"Their abode": that is, their dwelling and place of settling from which there is no escape for them, "is the Fire" — not what they were content with of the life of this world and its pleasures. "For what they used to earn" (﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾): from the inner deeds that were counted, and what those entail of sins; or that [the Fire is the requital for] what those [deeds] earned for them. The combination of the past and present forms is to indicate continuity. The preposition "bi" (ب, "for") is connected to what is indicated by the final clause, which comes as a predicate about the demonstrative noun; Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "jūzū" (requite/recompense them). The clause "ulā'ika" (those) is the predicate. Regarding His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect﴾ etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ in what must be believed in, and within which belief in the signs that the heedless have neglected is included as a primary inclusion; and it may be that the object of the belief is specified by this, in view of the context. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, i.e., deeds that are righteous in themselves and befitting of faith; the noun modified is omitted because the adjective functions in the manner of nouns. ﴿Their Lord guides them by their faith﴾, i.e., He guides them, because of their faith, to their abode and their destination, which is Paradise. It is mentioned only because it is clear and the soul is inclined toward it, especially when one considers what preceded concerning the abode of the disbelievers and the evil deeds that led them to it, and the allusions and explicit statements that followed.

The faith intended here, which has been made the cause, is the specific faith accompanied by righteous deeds, mentioned as such, not faith stripped of them, nor the more general faith. Two rams should not butt heads over this, and the verse is far from indicating anything contrary to what the community holds: that faith unaccompanied by righteous deeds leads in general to Paradise and that its possessor is not eternally abiding in the Fire. For its explicit meaning is that faith joined with righteous deeds is a cause of guidance to Paradise. As for the claim that everything that is a cause of it must be so, there is no indication in it or in anything else to that effect. How could there be, when His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, for them is security and they are guided﴾ calls to the contrary, based on what they have agreed upon in interpreting wrongdoing as polytheism? Even if it is taken at its apparent meaning, there enters into guidance one who believed but did no righteous deed, then died before committing a forbidden act or abandoning an obligatory one. To this interpretation of faith as we have stated went al-Zamakhshari, and he said: the verse indicates that the faith considered for guidance to Paradise is faith restricted by righteous deeds. He justified this by saying that it made the relative clause a combination of both matters, so it is as if it were said: "Those who combined faith and righteous deeds," and then it was said: "by their faith," meaning this faith to which righteous deeds are joined.

Some claimed that this was based on Mu'tazilism and the eternal abiding of the non-righteous in the Fire, then said there is no indication in the verse of what he mentioned, because it made the cause of guidance to Paradise the absolute faith. As for the claim that its addition to the pronoun of the righteous requires taking righteousness as a condition in the causation, this is disputed, for the pronoun refers to the persons regardless of their attributes. Furthermore, the relative clause being a cause of the predicate by way of implication does not contradict the explicit, stated cause. Moreover, not every predicate about a relative pronoun requires this; do you not see that a phrase like "the one who was with us yesterday did such-and-such" is free of what they mention in a phrase like "the one who believes enters Paradise." Al-Zamakhshari was defended by the argument that the combination of faith and righteous deeds clearly indicates that both are the cause, and the explicit statement of the causality of faith attributed to the pronoun of "those who believe and do righteous deeds" is like a specification that it is that faith accompanied by what accompanies it, not the absolute. However, it was mentioned for its originality and added nobility, and it does not follow from this that its re-mention is redundant or that it independently has causality.

This also contains a rebuttal of al-Qadi al-Baydawi, where he claimed that the concept of sequence, even if it indicates that the cause of guidance is faith and righteous deeds, yet the explicit words of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿by their faith﴾ indicate the independence of faith. In al-Kashf he also denied that what is explicit is that, and that the inference is based on making faith and righteous deeds occur in the relative clause so that they function as a cause. Then, when faith was repeated as an annexed noun, it became an indication of the faith joined with them, since it is established that the use of that is only where there is a known referent, and the known antecedent is this, and the default is the absence of anything else. Then he said: Even if it is granted that the explicit meaning is that, it would not harm al-Zamakhshari, because deeds would then be considered a condition, in combining the explicit and the implicit as far as possible; thus the accompaniment of deeds is not neglected, nor is the indication of causality. This is the benefit of mentioning it separately a second time, along with its originality and added nobility. No one among the community opposes this, because the disobedient are not guided. As for the claim that everyone who is not guided is eternally abiding in the Fire, it is rejected in the strongest terms. End of quotation. (And in the heart there is something about this rejection.) The better course is to rely on what we have already presented in establishing that the verse is far from indicating anything contrary to what the community holds. Guidance in this sense may be interpreted either as guidance that leads to the desired goal, or as mere indication; the first is preferred, though one who said that the meaning is "He guides them on the path to Paradise by the light of their faith" chose the second. That is either by supposing an omitted noun, or on the basis that their faith produces a light before them. It has also been said that the meaning is: He strengthens them by their faith to remain steadfast upon the path that leads to reward, and guidance upon it is in the first sense. It has been said too: the meaning is that He guides them to comprehend the realities of matters, so that they are revealed to them because of that. Whichever it is, the turn of speech in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿their Lord﴾ serves to honor them by attributing the Lord to them, along with an indication of the cause of guidance.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Beneath them rivers flow﴾, i.e., beneath their dwellings, or before them, is a resumptive statement, either grammatical or explanatory, so it has no place in the i'rab; or it is a second predicate of "inna", so its place is the nominative. It is permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He guides them﴾, on the assumption that what is guided to is what they desire in Paradise, as Abu al-Baqa' said. If it is made an anticipated circumstantial clause, there is no need to suppose this assumption, but it is contrary to the apparent meaning. When al-Zamakhshari explained ﴿Their Lord guides them﴾ as "He strengthens them" etc., he made this sentence an explanation of it and a clarification, because adherence to the cause of felicity is like arriving at it. It is not hidden that the manner of this explanation is the manner of an apposition, and al-Tibi explicitly stated this; in that case its place is the nominative, since it is the place of the sentence that is replaced. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is another predicate or another circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He guides them﴾, making it a coordinate circumstantial clause, or from ﴿rivers﴾, making it an interlocked one, or it is connected to "flow" or to "guides". What is meant, as has been said, by the guided-to is either their dwellings in Paradise or what they desire therein.

[p. 76]

*Da'wahum* means *du'a'uhum* (their supplication). It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and His saying, exalted be His majesty, *fihā* ("therein") is attached to it. His saying, glorified be He, *Subhānaka Allāhumma* ("Glory be to You, O Allah"), is its predicate (*khabar*). That is, their supplication is this utterance. Although *da'wā* is well known in the sense of "claim" (*id'ā'*), it is also used in the sense mentioned here. That the predicate is of the category of supplication is supported by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The most frequent of my supplication and that of the prophets before me at 'Arafat is: There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs the praise, and He is capable of all things." Apparently, applying the term "supplication" to this is metaphorical (*majāz*), and this is what the words of Ibn al-Athīr convey, where he said: "Tahlīl (saying 'there is no god but Allah'), tahmīd (saying 'al-ḥamdu lillāh') and tamjīd (glorifying Allah) are called supplication only because they have the same standing in obtaining the reward and recompense of Allah, the Exalted." In a hadith: "When My servant's praise of Me occupies him from asking Me, I give him the best of what I give those who ask." The word also comes in the sense of worship, as in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon other than Allah﴾. It has been permitted to intend this meaning here, and the intended sense would be the negation of obligation (*taklīf*), i.e., they have no worship other than this utterance, and that is not worship; rather, they are inspired to it and speak it out of delight, not as an obligation. A parallel to this is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾. There is obscurity in this, as is evident. It may be said that a similar case occurs in the verse if *da'wā* is intended in its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*), so the meaning would follow the pattern stated, namely that they have no request to make of Allah, the Exalted, other than that; and it is known that this is not a request, which implies that they have no request at all.

The purpose of this is to indicate that all their aims are fulfilled in actuality, so they have no need to ask for anything, although there is in this what there is.

*Subḥāna* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) for a deleted verb, obligatorily, and it has the meaning of tasbīḥ (glorification). The sentence is taken as a nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*), meaning: "We glorify You with glorification," because that is more eloquent. The sentences that follow it are similar. *Allāhumma* is, by estimation, *yā Allāh*; the particle of address was deleted and the *mīm* was substituted for it. The complete discussion of this and what precedes it has already been given to you earlier, so recall it. The expected order would be to place the august Name first, because the vocative precedes supplication, but it was used in tasbīḥ in this form. It has been said that this is because it is a declaration of freedom from all deficiencies, whereas in a vocative there may be an impression of a lack of proper manners.

﴿Their greeting therein﴾, i.e., that with which they greet one another, ﴿is "Peace"﴾, i.e., their being safe from every disliked thing. It is the predicate of *taḥiyyatuhum*, and *fihā* is attached to *taḥiyya*. *Taḥiyya* is honouring someone with an honourable state. Its original form is *aḥyāka Allāhu ta'ālā ḥayāt ṭayyiba* ("may Allah, the Exalted, give you a good life"). Its idafa (construction of genitive) here is to the object, and the subject is either Allah, glorified be He, i.e., the greeting of Allah, the Exalted, to them is that, and this is guided by His saying, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾; or the angels, peace be upon them, and this is guided by His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace."﴾

[p. 77]

It is also permitted that the idafa be to the subject, with a deleted modifier, i.e., the greeting of some of them to others is their last. It may also be considered that the deleted part is an object, so the idafa is to the object, and the subject is deleted. It has also been said that it is permitted that it be one of the cases in which the verbal noun is annexed to both its subject and its object together, when the meaning is "some of them greet others." A parallel in annexation to both subject and object is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, where *ḥukm* (judgment) is annexed to the pronoun of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, and they are the judges, while others are judged, namely those against whom judgment is passed. This is not from the category of combining literal (*ḥaqīqa*) and figurative (*majāz*) meaning, which is disputed, since annexing a verbal noun to its subject is literal, and to its object is figurative. There is no disagreement about permissibility of combining when the figurative meaning is intellectual (*'aqlī*); the disagreement is only when it is linguistic (*lughawī*).

﴿And the last of their call﴾, i.e., the conclusion of their supplication, ﴿is that "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ (10) That is, "that it is 'Praise belongs to Allah'." Here *an* is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, its subject is a deleted pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr sha'n*), and the nominal sentence is its predicate. *Inna* and its two operands form another predicate. It is not explanatory (*mufassira*) because its condition is absent, nor is it superfluous (*zā'ida*), because superfluity contradicts the original usage and there is no need for it. Moreover, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Mujahid, Qatada and Ya'qub read it with the heavy *inna* and *al-ḥamdu* in the accusative, and in this is evidence for what we have said. Apparently the realisation of the content of these sentences, because they are nominal, is by way of permanence and continuity, and there are reports that support this. Thus perhaps when these people entered Paradise, they attained knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, that they had not attained before, according to their different ranks.

Our master Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi clearly stated in one of his treatises, in the discussion of the variation of the people of Paradise in knowledge, saying: "The common believers in Paradise will be in knowledge like the scholars in this world, and the scholars there will be like the prophets, peace be upon them, in this world, and the prophets, peace be upon them, will be in that like our Prophet (ﷺ). Our Prophet, peace be upon him, will have from knowledge of his Lord, glorified be He, the highest extent that will not be possessed by any near angel or sent prophet. It is possible that this is the praised station. And it is not far from me that they, despite their variation in knowledge, will continue to ascend therein according to their ranks, and the journey in Allah, glorified be He, is endless, and reaching the essence is impossible. And then the variation is in knowledge of the attributes, and they are, as has been said, either negative, and they are called attributes of majesty (*Jalāl*) because it is said of them 'Exalted above such-and-such,' or otherwise, and they are called attributes of honour (*Ikrām*). And this is how the words of His exalted saying were explained: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾. So they will continue to call upon Allah, the Exalted, by glorification, which is an indication of describing Him with attributes of majesty, and by praise, which is an indication of describing Him with attributes of honour. And continuity is conventional, and it is more than can be counted." His saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in describing the people of Paradise, as in Sahih Muslim: "They glorify Allah, the Exalted, in the morning and evening," supports that by its apparent meaning. And what is meant by morning and evening, as al-Nawawi said, is their duration. The apparent meaning of the verse is that they put forward the description of Him by attributes of majesty and conclude their supplication by describing Him with attributes of honour, because the first precedes the second, as the removal of defects precedes the adornment. This is guided by His saying, glorified be He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾.

The preferred opinion according to me is that the agent of the greeting is Allah, the Exalted, or the angels, peace be upon them. In that case it is not far that the mentioned order corresponds to the order of occurrence. This would be by saying: when they begin the supplication, they glorify Allah, the Exalted, and declare Him free from imperfection, and so they are met with peace, which is a supplication for safety from every disliked thing. If it is from Allah, glorified be He, then it is undoubtedly metaphorical, because the literal reality of supplication directed at Him, the Exalted, is impossible. If it is from the angels, peace be upon them, then there is no obstacle to its remaining in its literal sense, but the request in it is directed to permanence, because the basic safety is already theirs. And if we say that it accepts increase, then there is no remoteness in directing a request for it. How delicate is the correspondence of glorification and declaration of purity with safety from disliked things, because of their closeness in meaning, as is not hidden from the fair-minded. Then they conclude their supplication with ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and thus continues their custom in the morning and evening, as the report of the Sahih indicates, and perhaps the absence of mention of praise in it is because of sufficiency with what is in the verse. This is what I have concerning it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "I was informed that when a bird passes by the people of Paradise and they desire it, they say: 'Glory be to You, O Allah,' and that is their supplication with it, and the angel comes to them with what they desired. When the angel brings it, he gives them greetings and they return the greeting to him. This is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Their greeting therein is peace﴾. Then when they have eaten their need, they say: 'Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds,' and that is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And the last of their call is that praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾." This is apparent in that the mentioned order also corresponds to the order of occurrence, but it indicates that *da'wā* means supplication, and the meaning of "Glory be to You, O Allah" being a supplication and request for what they desire at that time is that it is a sign of asking. A parallel to this is the glorification of a worshipper when something befalls him during his prayer. And in some reports it is said that this phrase is a signal between the people of Paradise and the servants at the meal, so when they say it, they bring them what they desire.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that when they say that, what they desire from Paradise comes to them from their Lord. There is no harm in that. Yes. Thus the praise after eating their need is the implication of His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And the last of their call is that praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, is obscure.

The judge (al-Qadi), may Allah whiten the brightness of his circumstances, said: "Perhaps the meaning is that when they enter Paradise and witness the greatness and majesty of Allah, glorified be He, they glorify Him and describe Him with attributes of majesty. Then the angels greet them with safety from calamities and success in the various kinds of honours, or Allah, the Exalted, greets them, so they praise Him and extol Him with attributes of honour." This is also apparent, and the order of mention would be as we said, except that it has been objected that the annexation of *ākhir* (last) to *da'wāhum* (their call) rejects it. The apparent basis for the rejection, as has been said, is that according to this view it would be the last state, and that considering success through honours as part of the meaning of peace is not apparent. Perhaps the matter in this is easy.

Shaykh al-Islam said: "Perhaps they say: 'Glory be to You, O Allah' when they witness the wonders of the traces of His power, the Exalted, and the results of His mercy and compassion, what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, sanctifying His station, the Exalted, from the defects of incapacity and deficiency, and declaring His generous promise free from the marks of breaking it. And the conclusion of their supplication will be that they say: 'Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds,' as a description of Him, the Exalted in majesty, with attributes of honour after describing Him with attributes of majesty. The meaning is that their supplication is confined to what has been mentioned, since they have no awaited object that they would arrange within the string of supplication. Perhaps the placement of mention of their greeting in the middle, between their supplication and its conclusion, is for the purpose of reaching the conclusion of the narrative with praise, seeking blessing, although the greeting is not entirely foreign." The end. It seems he meant by the greeting not being entirely foreign, that it is in meaning a supplication, and his words are explicit that the actual order differs from the order of mention. It is not hidden that the justification for placing the mention of the greeting in the middle by what he mentioned is hardly acceptable to any fair-minded person. Moreover, he and the rest of the commentators whose words we have seen overlooked explaining the nominal form of the sentences, so understand. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

**[Page 78]**

﴿And if God were to hasten for people﴾ it is those who do not expect to meet God, mentioned in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us﴾, and so on. The verse is connected to that and indicates that they deserve punishment, and that He, glorified is He, only grants them respite as a gradual lead-on (istidraj). The mention of the believers came in between for completion (tatmim) and contrast (muqabalah). And "people" was used in place of their pronoun to express the gravity of the matter.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (Guidance of the Sound Mind): they were introduced by the generic noun because the hastening of good for them does not depend on their described attribute, since not all of that comes by way of istidraj. The meaning is: if God, exalted is He, were to hasten for them ﴿the evil﴾ which they were seeking hastily, in denial and mockery. For they used to say: "O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment," and they would say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" and the like.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that he said: it is a man's supplication against himself and his property with what he dislikes, that it be answered for him. And both of them related from Mujahid that he said: it is a person's saying to his child or his property when angry: "O God, do not bless it, O God, curse it." In this there is an application of "people" to the general sense, but the preferred view is the first. It is supported by what is said: that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: "O God, if this is the truth..." etc.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿their seeking of good hastily﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). The original, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is "hastening similar to their seeking hastily," so "hastening" (ta'jilan) was omitted together with its descriptive attribute (which is the genitive phrase), and the noun in the genitive took its place.

In al-Kashshaf: he placed "their seeking of good hastily" in the position of "His hastening it for them," to indicate the swiftness of His response to them and His granting them their request, so that it is as if their seeking of good hastily were a hastening of it. This is a sound statement, indicating the precision of its author's reasoning, as Ibn al-Munir said, since a confirmatory verbal noun is hardly ever placed in the Noble Book alongside something other than its own verb without this great benefit. The grammarians say about this: the verbal noun is treated as governed by an implied verb indicated by what is mentioned, and they add nothing to that. But if the discerning person reviews his intuition and communes with his thought, he will know that it was paired with a verb other than its own for a purpose. That purpose, in His saying: ﴿And God caused you to grow from the earth as growth﴾, is to alert to the penetration of power in what it acts upon and the swiftness of the execution of its command, so that it is as if God's causing you to grow were the very act of your growing: when the causing occurs, the growing occurs necessarily, so that each is the other, and so it was paired with it.

Al-Tibi said: the original wording was "if God were to make evil come to people, its hastening," then the verb "seeking hastily" was put in its place, then it was attributed to them, so it was said "their seeking of good hastily." This is because the intended meaning is that His mercy preceded His wrath, so the intensification is increased. Their seeking of good is swifter than God's hastening it for them, for man was created hasty, whereas God is patient and forbearing: He delays for the many interests that human reason cannot discern, and yet He grants them their requests and speedily answers them.

Abu Hayyan required that the estimate be "hastening similar to their seeking hastily," or that there is an omitted element indicated by the verbal noun, namely: "if God were to hasten evil for people when they seek it hastily, the seeking of good." He said: because the meaning of "hastened" (ajjala) differs from the meaning of "sought hastily" (ista'jala), since "ajjala" denotes occurrence while "ista'jala" denotes the request for hastening; and the former is from God, exalted is He, while the latter is attributed to them. Therefore what al-Zamakhshari and his followers established is not permissible. Al-Safaqsi answered that the form "istaf'ala" here indicates that the act falls upon its request, like "istaqarra" in the sense of "aqarra." His saying "and this is attributed to them" is based on the view that the verbal noun is attributed to the agent, though it may be attributed to the object. None of this is hidden, but all of it arises from little reflection.

The meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿their term would have been decreed for them﴾ is: they would surely have been made to die and destroyed completely. It is said: "its term was decreed for him," meaning: its duration in which his death was determined was brought to an end for him, so he perished. In choosing the passive form there is conformity with the ways of Majesty, together with an announcement that the agent is definitively specified. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read ﴿la-qada﴾ (in the active voice). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿la-qadayna﴾. In this there is a shift (iltifat). The choice of the non-past form in the conditional, though the meaning is past, is to convey that the non-decreeing of the term is due to the continuing absence of hastening. For a negated present verb in the position of the past does not explicitly convey the negation of the continuation of the act; rather, it may convey the continuation of its negation according to context, as has been verified in its proper place.

Some verifiers have mentioned that the antecedent here is not the mentioned hastening itself, but rather the will for it, which entails the aforementioned decreeing, existentially and non-existentially. For the decreeing is not something distinct from the hastening of evil in itself; rather, it is either itself or a particular of it, like the rest of its particulars, with no distinction from the rest, since its concept does not include what is not in the concept of the hastening of evil, namely the severity and terror. Therefore its consequence upon it, whether existence or non-existence, does not add a benefit that justifies making it follow from it. So this is not like His saying: ﴿If he obeyed you in much of the matter, you would surely be in difficulty﴾, nor like His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾, nor like His saying: ﴿If God were to seize people for what they earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, when the answer is interpreted as annihilation. Moreover, in the consequence following upon the will of the antecedent there is what is not in its following upon the antecedent itself: a indication of exaggeration and the magnification of the matter, and an indication that affairs are contingent upon His will, which is founded upon profound wisdoms.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us﴾, that is, We leave them by granting respite and gradual lead-on, ﴿in their transgression﴾, which is their not expecting the meeting and their denial of resurrection and recompense, and what follows from that of evil deeds and shameful sayings, ﴿wandering blindly﴾ (11), that is, they vacillate and are bewildered. It is not correct to coordinate it with the protasis of "if" (law) or with its apodosis, because that would negate what is intended to be affirmed. And "law" here does not mean "that," as has been said. Rather, it is either coordinated with the whole conditional sentence, since the sentence has the meaning of "He does not hasten it for them" and carries its force, so it is as if it were said: He does not hasten, but rather leaves them; or it is coordinated with an implied element indicated by the conditional, namely: "but He grants them respite," or "but He does not hasten and does not decree, so He leaves them." Some have said each of these. It is also said that the sentence is resumptive, and the estimate is "so We leave them." And it is said that the fa' (so) falls in the apodosis of an implied condition, and the meaning is: if God, exalted is He, were to hasten what they sought hastily, He would have annihilated them; but He grants them respite so that they increase in their transgression, then He will uproot them. And if that is so, then We leave those who do not expect to meet Us in their transgression, wandering, then We cut off their remnant.

The author of al-Kashf, after establishing that the connection of "And if God were to hasten..." to "Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us..." and that the mention of the believers came in between for completion and contrast, and is not extraneous, said: there is no need to make this the apodosis of an implied condition. And in placing the relative pronoun in the position of the personal pronoun there is a kind of clarification of the transgression by what is in the relative clause, and an indication that it is the cause of the leaving and the respite.

**[Page 79]**

[p. 80 is omitted from the translation.]

﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, whether lying on his side, sitting, or standing.﴾ That is, when a kind of harm, from illness, poverty, or other hardships, befalls him, a minor affliction. It is also said to mean harm in general. ﴿He calls upon Us﴾ to remove it and relieve it. ﴿On his side﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). For this reason he joins to it the explicit circumstantial phrases, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿or sitting, or standing﴾. That is, he calls upon Us lying down, or stretched out on his side. The preposition lām (on his side) is in its literal sense. It is also said that it means ʿalā (upon), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ (17:107). There is no need for this. The preposition ʿalā is sometimes used here, and it indicates his being elevated over it. The lām indicates the specificity of his state of being and his settling on his side, since he cannot remain in any other posture. So there is additional emphasis.

There is disagreement about the subject of the circumstantial phrase. It is said that it is the subject of ﴿called﴾. It is also said that it is the object of ﴿touches﴾. This view is considered weak for two reasons. The first is that the circumstantial phrase is placed out of its proper position without a reason. The second is that the meaning would then be that he calls upon Us often in all his conditions, but that the specified states were singled out for mention because a person is usually not free of them, not that harm touches him in all his conditions. It is answered that there is no problem with this, for if harm touches him in these states, then his calling upon Us in them follows as well, because the condition in the conditional clause is also a condition in the consequent. So when you say, "If Zayd comes poor, we treat him well," the meaning is "we treat him well in his state of poverty." You know that the more apparent view is the first.

Some scholars considered distributing these states among individual human beings, meaning that some people call upon Us in one of these states and others in another. Others have mentioned that these states may be intended to generalize the kinds of harm, because they are either mild, not preventing a person from standing; or moderate, preventing him from standing but not from sitting; or severe, preventing him from both. Their meaning is understood from them with the help of the context. As for ﴿when﴾ (idhā), it is said that it is in its original sense, and it is said that it refers to the past.

﴿But when We remove from him the harm that touched him﴾, after he called upon Us, as the fāʾ (then) indicates. ﴿He passes on﴾, that is, he goes on and continues in his former state, forgetting the condition of hardship and trial. Or it means he moves away from the place of supplication and entreaty and turns his side away. The sense of passing on in the first case is figurative, while in the second it is literal, and it becomes a metonymy for not calling upon Us. ﴿As though he had never called upon Us﴾, that is, as though he had never called upon Us. The verb has been lightened and the dummy pronoun (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) has been omitted. A similar example is the verse:

*"And a face bright at the throat, as though its two breasts were two small caskets."*

The original form is "ka-annahu," and the verb has been lightened, and the dummy pronoun has been omitted. However, Ibn Hisham stated in his commentary on the examples that this is not necessarily fixed, since the pronoun may refer to the face or to the chest, according to one transmission, "wa-ṣadrin." It is also transmitted as "ka-anna thadyayhi" (as though his two breasts), in which kaʾanna governs a noun already mentioned. It is not far-fetched that this is permissible in the first transmission according to some dialects. The comparative clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the subject of ﴿passes on﴾, that is, he passes on, likened to one who had never called upon Us ﴿to a harm﴾, that is, to its removal, because that is what is called upon. It is also said that there is no need to supply a word here, and that "ilā" is used in the sense of "li-" (for), meaning "for a harm ﴿that touched him﴾." The apparent view is that this is a description of the human species in general, or of the disbelieving part of it, taking into account the state of some individuals who possess these characteristics.

Al-Shihab mentioned that the exegetes have three views on the meaning of "man" here. It is said that it means the species. It is said that it means the disbeliever. It is said that it means a specific person. According to the last view, no qualification is needed, but there is no point in it. ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that wondrous adornment, ﴿it has been made attractive to the extravagant﴾, that is, to those characterized by the blameworthy qualities mentioned, ﴿what they used to do﴾ (10:12), namely turning away from the remembrance and supplication, and immersion in desires. Extravagance (isrāf) means exceeding the limit. Those people are called extravagant because God, exalted is He, gave them faculties and senses so that they would direct them to their proper ends and use them for what they were created for, namely knowledge and righteous deeds. But they directed them to what is not fitting, even though these faculties were their capital. The agent of the adornment is either the Owner of the Kingdom, exalted is His majesty, or Satan, upon whom be the curse. This has been investigated before. The same applies here, so consider it.

As for the connection of this noble verse with what precedes it, it is said that in each of them there is a respite given to the disbelievers in the manner of istidrāj (gradual leading on, the granting of respite to the wrongdoer), after being saved from the evil established in the first verse and from the harm established in the second.

The Imam mentioned two aspects of the connection with the first verse. The first is that God, in the first verse, showed that if He sent punishment upon the servant in this world, he would be destroyed. This verse confirms that, since it indicates his extreme weakness and utter helplessness. The second is that God, glorified is He, pointed in the first verse to the fact that the disbelievers hasten the coming of the punishment, and in this verse He, exalted is His majesty, showed that they are lying in that demand, since it indicates that if the smallest thing he dislikes befalls a human being, he will humble himself before God, exalted is He, to remove it from him. End of quotation. Each has its own direction.

In this verse there is a rebuke for one who abandons supplication in ease and rushes to it only in hardship. What befits the perfect believer is humility before his Master in both ease and hardship, for that is more likely to bring about an answer. Thus in the hadith: "Get to know God in ease, and He will know you in hardship."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Call upon God on the day of your ease, and He will answer you on the day of your distress." In a hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Hakim narrated it from Salman, and said: its chain is sound: "Whoever would like God to answer him in times of adversity and calamities, let him increase supplication in ease." The reports on this matter are numerous.

[p. 81]

﴿And We had certainly destroyed the generations﴾ like the people of Nuh, ʿAd and Thamud. The word *qurūn* is the plural of *qarn* (with a fatḥa on the qāf), which means the people of a particular era. It is derived from *al-iqtiran* (coming together), as if the people of that era were joined together in their deeds and conditions. It is said that a *qarn* is forty years, or eighty, or a hundred. It is also said that it refers to time in general. The meaning intended here is the first one. The same applies to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them." And to the line of poetry:

*When the generation in which you live passes away, and you are left behind in another generation, then you are a stranger.*

﴿from before you﴾ means from before your time. The address is to the people of Makkah, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), for the sake of intensifying the warning, after confirming it with an oath. The prepositional phrase is connected to *ahlaknā*. Abu al-Baqāʾ prohibited it from being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of *al-qurūn*.

﴿when they committed wrong﴾ means at the time they committed wrong through denial, persistence in error and misguidance. The temporal clause is connected to *ahlaknā*. Making *lammā* a conditional particle with an implied answer, *ahlaknāhum* (We destroyed them), supported by what precedes it, is an unnecessary strain.

The statement ﴿and their messengers came to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *ẓalamū*, with *qad* implied. The statement ﴿with clear proofs﴾ is connected to *jāʾat-hum*, with the *bāʾ* being for transitivity (*taʿdiya*), or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from *rusulihim*. This indicates the extent of their wrongdoing and their excessive obstinacy. That is, they committed wrong through denial, while their messengers had come to them with clear signs indicating their truthfulness, or while they were present with them at a time when there was no room for denial.

Abu al-Baqāʾ and others permitted that it be conjoined to *ẓalamū*, in which case it has no place in grammatical analysis (*iʿrab*). Or its place is the genitive, according to those who hold that a temporal noun may be annexed to the thing it is conjoined to. The order of mention does not have to match the order of occurrence, as in His statement: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration﴾. There is no need for this excuse, on the basis that wrongdoing is not limited to denial but encompasses all kinds of wrongdoing. Denial is understood from His statement: ﴿and they would not have believed﴾, in the most emphatic and forceful manner, since the *lām* is for emphasizing the negation.

This sentence, on the first view, is conjoined to *ẓalamū*. It is not at all an explanatory conjunction (*ʿaṭf tafsīrī*), contrary to what the author of al-Kashf said, differing from al-Ṭībī. This is because the first informs of the occurrence of denial, while this one informs of persistence in it. On the second view, it is conjoined to what precedes it that was conjoined. It is also said that it is an interjected statement (*iʿtirāḍ*) for emphasis, placed between the verb and what functions as its comparative verbal noun, namely His statement: ﴿Thus﴾. The recompense referred to is an expression for its verbal noun, meaning like the dreadful recompense, that is, the severe destruction, which is total annihilation. ﴿We recompense the criminal people﴾, meaning every criminal group, so that it encompasses the generations. Taking *dhālika* as an expression for them is not appropriate to the context.

It was also read as *yajzī* with the third person masculine, shifting from the first person plural in *ahlaknā* to it. The essential meaning on the view of conjunction is that the cause of their destruction was their denial of the messengers, and that it was not valid or proper for them to believe, because of the corruption of their readiness and God's abandonment of them. On the view of interjection, the first matter alone is stated in explaining the result. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, in place of the second matter, God's knowledge that there is no benefit in giving them respite after they had been held to the proof through the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them. He made it an explanation on both views. There is in this what requires unveiling, so reflect upon it. The explanation of their not believing by abandonment and the like is evident. The words of al-Qāḍī are explicit in explaining it also by God's knowledge that they would die in disbelief. This was objected to as contradicting the statement of the scholars that knowledge follows the known. Some learned scholars strained greatly to correct this, but they did not produce anything.

[p. 82]

Some researchers said: the meaning of knowledge following the known is that His knowledge, from eternity, of the specific contingent known thing follows its quiddity. That is, the particularity of the knowledge and its distinction from other knowledges is only by virtue of its being knowledge of this quiddity. As for the existence of the quiddity and its actuality in what is ongoing, it follows His eternal knowledge, which follows its quiddity. That is, when He, may He be exalted, knew it from eternity with this particularity, it necessarily follows that it is realized and comes into existence in what is ongoing with this particularity. So the very fact of their dying in disbelief and their not believing is what is followed by His eternal knowledge, and its occurrence follows it. This is not doubtful at all, and it is the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah, may God have mercy on them. By it many difficulties are resolved, so retain it.

Our master Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani mentioned that the meaning of knowledge following the known is that it is related to the known, revealing it as it is. He built upon this that quiddities are established and not made, in their being established. The claim of this following is what Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, held. ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Jīlī disputed this. Shaykh Muḥammad ʿUmar al-Baghdādī, may God's mercy be upon him, said: the knowledge following the known, considered with respect to the presence of the eternal entities which gave God the detailed knowledge of them, and considered with respect to general comprehensive knowledge, the known follows the knowledge. This is because when God, may He be exalted, manifested Himself from His essence to His essence through the most holy emanation, the entities and their readinesses came into being. They did not come about from ignorance, may God be exalted far above that with great exaltedness. In that case there is no disagreement between Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, and al-Jīlī. Even if some disagreement remains, the truth is with the Shaykh, because al-Jīlī in relation to him is a bee buzzing around the sanctuary, and the proof is also with the Shaykh like fire on a mountain. But he (al-Jīlī), may God be pleased with him, went too far in his words: "Knowledge follows the known, and the known is you, and you are He." The inquiry is a rugged path with a difficult ascent, and the complete discussion of it is sought in its proper place.

The derivation of the meaning of knowledge here, as it is said, is from the emphasis which the *lām* conveys. In the verse there is a severe threat and a firm warning to the people of Makkah, because they and those destroyed share in what necessitates destruction. It is known from what has been established that the pronoun in *kānū* refers to the generations, which is evident. Muqātil permitted that the pronoun refers to the people of Makkah, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Likewise he permitted that by "the criminal people" is meant the people of Makkah, in the manner of placing an apparent noun in place of a pronoun of address, to indicate that they are foremost in criminality. The mention of ﴿the people﴾ indicates that the punishment is one of total annihilation.

The comparison on this view is evident, since the meaning is: He will recompense you with the like of the recompense of those before you. As for the first view, it is in the manner of ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ and its like. This too is somewhat far-fetched. Indeed, some researchers said: it rejects it entirely.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 14:

His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them﴾. This is explicit that it is the beginning of an admonition regarding their affairs, and that what is set out in it are the initial stages of their circumstances, to test how they conduct their deeds, in a manner that conveys an inclination toward them towards faith and obedience. Thus it is impossible that this should come right after the statement of the final outcome of their affair and the decisive pronouncement of their destruction for the completeness of their crimes. The conjunction is with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We had destroyed﴾, not with what precedes it. The meaning is: then We made you successors in the earth after the destruction of those generations whose reports you hear and whose traces you witness (﴿so that We may observe how you act﴾, 14). That is, so that We may know what deeds you do. So "kayfa" (how) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of ta'lamun (you do). In al-Mughni (Ibn Hisham's Mughni al-Labib) he has explicitly stated that kayfa comes in this way, and that among its instances is ﴿How did your Lord deal﴾. It is not governed by ﴿linanzura﴾ (so that We may observe), because the interrogative has priority of position, so what precedes it is prevented from acting upon it. Hence it is obligatory to place it before its governor here.

It has also been said: its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿ta'malun﴾, as is the well-known view of it when a verb follows it, as in "kayfa daraba Zaydun" (in what state did Zayd strike), meaning: in what state do you do the deeds fitting for succession, of the qualities of goodness. In this there is an emphasis on deterrence from evil deeds that is considerable.

It has also been said: its place is the accusative as the direct object (maf'ul bih) of ta'lamun, meaning: what deed you do, good or bad. They have explicitly stated that it comes in this way as well, and they took as instances of it such constructions as "kayfa zananta Zaydan" (how did you consider Zayd). Al-Zamakhshari explained the verse in accordance with this, and al-Qutb followed up on him with what he followed up on. Then he said: "Perhaps he made kayfa here a metaphor in the sense of 'what thing', due to the indication of the context."

Some of the verifiers have mentioned that the truth is that the meaning of kayfa is asking about states and attributes, not about essences and other things. So the question here is about their states and their deeds, and there is no meaning to asking about a deed except whether it is good or bad, and whether it is virtuous or wicked. Thus kayfa is not a metaphor, but remains in its true sense. Then, the use of "nazar" (observing) in the sense of "'ilm" (knowing) is a metaphor, in that it is likened to the gaze of the one who looks and the direct witnessing of the one who beholds, in its realisation. The statement is a metaphorical allegory built upon a subordinate explicit metaphor. The meaning is: He deals with you in the manner of one who seeks knowledge of your deeds, in order to recompense you according to them, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿That He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. It has been said: it is possible to say that what is meant by knowledge is the known, and in that case this is a metaphor built upon a metaphor. In any case, it does not follow that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, was not knowing of their deeds before their succession. The interpretation of observing as knowing is not based on the denial of sight, as is the doctrine of some of the Qadariyyah who say that He, majestic is His affair, neither sees nor is seen. For we, and to Allah, exalted is He, be praise, are of those who say that He, blessed and exalted is He, sees and is seen. The conditions in the case of the witnessed are not rational, as has been verified in its proper place. Sight is an attribute distinct from knowledge, and likewise hearing. And among those who also say: the forms of the contingent quiddities are witnessed by Allah, exalted is He, eternally, in their state of non-existence in themselves, in the mirrors of the fixed quiddities that are with Him, majestic is His affair. Rather, it is based on the meaning requiring it for Him. For when you say: "I honoured you so that I may see what you do," its meaning is: I honoured you so that I may test you and know your doing, so that I may recompense you for it. From here it is known that interpreting observing as waiting and expecting, as is one of its meanings, is nothing, and some people interpreted the words of some of the eminent scholars in this way, and committed an excess and spoke an error.

(This.) It is also read ﴿linazzura﴾ with a single nun and the ẓā' doubled. The reason for that is that the second nun was changed into a ẓā' and assimilated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ is an *iltifat* (a shift from direct address to the third person, a grammatical change of person). It turns away from them and directs the address to the master of those addressed, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, by enumerating their crimes, which oppose what was intended for them through the vicegerency (*istikhlaf*): denial and disbelief in the clear verses and other things, like the practice of the destroyed generations before them. The use of the present tense (*sigha al-mudari'*) indicates the renewal of their answer, which comes in line with the renewal of the recitation. By "the verses" is meant the verses that indicate Divine Unity (*tawhid*) and the invalidity of association (*shirk*).

It has also been said that it refers to something more general than that. The idafa (genitive construction) serves to honour the thing it is attached to and to encourage belief in it and warn against denying it. The word ﴿clear﴾ (*bayyinat*) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier), meaning: in a state of being clear in indicating what they contain. The verb of recitation is placed in the passive voice, with the verses as its subject, rather than the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, being the subject in the active voice. This implies that there is no need to specify the reciter, and indicates that their speech is about the recited text itself, even if a great man from one of the two cities had recited it. ﴿Those who do not hope for meeting Us say﴾: he placed the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that what is in the clause of the relative is the cause, the great and reported thing from them, and to blame them for it. That is, they said to the one who recites them to them, who is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this.﴾ They pointed by "this" to the Qur'an containing those verses, not to the verses themselves alone, intending to remove the whole thing from the scene, meaning: bring another book that we may read, [Page 84] which contains nothing we find improbable concerning the Resurrection and its consequences, nor what we dislike, such as the reproach of our gods and the threat for worshipping them. ﴿Or change it﴾: by putting in place of the verse containing that another verse. Perhaps they only asked this as a trick and with hope of his answering, peace be upon him, so that they could use it to make him accountable and to mock him, and it was not their intention that if he answered them they would believe.

﴿Say﴾, O Messenger, to them: ﴿It is not for me to change it﴾. The verbal noun (*masdar*) is the subject of *yakunu* (it is/becomes), and this is from *kana* in its complete sense (meaning "to exist"), and it is interpreted as *wajada* (to find/exist). The negation of existence may be meant to negate validity, for the existence of what is not valid is like non-existence. So the meaning here is: it is not valid for me at all to change it. ﴿Of my own accord﴾, that is, on my own part and from myself. The origin of *tilqa'* is a verbal noun on the pattern *tif'al* with the letter *ta'* and no other verbal noun came with its *kasra* except this one, and except *tibyan* in the well-known usage.

It was read anomalously with a *fatha* (*tilqa'a*), which is the regular form for verbal nouns indicating repetition, like *tawaf* and *tajwal*. Here it has moved from that to the figurative adverbial sense (*zarfiyya majaziyya*), and prefixing it with *min* does not remove the noun from its adverbial status. For this reason, the adverbs that are not inflected, such as *'inda*, are specific to being prefixed by it.

Some people have erred regarding this and restricted the answer to demonstrating the impossibility of what they proposed in their second proposal, to indicate that the impossibility of what they proposed first is so evident that there is no need to show it, and because what proves the impossibility of the second also proves the impossibility of the first, all the more so. So in effect and reality it is an answer to both matters.

﴿I follow only﴾, that is, I only follow what I am revealed in what I do and leave, ﴿what is revealed to me﴾ without changing anything in it at all, in the sense of restricting his state, peace be upon him, to following what is revealed, not restricting his following to what is revealed to him, as is the more immediate understanding from the apparent expression. So it is as if it were said: I do nothing but follow what is revealed to me. The clause is an independent sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining what would happen, for it is his nature to follow the revelation in the state that it is, and he does not independently do anything without it at all. It has been said that in this there is an answer to a presumed objection, which is: how is this so, when some verses have been abrogated (*naskh*) by others? It also refutes what they suggested by this question, that the Qur'an is his own speech, peace be upon him. Likewise, restricting the change in the answer to his words ﴿of my own accord﴾ rebuts their insinuation that it is from him, peace be upon him. For this reason he also called it a great disobedience, bringing about a great punishment with the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ [Verse 15] This is a justification for the content of what came before it, regarding the impossibility of changing and limiting his command, peace be upon him, to following the revelation. That is: indeed I fear, if I disobey Him, Exalted is He, by attempting the change and turning away from the revelation, the punishment of a great day, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Meeting that they do not hope for. In this there is an allusion that they deserved punishment by this proposal, because proposing what necessitates something also deserves it, even if it is not the same as doing it. The mention of the title of Lordship, with the addition to His pronoun, peace be upon him, is to magnify the matter of disobedience and to show the perfect purity of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. In the use of "day" with the emphatic (*tafkhimi*) nunation and describing it as great, there is what is not hidden of the magnitude of the punishment and its horror.

Al-'Allama al-Tibi allowed that the answer mentioned could be an answer to both proposals without any need for anything else, by interpreting the change in it as encompassing the change of an essence into another essence, like "I exchanged the dinars for dirhams." This is what they pointed to with their words: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾. And the change of an attribute into another attribute, like "I changed the ring into a loop," is what they pointed to with their words: ﴿or change it﴾. It was objected to this that restricting the change by his words, glorified is He: ﴿of my own accord﴾ prevents interpreting it in the more general sense, because it implies that this is within his capacity, peace be upon him, but he does not do it without the permission of Allah, Exalted is He. The change they first pointed to is not within his capacity, peace be upon him, so much so that the proposers know that this is impossible, yet they proposed it [Page 85] for the reason that has passed, and said: "If we wished, we would say the like of this," out of arrogance and obstinacy.

Then, the apparent meaning is that they proposed the change and bringing it through the way of fabrication. It has been said: there is no room for saying that they proposed that from the direction of revelation. So it is as if they said: bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it, from the direction of revelation, just as you brought the Qur'an from its direction. The meaning of his words: ﴿It is not for me﴾ etc. would be: it is not facilitated for me, and I cannot change it. This is because of what is in al-Kashshaf that his words ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾ refute that. It was justified that they did not request what is disobedience on this assumption, so that he would have to say in answer to them what he said. It was examined that requesting without permission is disobedience. If "it is not facilitated for me" is not interpreted as meaning that it is because it is not permitted, then the answer does not correspond to their question, because the question was about a change from Allah, Exalted is He, and he, peace be upon him, said: I cannot change it of my own accord in the answer. And if it is interpreted that way, then the disobedience is also to be understood in the same way. It was answered that the author of al-Kashshaf interpreted "it is not for me" as meaning that it is impossible and not facilitated, and disobedience falls on what is possible and within capacity, not that they requested what is disobedience or not. The correspondence is achieved, indeed in its strongest form, because what results is either the change of his own accord, which is impossible, or from the direction of revelation, in which case I am a follower and not one who is followed. Yes, it is not denied that another aspect could come, by interpreting it as meaning that it is not lawful for me to do that without permission. But the author of al-Kashshaf did not negate it.

Some verifying scholars mentioned that there is no room to interpret their proposal as being from the direction of revelation, because of the justification by "Indeed, I fear" etc., since what is mentioned in it aims at the disobedience of fabrication, as the explicit text that follows it of the two noble verses guides to. In that case, that disobedience is not realized in it, and the disobedience of requesting the change of what the legislative wisdom has required, especially on the basis of the disbelievers' proposal, is not intended, so realizing it does not help. This is a sound statement, from which one learns what is open to scrutiny in the preceding discussion.

It remains that some reports imply that they requested the coming from the direction of revelation. From Muqatil: the verse was revealed concerning five men: Abdullah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Mukarraz ibn Hafs, Amr ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Qays al-'Amiri, and al-'As ibn 'Amir ibn Hisham. They said to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "If you wish us to believe in you, then bring a Qur'an that does not contain abandoning the worship of al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat, and does not contain criticism of them. And if Allah, Exalted is He, has not revealed it to you, then say it yourself, or change it: put in place of a verse of punishment a verse of mercy, and in place of the forbidden something lawful, and in place of the lawful something forbidden." It may be said that this, even if its authenticity is granted, does not preclude that what is in the verse is what the second conditional clause's *tali* (the consequent, the following part) pointed to from their words. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 16:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you﴾ is a confirmation of the truth of the Qur'an and that it is from Him, the Exalted, following the explanation of the falsehood of what they proposed, in the most complete manner. It begins with the independent command to show perfection, to give attention to its matter, and to announce its independence in meaning and style. For it is a proof indicating that it is by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and His will, as you will know, Allah willing. What preceded is merely a report of the impossibility of what they proposed. The object of the will (maf'ul al-mashi'ah) is omitted, indicated by the apodosis (jaza', the consequent clause), as is customary in such cases. Some of them appear to understand otherwise from the apparent meaning of their words, but that is not so, and it is evident. The meaning is that the whole matter is contingent upon the will of Allah, the Exalted, and I have no share in it at all. If Allah, glorified is He, had willed the non-recitation of it to you and your non-awareness of it through me, by not sending it down upon me, and not commanding me to recite it, He would not have had me recite it to you. ﴿Nor would He have made you aware of it﴾, that is, nor would He have informed you of it through me. The consequent, which is the non-recitation and the non-informing, is negated, so the antecedent, which is His will of non-existence, is negated. The will of non-existence entails the non-will of existence, so the negation of the one entails the negation of the other, and this occurs only when the will of existence is realized. Thus it is established that His, the Prayer and peace be upon him, recitation of the Qur'an and His, the Exalted, making you aware of it through him, occur by His will, the Exalted.

The restriction of the making-aware to this is what the context requires. Since some have limited the object supplied in the conditional clause to the non-recitation alone, they gave as the reason for the restriction that the non-informing in absolute terms is not among the necessary implications of the condition, which is the non-willing of His recitation upon him, Prayer and peace be upon him. Therefore it is not permissible to place it in the same series as the consequent. But the reason for limiting it to that is not apparent, nor for not joining the non-making-aware to it, although the conjunction (al-'atf) is clearly applicable to it. Attributing the non-making-aware to Him, the Exalted, which indicates that the making-aware is ascribed to Him, the glorified, is an announcement that he, Prayer and peace be upon him, has no part in that, as the context also requires. In the transmission of Abu Rabi'ah from Ibn Kathir, it is read ﴿wa-la-adraakum﴾ with the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid), which is the one occurring in the answer to ﴿law﴾ (if). That is: If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, and He would have made you aware of it through the tongue of another, in the sense that it is the truth from which there is no escape. If I had not been sent with it, He would have sent another with it. The lam is used here to announce that informing them of it through the tongue of someone other than him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is more definitively negated and stronger. Perhaps the (la) in the first reading is due to the fact that what is not tolerated in the principal (matbu') may be tolerated in the follower (tabi'). Otherwise, it does not occur in the answer to ﴿law﴾, so one does not say: "If Zayd had stood, 'Amr would not have stood," but rather "ma qama" (he did not stand). From here, al-Samin explicitly stated that it is a superfluous particle emphasizing the negation. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Sirin that they read ﴿wa-la-adra'tukum﴾, attributing the verb to the pronoun of him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, like the preceding verb. The original form is "wa-la-adaituka," so the ya' was changed to alif according to the dialect of those who change a sukun ya' preceded by a fatha into alif. This is the dialect of Bil-Harith ibn Ka'b and tribes of Yemen, to the extent that they changed the ya' of the dual into alif and made the dual in all cases of one form. Qutrub related this from 'Aqil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others related from al-Hasan that he read ﴿wa-la-adra'tukum﴾ with a sukun hamza. It is said that it is substituted from the alif which was changed from the ya', as you have heard. It is also said that it is substituted directly from the ya', as is said in "labaytu" becoming "labi'tu." In both views, it is not original, and this occurred in some dialects, as explicitly stated by more than one scholar. It is also permitted that it be original, the verb being from al-dar' (to repel, to prevent), and it is said "adra'tuhu," meaning "ja'altuhu dari'an," i.e., I made him a repeller, i.e., a repeller. The meaning is: nor have I made you, through his recitation, adversaries who repel me with disputation. It was also read ﴿wa-la-adrakum﴾ with and without hamza, with the verb attributed to the pronoun of Allah, the Exalted. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, used to read ﴿wa-la-andhartukum bihi﴾ (nor would I have warned you with it). ﴿So I have remained among you a lifetime﴾ is a kind of reasoning for the necessary implication that this is by the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as has passed just now. Al-lubth (remaining) is residence. The accusative of ﴿'umuran﴾ is by analogy with the adverb of time, and what is meant by it is a period. It is also said that it is by the supposition of an omitted genitive, i.e., "the measure of a lifetime." It is with a damma on the mim. al-A'mash read it with a sukun for lightness. The meaning: I have dwelt among you for a lengthy period, which is the measure of forty years, during which you preserve the details of my conditions and know the news of my words and deeds. ﴿From before it﴾, that is, from before the revelation of the Qur'an, or from before the time of its revelation. The return of the pronoun to the recitation is not correct. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, that is, will you not observe this, so that you would not reason the impossibility of its issuing from someone like me, and the necessity of its being sent down from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. For that is not hidden from one who has a sound intellect and an upright mind. Indeed, by my life, whoever has even a little measure of intellect, if he reflects on his affair, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and that he grew up among them this long age, without associating with the scholars in any matter, and without consulting them in any art, and without mixing with the eloquent in discourse and debate, and without engaging with them in composing sermons and in opposition, then brought a book whose eloquence overwhelmed everyone of refinement, whose rhetoric bewildered the most eloquent of the Arabs, which contains the wonders of the kinds of sciences and the subtle realities of the explicit and the implicit, which became revealing the secrets of the unseen that conjecture can reach, and expressing the tales of the earlier peoples and the stories of the later generations of the ages, confirming what is before it of the revealed books and being a guardian over them in its decisive and detailed rulings, there remains with him no doubt that it is a revelation sent down from Allah, of majestic majesty and pervasive bounty. This is what the consensus of the majority agreed upon, and it is more fitting for refuting them, as is not hidden from the reflective person.

It is said: The more suitable reading for building the answer in what preceded upon the impossibility of his, Prayer and peace be upon him, issuing change or alteration, because it is a disobedience that entails great punishment, and his, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, restriction to following the revelation and refraining from arbitrary opinion, without any reference there or here, because the Qur'an in itself is a matter beyond the capacity of humans, nor because he, Prayer and peace be upon him, was unable to produce its like, is it to be cited here with what suits that from his, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, constant conditions during that long period, of the perfection of his purity, Prayer and peace be upon him, from what might suggest any trace of uttering lies and fabrication from him against anyone whoever he may be, as is indicated by its following with the condemnation of the one who fabricates against Allah, the Exalted. The meaning: I have dwelt among you before the revelation, never confronting anyone with arbitrariness or disputation, nor hovering around a statement containing any trace of doubt, let alone what contains lying and fabrication. Will you not observe this? Will you not reason that one whose condition is this, consistent through this long period, cannot possibly fabricate against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and impose on all creation commands and prohibitions that entail the seizing of property, the shedding of blood, and other things, and that what he brought is a clear revelation, a sending down from the Lord of the worlds. End.

You know that this is not what comes to mind, and that the first statement indicates in general that the Qur'an is a matter beyond the capacity of humans, and that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is unable to produce its like. Moreover, it is a remoteness that is not free from dispute, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 17:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾ is a rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) whose meaning is negation, i.e. there is no one more unjust than that. The negation of greater wrongdoing, as is well known, is a metonymy (kinaya) for the negation of equality; so the meaning is that he is more unjust than every wrongdoer. The verification of this has already passed.

The verse is connected to what precedes it, in that its purpose is to clear the Prophet (ﷺ) of what they hinted at, namely attributing the invention of a lie against Allah, the Exalted, to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and far be it from him. It also declares the polytheists to be wrongdoers for their denial of the Qur'an and their disbelief in it. The addition of ﴿lie﴾ (kadhiban), although inventing against Allah is necessarily only that, serves to indicate that what they hinted at and attributed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, explicitly, while it is a lie against Allah, the Exalted, is itself a lie in its own right. Thus an invention may be a lie only in its attribution, as when you attribute the sin of Zayd to 'Amr. This is an emphasis by him, peace and blessings be upon him, in clearing himself of what has been mentioned.

The fa' (then) is for the ordering of the speech upon what preceded, namely the explanation that the Qur'an is by the will and command of Allah, the Exalted. That is: since the matter is so, whoever invents against Him, the Exalted, by creating speech and saying, "This is from Allah, the Exalted," or by substituting some of His verses for others, as you permit that regarding me, and likewise whoever denies His signs, may He be glorified, as you do, is the greatest wrongdoer of all wrongdoers.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of the verse is to declare the polytheists wrongdoers for their invention against Allah, the Exalted, in their saying that He, may He be exalted above what they say, has a partner and a son, and for their denial of His signs, glorified is He. The verse is connected either also to what precedes it, in the sense that I did not invent against Allah, the Exalted, nor did I lie about Him, and the proof of that has been established, while you have done so by claiming that Allah, the Exalted, has a partner and that He has a son, and by denying His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and what he brought from Him, glorified is He.

As for connecting it to His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We destroyed generations before you when they did wrong﴾ and so on, with the words ﴿Then We made you successors﴾ and His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them﴾ up to here, as a notification that the polytheists to whom the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent followed the ways of those before them in denying the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and the messengers, peace be upon them; and this would be a return to the first subject after finishing the story of the polytheists.

It has also been said that the connection to what preceded is that they had asked him, peace and blessings be upon him, to change the Qur'an because of its condemnation of their gods, whom they had invented as deities. It has also been said that the verse is a preparation for what follows. But it is not hidden that the first view is the most suitable to the context, most in accord with the fa', furthest from artificiality, and closest to the sound mind's understanding.

﴿Indeed(anahu), the matter is that the criminals will not succeed﴾ (la yuflihu al-mujrimun). That is: they will not be saved from what is feared, nor will they win what is sought. The intended meaning is the category of criminals, so the inventor and the denier are included in it in the first instance. And there is no concealing the significance of choosing the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), which conveys attention to the subject of what is mentioned after it from the very beginning.

﴿And they worship, besides God, that which can neither harm them nor benefit them.﴾ This is a report of another of their offenses, and it is coordinated with His words, glorified is He, ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them...﴾ (the verse), a coordination of one narrative with another. "Besides God" (min dūni Allāh) is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relative to the subject of "they worship," meaning: going beyond God, either in the sense of abandoning His worship entirely, since worship is not valid and does not occur when there is association (shirk), or in the sense of not being content with Him and making Him a partner alongside the worship of others, glorified is He, as some have chosen. The "mā" (that which) is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a descriptive (mawṣūfa), and it refers to the idols. The meaning of their not harming or benefiting is that they have no power to do so, because they are inanimate objects (jamādāt). The purpose of this attribute is to negate that they are valid objects of worship (ma'būd), because it is a characteristic of one who is worshipped to have the power to do what has been mentioned. It was also said: the meaning is that they do not harm them if they abandon worshipping them, and do not benefit them if they worship them. The purpose here too is to negate the validity of their being worshipped, because it is a characteristic of the one who is worshipped to reward his worshipper and punish whoever does not worship him. The difference between the two interpretations, as al-Quṭb stated, is that the first leaves harm and benefit unrestricted, while the second restricts them to worship and abandoning it.
