It was also said: according to the first interpretation, the relative pronoun refers specifically to the idols themselves, and according to the second, it refers to whatever lacks the attributes of being worshipped. It is permissible for other than idols to be included in it, such as the angels and the Messiah, peace be upon them. The apparent meaning here is that the reference is to idols, because the Arabs were only worshipping them, and the people of al-Ṭā'if worshipped al-Lāt, the people of Makkah worshipped Manāt, Hubal, Isāf and Nā'ilah.

﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors with God."﴾ Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith used to say, "When the Day of Resurrection comes, al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā will intercede for me," and the verse was revealed concerning him.

It is apparent that the rest of the polytheists also used to say this statement, and perhaps they said it as a supposition and hypothesis, meaning: if it is true that he (ﷺ) was sent as you claim, then these will intercede for us. It cannot be said that what is understood from intercession with God, exalted is He, is that it occurs in the Hereafter, which implies resurrection, and they deny it, as His words indicate, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not resurrect whoever dies.﴾ Likewise is what preceded a moment ago, His words, glorified is He: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say...﴾ Thus there would be a contradiction between the implications of the verses. Perhaps for this reason al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him, said: they meant by this intercession the intercession in this world, for the improvement of livelihood, and in that case there is no contradiction. The majority hold the first view, and whoever examines the condition of these people finds them hesitant, and for this reason their statements differed. The attribution of intercession to the idols is said to be by way of causation, because, as is well known, they fashioned them in the forms of righteous men who had standing among them, and they believed that whenever they occupied themselves with worshipping them, those men would intercede for them. It was also said that they believed the ruler of each region was a particular spirit from among the spirits of the celestial spheres, so they designated for that spirit an idol from among the idols and occupied themselves with worshipping it, intending by it the worship of the stars. Other explanations were also given. The truth is that among the idols are those made in the first manner, and among them are those made to be like temples (hayākil) for the spiritual beings.

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them: ﴿Do you inform God of what He does not know...﴾, meaning: do you inform Him, glorified is He, of something that has no existence and no reality at all, namely that the idols are their intercessors before Him, majestic is His glory. For what the All-Knowing of the unseen, whose knowledge encompasses universals and particulars, does not know, has no reality whatsoever. They mention that the like of this is not called a "thing" (shay'), based on what Sībawayh said: a thing is that which may be known and reported about, and this includes both the existent and the non-existent, as some of our companions, such as the Muʿtazilah, have verified. They called what is not known "the negated," such as a partner or the joining of two opposites. Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kūrānī verified this in an independent treatise, in which he brought wonders. It is also permissible that the relative pronoun refers to the fact that He, glorified is He, has a partner. The purpose, according to both interpretations, of mentioning that God is informed of what has no reality and of which His knowledge does not encompass, is mockery and ridicule of them; otherwise there would be no information at all.

﴿in the heavens or on the earth﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relative to the omitted returning pronoun (ʿāʾid), meaning: of what He does not know existing in that. Its purpose is to emphasize the negation implied by what precedes it, for it has become customary to say, when emphasizing the negation of something, "this is not in the heaven or on the earth," because the common people believe that everything that exists is either in the heaven or on the earth, as is the view of the theologians regarding everything other than God, exalted is He, since He, glorified is He, is the worshipped One, exempt from indwelling in place. The verses whose apparent meaning is that are among the ambiguous verses (mutashābih), and the positions on them are well known. This applies when "heaven" and "earth" are meant as the two directions of height and depth. It was also said: the statement is argumentative, to match the claim of the disbelieving addressees that the matter is so. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is, "Do you inform Him, exalted is He, of a partner or an intercessor who knows nothing in the heavens or on the earth," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship, besides God, that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens or the earth.﴾ But this is not valid.

﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ That is, above their associating, which implies that statement which is false, or above their partners whom they believe to be partners.

It was read as "Do you inform" (a-tunabbi'ūna) with lightening (takhfīf). Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "you associate" (tushrikūna) with the second-person ta', on the basis that it is part of the speech commanded to be said. According to the first reading, the phrase is a parenthetical interjection of humiliation from Him, glorified is He and exalted is He.

And the people were not but one community: That is, from the beginning, all people were in agreement upon the truth and the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), without disagreement. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Mujahid, al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim, and it is supported by the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "And the people were not but one community upon guidance." This was from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until Qabil (Cain) killed Habil (Abel). It is also said: until the time of Idris, peace be upon him. It is also said: until the time of Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him, and they were ten generations. It is also said: they were like that during his time, peace be upon him, after no dwelling of the disbelievers remained on the earth, until disbelief appeared among them. It is also said: from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, until 'Amr ibn Luhayy made the worship of idols appear. This is what is related from 'Ata', and according to it, the word ﴿the people﴾ refers specifically to the Arabs. This is the most suitable reading for the placing of this noble verse right after the account of what was reported of them of blunders, and for the exoneration of the sanctuary of Majesty from that.

Page 90

﴿But they differed﴾: some of them disbelieved, while the others remained upon what they were upon, so each of the two groups opposed the other. The fa' (then) here indicates sequence, and it does not contradict the extension of the period of agreement, since the intended meaning is to explain that the disagreement occurred after the period of agreement had ended, not immediately after it began. ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: that is, the postponement of judgment between them, or of the punishment that would decide between them, until the Day of Resurrection, for it is the Day of Decision and Recompense. ﴿Surely the matter would have been decided between them﴾ immediately, ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ (19). That would be by sending down upon them signs compelling them to follow the truth and to end the disagreement, or by destroying the falsifier and preserving the one upon truth. The form of the present tense here is to narrate a past situation and to indicate continuity. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that it serves as a confirmation of what was indicated, namely that tawhid is the true religion, since it conveys that it is an ancient creed upon which all nations were united, and that shirk (associating partners with God) and its branches are ignorances invented by the misguided, in opposition to the majority and in splitting the unity of the community. It is also said that the connection is this: He, glory be to Him, previously explained the corruption of the people through the worship of idols, and in this verse He explained that this doctrine was not the doctrine of the Arabs from the beginning, but rather they were upon the true religion, free of the worship of idols, and the worship of them only arose among them through the enticement of the devils.

It is said: the purpose of this is that when the Arabs know that what they are upon today was not among them before, and that it arose after it did not exist, they would not be zealous in its defense, and would not be pained by its being shown to be false and invalid. It is related from al-Kalbi that the meaning of their being one community is their agreement upon disbelief, and that this was in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. A similar report is related from al-Hasan, except that he said: they were like that from the death of Adam until the time of Nuh, peace be upon them both. Then whoever believed believed, and whoever remained remained upon disbelief. The benefit of mentioning this statement in this context is to console him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, as if it were said: Do not hope that everyone you call to faith and tawhid will respond to you and accept your religion, for all people were upon disbelief, and faith only arose among some of them after that. So how can you hope for the agreement of all upon it?

It has been objected that this implies the earth being empty, in some era, of a believer in God who knows Him. They have said: the earth is never empty of such a person at any time. It is answered that the non-emptiness is subject to dispute. It has been reported in some traditions that before the Day of Resurrection there will be no one among the people who says "Allah, Allah." Even if we accept it, the intended meaning of agreement upon disbelief is the agreement of the majority.

The truth is that this statement in itself is weak, so it is not appropriate to refute what objects to it, and something weaker than it is even less worthy of refutation. Indeed, it hardly holds true that the meaning is that they were one community and then differed, by each of them establishing a separate creed from among the creeds of disbelief, opposing the creed of the other. This is because the discourse is not about that kind of disagreement, since at that point each of the two groups is a falsifier, and it cannot be conceived that judgment would be made between them by preserving the one upon truth and destroying the falsifier, or by compelling one of them to follow the truth so that the disagreement is removed, as is not hidden.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishara) meanings in the verses: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾: the alif indicates the Essence (al-Dhat), which is the first of existence. The lam indicates the Intellect called Jibril, peace be upon him, which is the middle of existence, that which overflows from the Origin and pours forth to the End. The ra indicates Mercy, which is the Muhammadan Essence (al-Dhat al-Muhammadiyya). In reality, it is first, middle and last, but the considerations differ. It is as if this is an oath by Him, exalted is He, by the Muhammadan Reality, that what the surah or the Qur'an contains of verses is the verses of the Firm Book. It is also said: the meaning is that what is indicated by these letters are the foundations of the Book of the All, which is full of wisdom, or the firm (muhkam) Book, and most of its details.

﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them?﴾ This is a denial of their astonishment at God's established practice, which is revelation to a man. That astonishment was due to their remoteness from his station, the incompatibility of their condition with his condition, and the conflict of what he brought with what they believed. ﴿That warn the people﴾: that is, frighten them ...

Page 91

from associating anything with Me. ﴿And give good news to those who believe that they have a sure standing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾: that is, a great precedence and a nearness that no one else has. It is also said: a precedence of mercy which He deposited in Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. ﴿The disbelievers said﴾: that is, those veiled from God, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is clearly magic.﴾ That is, the Book that Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, brought. When they saw it exceeding their measure, and they were veiled by devilishness from standing upon the reality of the situation, they said this. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾: that is, periods, each day of which equals one complete revolution of the greatest sphere, as the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar) explicitly stated. The number six is a perfect number, and God chose it for what it contains of secrets. ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾: that is, the dominion, ﴿arranging the affair﴾ within it according to His wisdom, by the hand of His power. The Throne may also be interpreted as the heart of the perfect person, and the statement is then an allusion to the creation of the human being in whom the whole world is folded. ﴿There is no intercessor﴾ who intercedes for anyone to avert what harms him or to bring what benefits him, ﴿except after His permission﴾ through the bestowal of readiness (isti'dad) and the facilitation of the causes. ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾, described by these noble attributes, ﴿who nurtures you and arranges your affairs. So worship Him, single Him out for worship, and recognize Him by these attributes. Do not worship the devil, and do not veil yourselves from Him, exalted is He, so that you attribute His word and His act to the devil.﴾ ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ His signs, which He inscribed by the hand of His power in the pages of the horizons and the souls, so that you may reflect upon them and refrain from associating partners with Him, glory be to Him. ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾: by returning to the very essence of the absolute gathering at the Lesser Resurrection, or to the essence of the gathering of the Essence through annihilation in Him, exalted is He, at the Greater Resurrection. Thus it is said. One of the gnostics (arifin) said: the return of lovers is to His beauty, the return of the knowers is to His majesty, the return of the monotheists is to His greatness, the return of those who fear is to His magnificence, the return of those who yearn is to His union, the return of those who love is to His nearness, and the return of the people of special care is to His Essence. Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said concerning the verse: from Him is the beginning and to Him is the end, and between them are the fields of His bounty and the successive flow of His favors.

﴿The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾: that is, He originates it in the first creation, then repeats it in the second creation. Or it means He originates creation by bringing them from concealment into manifestation, then repeats it by annihilating them and manifesting Himself. ﴿That He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice, and those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾: that is, He does this so that He may recompense the believer and the disbeliever according to what the deeds of each require. ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance﴾: that is, He made the sun of the Spirit a light of existence ﴿and the moon a light﴾: that is, the moon of the heart. ﴿And determined for it stages﴾: that is, stations (maqamat), ﴿that you may know the number of years﴾: that is, the years of your ranks and your stages in journeying toward Him and in Him, exalted is He, ﴿and the reckoning﴾: that is, the reckoning of your degrees and the places of your feet in each station and rank. It is also said: He made the sun of the Essence a radiance for the knowing spirits, and made the moon of the Attributes a light for the loving hearts. So the spirits perished through the assault of the Essence within the Essence, and the hearts remained through witnessing the Attributes within the Attributes. This sun that is indicated never sets at all from the insights of the spirits, and for this reason one of them said:

It is the sun, except that the sun has an eclipse,
and what we mean does not set.

﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night﴾: that is, the dominance of the darkness of the soul over the heart, ﴿and the day﴾: that is, the day of the radiance of the light of the Spirit upon it, ﴿and what Allah has created in the heavens﴾: that is, the heavens of the spirits, ﴿and the earth﴾: that is, the earth of the bodies, ﴿are signs for a people who are wary﴾: of veiling by the attributes of the commanding soul (nafs ammara). ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord guides them by their faith﴾: that is, He brings them to the three gardens according to the light of their faith. So His word, glory be to Him: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them in gardens of bliss﴾ serves as an explanation of that. ﴿Their prayer therein﴾ (their readiness-claim, al-da'wa al-isti'dadiyya) ﴿is: "Glory be to You, O Allah!"﴾: an indication of His transcendence. The transcendence in the first is from shirk in acts, by disclaiming their own power and strength; in the second, from shirk in attributes, by stripping away their attributes; and in the third,

Page 92

from shirk in existence, by their annihilation. ﴿And their greeting therein is peace﴾: that is, the outpouring of the lights of purification and the sustenance of purity, or the shining of the lights of manifestations and the sustenance of abstraction, and the removal of afflictions. ﴿And the last of their prayer is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾: that is, the last thing their readiness requires is their standing through Allah, exalted is He, in the manifestation of His perfections and the attributes of His majesty and beauty upon them. This is the true praise from Him and to Him, glory be to Him. ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing﴾: that is, he spends his times in supplication. ﴿But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us against a harm that touched him.﴾ This describes those who did not perceive the realities of servanthood in the stations of Lordship. When the night of trial darkens over them, they rise to kindle the lamp of supplication. When the darkness clears from them by the shining of the lights of the dawn of relief, they forget what they were in and pass on as though they had never called upon their Master to remove what troubled them:

As if the youth had never been in need on the day he was clothed,
and had never been a pauper when he grew wealthy.

Had they been gnostics, they would not have left the abode of humble supplication and the manifestation of servanthood before Him, exalted is He, at every moment. ﴿And the people were not but one community﴾: upon the nature (fitra) upon which Allah created people, turning toward tawhid, illuminated by the light of the original guidance. ﴿But they differed﴾: by the requirements of creation and the differences of temperaments, inclinations, customs and associations. ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: which is His eternal decree, exalted is He, by determining the terms and sustenance, ﴿the matter would have been decided between them concerning that over which they differ﴾: by destroying the falsifier and preserving the one upon truth. The meaning is that the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, required that each of them reach the direction toward which he turned his face, through the deeds he performs and the manifestation of what was hidden in his soul. Glory be to Allah, the Wise, the All-Knowing.

﴿And they say﴾, a narration of another of their crimes. In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, Zamakhshari's Qur'anic commentary), the present tense is interpreted as the past, i.e., "and they said." He made this a sign that the conjunction is not with ﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors"﴾, as the apparent wording would suggest, but rather with His words, glorified be He: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us said: "Bring a Qur'an other than this"﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. The present tense was preferred over the past to indicate the continuity of this utterance and that it is among their habits and customs, along with what that carries of bringing to mind its shameful image.

It is also permissible that the conjunction is with (they worship), which is what some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) restricted themselves to. Some of them left the verb on its apparent meaning, and it has a basis. The speakers are the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ They meant a sign from among the signs they had proposed, like the sign of Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both. The meaning of its being sent down to him is God Most High's manifesting it through his hand, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. They asked for that out of obstinacy and stubbornness. Otherwise, he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, came with clear signs and dazzling miracles that rise above all signs and surpass all other miracles, especially the Great Qur'an, whose inimitability remains for all time until the Day of Resurrection. By my life, if they had been fair, they would have dispensed with every sign other than him, peace be upon him, for he is the Greatest Sign. Whoever sees him and examines his circumstances would hardly doubt that he is the Messenger of God, may God Most High's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿Say﴾ to them in reply: ﴿The unseen belongs only to God, so wait; I am with you among those who wait.﴾ This is a reply according to what al-Tibi (al-Tibi, the commentator) established, in the manner of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), for when they asked what they asked despite the presence of abundant signs, this indicated that their question was for the sake of obstinacy, as you have just understood. So they were answered with what they were answered, to indicate that their question was the question of those who propose, for which they deserve God's vengeance and the descent of His punishment. It means that He will certainly uproot your root, but I do not know when it will be, and you are in that state, because that is from the unseen, which belongs exclusively to God Most High; no one knows it except Him, may His majesty be exalted. Since that is so, then wait for what your proposal necessitates; I am with you among those who wait for it.

It has also been said: the meaning is that He, Most High, is the one exclusively knowing the unseen, and what prevents the sending down of the proposed signs is a hidden matter, so no one knows it except Him. This was objected to on the grounds that it is specific, namely their obstinacy. God Most High said: ﴿And what makes you know that when it comes they will not believe?﴾

Page 93

It is answered: We do not concede that their obstinacy is what prevents it; the obstinate may be answered, and the verse, though it indicates their persistence in obstinacy, even if it [the sign] came, does not indicate that obstinacy is what prevents it.

Some of the verifiers chose that what you have proposed, and claimed to be among the requirements of prophethood, and made your faith conditional on its descent, belongs to the hidden matters exclusive to Him, glorified be He, of which I have no knowledge. So wait for its descent; I am with you among those who wait for what God Most High will do to you for your audacity toward such a great matter as denying the signs and proposing others. This view was objected to on the grounds that the ordering of the command to wait upon the exclusivity of the unseen to God Most High is incompatible with it. What comes to mind is that the people's question, may God Most High fight them, contains a claim that the good lies in sending down a sign of what they proposed, since they did not take into account what had been sent down and did not pay attention to it. It is as if they said: "There is no good in the sending down of what has been sent down; the good lies only in sending down a sign of what we propose. So why is it not sent down?" This contains, without doubt, a claim to knowledge of the unseen. So they were answered: the unseen belongs exclusively to God, for He is the one who knows what is good, not you nor anyone else. Then He, glorified be He, said: ﴿So wait﴾, etc., in the sense: since the knowledge of the unseen belongs exclusively to God Most High, and you have claimed of it what you have claimed and have slandered what you have slandered, then wait for the descent of punishment upon you; I am with you among those who await it. This objection does not apply to this view, nor what might be raised against it. So reflect.

[p. 94]

*"And when We let people taste mercy"* (﴿وإذا أذَقْنا النّاسَ رَحْمَةً﴾), such as health and abundance, *"after adversity had touched them"* (﴿مِن بَعْدِ ضَرّاءَ مَسَّتْهُمْ﴾), meaning it had afflicted them until they felt the evil of its effect upon them. Attributing the touching to adversity, after attributing the tasting to the Divine Name (*Damir al-Jalalah*), is one of the Qur'anic courtesies (*al-adab al-Qur'aniyyah*), as in His saying, *"And when I am ill, it is He who cures me"* (Q 26:80), and its like. It is fitting to observe this courtesy in such matters. Thus in a report: "O Allah, the good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You."

By *"the people"* is meant the disbelievers of Makkah, according to what has been said, because it is reported that Allah the Exalted imposed upon them a drought for seven years, until they nearly perished. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to supplicate for them for fertility, and they promised him that they would believe. When he supplicated for them, and Allah the Exalted had mercy on them with rain, they began to slander His signs and to oppose him (ﷺ) and to plot against him. This is His saying, Glorified is He: *"Then, behold, they have a scheme concerning Our signs"* (﴿إذا لَهم مَكْرٌ في آياتِنا﴾), meaning by slandering them, not regarding them, and devising means to repel them. The apparent meaning is that by *"the signs"* are meant the Qur'anic verses. It has also been said that by them are meant the cosmic signs (*al-ayat al-takwiniyyah*), such as the sending of rain, and their scheme in them is ascribing them to the idols and the stars. It has also been said that *"the people"* is general, covering all disbelievers, and it is not permissible to take it to include the disobedient, as is not hidden.

The Arabs used to ascribe rains, and likewise winds, heat and cold, to the *anwa'* (star-risings, sing. *nawʾ*). *Nawʾ* is a verbal noun from *nāʾa yanūʾu*, meaning to rise with effort and hardship, and it is also said of setting, so it is one of the words with contrary meanings (*min al-adhdad*). It is also applied to the star which is one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions that we mentioned earlier, and this is what is meant in their speech. However, the attribution to it is in terms of its setting together with the dawn and its disappearance, as is well known, or in terms of its rising at that time, as al-Asma'i said.

The one who holds that the *anwa'* have an influence has been considered a disbeliever. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Zayd ibn Khalid, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted said: *'In the morning there are among My servants one who believes in Me and disbelieves in the star, and one who disbelieves in Me and believes in the star. As for the one who says, "We have been given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy," he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star; and as for the one who says, "We have been given rain by such-and-such a star-rising," he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star.'"*

Perhaps the reason this is disbelief in Allah the Exalted is based upon the belief that the stars have an independent, volitional influence in this matter. Otherwise, believing that the influence is with them and not by them, as is the well-known position of the Ash'arites concerning all causes, is not disbelief, as al-⁠ʿAllamah Ibn Hajar explicitly stated. Likewise, believing that the influence is by them in the sense that Allah the Exalted has deposited in them an influential power by His permission, so that when He wills, they have influence, and when He does not will, they have no influence, is the position of the Salaf concerning causes, as established by Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani in *Maslak al-Sadad*. Had the attribution of influence absolutely to the *anwa'* and the like of the upper bodies (*al-ʿulwiyyat*) been disbelief, the matter would have been too wide, and it would have necessitated declaring many people disbelievers, including their most excellent, because of their saying that much of the world of generation and corruption (*ʿalam al-kawn wa'l-fasad*) is attributed to the upper bodies, which they call the "upper fathers." The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, has explicitly stated that the wandering stars (*al-sayyarat*) and others have an influence in this world, but knowing the determination of its particulars is something that only the masters of unveiling and inner observations (*arbab al-kashf wa'l-arsad al-qalbiyyah*) are aware of. His intention, may his secret be sanctified, and likewise the intention of whoever stated influence absolutely, is nothing other than what either of the two groups concerning causes has held. Far be it, and far again, that those excellent scholars should be among those who believe that there is in existence an influencer other than Allah the Exalted. Rather, whoever comprehends the true meaning of the words of the philosophers, who are far removed from the noble Shari'ah, finds them agreed that existence is an effect (*maʿlul*) of Him, the Exalted, absolutely. Bahmanyar said in *al-Tahsil*: "If you ask for the truth, it is not valid that the cause of existence should be anything except that which is free from every aspect of the meaning of potentiality (*maʿna ma bi'l-quwwah*), and this is the First Principle and nothing else." As for what is reported from Plato, that he said: "The world is a sphere, the earth is its center, the human is its target, the spheres are bows, the events are arrows, and Allah the Exalted is the Archer, so where is the escape?"—this indicates that (*yushʿir bi-dhalika aydan*)—

[p. 94 continues]

*(Yes)*, they did speak of intellectual conditions (*al-sharaʾit al-ʿaqliyyah*), and these are what is meant by the intermediaries (*al-wasaʾit*) in the speech of some of them, and this is contrary to the correct doctrine. In summary, one who says that the stars are influential, in the sense that the influence is with them or by them with the permission of Allah the Exalted, does not become a disbeliever. Rather, his ruling is the ruling of one who says that fire burns and water nourishes, for example. There is no difference between the two statements except what might be said: that the influence in the case of fire and water is a sensible, observed matter, whereas the influence in the stars is not so, and the claim concerning it is "casting stones at the unseen" (*rajm bi'l-ghayb*). But this, even if granted, does not necessitate that one of the two statements be disbelief and not the other, as is not hidden from the fair-minded. Nevertheless, the more cautious course is to avoid attributing influence absolutely to the stars, and to refrain from uttering words like those with which Allah the Exalted declared the utterer a disbeliever. This is so.

*(And when)* the first is conditional, and the second is sudden (*fujaʾiyyah*), linking the response. The indefiniteness of *"scheme"* (*makr*) is for magnification, and *"in"* (*fi*) is connected to the stability (*al-istiqrar*) to which the *lam* is connected.

*"Say: Allah is swifter in scheme"* (﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ أسْرَعُ مَكْرًا﴾), meaning swifter than you. *Asraʿu* is a comparative form (*afʿal al-tafdil*), and it is derived either from the triliteral *saraʿa*, as al-Farisi related, or from the augmented *asraʿa*. However, there is a difference of opinion about deriving the comparative from the augmented form. Some prohibited it absolutely, some permitted it absolutely, and some said: if the hamza is for transitivity it is prohibited, otherwise it is permitted. The construction of the exclamatory form (*bina' al-taʿajjub*) is similar in this regard. The attribution of swiftness to the one surpassed indicates the suddenness. The validity of using *asraʿa* in this sense does not depend upon the speech indicating what has been mentioned, contrary to what the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words requires. The root meaning of *makr* is concealing a plot and harm, and what is meant by it here is requital and punishment for the scheme, as a figurative usage by a looser connection (*majaz mursal*) or by correspondence (*mushakalah*). The latter does not contradict this, as in the commentary on *al-Miftah*. It has become well known that it is not used of Him except by way of correspondence, but this is not so, as has been verified in its proper place.

*"Indeed Our messengers"* (﴿إنَّ رُسُلَنا﴾), the guardians (*al-hafazah*) from Our side, *"record what you scheme"* (﴿يَكْتُبُونَ ما تَمْكُرُونَ﴾), meaning your scheme, or what you scheme. The manner of recording that is not necessary to know, and there is no need to make this figurative for knowledge. This is a confirmation of retribution against them and an alert that what they devised in concealing is not hidden from the scribes, let alone from the One who sent down the Book, from whom no hidden thing is concealed. In this there is also a rebuke of them, as is not hidden. The apparent meaning is that this sentence is not included in the quoted speech, like His saying: *"And if We brought the like of it as a supplement"* (Q 18:109). It is a reason (*taʿlil*) for the swiftness of His scheme, Glorified and Exalted is He. It has also been allowed that it is included in that, and in

[p. 95]

*"Indeed Our messengers"* there is a shift (*iltifat*), for had it been left in line with His saying, Glorified is He, *"Say: Allah,"* it would have said: "Indeed His messengers." There is no difficulty in this, since there is no reason for commanding the Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them: "Indeed Our messengers," the pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted and not to him (ﷺ), with the supposition of an omitted genitive, i.e., "the messengers of our Lord," or by attribution for the slightest connection, as has been said.

Some have said in answer: it is a report of what Allah the Exalted said, with the intention of conveying this meaning, not with this wording.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid read *"yamkurūna"* (they scheme) in the third person (*lafz al-ghaybah*), and this was also narrated from Nafi' and Ya'qub. In it there is continuity with what preceded in His saying, Glorified is He: *"touched them"* and *"to them"*. The address (*al-khitab*) is more fitting, as the rest read it, if the sentence is included within the scope of the saying, since the meaning is "Say to them," and the fittingness of the address is then evident. In it there is also an emphasis in informing them of their scheme. Some of the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqin*) took it, in that reading and in its not being included within the scope of the saying, as a reason for the swiftness, or for the aforementioned matter. The form of the future tense in the two verbs is to indicate continuity and renewal, and likewise in His saying, Glorified is He:

He is the One who enables you to travel on land and sea. According to what has been said, this is a resumptive statement (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes), brought to explain another of their offenses, which is based on what was mentioned just before: the variation in their condition according to the variation of the harms that afflict them. It is also reported from Abu Muslim that it is an explanation of part of what was stated in general terms in His words, "And when We let people taste mercy..." etc. This is close to the view of al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi), that when God said, "And when We let [them] taste..." (the verse), this is a universal statement, and it was presented to them as an example so that what they are upon would become clear and manifest.

Some have claimed that it is connected to the preceding proofs of God's oneness, so it is as if it were said: Your God is the One who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light. "He is the One who enables you to travel..." etc. The "enabling of travel" (at-taysir) is interpreted as causing one to move and empowering one to move. The reason for this, it is said, is that "until, when you are in the ships" cannot be taken as a limit (ghayah, the endpoint) of the travel at sea, even though it precedes it, and the limit of a thing must necessarily come after it. But after this interpretation, there is no difficulty in taking what is mentioned as a limit of what precedes it.

It has also been said: this is to block the implication of combining the literal and the metaphorical, because the one who makes one travel at sea is God, Exalted, since He, glory be to Him, is the one who originates those movements in the ship by means of the wind, and the servant has no part in it, but only in its preliminaries. As for travel on land, it is among the voluntary acts issued by the addressees themselves, if they are on foot, or by their animals, if they are riders; God's enabling of travel on land is the provision of the instruments and tools. The implication of combining the two is evident. The answer to this objection is that what is meant by "enabling" is what has been mentioned, which is a figurative meaning that encompasses both the literal and the metaphorical.

Some have claimed that the enabling of travel on land and sea is one and the same, and it has been used as evidence that the actions of the servants are created by God, Exalted. It has been objected that this is a far-fetched strain (takalluf). Al-Zamakhshari did not interpret "enabling" in the way we mentioned, but made the limit (ghayah) the content of the conditional sentence that follows "until" together with what is within its scope, as if it were said: He enables you to travel until, when this event occurs, and such-and-such happens, namely the coming of a violent wind, the piling up of waves, the thought of destruction, and the supplication for deliverance, rather than being in the sea. Al-Qutb has criticized this, saying that if being in the ship is taken together with what is conjoined to it, namely His words, "And they sailed with them with a good wind, and they rejoiced in it," it would suffice, and there would be no need to consider the whole conditional and its response together. Then he said: The truth is that if the limit is defined as what a thing reaches essentially, then it is nothing but what occurred as the condition in such a case; and if the limit is defined as what a thing reaches absolutely, whether essentially or through an intermediary, then it is the whole of the condition and its response. Clarify this from your saying: "I walked until, when I reached the town, I traded." What the walking reaches essentially is arrival at the town, and as for the trading, it is a matter that follows from that, so it is among what the walking reached through an intermediary.

The doubling in (yusayyirukum) is for transitivity (ta'diyah, making a verb take a direct object). You say: "The man traveled" (sara ar-rajul) and "I made the man travel" (sayyartuhu). Al-Farisi said: sara is transitive like sayyara, because the Arabs say: "sirtu ar-rajul" and "sayyartuhu" with the same meaning. From this is the saying of the Hudhali (poet):

"So do not be distressed over a year whose delight you are,
for the first to be content is the year of its traveler."

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it is said: "The animal traveled (sarat ad-dabbah) and its owner made it travel (sarraha sahibuha); it is transitive and intransitive." He cited this verse, and the grammarians, since they did not approve of that, began it with (the line before it).

Al-Fulk (the ships) is singular and plural alike, and the difference in vowel patterns between them is conventional (i'tibari). In al-Sihah it is said that it is singular and plural, masculine and feminine. It seems that this is with respect to the vessel and the ship. Sibawayh used to say: al-Fulk, which is a broken plural (jam' taksir) of al-Fulk which is singular, is not like junub, which is singular and plural, or tifl and similar nouns, because fa'al and fu'l share in one thing, like al-'arab and al-'urb, al-'ajam and al-'ujm, ar-rahab and ar-ruhb. Therefore, since fa'al may be pluralized as fu'l, like asad and usud, it is not impossible that fa'al be pluralized as fa'l.

The pronoun in (jarayna) refers to al-fulk (the ships), and the pronoun in "bihim" refers to those who are in them. This is an iltifat (shift from address to third-person reference) for the sake of emphasizing the repulsiveness of their condition, as if He had turned away from addressing them, and reported their evil conduct to others. It has also been said: there is no iltifat; rather the meaning of His words, "until, when you are in the ships," is "until, when some of you are in them," since the address is to all, and among them are those who are traveling on land. Thus the absent pronoun refers to that omitted (mudaf muqaddar, an understood genitive construction). Compare His words: "Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave..." (24:40), for it is in the sense of "or like one in darkness, in a deep sea, covered by a wave." The first "bi" is for transitivity, and the second, and likewise the third, is for causation. Therefore the two particles are attached to one governing element. Otherwise, they have prohibited attaching two particles with the same meaning to one governing element. Considering the attachment of the second after the attachment of the first to it, and attending to it together with it, removes the unity of the governing element.

It is also allowed that the second "bi" be for a circumstance (hal), meaning: they sailed with them while it was accompanied by a wind, so it is attached to an omitted element, as in "in the sea." The first may also be taken as expressing accompaniment (mula-basah). "And they rejoiced" is conjoined to (jarayna), and it is conjoined to "kuntum." It may also be taken as a circumstantial clause with qad understood. The pronoun in "bi-ha" refers to the wind. Al-Tabarsi related that it refers to the ship, but this can hardly be written with a pen. What is meant by "good" (tayyibah), as the context requires, is gentle in its blowing, agreeing with the intended destination.

The apparent sense of the verse, as reported from al-Imam, requires that the rider of a ship moves by its movement, contrary to those who say he is stationary. There is no basis for this disagreement, as some researchers have said, for he is stationary in essence and moving through an intermediary.

Ibn 'Amir read (yanshurukum) with the nun, the shin with a dot, and the ra' without a dot, from al-nashr, the opposite of folding, meaning: He scatters you and disperses you. Al-Hasan read (yunshirukum) from anshara, meaning "revive." Some Syrian readers read (yunashhirukum) with shaddah for intensification, also from nashr. From Umm al-Darda it is reported that she read "fi al-fulki" with the addition of the two ya' of nisbah (relative ending). The reason for this: the two ya' are additional, as in al-kharijiyy and al-ahmariyy, and this is not restricted to adjectives, as in the forms dudawi and ana as-Salatani in the verse of as-Salatan. It is also possible that what is meant by it is the deep sea, the great water in which ships sail only in it.

His words, "There came to them," is the answer (jawab) to "idha" (when). The pronoun in the accusative refers to the ship or to the good wind, in the sense of: it encountered them and overpowered them from a direction opposite to them. For the blowing in accordance with their course is not called, according to what is said, a coming of another wind usually, but rather a strengthening of the first wind. The second interpretation was preferred because it is more evident, since it necessarily implies the first without the converse, for blowing in the direction of a gentle wind is considered a coming with respect to the ship, but not with respect to the gentle wind, while it does not entail a clash of waves, which necessitates its coming from every place. Also, because the terror in describing its overpowering them is greater with respect to what they rejoiced in and attached the ropes of their hopes to. Consider this carefully.

"A violent wind" (rih 'asif) means a wind with violent force (dhat 'asf). It is of the type of nisbah (relative formation), like laban and tamir, and it applies equally to masculine and feminine, as the grammarians have stated. Therefore it did not say "'asifah," even though the wind is feminine, which is not made masculine without a reinterpretation.

It has also been said: it did not say "'asifah" because violence (al-'usuf) is specific to the wind, so it is like "hA'id" (menstruating, applied to a woman), so no distinguishing marker is needed. Or it is said that masculinity was considered with respect to the wind, just as femininity was considered in it. The first view that we presented is better. The root meaning of al-'asf is breaking, and the broken plant; what is meant is violent blowing.

"And the wave came to them" (wa-ja'ahumu al-mawj): it is what rises and is elevated from the agitation of water. It has been said: it is the agitation of the sea. The first is the well-known view.

"From every place": that is, from the places where waves usually come. It may also happen that it comes from directions due to causes that coincide for that.

"And they thought that they were encompassed" (wa-zannu annahum uhita bihim): that is, they were destroyed, as Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Juraij. Thus there is a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) in the speech. It has also been said that encompassing is a metaphor for blocking the paths of escape, likening it to the encirclement of a person by an enemy; then by that metaphor the destruction is alluded to (kinayah), because it is among its concomitants and necessary consequences.

It has also been said that this is an example for destruction, and "zann" (thinking) in its usual sense. It is allowed that it means certainty, based on the realization of its occurrence in their belief, or that the allusion is to proximity to destruction.

"They called upon God": making it, according to more than one, a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, a substitute that is connected to its antecedent by a relation rather than identity) for "zannu," because their supplication is among the necessary consequences of their thinking of destruction, so there is a connection between them that justifies the substitution. It has also been said: it is the answer to what the meaning contains of the sense of a condition, meaning: when they thought they were encompassed, they called upon God, etc.

Abu Hayyan made it a clarificatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What was their state at that time?" and it was answered: "They called upon..." etc. The view that it is a substitute was preferred over this, because it is more closely connected to the flow of speech, and the meaning is more explicit as being the intended point, while it conveys what is derived from a resumption and dispenses with assuming a question. You know that assuming a question is not a real assumption but a notional matter, and in it there is brevity as much as there is. It is not more far-fetched than what was strained for the substitution view. The statement of some of them suggests that it may be the answer to the conditional, and "there came to them" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, as in His words: "So when they board the ships, they call upon God..." (29:65). It has been objected that the need for an answer requires directing what is suitable for it toward it, not toward a supplementary circumstance that requires the assumption of qad. Moreover, the conjunction of "and they thought" to "there came to them" rejects the circumstantial sense, and rejoicing in the good wind does not occur at the time of the violent wind's coming. The meaning is based on the realization of the coming, not on supposing it, so that it may be made a hypothetical circumstance. This is not without merit. The apparent point is that what he counted as an impediment to the circumstantial sense is not shared between it and its being the answer to (idha), because it requires that the two be in one time, as is not hidden from anyone who has even minimal acquaintance with the styles of speech.

His words, "sincere to Him in religion" (mukhlisina lahu ad-din), are a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "da'aw" (they called). "Lahu" is attached to "mukhlisin," and "ad-din" is its object, meaning: they called upon Him, Exalted, without associating anything with Him, because when they return from intense fear to the primordial nature (al-fitrah) upon which every person is created, which is monotheism, and that none has any power except God, Glory be to Him, which is fixed in the natures of the world. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

From a hadith that Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: When the day of the conquest (of Mecca) came, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl fled and boarded the sea, and a violent storm struck them. The companions of the ship said to the people of the ship: "Be sincere (to God), for your gods will not avail you anything." Ikrimah said: "If nothing saves me at sea except sincerity, nothing else will save me on land. O God, I make a covenant with You: if You grant me well-being from what I am in, I will come to Muhammad (ﷺ) until I place my hand in his hand, and I will surely find him pardoning and generous." He said: So he came and embraced Islam.

In the narration of Ibn Sa'd from Abu Mulaykah: When Ikrimah boarded the ship, and the wind seized them, they began to call upon God, Exalted, and to declare His oneness. He said: "What is this?" They said: "This is a place where nothing benefits except God, Exalted." He said: "Then this is for Him. Muhammad (ﷺ) is the one who calls us to it. Return with us." So he returned and embraced Islam.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the intention is not restricting the supplication alone to Him, Glory be to Him, but also restricting worship to Him, Exalted, because by merely this they would not be "sincere to Him in religion."

Whatever the case, the verse indicates that the polytheists do not call upon anyone other than Him, the Exalted, in that state. And you know well that people today, when a grave matter or a mighty calamity befalls them on land or sea, call upon those who neither harm nor benefit, neither see nor hear. Among them are those who call upon al-Khidr (al-Khadir) and Ilyas (Elias); among them are those who cry out to Abu al-Khamis and al-Abbas; among them are those who seek help from one of the imams; and among them are those who humble themselves before a shaykh from among the shaykhs of the community. You will not find among them anyone who singles out his Lord with his supplication and his call, nor does it scarcely occur to him that if he were to call upon Allah alone, he would be saved from these terrors. So, by Allah, the Exalted, tell me: which of the two groups, from this standpoint, is more rightly guided in the way, and which of the two callers speaks more upright a word? And to Allah, the Exalted, is the complaint made, of a time in which the winds of ignorance have raged, the waves of misguidance have crashed, the ship of the Shari'ah has been holed, seeking help from other than Allah, the Exalted, for deliverance has been taken as a pretext, and for those who know the good, enjoining it has been made difficult, and the various kinds of calamities have prevented forbidding the evil. Furthermore, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful﴾ [10:22] is in a place of accusative (nasb) by an implied verb according to the Basrans, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the preceding pronoun. The view of the Kufans is to treat the supplication as having the status of speech, since it is one of its types, and to make the clause quoted by it; the first view is the preferable one here. The lam is a preface to an implied oath, and ﴿we will surely be﴾ is its answer.

The pointed-to in this state in which they are: that is, "By Allah, if You deliver us from what we are in of hardship, we will surely, after that, forever be grateful for Your favors, of which this favor being asked for is one." The deviation from "we will thank" (lanashkuranna) to what is in the sublime composition is for the sake of emphasis in indicating the firmness in gratitude and persistence in it.

[p. 99]

﴿So when He had delivered them﴾ from the hardship and distress that had befallen them. The *fa'* (then) indicates swiftness in the response. ﴿Behold, they were committing outrage﴾ on the earth. That is, they hurriedly rushed into corruption on it, eagerly pursuing it and going to extremes in it, from their saying *baghā al-jurḥu* (the wound spread) when it spread into corruption. The addition of ﴿on the earth﴾ indicates that their outrage extended to all its regions. The present tense (*muḍāri'*) indicates renewal and continuation. As for His, glorified and exalted, saying ﴿without right﴾, it emphasizes what *al-baghy* (outrage) already conveys, for its meaning is that it is without right even in their own view, being manifest injustice whose ugliness is not hidden from anyone. It has been said something similar concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾. *Al-baghy* has also been explained as corrupting the form of a thing and destroying its benefit. ﴿Without right﴾ was introduced to exclude what is done by right, such as the raiders' devastation of the lands of the unbelievers, cutting down their trees, and burning their crops, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did to the Banu Qurayza.

It has been objected that the sublime structure of the verse does not support this, because *al-baghy* in the first sense is the one befitting the state of the corrupters, so the discourse should be built upon it. Al-Zamakhshari chose that this phrase serves to exclude what was mentioned. The *Kashf* mentions that by this he pointed out that linguistic corruption is the removal of a thing from benefit, so not every outrage (i.e., corruption) on the earth and domineering in it is like that, as you know, even though its conventional meaning is domineering without right. But the consideration is toward its original meaning. It has also been said: the *baghy* that is transitive with *fī* means destruction and corruption, and it may be right or other than right; while the one transitive with *ʿalā* means injustice. Restricting the first with ﴿without right﴾ is for exclusion, and restricting the second with it is for emphasis. Perhaps whoever takes *al-baghy* here to mean injustice would say: the meaning is that they transgress against the Muslims, for example. Understand this.

﴿O mankind﴾: the address is directed to those outrageous ones, for the intensification of the threat and the emphasis of the warning. ﴿Your outrage﴾ which you engage in, is the subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate is His, glorified, saying: ﴿is against yourselves﴾. That is, it is against you in reality, not against those you transgress against, even if they think otherwise. His, exalted, saying ﴿the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) emphasizing a verb understood by way of resumption (*isti'nāf*), that is: you enjoy the enjoyment of the life of this world. The purpose of this is to show that the benefit gained by outrage is a fleeting one, not worth counting, quick to vanish, and lasting in its consequence. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*), meaning: enjoying, and the governing element is the stability (*al-istiqrār*) contained in the predicate. It is permissible that it be the outrage itself, because it is not permissible to separate the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate; also, one does not predicate something of a verbal noun until its relative clause and complements are complete. It has been objected that there is no meaningful significance in restricting the fact that their outrage is against themselves to the state of their enjoying the life of this world.

It has been said: it is in the accusative as a time adverb, like *maqdam al-ḥājj* (the arrival time of the pilgrim), meaning: the time of the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the governing element is also the stability, and the objection to the previous applies here. It has been said: it is in the accusative as an object of a verb indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: you seek the enjoyment of the life of this world. It was objected that this requires that *al-baghy* mean seeking, because that is the form which takes a direct object, and the verbal noun does not indicate it. Also, making the verbal noun mean its own meaning disturbs the eloquence of the sublime composition, because the resumption is to explain the evil outcome of what was related of them of outrage, interpreted by the chosen view as excessive corruption suited to their condition; and then the connection is negated and the coherence is lost. The first also was taken in its own meaning, which obliges one to exalt the sanctuary of the revelation from it.

It has been said: it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*), meaning: for the sake of the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the governing element is the stability. It was objected that what is given as the cause is the outrage itself, not that it is against themselves. It has been said: the governing element is a verb indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: you seek for the sake of the enjoyment of the life of this world, with the sentence being a resumed one. It has been said: it is in the accusative as a direct object of the verbal noun, and ﴿against yourselves﴾ is attached to it, not a predicate of *mā* as mentioned before. The meaning of ﴿yourselves﴾ is the genus, and the predicate is omitted because of the length of the speech. The estimate is: your outrage against the sons of your kind is the enjoyment of the life of this world, which is blameworthy, or forbidden, or misguidance, or manifest corruption, or something like that. In this lies the basing on the view that *al-baghy* means seeking, and you already know what is in it. Yes, if its accusative were taken as the cause, meaning: your outrage against the sons of your kind for the sake of the enjoyment of the life of this world is blameworthy, as some of them chose, it would have some validity in general. But the truth required by the eloquence of the composition is the first.

Al-Jumhur read *matā'u* in the nominative.

The author of *al-Murshid* said: In it there are two possibilities. The first is that it is the predicate, with the adverbial phrase being the complement of the verbal noun. The second is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that, or it is the enjoyment of the life of this world. Another possibility was added, that it is a predicate after a predicate for *bagh-yukum* (your outrage). The preferred view, rather the one that is fixed according to the first possibility, is that the intended meaning of ﴿yourselves﴾ is the sons of your kind or your likes, by way of metaphor. Referring to them by this is for compassion and for urging them to abandon preferring the mentioned enjoyment over what is due in rights. And on the last two possibilities there is no obstacle to taking the words in their literal sense, as our master Shaykh al-Islam explained. It was also read with the accusative for *matā'* and *al-ḥayāt*. The accusative of the first is explained as before, and the second is put in the accusative as a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-ishtimāl*) of the first.

It has been said: it is in the accusative as an object of purpose when its accusative is not as a verbal noun, because the emphasizing verbal noun does not govern. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that it was read with both in the genitive, with the second being a genitive complement of the first, and the first an adjective of ﴿yourselves﴾, meaning: possessing enjoyment. It was also permitted that the verbal noun be in the sense of the active participle, meaning: enjoying. It was considered weak to make it an apposition, since it is possible to make it a qualifier ﴿this﴾.

In the verse there is a sufficient warning against outrage, as is not hidden.

Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Khatib, al-Daylami and others narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Three things return upon their people: deception, breach of covenant, and outrage." Then he, upon him be prayers and peace, recited: ﴿O mankind, your outrage is against yourselves﴾ and ﴿And evil deception does not encompass anyone except its people﴾ and ﴿Whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Bakra, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "No sin is more deserving of having its punishment hastened for its doer than outrage and severing the ties of kinship." He also narrated through the chain of Bilal ibn Abi Burda, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said: "No one transgresses against people except the child of an adulteress, or in whom there is a trace of that."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "If a mountain were to transgress against a mountain, the transgressor of the two would be crushed."

Al-Ma'mun used to recite these two verses to his brother:

O possessor of outrage, outrage is a fall,
so refrain; the best deed of a man is its most just.
If a mountain on a day were to transgress against a mountain,
its heights and its depths would be crumbled from it.

Al-Shihab set this out and said:

If one who transgresses against you exceeds, then leave him,
and watch for a time for the vengeance of the transgressor, and beware
of the grievous outrage, for if a mountain transgressed against a mountain,
the transgressor would be crushed.

﴿Then to Us is your return﴾: it is a conjunction with what preceded of the resumed, implied sentence, as if it were said: you enjoy the enjoyment of the life of this world, then you return to Us. The composition was changed to what is in the sublime structure to indicate permanence and brevity.

﴿So We will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in the world, continuously of outrage. Thus it is a warning and threat of recompense and punishment. The discussion of its parallel has already preceded.

[p. 100]

[Page 101]

﴿Indeed, the likeness of the worldly life﴾ is a resumptive sentence (al-istinaf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it) that explains the state of the worldly life and how brief the period of enjoying it is. The original meaning of "mathal" (likeness) is that the thing used as an example is compared to the thing it illustrates, and the word is borrowed for a strange and remarkable matter. The meaning is: its state is one of rapid passing away and the cutting off of its blessings after they have come and after people have been deceived by them. ﴿Like water which We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it﴾, that is, they grew abundantly because of it, ﴿until﴾ some of them intertwined with others. Here the "ba'" (with) indicates causation. Some scholars kept it in the sense of accompaniment and took the mingling to be with the water itself, since water serves as nourishment for plants, so it flows into them and mixes with them. The first view is the one implied by the words of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. ﴿of which men and cattle eat﴾, such as herbs, crops, grass and pasture. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wal-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the plants. ﴿Until, when the earth took on its adornment﴾, that is, it completed and perfected its ornament (zukhruf), meaning its beauty and brightness, ﴿and was decked out﴾ with the varieties, shapes and different colours of plants:

"Like the trailing hems of a graceful maiden who came forward in dyed, sheer garments, some longer than others."

Many have mentioned that the verse contains an implicit metaphor (isti'ara bil-kinaya, a metaphor in which the likened item is omitted and only its attribute is indicated), in that the earth is likened to a bride, the thing likened-to is omitted, and the likened thing (the earth) is put in its place. Attributing the taking of ornament to it is an imaginative device (takhyil), and what follows it is a supporting element (tarshih). It has also been said that "zukhruf" means gold, borrowed for freshness and a dazzling appearance.

[Page 102]

The original form of "izzayyanat" is "tazayyanat," in which the "ta" was assimilated into the "za" and the letter was made sukun (vowelless), so a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza, a hamza pronounced only when beginning speech) was added to allow pronunciation at the start of the word with a sukun. Following the original form, 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read it so, and al-A'raj, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliya, Nasr ibn 'Asim and al-Hasan read it differently: "wa-azyanat," in the pattern "af'alat," like "akramat." Its regular form would have been to undergo i'lal (morphological weakening, changing a weak letter), converting its "ya" into an "alif," so one would say "azanat," since this is the regular pattern for verbs with a weak middle radical. However, it came contrary to this, as in "aghlayat al-mar'a" when a woman gave her child al-ghayl, which is the milk of her pregnancy, while she was pregnant. Yet "aghalat" has also come according to the regular pattern.

The meaning of the verbs here is becoming (al-sayrura), that is, she became one who possesses adornment, or she made herself so. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read "izyanat" with a hamzat al-wasl followed by a sukun "za," an open "ya," a hamza, likewise, a shaddah on "nun," and the feminine "ta." Its original form was "izyanat" in the pattern "ihmarrat," with a clear "alif." Since they disliked two consecutive sukun letters, they converted the "alif" into an open hamza, as was also read in "al-dallin" (wa-la al-dallin). Also attested is "ihma'arrat" with a hamza, as in the line:

"When the leading ones, smeared with fresh blood, turned red."

'Awf ibn Jamil read "azyanat" with an "alif" without any substitution. It was also read "azayanat" intending intensification (al-mubalagha).

﴿And its people thought they had power over it﴾, that is, over the land, meaning they thought they were able to benefit from it, to obtain its fruit and to harvest its produce. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the crops, or to the fruit, or to the adornment, since that is understood from the context. ﴿Then Our command came upon it﴾: this is the answer to "idha" (when), meaning that the punishment We had decreed befell it, namely the destruction of its crop by calamities and blights such as hail, locusts, mice, a fierce wind, the simoom and other things. ﴿by night or by day﴾, that is, in the night or in the day. The apparent purpose is to indicate that there is no difference, in the coming of punishment, between the time of their heedlessness and the time of their alertness, since nothing prevents it and nothing repels it. ﴿So We made it﴾, that is, We made its plants ﴿a harvest﴾, that is, like something reaped from its root. The apparent view is that this is a simile, since both parties are mentioned, for what is omitted is in effect what is stated. It is also permitted that there is an explicit metaphor here, the original being: "We made its plants perished," so the perished was likened to the reaped, and the name of the likened-to was put in its place. This does not conflict with the supposition of an omitted modifier, as some have thought, because it did not liken the crop to the harvest but likened the perished to it. Al-Sakkaki held that the verse contains an implicit metaphor, in that the adorned and decorated earth is likened to lush, beautiful vegetation which was struck by something that removes and destroys it, and the reaped was taken as imaginative. Its weakness is not hidden. ﴿as if it had not flourished﴾, that is, as if its plants had not flourished, meaning had not remained or stayed. Thus "taghann" (flourish) derives from "ghanija bil-makan" when one stays and dwells in a place, and from it the dwelling is called "mughan." The modifier has been omitted here and in what precedes it, so the pronoun in the genitive became accusative in the first and implicit nominative in the second. Omission was chosen for intensification, since the apparent meaning indicates that the earth itself was made a harvest, and as if it itself had not been flourishing, since it would not change through the change of what is in it. Some have also linked "upon it" ('alayha) to the two preceding clauses, because the intended meaning there is "upon its plants," so the modifier is omitted and the pronoun is governed by "'ala." This is not far-fetched, except that there is some uncertainty as to whether omission for intensification applies here too. It has also been said that the pronoun in "tughni" and what precedes it refers to the crop, as it was said about the pronoun in "'alayha." It has been said that they refer to the earth, with no omission, but the figurative usage lies in the attribution (al-tajawwuz fil-isnad). You know that returning all the pronouns to the earth, even with the figurative use in attribution, is preferable to returning them to something else whatever it may be. Indeed, it is possible to return the pronoun to it in al-Hasan's reading "yughni" with a yā' (the verb being third-person masculine), and to make that of the type of "wa-la ard abqal abqaluha" (there is no land with more herbs than its herbs). As you see, it should refer to the plants or to the crop, for example, and the meaning comes to "as if it had not been growing." ﴿yesterday﴾, that is, in a time shortly before Our command came, since "yesterday" is a proverbial expression for this. The comparative clause may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or it may be a new sentence with no grammatical place in the sentence, as an answer to an implied question. The thing exemplified in the verse, what is understood from the context, is the sudden disappearance of the plants' greenness and their going away as chaff, leaving no trace after having been fresh and tender. The plants had intertwined, and the earth had been adorned with their colours until people hoped and thought it had been spared from calamities. The likeness is not with the water even though the particle of comparison (ka) enters it, since it is a compound simile (tashbih murakkab) together with the speech itself containing matters which are literal and matters which are figurative, with a subtlety that is not hidden. It is reported from Ubayy that he read: "As if it had not flourished yesterday, and We did not destroy them except for the sins of their people."

﴿Thus﴾, that is, in the same manner as this wonderful detailing, ﴿We detail the signs﴾, that is, the Qur'anic signs, of which this sublime verse, which warns about the states of the worldly life, is one. That is, We make them clear and explain them. ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ ﴾24﴾ on their meanings and understand their realities. Their being singled out is because they are the ones who benefit. It is also permitted that by the signs is meant the created things and the perishable things mentioned during the illustration, and by detailing them is meant their being turned around in the order described, in terms of coming into being and passing away, since they are signs and indicators by which the one who reflects may infer the states of the worldly life, both in its present condition and its outcome. The first is the apparent view. It is reported from Abu Mijlaz that he said: "It used to be written beside this verse, but it was erased: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would wish for a third valley, and nothing fills the soul of the son of Adam except dust, and Allah turns in forgiveness to whoever repents.'"

﴿And God invites to the Abode of Peace﴾: an exhortation to people toward the everlasting life of the Hereafter, following His exhortation away from the transient life of this world. That is, He invites all people to Paradise, by commanding them with what leads to it. Paradise is called *dar al-salam* for one of these reasons: because its people are safe from every pain and calamity; or because God Himself greets them with peace; or because its guardians say to them, "Peace be upon you, you have been made good"; or because some of its inhabitants greet one another with peace.

As for *al-salam* (السَّلام), it may mean *al-salamah* (safety), or *al-taslim* (greeting), or, since *al-Salam* is among God's names, the meaning is "He from whom and by whom is safety," or "the One who possesses safety from all deficiencies." It is then attributed to Him, glorified is He, for honour, as in the House of God for the Ka'bah. Also, because no one other than Him has any ownership in it, outwardly or inwardly, may He be exalted in status. And it alludes to the fact that whoever is in it is safe from what has passed, by considering the meaning of safety in its origin. The fact that it is specifically attributed to Him, and not to any of His other names, indicates this intention.

﴿And He guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance, ﴿to a straight path﴾, [a path] that leads to that abode, which is the true religion. In the verse there is an indication that guidance is other than invitation to that, and that command (*al-amr*, الأمر) is different from will (*al-iradah*, الإرادة), since He, glorified is He, generalised the invitation by omitting its object, and restricted guidance to will (*al-mashiyyah*), which is equivalent to *al-iradah* according to the well-known view, since He qualified guidance by it. This is the view taken by the *al-Jama'ah* (the majority of the scholars of the Sunnah). The Mu'tazilah said: the meaning of guidance is *al-tawfiq* (divine enabling) and *al-lutf* (divine kindness), and the difference between invitation and command for this reason is clear, for the disbeliever is commanded but is not enabled. And "whom He wills" means: whom He knows that kindness will benefit, because His will, exalted is His state, follows wisdom. So whoever He knows kindness will not benefit, He does not enable and does not show kindness to, since enabling someone whom God knows will not benefit him would be futility, and wisdom is incompatible with futility. Thus He, exalted and high is He, guides whom kindness benefits, even though He wills the guidance of all.

﴿For those who did good﴾, i.e., who performed good deeds, by doing what was commanded and avoiding what was forbidden. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained *ihsan* (excellence in worship) in his saying (peace be upon him): "That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."

﴿the best reward﴾, i.e., the best abode, which is Paradise. ﴿And more﴾, which is looking upon the Noble Face of their Lord, majestic is His majesty. This is the interpretation transmitted (*ma'thur*) from Abu Bakr, Ali, may Allah honour his face, Ibn Abbas, Huthayfa, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and others. It is also reported *marfu'* (traced back explicitly to the Prophet) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through many chains. Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim
(page 103)
Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Hibban, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* have all narrated from Suhayb that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, ﴿For those who did good﴾, and so on, then said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise which He wishes to fulfil for you.' They will say: 'And what is it? Has He not made our scales heavy, whitened our faces, admitted us into Paradise, and removed us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil will be lifted from them, and they will look upon Him, glorified is He. By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than looking upon Him, nor more pleasing to their eyes."

As for relating this interpretation with the word "it is said" (*qila*), as al-Baydawi did, may Allah pardon him for what is not fitting; and al-Zamakhshari's statement, may Allah treat him with His justice, that the hadith is *marquq* (with a qaf), meaning fabricated, which issues only from a base fellow (*raqi'*), is incorrect, for it is agreed upon as sound, and it has been related by memorizers in whom there is nothing that can be criticized.

Yes, other explanations of this have come down besides what has been mentioned, but they do not reach this level of authenticity, nor is the Prophet's elevation (*raf'*) explicitly stated in them. Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that he said: "The increase is forgiveness and good pleasure." He related from al-Hasan that it is the multiplication of a good deed tenfold up to seven hundredfold. He related from Ibn Zayd that it is that He will not call them to account for what He gave them in this world. He related from al-Hakam ibn Utayba, from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that it is a single chamber of pearl with four doors. Ibn al-Jawzi criticized this, saying it is not sound. It has also been said: the increase is that a cloud passes over them and says, "What do you want? I shall rain upon you," and whatever they desire, it rains upon them.
