Some scholars reconciled the reports by saying there is no barrier to Allah bestowing all of what has been mentioned upon them, and it qualifies as an increase over the Paradise He has granted them. This is supported by what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related from Sufyan, who said: "There is no disagreement in the interpretation of the Qur'an; rather, it is a comprehensive statement which intends this and that." What led al-Zamakhshari to disregard the explicit reports that the increase refers to seeing Allah is his corrupt assumption, like that of his companions, that Allah cannot be seen. You already know the source of that assumption, and the People of the Sunna have refuted it on several grounds.

﴿Neither dust nor humiliation shall cover their faces﴾, i.e., no dust (*ghabara*) in which there is any blackness will cover them, nor any trace of disgrace whatsoever, nor the gloom of distress. The meaning is that there will not befall them what befalls the people of the Fire, or that there will not befall them anything that would cause such sorrow and bad state. The statement is literal (*haqiqa*) according to the first meaning, and metonymic (*kinaya*) according to the second, because the absence of such covering is a necessary consequence of the absence of what causes it. So the necessary consequence is mentioned in order to move from it to what it implies. This was preferred on the ground that it is more praiseworthy, and the purpose is to show that their bliss is free from the blemishes of hardship, following the statement of the bounty with which He has favoured them. It has also been said that this mention is to remind them of what has saved them from it, for when they recall it, their joy and delight increase, just as when the people of the Fire recall what bliss they have lost, their grief and regret increase. It has been said too that the aim is to bring joy to them by reminding them of the state of their enemies, the people of the Fire, for when a person knows that his enemy is in humiliation and bad condition, his happiness increases. We have indeed witnessed people who are content with the harm befalling their enemy in place of any benefit to themselves, indeed who are pleased by their enemy's harm even when it harms them too.

The placing of the object before the subject is for emphasis, to show that what is protected from covering is the noblest of their limbs (i.e., their faces), and for suspense, leading to what is delayed, and because the subject involves a detail of particulars.

﴿Those﴾, i.e., those mentioned, by virtue of their being characterized by what preceded, ﴿are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾, i.e., remaining without cessation, and this entails the non-cessation of its bliss.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 27:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئَاتِ﴾ That is, shirk and sins. It is a subject (mubtada') with an omitted modifier (mudaf) understood, and its predicate (khabar) is His, glorified be He, statement: ﴿جَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِهَا﴾ ("the recompense of an evil is its like"). The bāʾ (bi-) is connected to jazāʾ, which is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of the passive form, not a noun meaning "compensation," as in some of the following interpretations.
[Page 104]
According to what has been said, the meaning is: the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is that one evil be repaid with one like it, meaning without any increase, in accordance with justice. Otherwise there is nothing preventing pardon, in accordance with generosity. But that applies to other than shirk.

It is also permissible for ﴿جَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِهَا﴾ to be a sentence consisting of a subject and predicate, which is the khabar of the subject. In that case there is no need to assume an omitted modifier, but the returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) is omitted, meaning: the recompense of an evil from them is with its like, following the pattern of "butter is two manns for a dirham" (al-samn manawān bi-dirham).

Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) permitted that jazāʾ be a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: for them is the recompense of an evil with its like. The word "lahum" ("for them") is omitted because of an indicator, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا﴾ ("for those who did good"). The whole sentence is the predicate of ﴿الَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا﴾. In that case there is no need to assume a returning pronoun, just as there is no need to assume an omitted modifier. Several scholars permitted that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ be coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the preceding ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ in the genitive position, which together with its preposition is a predicate, and that ﴿جَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ﴾ be coordinated with ﴿الْحُسْنَى﴾, which is the subject. In that coordination there is the matter of coordinating over two governing elements of different types (ʿamalayn mukhtalifayn), and there are several positions on it: the prohibition in all cases, which is the position of Sibawayh; the permission in all cases, which is the position of al-Farrāʾ; and the distinction that if the prepositional phrase comes first, as in "fī al-dār Zayd wa-al-ḥujrah ʿAmr," it is permitted, otherwise it is prohibited. Those who prohibit treat such examples as having an implied preposition, and make this a general rule, as in his saying:

Is every man you think a man,
and is a fire kindled at night a fire?

It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is the sentence ﴿مَا لَهُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عَاصِمٍ﴾ ("they will have no protector from God"), or ﴿كَأَنَّمَا أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ ("as if their faces were covered"), or ﴿أُولَئِكَ أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ﴾ ("those are the companions of the Fire"), and what comes between is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ). There is a disagreement among the grammarians about multiple parenthetical interjections. In that case ﴿جَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ﴾ is a subject, ﴿بِمِثْلِهَا﴾ is connected to it, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "will befall." Or ﴿بِمِثْلِهَا﴾ is the predicate, on the basis that the bāʾ is superfluous, or the prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate, on the basis that the bāʾ is not superfluous. It is better to specify the connected element as a particular one, such as "occurs," while it is also valid to assume it as a general one. The claim that there is no meaning to it is an evident delusion. In any case, there is no indication in the verse that the increase (ziyādah) is the grace (faḍl) rather than the vision (ruʾyah). You already know that interpreting it as grace is what is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) and a group of the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ). So one should not depart from it because of what appears to contradict it, especially since the Imam (al-Razi) and others have brought numerous proofs that it means that. The two verses were not expressed in one style, in order to observe the complete distance and contrast between the two groups. The mention of "earning" (kasb) is to indicate that this is only through their bad conduct and their crime against themselves.

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ﴾ That is, great humiliation. The tanwīn here is for magnification, unlike the tanwīn in what came before, as we have indicated. Attributing the covering (rahaq) to their selves rather than their faces indicates that it encompasses them and envelops them.

It was read ﴿يُرْهِقُهُمْ﴾ with the yāʾ, because the subject is apparent and its feminine marking is not real. It has also been said that the masculine form is used because the intended meaning of humiliation is its cause, figuratively, but there is no need for that, as is clear, because the masculine form with a figuratively feminine noun is very common, especially when separated.

The wāw, according to several scholars, is for coordination, and what follows it is coordinated with ﴿كَسَبُوا﴾. Abu al-Baqāʾ considered this weak, because the future tense is not coordinated with the past tense. It was answered that this is denied. In this coordination there is an exaggeration that is evident, since it presents the attribution of the covering to them on the Day of Resurrection as something known, as this is made, through the coordination, the relative clause of the relative pronoun. It has also been said that it is coordinated with what precedes it in meaning, as if it were said: "And those who earned evil deeds, their evil will be repaid with its like, and humiliation will cover them." And this is perhaps better than the first. As for making the wāw circumstantial, with the sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿كَسَبُوا﴾, its state is not hidden.

﴿مَا لَهُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عَاصِمٍ﴾ That is, there is no one for them who will protect them and prevent them from the wrath of God and His punishment. The first min is connected to ʿāṣim, and the speech has an omitted modifier. The second min is superfluous, for generalizing the negation. Or it means: "they have no one from His side, and with Him, who would protect them, as there is for the believers." In that case the first min is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from ʿāṣim. It has also been said that it is connected to the stability (istiqrār) understood from the adverbial phrase, and there is no omitted modifier in the speech, and the second min remains as it is. The sentence is either resumptive or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿تَرْهَقُهُمْ﴾. In the negation of a protector there is an exaggeration in the negation of protection that is evident.

﴿كَأَنَّمَا أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعًا مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ That is, as if they had been clothed with that because of the intensity of its blackness and darkness. The prepositional phrase is an adjective of ﴿قِطَعًا﴾, and His statement, glorified be He, ﴿مُظْلِمًا﴾ ("dark"), is a circumstantial clause from ﴿اللَّيْلِ﴾, and its governing element is the connected element of the prepositional phrase, whether it is a verb or a noun.

Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from ﴿قِطَعًا﴾, or an adjective of it. The required form would be the plural, because ﴿قِطَعًا﴾ is the plural of qiṭʿah, but its circumstantial clause or adjective was given in the singular on account of interpreting it as a collective (ta'wil dhalika bi-kathir). It is not hidden that this is an unnecessary affectation. The apparent meaning is that min is partitive (tabʿīḍ). Some researchers said: "Al-layl has two meanings: a time in which the sun is hidden, a little or a lot, as one says: 'the night has entered' and 'now it is night'; and the period between sunset and its rising or its nearness to rising. So min is either partitive according to the first, or explanatory (bayānīyyah) according to the second." Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the governing element of the circumstantial clause, ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾, could be connected to ﴿مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾, as the adjective of ﴿قِطَعًا﴾, so its reaching to the modified noun is like its reaching to the adjective. The author of al-Taqrib said: "In this there is an issue, because ﴿مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ is not the complement of ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ so that it would govern the genitive noun; rather the assumption is that it is an adjective, so the governing element in it is the stability. Also, the adjective is ﴿مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾, and the one qualified is the night, so ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ is not a governing element in the qualified noun, although that is the intended meaning." It may be said: min is explanatory, and the assumption is "existing from the night," so ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ governs the adjective, which is existing, so it is as if it governs "the night." This is based on the principle that the governing element of the governing element of a thing is a governing element of it, and this is invalid. The correct view is to say: min is partitive, meaning "part of the night," and it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿قِطَعًا﴾, and ﴿مُظْلِمًا﴾ is made a circumstantial clause from the part, not from ﴿مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾, so that the governing element of the qualified noun is ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾. It is not hidden that this is a view that covered "pieces" with a night of affectation and strain, dark.

Imam Amin al-Din answered that the attribution of ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ to ﴿قِطَعًا﴾ is only with regard to its undetermined essence, which is explained by "night," not with regard to the concept of the pieces in themselves. The pieces were mentioned only to clarify the quantity with which their faces were covered, which is the dark night. So the reaching of the verb to ﴿قِطَعًا﴾ is with regard to what the intended meaning cannot be completed without, just as the verb reaches to it when one says: "I bought pounds of oil, clear," for the thing bought is the oil, and the pounds are built to express the quantity of what was bought, clear. So the governing element of the circumstantial clause is actually the verbal governing element, and the meaning of the verb is not considered in the prepositional phrase from the aspect of governing, because the verbal governing element is more prominent in appearance. What is in it is not hidden.

In Al-Kashf it is said: Al-Zamakhshari held that ﴿أُغْشِيَتْ﴾ has a connection with His statement, exalted be He, ﴿مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾, since the adjective and the qualified noun are united, especially as the pieces are part of the night. So it is permissible for it to be the governing element of the adjective on that basis, and as if it were said: "Its faces were covered as the night, dark." This is like what was permitted in His statement ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا﴾ ("and We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts, as brothers"), that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun on the basis of its unity with the genitive noun. And as if it were said: "and We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts, as brothers." And like what was permitted in ﴿مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf"), because the religion is like a part, as if it were said: "follow Abraham, a ḥanīf." This is what al-Zamakhshari held, and it is the secret of this place, not what many have lengthened, especially taking min as abstractive (tajrīd). For although the meaning is partitive and not explanatory, not every explanatory min is abstractive, and its purpose is not complete. End of quotation.

He has in this made an oblique criticism of his teacher, the scholar al-Tibi, for he, may God have mercy on him, went to great lengths in strain. The fairness is that what al-Zamakhshari permitted here is not appropriate, and striving to correct it, while there is a clear reading that is not clouded with dust, comes close to being futile.

Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Sahl read ﴿قِطْعًا﴾ with a sukun on the ṭāʾ. It is a singular noun whose meaning is a portion of the night, or the darkness of its end, or a collective noun for qiṭʿah. They cited:

Open the door and look at the stars,
how much of the dark night is upon us!

On this basis it is permissible for ﴿مُظْلِمًا﴾ to be an adjective of it or a circumstantial clause from it without any strained interpretation. It was also read: "as if a piece of the night, dark, were covering their faces" (كَأَنَّمَا يَغْشَى وُجُوهَهُمْ قِطَعٌ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِمٌ). The discussion of it is evident, and the sentence, like the one before it, is either resumptive or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿تَرْهَقُهُمْ﴾.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ That is, those described with the blameworthy attributes mentioned. ﴿أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ﴾ ("are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever") — they will not leave it ever.

The Wa'idiyya (the Khawarij and Mu'tazila who held that the grave sinner is eternally damned) used this verse to support their corrupt position on the eternal abiding of the people of major sins. It was answered that "sayyi'āt" (evil deeds) includes disbelief and all other sins, and evidence has been established that the people of sins will not abide eternally, so the verse is specified to those other than them. Also, it may be said that they are included among "those who did good," based on what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-Shaykh from Qatada, that they are those who bore witness that there is no god but God, meaning the believers in general. So they do not enter the other category, because the two rulings conflict. It has also been said that if the "al-" in "al-sayyi'āt" is for totality (istighrāq), then the intended meaning is whoever did all of that, and the view that he abides eternally in the Fire is agreed upon. But this is not the right position.

[Page 107]

﴿And on the Day We gather them﴾: this is a new (resumed) statement, brought to explain another of their dreadful conditions. Its placement after the earlier items, although it precedes some of their states mentioned previously, is, as some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said, to indicate that each of what precedes and what follows is independent in consideration. If the external order had been observed, all of it would have been counted as one thing, and for this reason it is separated from what came before it. Al-Tabarsi (d. 548 AH) claimed that when God had mentioned the recompense, He explained by this the time of that (recompense), and according to this the verse is connected to what was mentioned just before. But it should not be overlooked that this does not take the form of explanation. Better than this is to say: the connection with what precedes it is that it contains an emphasis on His words, glorified is He: ﴿They will have no protector from God﴾, in terms of its indication that the partners will not benefit them.

﴿Yawm﴾ (the Day) is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, such as "remind them" and "warn them". The pronoun in ﴿We gather them﴾ refers to both groups: those who did good (ahsanu al-husna) and those who earned evil deeds. This is because it is what is immediately understood from His words ﴿all of them﴾, and because one of the members of the second group is mentioned in His words ﴿Then We will say to those who associated﴾, i.e., to the polytheists among them. Also, because rebuking and threatening them before all witnesses is more dreadful, and the announcement of the gathering of all in the terror of the Day is more fitting. To this view went al-Qadi al-Baydawi and others. That their intended meaning by the two groups is the two groups of disbelievers and polytheists is extremely contrary to the apparent sense.

It is said: the pronoun refers only to the second group, so ﴿those who associated﴾ is a relative pronoun placed in the position of a pronoun. The point of specifying the description of their associating within the relative clause, out of all the evil deeds they acquired, is that the rebuke and reproach are based upon it, together with what it implies of it being the greatest of their crimes and the chief of their evil deeds. This is the reason for the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun, according to the last opinion.

﴿Makanakum﴾ (your place) is an adverbial phrase of place governed by a verb that has been deleted, and that (adverb) takes its place. It is in construction (idafa) with the kaf, and the mim is the sign of the plural. That is: "Remain in your place." The meaning is: wait until you see what will be done to you. From Abu Ali al-Farisi (d. 377 AH) it is reported that makan is an ism al-fi'l (verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb), and its vowel is a built (mabni) vowel. Is it an ism al-fi'l meaning "stay" (ilzam) or "remain firm" (ithbat)? The apparent sense of some of them is the first, and what is reported from the commentary on al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil) is the second, because on the first view it would necessarily be transitive like "ilzam" (stay), although it is intransitive. It is answered that the necessity is denied. Al-Saffaqsi (d. 742 AH) said: in the words of al-Jawhari (d. 393 AH) there is something that indicates that ilzam is both intransitive and transitive, so perhaps what is an ism al-fi'l for it is the intransitive. The Kufans mentioned

[Page 108]

that it is transitive, and they heard from the Arabs: "Makanaka Zaydan" meaning "wait for him." Al-Damamini (d. 827 AH) in his commentary on al-Tashil chose that it is not an ism al-fi'l, saying: "I do not know what motivates making this adverb an ism al-fi'l, whether intransitive or transitive. Why did they not make it an adverb in its own right, and not remove it from its original state, meaning: 'Establish your place' or 'Wait in your place'?" The claim of an ism al-fi'l is only appropriate where it is impossible to combine that noun with that verb, such as "sahi" (be quiet), "alayka" (upon you), and "ilayka" (to you). But where it is possible, as with "waraaka" (behind you) and "amamaka" (in front of you), it is not. And in this there is clear objection.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿You﴾ are an emphasis of the pronoun that moved to the adverb from its governing verb, according to the first opinion, and of the hidden pronoun in the ism al-fi'l according to the second opinion. His words, glorified is He: ﴿and your partners﴾ are coordinated with that. It is said: ﴿You﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning "humiliated" or "to be recompensed." This is contrary to the apparent sense, along with what it involves of disturbing the arrangement of the composition. It is also said that the reading ﴿and your partners﴾ in the accusative (wa-shurakaakum) rejects it, since it would then become like "every man and his property," and such a construction is not valid here, because there is no governing element for it. The governing element on the first interpretation is clear, because of the position of ﴿your place﴾.

﴿Then We will separate them﴾: that is, "then We will divide them." It is from zilt al-shay' 'an makanihi (I removed the thing from its place), i.e., azaltuhu (I removed it), and the doubling (of the letter) is for intensification, not for transitivity. It is from the root y (ya'), and its measure is fa'ala, as evidenced by zayala (to part), and it has been read with that. It has the same meaning, like kallamtuhu and kalamtuhu, and sa''ara khaddahu and sa'ara khaddahu.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is from the root w (waw), because it is from zala yazulu, and the waw was changed to ya' because it is of the form fay'al. But the first is more correct, as you know, and because its verbal noun is tazyil, not zuyula. Moreover, the verb (fi'l) is more common than fay'al. The accusative of "bayn" (between) is as an adverb of place, not as a direct object, as has been mistakenly supposed. The meaning of separation is cutting off the bonds and connections that existed between them and their partners in the world. It is said: the separation is physical. But the apparent sense of the sublime composition does not support this.

The coordination is with ﴿We will say﴾. The choice of the past tense form is to indicate certainty, for increased rebuke and regret. The fa' (then) indicates that the separation and its beginnings occur immediately after the address, without any delay, to show the complete weakness of the relationship and connection between the two groups.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿And their partners will say﴾ are coordinated with what precedes. It is permitted that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with qad (indeed) implied or not, according to the difference of opinion. The attribution (idafa, "their partners") is in consideration that the disbelievers are the ones who took them as partners to God, exalted and glorified is He.

It is said: because they made for them a share of their wealth, and so they made them partners to themselves in that. By "these partners" is meant, it is said, the idols, for the people of Mecca only worshipped them, and they are the ones principally addressed in most of these verses. Attributing speech to them is not far from His power, exalted is He, so God makes them speak, the One who made everything speak in that station, and they say to them: ﴿You did not worship us﴾ (10:28-29). What is meant by this is their disavowal of their worship, and that in reality they worshipped only their own desires that prompted them. How great is this, in place of the intercession which they were expecting from them!

It is said: what is meant by them is the angels and the Messiah, peace be upon them, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels: "Did these used to worship you?"﴾ (34:40). And His words, glorified is He: ﴿Did you say to the people: "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?"﴾ (5:116), and the verse. What is meant by that speech is what was intended by it first as well, because denial of worship is not valid, since it did occur in reality, and lying does not happen on the Day of Resurrection from one who was (a worshipper). It is said that the speech of the partners is taken according to its literal reality, on the basis that that station is a station of astonishment and bewilderment, so that lying would be like the lying of children and the mad who are astonished. It is also possible to say:

[Page 109 is not shown; continuing from the text as given]

It may also be said: they did not give any weight to the deeds of the disbelievers, and considered them as nonexistent because of their invalidity, and therefore they denied their worshipping them. Or it may be said: since the polytheists imagined in what they worshipped many attributes that did not in fact exist in it, they were in reality worshipping essences described by those attributes. Since the essences of the partners were devoid of those attributes, it is correct to say that the polytheists did not worship the partners. This is better than the first two views; indeed, one scarcely turns to either of them. It seems that the meaning according to it is: "You worshipped the one whom you claimed was able to intercede for you and deliver you from punishment, and was described with such-and-such. So seek him, for we are not like that." What is meant by this is the cutting of the ropes of their hopes and casting them into complete despair of obtaining what they used to hope for and believe concerning them. Perhaps despair was already present in them from the moment of death and their being afflicted with punishment, but by what is mentioned there arises a rank above that rank.

It is said: what is meant by them are the devils, and the cutting of connection in this case is from both sides, not from the side of the worshippers alone, as the preceding context suggests. What is meant by their words is in the manner of what preceded. An objection to the view that what is meant is the angels and the Messiah, peace be upon them, is that it does not fit His words, exalted is He: ﴿Your place, you and your partners﴾, since what is meant by it is a threat and warning, and the apparent sense of the coordination is that this applies to the partners as well. And threatening those noble ones, upon them be prayers and peace, is something scarcely to be advanced as a view.

It is answered: this objection applies equally, for it also falls upon the first view, since there is no meaning to threat and warning regarding idols when nothing has proceeded from them that would necessitate it. There is no escape except by holding that the threat and warning are for the addressees alone, or for the whole group by consideration of them.

It is answered: it is permissible that the threatening of the idols is like their being cast into the Fire together with their worshippers, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ (21:98). Likewise His words, glorified is He: ﴿So guard yourselves against the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ (2:24), according to what a group of the exegetes held. The claim of a difference between threatening and casting into the Fire requires proof. Yes, they said: on the view that what is meant is the angels, peace be upon them, it is necessary that the heedlessness in His words, glorified is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 29:**

﴿So Allah suffices as a witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship.﴾ [It is to be understood] as [meaning] non-approval, not lack of awareness, because the angels' lack of awareness of their worship is not evident. Indeed, even if it were said that this interpretation is required, on the view that the intended referent is also al-Masih (Jesus, peace be upon him), it would not be far-fetched, since his lack of awareness of their worship is [still plausible], even though he will descend and break the cross, for the same reason. The interpretation according to the apparent meaning can hardly be sound unless the intended referents are idols, for their lack of awareness of this is evident. It has been objected that there is no evidence that the angels, peace be upon them, are aware of their worship, so that the wording could be diverted from its literal meaning to this. These worshipped beings are not the guardian angels (al-hafazah) or the scribes (al-kataba), but other angels, who may be occupied with carrying out what they have been commanded and so not turning their attention to what is in this world. We do not claim for the angels, peace be upon them, what the philosophers claim, for they are the ones who said on the day they were asked about the names: ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾. Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, is among the most eminent of them in rank, and yet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) often asked him about things, and he would say: "I do not know, and I will ask my Lord." Likewise, there is no evidence that al-Masih, peace be upon him, was aware of the worship of these addressees at the time it was performed, and his future descent to break the cross does not require awareness of it in that manner, as is not hidden. It may be cited as supporting evidence for his lack of awareness [of it] what Allah, the Exalted, relates of his answer to His question to him, peace be upon him: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things﴾. The latter view has been objected to, on the ground that it is not valid in this view at all, because it was the devils who adorned for them this vile abomination and incited them to it. How, then, can it be said that they are truly unaware of it, or that they do not approve of it? Perhaps whoever holds this view is committed to lying and says that it is permissible to occur on the Day of Resurrection.

And it has been said: the first view is also not valid with this view at all, because idols do not truly possess the attribute of heedlessness. Heedlessness, as is understood from the Qamus (the lexicon), is a name for abandoning a thing and the mind turning away from it to something else, and this is the condition of those who possess hearts, whereas idols are not of that kind. Likewise, they cannot be described with it metaphorically as meaning non-approval, since what is apparently meant by non-approval is anger and dislike, and it is evident that idols cannot be described with anger or approval, since these two follow perception, and they have no perception. Whoever affirms perception for inanimate things according to their own mode of existence, for him the matter is easy; but whoever does not affirm it says that it is a metaphor for lack of awareness. It may also be said that what is meant by their heedlessness of the worship of the polytheists is their lack of a potential demand for it, which ultimately returns to negating that they deserve worship for themselves and affirming wrongdoing against those who worship them.

In that case, the more apparent view is that by "the partners" is meant everything that was worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted, whether rational beings or others, and all of them are truthful in this statement. It may also be meant that the lack of demand includes both the present and the future lack of demand, if it is considered that the speaker is one to whom such a statement may be attributed, such as the angels, peace be upon them. This view does not depend on the partners being aware of their worship or on their not being aware of it; so it is possible that they have awareness of it, and it is possible that they do not. The apparent view, that the explanation of heedlessness as non-approval, meaning anger and dislike according to what has been said, requires awareness, since the dislike of a thing without awareness of it is hardly conceivable; and to attribute it to all the partners, even in general, at some time in worldly life, is not accepted. Perhaps the expression "heedlessness" is more reproachful to the addressees and to their worship than an expression such as "lack of demand" would be; so reflect.

The *ba'* in ﴿bi-Allah﴾ is a supplementary particle (silah), and ﴿shahidan﴾ is a specifying accusative (tamyiz). ﴿In﴾ is the lightened form of *anna*, and the *lam* is the one that distinguishes the lightened from the negative. The adverbial phrase is connected to ﴿ghafilin﴾, and the fronting is for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah). The meaning is: "Allah suffices as a witness, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, who has full knowledge of the reality of the situation: indeed we were heedless of your worship." The apparent sense of the words of some of the scholarly researchers is that ﴿So it suffices﴾ and so on is a proof for the preceding negation, not for the subsequent affirmation.

﴿Hunalika﴾ means: in that station, the place of slipping and bewilderment, which is the station of the Gathering. Here ﴿hunalika﴾ remains in its original sense, an adverb of place (al-zarfiyya al-makaniyya). It has also been said that it is used as an adverb of time (zarf zaman) by figurative usage (majaz), meaning: at that time. ﴿Tabluu﴾ means: is tested. ﴿Kullu nafs﴾ (every soul), whether believing or disbelieving, ﴿ma aslafat﴾ (what it sent forward) of deeds, so that it witnesses their benefit and harm in the fullest witnessing.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tatluu﴾ from al-tilawa (recitation), in the sense of reading. The intended meaning is reading the scrolls of what it sent forward. It has also been said that this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the manifestation of deeds. It is also permissible that it derives from al-tilw (following), in the sense that the deed takes on a physical form and appears, so its doer follows it until it brings him to Paradise or to Hell. Or it is a figurative depiction (tamthil).

Asim, in one narration from him, read ﴿nabluu﴾ with the single ba' and the nun, and ﴿kulla﴾ in the accusative. The subject of ﴿nabluu﴾ is His pronoun, exalted is He, ﴿kulla﴾ is its object, and ﴿ma﴾ is a comprehensive apposition (badal al-ishtimal) of it. The statement is an extended metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), meaning: there We deal with every soul as one who tests it and seeks to know its states of happiness and misery, by examining what it sent forward of deeds. It is also permissible that the meaning is: We afflict with trial, that is with punishment, every disobedient soul because of what it sent forward of evil. Then ﴿ma﴾ is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, which is the causal ba' (bi-sababiyya).

﴿Wa-rudduu ila Allahi﴾ (and they are returned to God) is coordinated with ﴿zayyalna﴾ (We separated). The pronoun refers to those who associated partners. What lies between is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraadh) within the narration, confirming its content. The meaning is: be returned to His recompense and punishment, or to the place of that. Thus the return is either figurative or literal. The Imam said: the meaning is that they were made compelled to acknowledge His divinity, exalted is He.

﴿Mawlahumu﴾ means: their Lord. ﴿Al-Haqqi﴾ means: the one whose lordship is truly established and true, not what they took as a false lord. It was also read ﴿al-haqqa﴾ in the accusative, as praise (madh). The intended meaning is God, exalted is He, and it is one of His names, exalted is He. Or it is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), and the intended meaning is what is opposite to falsehood.

There is no contradiction between this verse and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾, since the meaning of "mawla" differs in each. Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi that the first is abrogated (mansukha) by the second, but what is in this is not hidden.

﴿Wa-dalla﴾ means: was lost and went away. ﴿'Anhum ma kanu yaftaruna﴾ (what they used to fabricate has vanished from them), namely that their deities would intercede for them, or what they used to claim as partners of God, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Ma﴾ may be relative (mawsula) or verbal-masdar (masdariyya), and the clause is coordinated with His saying, exalted is He: "rudduu" (be returned). Some people made it coordinated with "zayyalna," and the clause "rudduu" is coordinated with the clause "tabluu" etc., falling within the parenthetical interjection. The plural pronoun refers to the souls implied by "kullu nafs." The shift to the past tense serves to indicate certainty and establishment, and the choice of the plural form signifies that their return to Him, exalted is He, will be collectively. What we have mentioned is more preferable in wording and meaning.

Shaykh al-Islam criticized the view that the pronoun refers to the souls and that "rudduu" is coordinated with "tabluu" etc., saying that it does not fit with mentioning the attribute of truth in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their true Lord﴾, since it is an allusion to those who were returned. He then said: Even if it is enough to take it as an allusion to some of them, or if ﴿al-Haqq﴾ is taken to mean justice in reward and punishment, that is, with "mawla" interpreted as the one who manages affairs, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and was lost﴾ and so on is something in which there is absolutely no room for the amendment, since the three pronouns in it refer to the polytheists, and so it necessarily entails disconnection. And restricting "kullu nafs" to the polytheist souls, despite the generality of the trial to all, is rejected by the context of magnifying the situation, end of quote. The apparent meaning is that he considered the coordination of ﴿wa-dalla 'anhum﴾ and so on with "rudduu" while its pronoun refers to the souls, which is other than what we have mentioned, so do not overlook this.

**[Page 111]**

﴿Say﴾, that is, to those polytheists whose conditions I have related, and whose actions, which are more foolish for them, lead to what follows. This is an argument for the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsehood of the polytheism (shirk) they hold.

﴿Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ That is, from both of them together. Provision comes through heavenly causes, such as rain and the ripening heat of the sun, and through other things, and through earthly materials. The first is like the agent (fa'il), and the second is like the recipient (qabil). Or it means from each of them independently, such as rain and manna and earthly foods, as a widening of provision for you. In this case, "min" (from) is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). It has also been said that "min" is for explanation (li-bayan), with an elided noun (ʿala taqdir al-mudaf). It has also been said that it is partitive (tab'idiyyah) on that assumption, meaning: from the people of the heaven and the earth.

﴿Or who controls hearing and sight?﴾ "Am" (or) is disconnected (munqati'ah), with the meaning of "bal" (rather). The shift is a transition (intiqali), not a negation (ibtali). In this there is an alert to the sufficiency of this interrogation for what is intended. That is: who is able to create them both and shape them in this wondrous natural disposition? Whoever has studied their anatomy has come upon what dazzles the intellects. Or: who protects them from afflictions, despite their multiplicity and the speed with which they are affected by the slightest thing that touches them? Or: who disposes of them by taking away and by preserving? "Control" (al-mulk) in every case is metaphorical. It has been said: the first meaning is more suitable to the arrangement of the attribute of creating together with the attribute of providing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ (35:3).

﴿And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?﴾ That is: who produces the animal from the sperm-drop, for example, and the sperm-drop from the animal? Or who gives life or causes death, such that "bringing out" means "producing", from the expression "the outcome is such-and-such" (al-kharij kadha), i.e., the result. That is: who produces the living from the dead, by bestowing life upon it, and produces the dead from the living, by bestowing death upon it and stripping it of life? The outcome is as you know. Some people have interpreted "the living" and "the dead" here as the believer and the disbeliever, but the first (interpretation) is better.

﴿And who manages the affair?﴾ That is: who undertakes the management of the affairs of the whole world? This is a generalization after the specification of what is included under it, the apparent matters, which were mentioned explicitly. In it there is an indication that everything comes from Him, glorified is He, and returns to Him, and that you cannot know its details.

﴿Then they will say﴾
[page 111]
﴿Allah﴾ without hesitation or delay, since there is no room for stubbornness or obstinacy in any of that, given its utmost clarity. The noble name is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is elided, i.e., Allah does what has been mentioned of these acts, not another.

﴿So, this is it.﴾ Perhaps the verse may be used as evidence, on the assumption that "min" is not for the beginning of the extent, that it is permissible to say that Allah, glorified is He, is from the people of the heaven and the earth. The meaning there being other than Allah, exalted is He, does not suit the answer. As for one who does not see it as permissible, meaning, as one who sees it as based on the apparent meanings of the verses that indicate that He, exalted is He, is in the heaven, and on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning the slave girl who pointed to the heaven when she was asked: "Where is Allah?" He said: "Free her, for she is a believer." And on his approval of Husayn when he said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: "How many gods do you worship, O Husayn?" He said: "Seven: six on the earth and one in the heaven." The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Then which one have you prepared for your desire and your fear?" Husayn said: "The God who is in the heaven." He left the verse according to what its apparent meaning requires. But you know that there is no explicit report that He, exalted is He, is from the people of the heaven and the earth, although there is a report that He, may His majesty be exalted, is in the heaven, in a sense befitting His majesty. So I do not see the permissibility of that, and there is no need to remove "min" from the beginning of the extent, so that effort would be required to refute the argument, as is not hidden. In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) it is said that this verse is a direct rebuke to the faces of the Qadariyyah (the Qadariyyah, the early group who denied divine predestination of human acts), who claim that provision is divided: some of it is what Allah has provided for the servant, which is the lawful, and some of it is what the servant has provided for himself, which is the unlawful. So it rebukes them for this hidden shirk, if they would only listen: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, even if they do not understand?﴾ (10:42). Likewise, it has been said, it rebukes some people who claim that the one who manages the affair in every age is the qutb (the pole, the chief of the saints), who is, in their view, the pillar of the heaven, and that without him it would fall upon the earth. So I imagine you, if you asked them who manages the affair, they would say: the qutb. It may be excused for them by saying that they mean he is the manager by Allah's permission, exalted is He. The application of "manager" in this sense to other than Allah, exalted is He, has come in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And by those who manage affairs﴾ (79:5).

It may be said: there is no difference in their view between Allah, exalted is He, and the qutb, except by consideration, because he is the one who has attained nearness through the supererogatory and obligatory acts in the most complete way, so otherness is removed. Thus the statement that the qutb is the manager is like the statement that Allah, glorified is He, is the manager, with no difference.

This has been objected to, on the grounds that it is an assertion of the doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud), and most of the theologians (mutakallimun) and some of the Sufis, such as the Imam al-Rabbani, may his secret be sanctified, deny that. The first (objection) is that the polytheists could have answered that question by saying: the angels or Jesus, peace be upon them, for example, in the sense that they are the managers of the affair by Allah's permission, exalted is He. Thus those mentioned would be to them like the qutbs are to those (Sufis). It is answered that the question is only about whoever the affair ultimately reaches, so they had no choice but to give the answer mentioned. Perhaps, if people other than the adherents of unity were asked in the same way, they would not have deviated in their answer from Him, glorified is He. As for the adherents of unity, may Allah sanctify their secrets, they have expressions that the polytheists would not say, and by my life, they are beyond the reach of reason. For this reason the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) rejected them.

﴿Then say﴾ to them: ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ (31). The interrogative hamzah is for denying the non-occurrence of being mindful, in the sense of denying the reality, as in your saying: "Do you strike your father?", not in the sense of denying the occurrence, as in your saying: "Shall I strike my father?" The fa' (then) is for coordination with an assumed element to which the noble composition is linked, meaning: "Do you know that, then you are not mindful?" The disagreement about this type of construction is well known, and what we have mentioned is what some scholars hold. The object of ﴿mindful﴾ is elided, and the verb is transitive with one object, meaning: "Will you not then be mindful of His punishment, which is for you, because of your engaging in associating with Him that which does not share with Him in anything of what has been mentioned of the specific attributes of divinity?" The speech of al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) seems to imply that it is transitive with two objects, and that is not correct.

[p. 112]

﴿So that is God, your Lord, the Truth﴾: this is a summation (*fadhlakah*) of what has been established, and the demonstrative refers to the One characterized by the preceding attributes, as they acknowledged. The demonstrative is the subject (*mubtada'*), the noble name (Allah) is an attribute of it, and ﴿your Lord﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and (*al-Haqq*, the Truth) is a second predicate, or an attribute, or the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permissible that the noble name be the predicate, with ﴿your Lord﴾ in apposition to it (*badal*) or as an explanation of it (*bayan*), and (*al-Haqq*) is an attribute of the Lord, meaning: your Owner and the one who manages your affairs, whose lordship is established and whose divinity is verified beyond any doubt. ﴿Then what is there after the Truth but error?﴾ That is, there is nothing to be followed other than the Truth except error. Whoever transgresses the Truth, which is the worship of God alone, will inevitably fall into error, which is the worship of other than Him, glorified is He, whether alone or in association, because worship of Him, exalted is His station, when associated with others is not accepted.

﴿Then what﴾ (*fa-ma*): *ma* is an interrogative particle and *dha* is a relative pronoun. It is also permissible that both together form a single word in which the interrogative has come to dominate over the demonstrative, and it is the subject whose predicate is (*ba'da al-Haqq*, after the Truth), according to what is in *al-Nahr* (a work of tafsir). The interrogative is reprimanding, meaning a denial of the occurrence and its negation. And (*ba'da*, after) is used in the sense of (*ghayr*, other than), not in a figurative sense. And the Truth is what you know, and it is other than the first (Truth), which is why it is stated explicitly. The application of the term Truth to His worship, glorified is He, and likewise the application of the term error to the worship of other than God, exalted is He, is because the basis of worship is belief. It is also permissible that the Truth refers to the first (Truth), and the explicit mention is for the sake of greater affirmation and to observe the perfection of the contrast between it and error. What is meant by it is the idols. The meaning is: then what is there after the Lord, the Truth, whose lordship is established, but error, that is, the vain, lost, and perishing falsehood. It is called by the verbal noun (*dalal*) for emphasis, as if it were the very essence of error and loss. It has also been said: what is meant by the Truth and error is what encompasses monotheism and the worship of other than God, glorified is He, and other matters, and what the context requires here enters in the primary sense. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ashhab, who said: Malik was asked about the testimony of those who play chess and backgammon, and he said: as for one who is addicted to them, I do not see their testimony as valid. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then what is there after the Truth but error?﴾ So all of this is error.

﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ That is, how are you turned away from the Truth toward error? The interrogative is reprimanding, meaning a denial of what has occurred and a declaration of its improbability and a expression of wonder at it. In it there is an emphasis that does not exist in directing the denial at the act itself, for every existent must exist in some state, so when all states of its existence are negated, its existence is negated by the demonstrative method. The particle (*fa*, so) indicates the sequencing of the denial and wonder upon what precedes it. Perhaps that denial and wonder are, in reality, directed at the source of the turning away, since the turning away itself from Him, exalted is He, as the truth holds, has no sense of being denied or wondered at, as it is His act, exalted is His majesty. The verb is not attributed to an agent because no purpose attaches to it. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) held that the agent of the turning away is the polytheists themselves, that they are the ones who turned themselves away and deviated from the Truth toward error, based on their view that servants are the creators of their own acts. The matter of denial and wonder upon this view is clear. The verb is not attributed to their pronoun in the sense of agency, to indicate that the matter has reached such a degree of abomination that it should not be openly stated that it occurred from them. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 33:

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., just as the word of Lordship (al-rububiyyah) has been realized for God, glory be to Him, or just as there is nothing after the truth but error, or just as they are turned away from the truth. ﴿The word of your Lord has come true﴾, i.e., His judgment, ﴿against those who defied﴾, i.e., those who persisted obstinately in disbelief and went to its furthest limits. What is meant by them are those who are being addressed. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of their pronoun in order to reach their censure through the title of the relative clause and to indicate causation. ﴿That they do not believe﴾ is a substitute for "the word" — a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull) or a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), based on the view that "the judgment" (al-hukm) is in the verbal-noun sense or in the sense of that which is judged. The word may also be interpreted as the promise of punishment (al-'idah bi-al-'adhab), in which case this clause serves as the reason for its truth, i.e., because they ... etc. It has been objected that the result of the verse on this reading, in light of what has been established regarding "those who defied," is that the word of punishment has come true against those obstinate rebels because of their obstinacy in disbelief and because they do not believe — and this is a repetition with no benefit in it. It was answered that even if it is granted that there is repetition in the verse in an absolute sense, it is an explicit statement of what was known implicitly, and in it is an indication of the nobility of faith: that the punishment of those who persist in disbelief is due to the absence of faith.

**Page 113**

﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ This is another argument establishing the truth of monotheism and the falsity of associating partners with God. He did not join it with a conjunction, to signal that it stands independently in proving the intended point. The question is posed for rebuke and imposition of the argument (ilzam). God made the repetition (of creation) like the origination in the imposition of the argument against them, because the proofs for it are manifest. He did not concern Himself with their denial of it, because they are obstinate about it, and the obstinate person is not to be heeded. So it should not be said: such an argument only works against one who acknowledges that originating creation and then repeating it are among the exclusive attributes of divinity, so that its denial of the partners entails the denial of their divinity; and they do not acknowledge this. Rather, the verse indicates that repetition is a matter that is uncovered and evident, reaching such a degree of clarity that another claim may be established upon it. Al-Tibi regarded this as a case of embedding (idmaj, a rhetorical technique in which one purpose is embedded within another), like the words of Ibn Nubata:

*So I must have ignorant people in his union; so who will I have as a friend with whom I deposit my forbearance?*

Here he embedded in an amorous verse the boast of being forbearing, and boasting is a complaint of brethren.

﴿Say: Allah originates creation and then repeats it.﴾ It has been said that this is a command to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to make clear to them who does that. That is: say to them, "Allah, glorified is He, does both; no one else does, whoever he may be." It does not mean that the Prophet, peace be upon him, answers on their behalf, as many have said, because the command to speak is not the same as the answer that is desired from them, though it entails it, since the matter asked about is not "who originates creation and then repeats it," as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾. The command to speak would then be the very answer desired from them, and he would be answering on their behalf in that. Rather, what is sought is only the existence of one among their partners who does the origination and repetition. So the answer is required from them alone. Yes, the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to include it in his statement, to signal that it is determined and necessary, and to indicate that they do not dare to state it explicitly for fear of rebuke and being silenced, not out of obstinacy and stubbornness. End of quote.

It may be said: what is meant by His words, glorified is He, ﴿Is there any of your partners﴾ etc., is: "Is the originator and repeater God, or the partners?" And what is meant by His words, glorified is His majesty, ﴿Allah﴾ etc., is: "Allah originates and repeats, not any other of the partners." In that case the question and answer fit together, and the exclusive sense (hasr) is understood by implication (dalalat al-fahwa). For when you say, "Who gives thousands, Zayd or Amr?" and it is answered, "Zayd gives thousands," both convey exclusivity without doubt.

From what has been mentioned, one may know what is in the preceding discussion in refutation of what the group (al-Jam') said. Likewise, the refutation of what al-Qutb said, that this does not suit as an answer to that question, because the question was about the partners while this statement concerns God Most High. Rather, it is an argument for His divinity, and that He is the one who deserves worship because He is the originator and repeater, after the argument establishing the denial of divinity for the partners. So reflect upon this.

In repeating the whole sentence in the answer, without omitting any part, the predicate is present as in the earlier answer, for added emphasis and affirmation.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ The *ifk* is turning away and reversing from something. It is said: *afakahu 'an al-shay'* (he turned him away from the thing), *yafikuhu ifkan*, when he reversed him from it and diverted him. From this is the saying of 'Urwa ibn Udhayna:

*If you are turned away from the best of good deeds, then among others who have been turned away*

It is sometimes restricted, as in the Qamus, to reversal from an opinion, and this is perhaps most suitable to the context. That is: how are you turned from the truth to falsehood? The discussion of it is as has preceded in ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾.

[Page 113]

﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?﴾ This is another argument against what has been mentioned, brought as a further proof upon a proof and a silencing upon a silencing. He detailed it to signal its excellence and its independence in establishing the intended point, as in the previous one.

The meaning is: Is there anyone who guides to the truth, by bestowing reason, sending the messengers, sending down the scriptures, granting success in reflection and contemplation through what He has set up in the horizons and within the selves, and so on, other than Allah, glorified is He, or are the partners [the guides]? Some commentators keep the statement to its apparent sense, as you heard earlier. Others restrict the way of guidance, but generalisation (taʿmim) better suits the context, which calls for complete rebuke and proof, as is not hidden.

﴿Say: Allah guides to the truth.﴾ That is, He, glorified is He, guides to it, not any other, exalted is His station. The discussion is on the same pattern as before.

The verb hidayah (guide) is transitive to two objects; the second is connected by means of a particle, either ilā (to) or the lām (to). It may also be transitive to both by itself, and this is said to be a dialect, just as it is used intransitively with the meaning of ihtadā (be guided). Al-Mubarrad denied this, saying that hudā in the sense of ihtadā is not known. But the authorities such as al-Farrāʾ and others did not follow him in this. Here the verb has been combined with both of its connecting particles, the ilā and the lām, for variety, and to indicate by ilā the sense of reaching a terminus, and by the lām to show that the terminus is the goal of the guidance, and that it was not directed to it by chance, but by intention of the act and making it its fruit. For this reason, that which is attributed to Him, glorified is He, is conveyed by lām, as you see.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then he who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed...?﴾, the intended meaning of it is generalisation, even though the actual agent is Allah, glorified is He, exalted is His station.

It has been said that the lām here is the lām of specification (lām al-ikhtiṣāṣ), but the majority hold the first view. The object is omitted in the three places. The permissibility of the intransitive use in the first case is something not to be considered. It is to be estimated in them in one pattern, like "the person" and similar.

It has been said that the estimate is: ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides another to the truth?﴾ ﴿Say: Allah guides whom He wills to the truth.﴾ ﴿Is then he who guides another to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not guide unless he is guided?﴾ (ʾamman lā yahiddi) with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, a kasrah on the hāʾ, and a shaddah on the dāl. This is the recitation of Yaʿqūb and Ḥafs, and its origin is yahtadī; the kasrah of the hāʾ is due to the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ḥammād and Yaḥyā, from Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read with a kasrah on the yāʾ and the hāʾ and a shaddah, and the yāʾ was given a kasrah in imitation of the hāʾ. Sībawayh held that the vowel of the present-tense prefix may be kasrah in dialect, except the yāʾ, because the kasrah is heavy on it. This recitation is a proof against him. Ibn Kathīr, Warsh from Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿĀmir read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and the hāʾ and a shaddah, and the origin is yahtadī. The fatḥah of the tāʾ was transferred to the hāʾ before it, then the tāʾ was changed to a dāl because their articulation points are close, and it was assimilated into it. Abū ʿAmr and Qālūn, from Nāfiʿ, read likewise, but he gave a rapid (ikhtilās) pronunciation to the fatḥah of the hāʾ, to indicate that the vowel on it is incidental. In some transmissions from Abū ʿAmr, he read with plain assimilation (idghām mujarrad), without transferring the vowel to the preceding letter, or with a kasrah on it because of the meeting of the two quiescent letters. This raised a difficulty, because it involves the joining of two quiescent letters. For this reason al-Mubarrad said: Whoever intends this must make a light vowel. Ibn al-Naḥḥās said: Without it, pronunciation is not possible. al-Qāḍī mentioned that he was not concerned about the meeting of two quiescent letters, because the assimilated letter is in the status of a moved letter. Some denied this recitation and claimed that he only read with rapid pronunciation. The truth is that he read with both, and this is also related from Nāfiʿ. Its detail is in Laṭāʾif al-Ishārāt and al-Ṭayyibah.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read yahdī like yarmī. This is either intransitive with the meaning of yahtadī, as it is one of the usages of the verb hidāyah according to what is relied upon, as you have learned just now; or it is transitive, meaning: he is not guided by another. This was preferred because it better fits what came before, since what is understood from it is the negation of guidance, not of being guided. The first may also be preferred, because in it there is agreement of the recitations in meaning, and agreement is better than disagreement. The negation of being guided is stated, though what is understood from what came before is the negation of guidance, as has been mentioned, because the negation of guidance usually entails the negation of being guided, since whoever is guided to the truth is not free of guiding others in some measure, and the least of it is that he is an example for another, so that he sees him and follows his path.

The fāʾ is for the ordering of the question upon what came before, as if it were said: If the matter is so, then I ask you: Who guides to the truth, and so on. The intended purpose of this is rebuke. The hamzah (interrogative particle) here is posterior in consideration, but it was placed first in the wording to show its prominence in requiring precedence, as is well known among the majority.

The form of the comparative may be on its true meaning, with the object of comparison omitted, as Makkī chose: ﴿Is then he who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed than he who is not guided, or is he who is not guided more worthy?﴾ Or it may mean "worthy" (ḥaqīq), as Abū Ḥayyān chose, and then it is a predicate of the relative clause. The separation by the predicate between ʾam and what is conjoined to it is the most eloquent, as al-Samīn said. It is sometimes not separated, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Is what you are promised near or far?﴾ Using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for added emphasis. ﴿That it be followed﴾ is in the place of accusative or genitive, after the deletion of the preposition, according to the known disagreement regarding such constructions, or it is "by that it be followed".

﴿Unless he is guided﴾ is an exceptive construction lacking its stated object (istithnāʾ mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances. That is: he is not guided, or he does not guide another, in any circumstance except when he is guided by Him, exalted is He, to guidance, or to the guidance of another. This is according to what is said by the majority: the notables among their partners, such as al-Masīḥ, ʿUzayr, and the angels, peace be upon them, but not the idols. This is because being guided, which is accepting guidance, and guiding another, are specific to those possessing knowledge, so they cannot be conceived for the idols. Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh and others reported that the intended meaning is the idols, and the reason for this is that it proceeds on their treating them as if they possessed knowledge. It has been said: the meaning is: or he who is not guided, from among the idols, to a place so that he is moved to it, unless he is moved to it, or unless Allah, exalted is He, transforms him from his state into a living being with responsibility, so that He guides him, and this is from your saying: The woman was guided to her husband, and she was guided to him.

It has been said: the first verse, ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ refers to the idols, or to what includes them and such as the angels, peace be upon them. And this one refers to the leaders of error, such as the rabbis and monks who took lords besides Allah. This is not far-fetched in my view. It is supported by the expression of following, for it requires acting by their commands and refraining from their prohibitions. This cannot be understood of idols except with strain. Although it can be understood of the notables among your partners, yet they call only to good, and following them in that is not blameworthy for any of them. Except that it may be said: the polytheists attributed to them commands and prohibitions, so He censured them for following them in that. He expressed it with following and did not express it with worship, saying: Is he who guides to the truth more worthy that he be worshipped, or he who does not guide unless he is guided? Although the verse includes the nullification of the validity of their worship, in that they do not guide. The least degree of worship is that the one worshipped guides his worshippers to what is good for their affairs. This is an exaggeration in deprecating their state of worship, because if following is not fine, then worship is not fine by a stronger argument. And if the state of that is ugly, the state of this is uglier. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

It was also read ﴿unless he is guided﴾ as ʾillā ʾan yuhadda, in the passive and with a shaddah, to indicate exaggeration in guidance.

﴿What is the matter with you?﴾ That is: what is the matter with you, in taking these powerless ones as partners of Allah, exalted is He? The statement is a subject and predicate, and the interrogation is for denial and wonder.

It is reported from some grammarians that a construction like this is not complete without a circumstantial phrase after it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is the matter with them, turning away from the reminder?﴾ So perhaps the circumstantial phrase here is omitted because it is evident, as if it were said: What is the matter with you, taking these as partners? It is not correct that His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ [10:35] be in the place of a circumstantial phrase, because an interrogative sentence does not occur as a circumstantial phrase. Rather it is another interrogation, also for denial and wonder, meaning: How do you judge with falsehood, which sound reason refuses and which judges its nullity, in taking partners with Allah, exalted is He? The fāʾ is for the ordering of the denial upon what has become manifest of the obligation of following.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 36:**

﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture.﴾ This is a fresh statement, not part of the preceding command. It comes from Him, exalted is He, to show the badness of their perception and their failure to understand what the clear proofs that compel monotheism contain, proofs that silenced them. That is, most of them follow in their beliefs and disputes nothing but a feeble conjecture resting on empty imaginings and invalid analogies, such as analogizing the absent to the present, or analogizing the Creator to the created on the basis of some slight, imagined similarity. They do not give heed to any single item of knowledge, let alone pursue the paths of sound proofs that guide to the truth, so that they would understand their content and ascertain their soundness and the falsity of what opposes them. So "following" here means submission in general, covering what accompanies acceptance and submission and what does not. The restriction (qasr) means what was pointed to: that there should be, in the course of their lives, some following of a single item of knowledge and some attention to it.

The indefiniteness of ﴿conjecture﴾ (ẓannan) is for specifying the kind. The specification of this following to "most" indicates that among them are some who may follow, and so arrive at the truth of monotheism, but who refuse to accept it out of arrogance and obstinacy. According to what they have said about the reason for the command to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that he should answer on their behalf, it points to the fact that their stubbornness and obstinacy prevent them from acknowledging this, since among them are those who knew and were obstinate. Perhaps the substitution here for all of them is by reference to this part. It is also permitted that the meaning be: most of them, throughout their lifetime, follow nothing but conjecture and never abandon it, for the negative particle entering on the present tense indicates the continuity of the negation according to the context. Thus "following" means acquiescence and submission, and the restriction is with respect to time. In the specification there is an allusion to what will come from some of them of following the truth and repentance.

It has also been said: the meaning is that most of them, in their affirmation of Allah, Exalted is He, follow nothing but conjecture, because it is a statement not supported by any proof in their view. And it has been said: the meaning is that most of them, in their saying to the idols that they are gods and that they are intercessors with Allah, follow nothing but conjecture. "Most" here means "all." This is like the use of "few" to mean "none" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So little do they believe﴾, and in the verse:

*"Few are those who lament calamities; he guards against the ends of tomorrow's talk for tomorrow."*

Placing an opposite on an opposite is a good and established practice. It should not be overlooked that these two views do not oblige reading "most" as "all"; it may be read in its ordinary sense as well. Some people have made the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refer to people in general, and then the ordinary sense must be taken without difficulty.

﴿Indeed, conjecture﴾ in any form ﴿does not avail against the truth at all.﴾ How, then, would corrupt conjecture avail? By "the truth" is meant knowledge and sound belief that corresponds to reality. The prepositional phrase is connected to what precedes it. ("At all") is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq), meaning "any kind of availing." It may also be a direct object, and the prepositional phrase in that case is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of it. The sentence is a resumption (isti'nāf) to explain the status of conjecture and its invalidity. In it is evidence for those who say that acquiring knowledge in matters of belief (i'tiqadiyyat) is obligatory, and that the faith of the muqallid (one who follows another's opinion without independent proof, by way of taqlid) is not valid. It was not taken in general to cover practical matters (amaliyyat) because of the existence of evidence for the validity of taqlid and for sufficing with conjecture in those matters, as has been established in its proper place.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ This is a warning to them concerning their ugly deeds, and it includes within it what is related of them concerning turning away from decisive proofs and following corrupt conjectures, by primary inclusion. It has been read as ﴿what you do﴾ (taf'alūn), with a shift to direct address to intensify the warning.

[Page 116]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 37:

﴿And it is not [possible] that this Qur'an should be fabricated apart from Allah﴾. This begins a discussion of their state with regard to the Qur'an, following the discussion of their state together with the proofs contained within it. Or it is a resumption, explaining what must be followed, and the proof for it, after the prohibition together with the following of conjecture. It has also been said that it is connected to what Allah the Exalted related of their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾. It has also been said that it is connected to the saying of the Glorified: ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ and so on. The remoteness of this is not hidden.

(Kana) here is defective (naqisa, i.e. the verb "to be" functioning as a copula in the sense of "was/is") according to many of the perfect scholars. (Hadha) is its subject (ism). (Al-Qur'an) is an adjective (na't) for it, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan). (An yuftara) with the interpretation of a verbal noun (masdar), i.e. "fabrication," is the predicate (khabar) of (kana), and it has the sense of a passive participle, i.e. "fabricated," as Ibn Hisham mentioned under the rule that a word may have one interpretation, and that interpretation may have another; and from this is his saying:

*By your life, youths are not those whose beards have grown.*

Some grammarians hold that (ma kana) means (ma sahha), "it is not valid," and that there is an implied lam (for emphasis of the negation). The original would be: "This Qur'an was not [such that it could be] fabricated," like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The believers should not all go forth﴾. Then (an yuftara) is the predicate of (kana), and (min dun Allah) is a second predicate, explaining the first. The meaning is: it is not valid nor proper that this Qur'an, filled with the various kinds of guidance that call for following, among which are those clear proofs that declare the truth of monotheism and the falsehood of polytheism, should come from other than Allah, the Exalted, in any manner whatsoever. Objections have been raised against this, but one should not depart from what he said regarding the position of ﴿apart from Allah﴾. What has been mentioned concerning the overall meaning is an acceptable matter, as is not hidden.

Al-Badr al-Damamini (Badr al-Damamini) permitted that (kana) be complete (tamma, i.e. meaning "exists/occurs"), and (an yuftara) be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for (hadha al-Qur'an). It was objected that this is not good at all, because "what exists of the Qur'an" would at first give the impression of denying its existence; and also, in substitution of inclusion there must be a connection between the substitute and the substituted, so the statement would have to be built on a connection between the great Qur'an and fabrication. And this is an implication of all that you see. He was answered with what I do not consider establishes any goodness at all. Some have limited themselves to considering the verbal noun without interpreting it as a passive participle, for the sake of intensification, on the pattern of what is said in "Zayd is just (adl)." The apparent view to me is that the intensification in this case returns to the negation, similar to what is said about the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, not that the negation returns to the intensification, as is not hidden. From here it becomes clear what is in the statement of some verifiers: that the statement of al-Zamakhshari in explaining the meaning of the verse, "and it is not valid, nor proper, and it would be impossible that such a thing in the loftiness of its matter and its inimitability be fabricated," perhaps suggests that it is on the omission of the lam, since the mere insertion of (kana) does not convey that. And the expression with the verbal noun has no connection to emphasizing the meaning of negation from the perspective of... Then they, as far as we have seen, did not consider the verbal noun here except as indefinite (nakira). The well-known position is the agreement of the grammarians that (an) and the verb interpreted as a verbal noun are definite, and for this reason one does not predicate it of an indefinite. It seems that this is based on what Ibn Jinni said in al-Khatiriyyat, that it may be indefinite, and it was mentioned that he presented it to Abu Ali and he approved it. Some have found this verse problematic, on the grounds that (an) makes the imperfect (mudari') specific to the future, as the grammarians explicitly state, while the polytheists only claimed that the Qur'an was fabricated in the past, as is indicated by what comes later, if Allah the Exalted wills. So how should it be that it is fabricated in the future? This has been answered by saying that the verb here is used for time in general, and Ibn al-Hajib and others have explicitly permitted this for the verb; al-Badr al-Damamini transmitted it in his commentary on Mughni al-Labib (Mughni al-Labib, a grammar work). Perhaps this is from the category of metaphor (majaz). In that case it is possible that the reason for shifting away from the explicit verbal noun, though it is the one used in their speech when no particular tense is intended, such as "your standing pleased me," is that the metaphor is more eloquent than the literal. It has also been said: perhaps the reason for this is that the predication works without interpretation, due to the difference between the explicit verbal noun and the interpreted one, as indicated by the commentator of al-Lubab and others. It is not hidden that this contradicts what was previously pointed out, that (an) and the verb are in the sense of a verbal noun, and that this in turn is in the sense of a passive participle.
