It has been said: It may also be answered regarding the root of the difficulty that it only negated in the past the possibility of fabrication's connection to it in the future, and of its being a locus for that; so the connection of fabrication to it by the verb is negated all the more. In that there is following the path of proof, so there is in the statement a primary or secondary metaphor. Abu al-Baqa' explicitly permitted that the predicate be omitted, and that the implied meaning is: "And it was not possible that this Qur'an be fabricated." Al-Allama Ibn Hajar said: the verse is an answer to their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾, which is a demand for fabrication in the future. As for the answer to their claim that he, peace and blessings be upon him, fabricated it, and far be that from him, it will come when their claim is related, so there is no difficulty. Moreover, the generality of making (an) specific to the future within the scope of negation: why should that not be the case in other than the predicate of negated (kana), as is indicated by the saying of the Glorified: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾? For it was revealed about a seeking of forgiveness that had previously occurred from them for the polytheists, as the leaders of the exegetes said. He extended his discussion on this in an appendix to his fatawa, so reflect.

﴿But [it is] a confirmation of what lies between its hands﴾: that is, of the divine books, such as the Torah and the Gospel. Thus the relative pronoun refers to the category. By "confirmation" is meant the clarification of truthfulness, which is the correspondence with reality and its manifestation. Its idafa (genitive construction) is either to its agent or to its object. The books confirm it in that the correct doctrines within it correspond to what is in them, and these are accepted by the People of the Book. As for others, if they acknowledge them, well; otherwise there is no consideration for them.

The making of the idafa to the object conveys emphasis in negating fabrication from it, because whatever is established and whose truthfulness is manifested through it is more deserving of truth. The aspect of its being a confirmation of them is that it indicates their descent from Allah, the Exalted, and includes the narratives of the earlier peoples as mentioned in them, and it is miraculous beyond them. So it is the one suitable to be a proof and evidence for them, not the reverse.

Some claimed that what is meant by ﴿what lies between its hands﴾ is the reports of unseen matters, and the idafa is to the agent, and its confirmation of it is its coming in accordance with what it reported. This is not correct. The accusative of "confirmation" is either by coordination (ʿatf) with the predicate of (kana), or because it is a predicate of an implied (kana). It has been said that it is accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) for an implied verb, i.e., "it was sent down for the confirmation of that"; and making the cause here what has been mentioned, although it was sent down for many matters, is because it is the appropriate one for the context of rejecting the claim of its fabrication. It has been said that it is accusative as a verbal noun for an implied verb, i.e., "it confirms the confirmation of," and so on. 'Isa ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "but it is a confirmation," and so on. He also read in the nominative in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and the detailing of the Book﴾, i.e., what was written and established of the realities and laws; and the coordination, whether in the accusative or the nominative, is upon "confirmation." The saying of the Glorified: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is another predicate of (lakin) or of the implied subject. It is set apart (fusil) because it is a sentence emphasizing what precedes it. It was permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book," even though it is a genitive construction, because it is an object in meaning. It was also permitted that it be a grammatical resumption with no place in the i'rab, or an explanatory resumption as an answer to a question about the state of the Book. The first is more apparent. The meaning: it is not befitting for a sensible person to doubt it, because of the clarity of its proof and the loftiness of its status. ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [37] is another predicate of (kana), or of the implied subject as in the previous one, or it is connected to "confirmation" or to "detailing," or to the verb whose cause is those two, or it is connected to an implied word that occurred as a circumstantial clause from "the Book." And "there is no doubt in it" is a parenthetical clause, lest the separation between the connected and the connected-to, or between the circumstantial clause and its owner, be made by a foreign element. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive in "in it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 10, verse 38:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ *Am* is disjunctive (*munqati'a*, introducing a new question after an earlier one), and it is taken to be governed by an implied *bal* (rather). According to Sibawayh and the majority, the interrogative *hamza* is present, meaning: "Rather, do they say...?" *Bal* here is transitional, and the *hamza* serves to deny the occurrence of the matter and to express its improbability, that is, "That should not have been the case." It is also permitted that the *hamza* be for affirmation (*taqrir*) so as to impose the proof. The two meanings, it is said, are close to each other. It has also been said that *am* is conjunctive (*muttasila*), with an implied counterpart (*mu'adil*), meaning: "Do you acknowledge it, or do you say, 'He has invented it'?" It has been said that it is interrogative in meaning of the *hamza*, and that it is coordinating in meaning of *waw*. The correct view is the first. In any case, the hidden pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ, even though he is not mentioned, because it is known from the context.

﴿Say﴾: as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of the invalidity of their corrupt claim, "If the matter is as you say."

﴿Then bring a surah﴾, whether long or short,

﴿like it﴾ in eloquence, excellence of connection, and solidity of meaning, "on the basis of invention." Its sum, it is said, is: "If that is an invention from me, then you invent a surah like it, for you are like me in Arabic and eloquence, and you are more practiced and accustomed in verse and prose." In this case, the intended meaning of the addressees bringing it is their composing it and speaking it from themselves, not something that includes quoting it from others who came before them. It is also permitted that the intended meaning be what has been mentioned. Perhaps this is the secret of the shift from "Say, a surah like it" as such to what is in the noble wording, namely: "If the matter is as you claim, then bring, from yourselves or from those of the eloquent and skilled Arabs who preceded you, such as Imru' al-Qays, Zuhayr and their like, a surah similar to it in its sublime attributes." Since you were unable to do that despite your great practice, and it is not found in the speech of those (and they are the ones for whom pulpits were set up at 'Ukaz, the eloquence and rhetoric, by whom the millstone of verse and prose turned, and whose days passed in composing and reciting), this indicates that it is not the speech of humans but the speech of the Creator of powers and destiny. It is also read as *bi-surati mithlihi* (with the construct), meaning: "with a surah of a book like it."

﴿And call upon﴾ for assistance and support

﴿whomever you can﴾ to call upon and seek help from, among your gods, which you claim are helpful to you in great affairs and in calamities and difficulties, those to whom you turn in everything you do and leave undone,

﴿apart from God﴾. It is connected to *ud'u* (call upon), as has been said, and *min* is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*), in the sense that the calling is initiated from other than Him, the Exalted; there is no connection between it and Him, glorified be His majesty, in any way. It is also permitted that it be connected to what precedes it, and *min* be explanatory (*bayaniyya*), meaning: "Call upon whomever you can from His creation." This is not without merit.

As for the benefit of this restriction, it is said: it is to emphasize their disassociation from Him, the Exalted, and that they are on the side of opposition and hostility. The intent is not to convey that He, the Exalted, is alone in power over what they were charged with, since that might give the impression that if they called upon Him He would answer them. It may be said: there is no harm in conveying this, because that exclusivity supports the intended point, which is that what he ﷺ brought was not from himself but from Him, the Exalted. The impression is not worth considering, since their calling upon Him, the Exalted, meaning their asking Him, glorified and exalted be He, to bring what they were charged with, exclusively by Himself, is something that can hardly be imagined, because it contradicts their earlier claim, as is clear. So reflect.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ 38, in that "I invented it," for that implies the possibility of bringing its like, and that in turn implies your power to do so. The answer to *in* (if) is omitted, because what is mentioned indicates it.

In this verse is evidence for the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an, because he, peace be upon him, challenged the most eloquent of the Arabs with a surah like it, and they did not bring that. Otherwise it would have been transmitted to us, because the motives to transmit it were strong. Some of the heretics (*mulahida*) claimed that their inability to bring that does not necessarily entail that it is from God, the Exalted, for a person may have a particularity that is not found in others, so it is possible that he, God's blessings and peace be upon him, was specially endowed with this rank of eloquence and rhetoric, distinguished from the rest of the Arabs, and so he brought what he brought, beneath them.

It has come by some routes that he, God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "I am the most eloquent of the Arabs, except that I am from Quraysh." It is answered that he, God's blessings and peace be upon him, although he was at the utmost heights of eloquence, to the point that it is as if God, glorified be His majesty and mighty be His power, churned the Arabic tongue and placed its cream upon his tongue, God's blessings and peace be upon him, so that no orator who confronts him fails to retreat with his limbs loosened, and no eloquent speaker who competes with him fails to return with an empty record. Nevertheless, his speech, peace be upon him, does not resemble what he brought of the Qur'an, and the speech of one person is uniform, as is not hidden from those of refined taste who are acquainted with the speech of the eloquent, past and present.

It has been objected that this does not dispel that claim, because it tacitly grants that his speech, peace be upon him, is a miracle that cannot be matched, and then the inability to match the Qur'an makes it lie between being His speech and being the speech of the Prophet ﷺ. Its being the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, is established only by adding its distinction over his speech ﷺ. The one who claims this has not asserted that it necessarily follows, from their inability to bring that, that it is from God, the Exalted, with certainty. Moreover, this granting contradicts what came earlier in explaining the sum of ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾, where the reason given was "you are like me in Arabic and eloquence," and so on. For this reason it has been said: the more appropriate answer is to commit to the view that his speech, God's blessings and peace be upon him, is not inimitable, even though he, peace be upon him, was the most eloquent of the Arabs, and there is no contradiction between the two, as is not hidden from the reflective. Some of them extended the discussion at this point; some introduced the question of the creation of acts (*khalq al-af'al*) into the matter and made the answer depend on the doctrine of al-Ash'ari concerning it. Perhaps the matter is sufficiently clear without lengthy discussion for one from whose eye of insight the veil has been lifted.

[p. 119]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 39:**

﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of, and its interpretation had not yet come to them.﴾ It has been said: this is a turning away (idrab) and a transition from demonstrating the falsehood of what they said about the Great Qur'an, through the challenge (tahaddi), to demonstrating it by showing that their speech arises from their not knowing its true nature and not having comprehended its sublime status. So "ma" refers to the Qur'an. This is what is reported from al-Hasan, and the verifying scholars of exegesis (tafsir) hold it. It has also been said that "ma" refers to what is mentioned in it that contradicts their religion, such as tawhid, resurrection and recompense. But this is not the correct view, whether the "ba'" is for transitivity, as is the most immediate reading, or for causation. The meaning is that they hastened to deny it without reflecting on what it contains, and without considering the evidences within it that indicate it is as described just above, and without knowing that it is not something that could be matched by bringing a surah like it. Expressing it with this designation, rather than saying "Nay, they denied it without encompassing its knowledge" or something similar, signals their complete ignorance of it, that they had known it only by the designation of not knowing it, and that their denial of it was only because of their failure to encompass its knowledge. This is because attaching a judgment to a relative clause (al-mawsul) indicates that what is in the clause of the relative is its cause. The original wording would have been "what they did not encompass with knowledge," but he turned away from it to what is in the noble arrangement, because it is more eloquent.

﴿And its interpretation had not yet come to them﴾ is a conjunction with the relative clause, or a circumstantial clause (hal) of the relative pronoun; that is, they had not yet come to understand its conventional and rational meanings, which reveal the elevation of its status and the brilliance of its proof. Thus ta'wil (interpretation) is a type of tafsir, and "coming" (al-ityan) is a metaphor for knowing and understanding. Perhaps its choice is to indicate that those meanings are directed to minds and are drawn to them of their own accord. It has also been permitted that by ta'wil is meant the occurrence of its referent, that is, its outcome and what it leads to, which is the real meaning according to some. Then "its coming" is a metaphor for its becoming clear and manifest; that is, the interpretation of the reports of unseen matters contained in it had not yet become clear to them, so that it would be shown whether it is true or false. The meaning is that the Qur'an is miraculous both in respect of its arrangement and its meaning, and in respect of its reporting of the unseen. They rushed to deny it before they had reflected on its arrangement and contemplated its meaning, or before they waited for the occurrence of what it reported of future matters. The negation of the coming of ta'wil with the word "lamma," which indicates the expectation of its negated object after the negation of encompassing its knowledge with the word "lam," is for emphasis of blame and intensification of reproach. The shamefulness of denying a thing before knowing it, when its coming is expected, is more heinous than denying it before knowing it in general.

Some have claimed that the turning away from denial is out of obstinacy, which is implied by His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say: "Then bring...﴾ and so on, for the argument of obligation (ilzam) comes only after the manifestation of incapacity. The meaning of this turning away is to blame them for imitation (taqlid) and abandoning reflection while they were able to do it. This is more severe in blame than obstinacy in one respect. This is because imitation is an admission by its holder of deficiency in intelligence, and then he is not excused for it. No person of intellect is content to imitate a man like himself without being preceded by intelligence and experience. As for obstinacy, some noble souls may praise it. Indeed, in their poetry there is an indication that they boast of it, as in the saying:

"So be obstinate toward whoever you are able to withstand in obstinacy."

And it is not objected that since obstinacy comes after knowledge, it is more deserving of blame. We do not concede that it is more deserving of blame than imitation; rather it is more deserving than ignorance before reflection without imitation being combined with it. And even if it is conceded, this too is more severe in one respect. The reproach has been made to fall upon their combining the two matters, and the combination in every case is more severe than singling out one of them, for which the turning away is valid. It is as if it were said: leave their challenge and their obligation, for they do not deserve address, because they are imitators, vacillating in the matter, not based on information or sound reason.

Al-Zamakhshari, in this context, mentions three opinions.

The first opinion: the estimate is "or did they say and claim it is fabricated," after knowledge of its inimitability, out of obstinacy. "Nay, they denied it before knowledge of the aspect of its inimitability came to them." So they continue in denial in both states, blamed for it, marked with the two vices of imitation and obstinacy, combining them in relation to two times. The reasoning is that ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of﴾ is explicit in their denial before knowledge of the aspect of inimitability. ﴿And its interpretation had not yet come to them﴾ indicates the extension of this denial until the expected interpretation comes, in relation to their denial before it, not in relation to the time of the report. Interpretation is also certainly occurring. In that case, either the denial has ceased, and so the blame for the first denial does not apply to them, or it continues, which is necessary so that it may be valid as blame against them for hastening to the denial, which is the explicit text. Therefore the conjunction must be upon His words, glorified is He: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾, and that is to show that they denied on the basis of knowledge, while this is to show their denial before it as well. Both aspects are considered, and they are blamed for both.

In sum: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾ is without doubt a denial after knowledge, because of the command that follows it. But since the expectation indicated by "lamma" was made to be for knowledge of the inimitability, it must be in relation to their first state, which is denial before knowledge. The Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, was expecting its disappearance through knowledge. The emphasis of "lamma" signifies the continuation of the denial for the entire period up to the time of the expected interpretation, at which time they denied out of obstinacy and rebellion.

The second opinion: taking ta'wil in the second meaning we mentioned. The meaning is: they hastened to deny before encompassing its knowledge, in order to know the inimitability of its arrangement. It has been said: the coming of the expected interpretation is what it leads to, namely the truthfulness of the reports of unseen matters. The intent of this is blaming them for their haste to denial from both aspects. But since with both aspects there is knowledge of what it contains, had they reflected, nothing would have remained expected. As for the second, since it is not so, there is something expected in it. He used the particle of expectation as an indication that this expected matter will occur, and it will become clear that they are wrong in it as well, as in the first. There is no consideration here of their being blamed in the two states of obstinacy and imitation. Rather, the intent is the complete manifestation of the obligation, that it is settled with their like, because of the aforementioned incoherence.

The third opinion: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾ is a blame of a group who denied on the basis of knowledge, and this is a blame of another group who denied on the basis of doubt. Since both kinds existed among them, the whole was attributed to the whole, and this is not unprecedented in the Qur'an. The purpose of the turning away is to generalize the denial, and that it was obligatory for the doubter to withhold judgment rather than hasten to denial. The meaning of expectation is that their doubt will cease, so some of them will know and some will remain as they are. The verse is silent on the detail and explicit about the cessation of doubt. There is no concealment that the doubter awaits, and likewise the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, was expecting the cessation of their doubt. End of quotation. It is not hidden that what we quoted first is more worthy of acceptance by people of intellect.

It has been objected to the claim that ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"﴾ is a denial after knowledge, that it arises from lack of knowledge, and that what is brought to prove it is within the scope of negation. The obligation comes after the challenge, and that statement comes before it, and its being preceded by the challenge mentioned in surah al-Baqarah refutes it, because that surah is Madinan and this one is Makki.

Yes, it may be said, to establish that this statement came after knowledge, that its quotation occurs in the noble arrangement after the quotation of the indication to its content, by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who do not hope for our meeting said, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it."﴾ And it is answered by what you have heard there, as the majority established. The explanation is that there was reported from them first the indication to attributing fabrication to the leader of the truthful, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, then reported from them the explicit statement of that. The apparent reading, as reported, is that the explicit statement occurred frequently after the indication, and a refutation of what they indicated has intervened in between. So it is possible that they understood and knew the truth but did not acknowledge it out of obstinacy and rebellion, and so they stated what they stated. That would be from them after knowledge. Because they progressed from indication to explicit statement, the obligation progressed as well, for this challenge is clearer in obligation than what preceded it, as is evident. But there is room for debate on this.

It comes to mind that it is possible that the turning away is from blaming them for denying the Qur'an to blaming them for hastening to deny what they did not encompass in knowledge, and that attaining knowledge of it is expected, whether it is the Qur'an or otherwise. So "ma" is general for both matters, and the Qur'an enters the generality primarily. Perhaps this is better than what has been said: that it is a turning away from an estimated matter. It is fitting that this "bal" be called eloquent (fasihah), for the meaning is: "They did not answer, or were not able to bring [the like], nay, they denied..." and so on.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like their denial without reflection and deliberation, ﴿denied those before them﴾, that is, they did the denial, or they denied their prophets in what they brought. ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ (39). This is addressed to the leader of those addressed, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and it may be general for everyone who is fit for it. By "the wrongdoers" are meant those before them. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is to indicate that denial is wrongdoing and its cause is what befell them of evil outcome, and to include these people, whose statements have been related, among them in the category of crime and threat, as a primary inclusion. The "fa'" is for the sequence of what follows upon an omitted matter that the speech implies; that is, "So We destroyed them. So see how..." and so on. "Kayfa" is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kana." It may be used so that it is placed in the position of the verbal noun, which is manner (kayfiyyah), and its interrogative meaning is entirely removed. Here it may bear that meaning, as in the statement of al-Bukhari, may God be pleased with him: "How was the beginning of revelation?" as al-Samin said. It is reported from him that the verb of seeing is suspended from acting because of "kayfa," since they treated it in every position as pure interrogation.

﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾: this describes their state after the expected ta'wil (the realization or fulfilment of the matter's outcome, as the ta'wil) has come, as has been said. For then it becomes possible to divide them into those who believe in it and those who do not, since belief in something without knowledge of it is impossible, and all of them shared in denial before that. Accordingly, the pronoun refers to the deniers. The meaning of believing in it is either merely the conviction of its truth, that is, among them are those who affirm in themselves that it is true when they comprehend its knowledge and the coming of its ta'wil, but they are obstinate and arrogant; or it is true belief, that is, among them are those who will believe in it and repent of disbelief. ﴿And among them are those who do not believe in it﴾, that is, they do not affirm it in themselves, just as they do not affirm it outwardly, due to their extreme dullness, which prevents them from comprehending its knowledge as it should be comprehended, or due to the feebleness of their intellect, the disorder of their discernment, and their inability to purify their knowledge from the conflict of the assumptions and illusions they have composed. So they remain in the doubt they were in. Or they will not believe in it in what is to come, but will die upon their disbelief, whether obstinate or doubting. ﴿And your Lord knows best the corrupters﴾ (40), that is, both groups according to the first interpretation, not only the obstinate, since they share in the root of corruption, which requires that they share in the threat intended by the speech. Or it refers to those who persist in disbelief according to the second interpretation.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 41:**

﴿And if they deny you﴾: that is, they persist in denying you after the proof has been established. This is interpreted this way because the root of denial is already present, so the future sense conveyed by the conditional particle is not appropriate here. Also, its answer, which is His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿Say: "To me is my deed, and to you is your deed"﴾, is meant as disavowal and leaving them be. This suits only persistence in denial and despair of their accepting the message. The meaning is: "For me is the recompense of my deed, and for you is the recompense of your deed, whatever they may be." The singular "deed" attributed to them is used in view of the generic unity, and to observe the perfection of the antithesis, as has been said. His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do﴾ is an emphasis on what the lam of exclusivity conveys, namely that the recompense of a deed does not pass to someone other than its doer. That is: you will not be held accountable for my deed, and I will not be held accountable for your deed. On this basis, the verse is muhkam (definitive) and not abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword, because its implication is that each is singled out for his own actions and their fruits, of reward and punishment, and the verse of the sword has not removed this. It is reported from Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd that it was abrogated by it, and it seems that this was because they understood from it abstention and leaving off confrontation. The reason for placing the ruling of the speaker first and then delaying it, and the reverse in the ruling for the addressees, is evident from what we have mentioned regarding the meaning of the verse, so understand.

* * *

Furthermore, of the allusive (ishari) meanings of the verses: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a scheme against Our signs﴾. This is their veiling from accepting the attributes of the Real. That is because with the abundance of apparent blessings and bodily desires, the soul's inclination toward the lower direction grows strong, so it veils itself from accepting that. Likewise, with various kinds of trial the soul's fury is broken, the heart is softened, and inclination toward the higher direction arises, along with readiness to accept that. ﴿Say: "Allah is swifter in planning"﴾, by concealing real subjugation within this apparent gentleness. ﴿Indeed Our messengers record what you plot﴾ on the tablets of the malakut. ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea﴾: that is, He makes your souls travel in the land of the spiritual struggles (mujahadat) and your hearts in the sea of contemplations (mushahadat). It has also been said: He makes your intellects travel in the land of actions, and your spirits in the sea of attributes and essence.

[p. 123]

﴿Until, when you are in the ship﴾: that is, the ship of eternal providence. ﴿and they sail with them on a good breeze﴾, which is the breeze of the northeast wind of His union, glory be to Him. ﴿and they rejoice in it﴾, because it announces that, and because it is perfumed with the scent of the abodes of intimacy and the pastures of holiness:

Oh breeze, what is with you? Every time you draw near to us, your fragrance grows sweeter.

I think Sulayma has learned of our sickness, so she gave you her perfume, and you came as a physician.

﴿There comes upon them a furious wind, and the waves come at them from every place﴾. That is the furious wind of subjugation and the waves of the attributes of majesty. This is the customary way with lovers: no state remains constant for them and no union lasts for them. How excellent is the one who said:

We spent the night in defiance of the envious, and between us was a drink like musk-scented wind, mixed with wine.

I placed her hand under my head, and I spent the night beside her, and I said to the night: "Stay long, for the full moon has gone to sleep."

When the dawn shone, it separated us. What bliss is there that time does not cloud?

﴿And they assumed they were encompassed﴾: that is, they were among those destroyed in those waves. ﴿they called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ by disavowing anything other than Allah, Exalted, saying: ﴿"If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful"﴾ to You, through You. ﴿But when He delivered them, behold, they transgress in the earth without right﴾. This is their exceeding the limit of servanthood by their intoxication in the beauty of lordship. That is like what befell al-Hallaj and his kind. Then He, glory be to Him, alerted them after their return from intoxication to sobriety that the matter lies beyond that, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, your transgression is only against yourselves﴾. That is: what you have claimed returns to you, not to Him, Exalted, for He, glory be to Him, is the Absolute Existent, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. Thus they have said. Ibn 'Ata' said regarding the verse: (until, when they embark) upon the vessels of knowledge, and the winds of providence have blown them along, and their souls and hearts have been delighted by this, and they rejoice in their turning toward their goal: ﴿there comes upon them a furious wind﴾, which effaces them from their states and their wills. ﴿and the waves come at them from every place, and they assume they are encompassed﴾: that is, they are certain that they are seized from themselves, and nothing remains for them, nor any attribute to which they could return, and that the Real has singled them out from among His servants by stripping them of themselves. ﴿They call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾, since He, glory be to Him, has purified their secrets and cleansed them of anything other than Him. ﴿But when He delivers them﴾: that is, He returns them to their attributes and their forms, and they return to what the common people are upon, of seeking livelihood for their souls. The commentary ends here.

It seems that he took baghy (transgression) to mean seeking (talab) and implied in it the meaning of occupation, that is: they seek in the earth, occupied with other than the Real, glory be to Him, and that is the livelihood by which their bodies subsist. And the threat that is announced by ﴿then We will inform you﴾, etc., is shaped according to this interpretation and what precedes it, because what occurs in intoxication carries no threat, and likewise the seeking of livelihood. Consider whether it is correct to say that the matter falls under the category of "the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near." Then He, glory be to Him, depicted the life of this world in the swiftness of its passing and the cutting off of its bliss after its arrival, and the deception of its possessor by it, by what He indicated with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Like water which We send down﴾, etc. In it there is an allusion to what befalls, God forbid, one whose wretchedness has preceded in eternity, from ruin after having been well: so while you see him, his states are fine and his years are free of the turbidity of troubles, the branches of his intimacy hang low and the gardens of his nearness are lovely, then time turns its back on him and attacks him with armies of tribulations. The winds of decree blow over those gardens, and the spacious expanse becomes narrow for him, joy and intimacy depart, and he is made like stubble, as if he had not flourished yesterday. The tongue of his state recites:

Stand by the abodes, for these are their traces; we weep for the beloved, out of grief and longing.

How often have I stood here asking, informed by a seeker of news, or a friend, or a compassionate one.

Then the caller of passion answered me in its ruins: "The one you love has departed, and the meeting has become rare."

[p. 124]

﴿And Allah invites to the abode of peace﴾, which is the spiritual world, sound from calamities. ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, in which there are no divisions. This is the path of unity. It may also be said: all are invited to His abode, and He guides the elite of the knowers to His union; or He invites the wayfarers to Paradise and guides the attracted ones (majdhubin) to witnessing. ﴿For those who have done good﴾, who are the elite of the elite: ﴿the best (husna)﴾, which is the vision of Allah, Exalted, ﴿and more (ziyadah)﴾, which is the continuance of the vision. Or: for those who have brought what makes their state good, of inward or outward goodness. The good reward is of the perfection that is poured upon them, and an increase in their readiness to accept good beyond what they were before. It may also be said: the husna is what the nearness of supererogatory acts requires, and the ziyadah is what the nearness of obligatory acts requires. ﴿Neither darkness nor humiliation shall cover their faces﴾: that is, the dust of shame does not afflict them, nor the humiliation of separation. ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾, which their deeds require. ﴿Therein they abide forever.﴾ Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of those who did evil, by His saying, exalted is His station: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds﴾, etc., and indicated that it is the reverse of the state of those noble ones. ﴿And on the day We gather them all﴾ in the great assembly, ﴿then We will say to those who associated: "Stay in your place, you and your partners"﴾: those are the veiled ones who stand with another in love and obedience. ﴿Stand together and wait for the judgment.﴾ ﴿Then We separate them﴾: that is, We cut off the bonds that were between them. ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not worship us."﴾ Rather, you worshipped things you invented in your corrupt imaginations. ﴿Allah suffices as a witness between us and you, that we were indeed unaware of your worship﴾: we did not seek it from you, neither by the tongue of state nor by the tongue of speech. ﴿There, every soul will test﴾: that is, it will taste and experience ﴿what it sent before﴾ in the world, ﴿and they will be returned to Allah, their true Master﴾, who undertakes their recompense with justice and equity. ﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾, from their inventions, their false fancies, and their vain wishes.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned, among what indicates tawhid, what He mentioned. Provision from heaven, according to the knowers, is the provision of spirits, and from the earth the provision of bodies. The living, in their view, is the knower, and the dead is the ignorant. ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾: this is a censure of them for lacking knowledge of what is necessary for their Lord, what is impossible for Him, and what is permissible. Almost none escape this censure except a few, and among them are those who knew Him, exalted is His majesty, through Him and not through thought. Indeed, knowledge may almost be confined to them, for the proofs of the people of the outward forms (ahl al-rusum), among the theologians and others, are mutually contradictory, and their statements pull against one another, so you scarcely see a proof free from "he said, she said," dispute, and argument. Attaining knowledge of that, despite all this, is a matter more distant than the Pleiades and rarer than the egg of the crow.

I have traversed all those sanctuaries, and roamed my gaze among all those landmarks,

and I found none but one placing the palm of a bewildered man under his chin, or another striking the tooth of a regretful man.

Whoever seeks salvation, let him do what those people did, so that it may first be attained for him. Let him follow the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) in what they were upon regarding the matter of their religion, unconcerned with the doctrines of the philosophers and of those theologians who follow their course, which increase the seeker of truth only in doubt. ﴿And it is not possible for this Qur'an to be fabricated apart from Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it﴾, from the Preserved Tablet, ﴿and a detailed explanation of the Book﴾, which is the Mother of the Book. That is: how could it be fabricated when it was established before it in two books, in summary and in detail? ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them﴾. This is a censure of them for hastening to deny the truth before reflection, contemplation, and attaining the reality. This is the habit of the deniers, the people of veiling, regarding the sayings of the people of the path: they hasten to reject them before reflecting upon them, contemplating their contents, and understanding the technical terms upon which they were built. The fitting course for them would have been deliberation and contemplation.

[p. 125]

And Allah, Exalted, is the Guardian of success.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 42:**

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ is an explanation that they are those whose hearts are sealed, such that there is no way for them to believe. (*man*) is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) precedes it. It is either a relative pronoun (*ism mawsul*) or an indefinite noun qualified by a following clause (*nakira mawsufa*). The clause after it is either a relative clause (*silah*) or a descriptive clause (*sifa*). The pronoun referring back to it is in the plural, in consideration of its meaning, just as it is in the singular afterward, in consideration of its wording. This may be to indicate the large number of those who listen, on the basis that listening does not depend on the conditions that reasoning depends on, whether customary or rational. The meaning is: "And among the deniers are those who, or people who, listen to the Qur'an, or to your speech, when the laws are known and the words reach their ears, but they do not benefit from them and do not accept them, like the deaf who do not hear." ﴿Then can you make the deaf hear﴾, that is, can you be able to make them hear? ﴿Even though they do not understand﴾, that is, even if their deafness is combined with their lack of understanding. This is because a deaf person who has understanding may perhaps be alerted when a sound reaches his ear canal, but when the loss of hearing and of understanding are combined, the matter is finished. They were likened to the deaf who have no understanding, despite being people of intellect, because their intellects have been struck by the affliction of imagination opposing them and the disease of following habit and blind imitation. For this reason it became impossible for them to grasp the meanings of the Qur'an, its precise rulings, and the perception of its elegant and refined wisdoms. So reciting words to them benefits them no more than the benefit animals derive from the speech of the one who shouts at them.

The placement of the subject (*musnad ilayh*) in ﴿Then can you﴾ is for emphasis (*taqwiya*) according to al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki, the Arabic rhetorician). Al-'Allama (al-Zamakhshari) took it to indicate restriction (*takhsis*). Thus, in placing the implied agent (*fa'il ma'nawi*) first and attaching to it the interrogative particle of denial (*hamzat al-inkar*), there is an indication that the Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, conceived in himself, out of his eagerness for the people's faith, that he was able to make them hear; or he was placed in the position of one who imagined that he was able to do so. And He, may His majesty be exalted, negated that from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and affirmed it for Himself, may He be glorified, by way of restriction, as if it were said: "You are not able to make those people hear; rather, We are the ones able to do so." This is what has been said, but there is something questionable in it. For this reason, the view of al-Sakkaki was chosen here, and the denial of making them hear was treated as a consequence of an implied preliminary premise (*muqaddima istidrakiyya matwiyya*) understood from the context, as has been indicated. In this view there is also the consideration that the interrogative particle is a fronted element displaced from its original position, because it requires precedence (*sadara*). This is the view of some scholars.

It has also been said that the particle is in its proper place, and the particle *fa'* (then) was introduced to deny that making them hear follows from their listening. But this is not by way of coordination (*'atf*) on the verb mentioned earlier, which occurs as a relative or descriptive clause, because that would cause the meaning to break down. Rather it is by way of coordination on a similar verb understood from the overall sense of the composition, not occupying its own place. As if it were said: "Do they listen to you, so that you make them hear?" Sometimes the intent is to deny the place where making them hear occurs after that listening and follows from it, as is indicated by the placement of "the deaf" in the position of their pronoun and by describing them as lacking understanding. The answer to *law* (even if) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The clause is coordinated on an assumed clause opposite to it, and the whole is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) relating to the object of the preceding verb. That is, "Can you make the deaf hear if they understood, and even if they do not understand," meaning "Can you make them hear in every hypothetical state?" It is said that this *law* is the concessive *law* (*law al-wasliyya*), and this is well known. The use of it here has been considered problematic, since the basic function of it is that the ruling holds on the assumption of the truth of what follows it, just as it holds on the assumption of its non-truth, though it is more likely on the assumption of its non-truth; but here the situation is reversed. It is answered that the connection of the concessive particle with affirmation proceeds in the usual manner, since its implied meaning is "You make them hear even though they do not understand." It is clear that making them hear while they have understanding is even more fitting. The interrogative is affirmative in its outward form, but if one looks at it as a denial, and as negative in meaning, it is considered to govern the whole after its connection. The same applies to what follows, so consider this carefully, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 43:

﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ and observe the clear proofs of your prophethood, but do not be guided by them, like the blind. ﴿Can you then make the blind to hear?﴾ — that is, can you guide them? ﴿And even if they cannot see﴾. That is: even if lack of sight were joined by lack of insight (al-basirah), for the purpose of sight is reflection (i'tibar) and discernment (istibsar), and the foundation of that is insight. For this reason the blind man of insight (al-a'ma al-mustabsir) makes shrewd guesses and perceives what the sighted fool (al-basir al-ahmaq) does not perceive. So it should not be said: how is seeing and sight affirmed for them first, and then negated of them second?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 44:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people﴾, i.e., He does not diminish for them ﴿anything﴾ of that with which their welfare and perfections are bound up, from the first principles of perception and the causes of knowledge and guidance to the truth through the sending of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and the setting up of proofs. Rather, He grants them all that as a favour from Him, exalted is His majesty, and as an act of generosity. ﴿But the people wrong themselves﴾ 44. I.e., they diminish what they diminish of that, by not using their faculties for what they were created for, by turning away from accepting the truth, by denying the Messengers, and by abandoning reflection on the proofs.

﴿Shay'an﴾ (anything) is the second object of yazlimu (wrong), on the basis that it is implicitly containing the meaning of yanquṣu (diminish), as has been said; or that it has the same meaning without any need to say that there is implication (tadmin), as we say: and that naqs (diminishing) is transitive to two objects, just as it is intransitive and transitive to one. The second object of the second object has not been mentioned because the purpose does not relate to it. The fronting of the first object may be for mere emphasis, while observing the rhyme (fāṣila), without intending to restrict the state of being wronged to them, according to the view of those who do not hold that fronting necessarily implies restriction, such as Ibn al-Athir and those who followed him, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾. It may also be that it is for restricting the state of being wronged to them, according to the view of those who hold that fronting necessarily implies that, such as the majority and those who followed them. Perhaps the choice of restricting the state of being wronged over restricting the state of being a wrongdoer to them is for the sake of emphasising the falsity of their actions and the feebleness of their minds, while the restriction of the first to them necessarily entails, as has been said, what the apparent situation requires of restricting the second to them, so the first restriction suffices instead of the second, while observing the benefit that has been mentioned.

Some have permitted that ﴿anfusahum﴾ (themselves) be an emphasis for "the people", and the object is then omitted, so it has the status of the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) in His exalted saying: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers﴾, in restricting the state of being wrongdoers to them. The expression of their act with the word naqs (diminishing), although it is a complete destruction, is for the sake of observing the aspect of its counterpart. The form of the present tense (muḍāriʿ) indicates continuity, in negation and affirmation. As for the second, it is evident; and as for the first, it is because the negative particle, when it enters upon the present tense, indicates, according to the context, the continuity of negation, not the negation of continuity, as has passed more than once.

It has been said: the meaning is that Allah does not wrong the people by punishing them on the Day of Resurrection with any of the wrong, but the people wrong themselves with a continuous wrong, for their continuous committing of evil deeds which necessitate punishment is itself their wronging of themselves. So wrong (ẓulm) is in its well-known meaning, and ﴿shay'an﴾ is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq). The negated present tense refers to the future, and the affirmed present tense refers to continuity. The context of the noble verse according to the first is to establish the proof, and according to the second is a warning. In both cases it is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for what preceded. Whoever makes it, according to the first, a concluding statement for all the obligations and narratives mentioned from the beginning of the surah, although it goes against the apparent sense, especially since what follows is not the start of a new narrative about others.

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that Allah does not wrong the people at all by taking away their senses and their minds, if He takes them away, because it is a disposal of His pure possession; but the people wrong themselves by corrupting that and diverting it to what is not fitting. It is an answer to a question that arose from the preceding verse, and the wrong in it is also in its apparent sense. It has been used as evidence that the servant has acquisition (kasb) and is not wholly deprived of choice, as the Jabriyya (determinists) held. The view preferred by many of the researchers is that the negation of the people's wronging Him, exalted is His majesty, is because He, glorified is He, is generous and wise, bestowing upon receptacles according to their pre-eternal preparedness fixed in knowledge. So there is no perfection or deficiency in the servant except that it is his perfection or his deficiency which his preparedness required. As the saying of the Most High, exalted is His majesty, guides to this: ﴿He gave everything its creation﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾. And that the affirmation of the people's wronging themselves is with regard to their preparedness, fixed in the pre-eternal knowledge, requiring what was bestowed upon them, by which they deserved punishment.

Some have mentioned that this preparedness is not something made (majʿūl), because making (ja'l) is preceded by the connection of power, which is preceded by the connection of will, which is preceded by the connection of knowledge; whereas preparedness is not like that, because knowledge has not been established except that it is connected to it, and rather to all other things as well, since connection to the known is one of the necessities of knowledge; and connection to what has no existence at all is not conceivable, since it is a relation, and a relation is not realised without the existence of both its sides. And this is not refuted by the claim that it entails the independence of existents from the influencer, because we say: if what is meant is their independence from that in view of the eternal knowledge-existence, then the matter is so and there is no objection to it; and if what is meant is their independence from that in view of their temporal external existence, then we do not grant the entailment. The verification of this, with what is for it and what is against it, is in its proper place. And in the verse, according to this, there is an indication that the fact of those deniers being as they were described arose only from their preparedness requiring it, and for that reason they were blamed for it, not from a mere decree upon them without their having any seeking of it through their preparedness. Perhaps calling the act contrary to what preparedness requires, if it were wrong, a metaphor, and treating the requirement as though it were ownership; otherwise the true meaning of wrong cannot properly be applied to any of His acts, exalted is He, in any way, since no one other than Him has true ownership of anything whatsoever. The apparent noun was placed in the resumptive clause (al-jumla al-istidrākiyya) in place of the pronoun, for the sake of additional specification and confirmation. Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿lakin﴾ with a light pronunciation and ﴿al-nās﴾ in the nominative.

**[Page 128]**

﴿And the day He gathers them﴾: read with the *ya'* (يَحْشُرُهُمْ), which is the recitation of Hamzah against ʿĀṣim. The rest read it with the *nūn* (نَحْشُرُهُمْ), as a shift from third person to first person (*iltifāt*, a change of grammatical person). According to most scholars, (يَوْمَ) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: "Remind them, or warn them, of the day when We shall gather them for the standing of reckoning." ﴿As if they had not remained﴾, meaning as if they were people who had not stayed (*lam yalbathū*) except ﴿for an hour of the day﴾, meaning a little of it. This is an image of extreme scarcity. It is specified as "of the day" because its hours are more clearly known than the hours of the night. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) relating to the object of (نَحْشُرُهُمْ), meaning: We shall gather them likened to those who did not remain in the world, or in the barzakh (the intermediate state), except for that small amount. The intended meaning of the comparison is not its apparent sense, as some have said. The author of *Sharḥ al-Miftāḥ* stated that a comparison is often mentioned while other meanings are intended that follow from it. So the intention is either regret over their not benefiting from their lifespans, or a wish that their stay before that had been longer, so that they would not witness what they witnessed of terrors. The sense of the clause in the Hereafter is therefore: We shall gather them full of regret, or wishing their stay before that had been long. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is: We shall gather them likened, in their outward conditions visible to people, to those who did not remain in the world and did not enjoy its pleasures except briefly. Whoever has lived in it for ages and enjoyed its comforts is not free of some traces of blessing and signs of delight, which contrast with the wretchedness of their appearance and the badness of their state. Some scholars took this view. The apparent sense is that it is an artificial reading, forced in order to keep the comparison on its outward level. The first view is better, as is not hidden. In any case, the benefit of the comparison is like a fire on a hill-top, and it is strange that someone who has not seen it says: the apparent meaning is that (كَأنَّ) expresses supposition. Some have claimed that the benefit of the restriction, if the intended meaning is staying in the barzakh, is to show the full ease of the gathering in relation to God's power, even after a long age, and to show the falseness of their disbelief and denial when they say: ﴿When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?﴾ and similar things. Or the benefit is to show complete correspondence between the two creations in forms and shapes, since brief staying in the barzakh is one of the causes of not changing or altering. Perhaps the final state on this view is: On the day We gather them in their forms and shapes, unchanged. Abū ʿAlī permitted the clause to be in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) of (يَوْمَ), with the connecting pronoun omitted, its estimated form being (كَأنْ لَمْ يَلْبَثُوا قَبْلَهُ), "as if they had not remained before it." Or it is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, with the connecting pronoun likewise, meaning a gathering as if they had not remained before it. This was rejected on the ground that such a connecting pronoun may not be omitted. The first was rejected on the ground that the adverbial noun (the qualified noun) is the Day of Resurrection, which is a specific day, and the estimated sentence is "the day of His gathering" or "the day of our gathering," so the qualified noun is definite while the clauses are indefinite, and a definite noun may not be qualified by an indefinite one. It is answered that the prohibition on omitting such a connecting pronoun is itself open to dispute, and that the clauses which are attached to time nouns may be interpreted as definite, so that what is attached to them is definite, or interpreted as indefinite, so that it is indefinite. Perhaps Abū ʿAlī strains to take them as indefinite, so that the qualified noun here is indefinite in his view, and the problem of qualifying a definite noun by an indefinite one disappears. You know that the answer only removes the impossibility and nothing more. The correct view is therefore to prefer the circumstantial reading (ḥāliyyah). His, glorified is He, words ﴿They shall recognise one another among themselves﴾ mean: some of them know others, as if they had been separated only briefly. This may be a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*, a new sentence), or it may explain the comparative clause and serve as evidence for it, as has been said. This is because, if the period were long, recognition would not remain, since a long period produces unfamiliarity and leads to mutual non-recognition. But recognition remains, so a long period is ruled out, and this is the meaning of ﴿they did not remain except an hour﴾. There is some weakness in this argument.

Abū al-Baqāʾ claimed that it is a supposed circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddarah*). There is no need to consider it supposed, because the evident point is that recognition among them is not delayed by a long time after the gathering, so as to need it. Scholars have stated that recognition among them occurs at the beginning of their emergence from the graves, and then it ceases because of the intense, bewildering terrors and the troubling states that befall them, which change their forms and shapes and turn them from one condition to another. My own view is that there is no certainty that it ceases, since the standings differ and the states vary. So they may recognise one another after not knowing one another in one standing and not in another, and in one state and not in another. Some reports support this. Some have claimed a contradiction between what this verse indicates and His, glorified is He, words: ﴿So there will be no ties of kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾ and His, exalted is He, words: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾, namely that there is no recognition, unless the two periods are taken into account. It has been said there is no contradiction, on the basis that the affirmed recognition is recognition for rebuke and reproach, while the denied recognition is recognition for companionship and compassion. Someone may object that the indication of these verses for the negation of recognition is not established, since what they show at most is the negation of the benefit of kinship and of one asking another. The recognition indicated by this verse does not contradict that. Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḥasan that he said about it: a man recognises his companion at his side, yet he cannot speak to him. Moreover, taking recognition (*taʿāruf*) to mean that they know one another is the well-known interpretation among the exegetes. It has also been said that what is meant is informing (*taʿrīf*), that is, that some inform others of the errors and disbelief they committed. But this has its own problems.

Some scholars permitted the earlier adverbial phrase to be connected to (يَتَعارَفُونَ). It has been said that it is then coordinated with what came before, but no proper basis for this is apparent. ﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have certainly lost﴾ is a resumptive clause, brought as a testimony from Him, exalted is He, to their loss, and as a matter of wonder at it. It is declarative in form and performative in meaning. It has also been said that it is a statement (*maqūl*) of an implied saying, placed as a circumstantial phrase relating either to the pronoun in (يَتَعارَفُونَ) or to the pronoun in (يَحْشُرُهُمْ), if the clause (يَتَعارَفُونَ) is also circumstantial, so that the circumstantial phrase is not separated from its owner by a foreign element. But the resumptive reading is more evident. Referring to them by the relative pronoun, although the context calls for a pronoun, serves to censure them by what is contained in the relative clause, and to indicate that this relative clause is the cause of what befell them. The apparent meaning is that the meeting with God, exalted is He, means every reckoning and recompense, and the loss means the depletion, that is, they were depleted in their trade, their dealings, and their purchase of disbelief in exchange for faith. It has also been allowed that the first (the meeting) means evil meeting, and the second (the loss) means destruction and misguidance, that is, they went astray and perished by denying that. ﴿And they were not guided﴾, that is, to the paths of trade, knowing its conditions, and they were not guided to the path of salvation. This clause is coordinated with the clause ﴿has lost﴾ and so on. It was also allowed that it be coordinated with the relative clause, on the ground that it serves as an emphasis for it.

[Page 129]

Its original form is *inna nurayannaka*, and *ma* is an added particle used to emphasize the meaning of the conditional (*sharṭ*). For this reason the verb is emphasized with the *nūn* of emphasis. The seeing (*ru'yah*) is visual, meaning: ﴿Whether We show you﴾ with your own eyes ﴿some of what We promise them﴾ of punishment, by punishing them during your lifetime, ﴿or We take you (in death) before that﴾, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾. This is the response (*jawāb*) of the conditional and of what is conjoined to it. The meaning is that their punishment in the Hereafter is established, whether or not they are punished in this world.

It was said that this is the response of *natawaffayannaka* (We take you), as if it were said: "Whether We take you in death, then to Us is their return, and We show it to you in the Hereafter." The response of the first clause is omitted, meaning: "Whether We show you, then that is the intended or desired outcome, or something similar." Al-Ṭībī said: meaning, "then that is true and right, or occurring, or established." Abū Ḥayyān preferred the first view. It has been objected to him that the return does not follow from that showing, so one would have to maintain that the conditional is incidental (*ittifāqiyyah*), arising from heedlessness of the intended meaning.

By ﴿We promise them﴾ is meant "We promised them," but the verb was shifted to the present form either to bring the scene vividly before the mind or to indicate renewal and continuity, meaning: "We promise them a renewed promise as wisdom requires, warning after warning."

Regarding the specification of "some" by mention, it was said that it is a hint that the promise is fulfilled by showing some of what was promised, and indeed the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown that on the day of Badr. ﴿Then Allah is witness over what they do﴾ of the evil deeds related about them. The intended meaning of "witness" is, metaphorically, its necessary consequence, which is requital and recompense. So it is as if it were said: "Then Allah is requiting them for what they do." It is also permissible that it means their being established and upheld through the speaking of the limbs, since Allah's witnessing in the sense of being watchful and guardian is a constant matter in both abodes. The *thumma* ("then") is not appropriate for that sense, and the apparent reading is that under these two interpretations it retains its literal meaning. According to al-Kashf and others, it is for gradation of rank (*tarākhī rutbī*) under the first interpretation, and literal under the second. The apparent sense of some scholars' statements is to prefer taking it as gradation of rank in all cases. I do not see any justification for departing from the apparent meaning after such a departure, nor that the conjunction with it is to the response, not to the whole conditional. You know that conjoining it to that would prevent the intended meaning of punishment or showing or the like from being what follows *thumma* and is consequent upon it. Perhaps what they considered there is not an explanation of "return," but rather a clarification of the intended purpose of the speech.

The explicit naming of Allah (the Divine Name) is to introduce awe, instill reverence, and emphasize the threat. Ibn Abī 'Abla read *thamma* with a fatḥah, meaning "there" (*hunālika*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 47:

﴿For every nation﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿there is a messenger﴾ to whom they are attributed and by whom they are called. ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾ to the place of standing, to bear witness against them regarding disbelief and faith, ﴿judgment is passed between them﴾ — that is, after he has borne witness — ﴿with justice﴾, meaning with fairness, and it is decreed the salvation of the believer and the punishment of the disbeliever. ﴿And they are not wronged﴾ 47 at all. It has been said that this sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil, a closing addition that reinforces what precedes it) that confirms what came before it.

It has also been said that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning that their not being wronged is continuous. A verse with this meaning, according to this view, is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And the prophets and the witnesses are brought, and judgment is passed between them﴾.

Or the meaning is: for every nation of the past nations there is a messenger who is sent to them with a law that wisdom required, in order to call them to the truth. ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾, and conveys to them and calls them, and they deny him and oppose him, ﴿judgment is passed between them﴾, that is, between every nation and its messenger, with justice, and it is decreed the salvation of the messenger and of those who believed in him, and the destruction of those who denied. The first interpretation is what Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Mujahid, and the phrasing (istiqbal) is upon it in its apparent sense, and it needs no supposition like that which was needed in the second interpretation. It has been given preference by His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 48:

﴿They say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"﴾ Based on the view that the apparent meaning of "the promise" they refer to is the worldly punishment that was promised, as the following context indicates. The apparent meaning of the verse raises a difficulty: God, exalted is He, has never left any nation without sending to each one of them a messenger. This is answered by saying that the people of the *fatrah* (the interval between messengers) had no messenger among them, as His saying, exalted is He, attests: ﴿so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾. It is answered that the generality of the verse does not require that the messenger be present with every nation among them, because his having preceded some of them does not prevent him from being a messenger to those ones, just as the preceding of our Messenger (ﷺ) does not prevent his being sent to us until the end of time. The most that can be said is that what occurred of confusion among the people during the time of the *fatrah* would lead to a weakening of the effect of the calling of the prophets, peace be upon them. (End of quotation.) And this is as you see.

It may be said: the intended meaning of "every nation" is every group whom God, exalted is He, willed to charge with obligation according to what His knowledge had preceded, or whom He willed to execute His word upon, or similar specifications (*mukhassisat*, restricting qualifiers) with which the ruling is not rendered void. It does not mean every group of people absolutely. Thus there is no difficulty at all, so reflect.

Then, this statement of the deniers is a demand for haste regarding what they were promised. Their purpose in it, as has been said, is to deem the promised matter remote and that it will not happen. The interrogative may be intended to express remoteness from the outset, since the context requires it and there is no obstacle to it. The claim that this is only the case from the outset with words like *ayna* and *anna* and the like, but not with *mata*, is not accepted. How so, when it is a figurative meaning, and there is no restriction on metaphor (*majaz*)? The address is to the master of those addressed, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the believers who recite to them the verses containing this. The answer to "in" (*in*, "if") is omitted, relying on what preceded it, meaning: "if you are truthful that it will come to us, then let it come to us quickly."

**[Page 131]**

Because the Prophet ﷺ was the intermediary in bringing about that (the promised punishment), and the promise was made concerning (the disbelievers) and not the believers, he was commanded to answer with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: I have no power over harm or benefit for myself﴾. That is, I am not able to bring about either of them in any way whatsoever. The mention of harm first is because the context of the noble composition is to show his inability regarding it. As for the mention of benefit, it is for generality, to show the complete extent of his inability. It has been said that it is an incidental addition (istitrad), lest it be assumed that this applies only to harm. The first view is preferable. As for what occurs in Surat al-A'raf, where benefit is mentioned first, it is to indicate its importance, and the context calls for it. The meaning is: I do not possess any of my affairs, whether to return it or to bring it forth, even though that (benefit or harm to myself) is closer to occurring. So how could I possess your affairs, so that I could bring about your promised punishment as you wish? ﴿Except what God wills﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati') according to a group (of scholars), meaning: "But what God the Exalted wills will occur." It has been said that it is a connected exception (muttasil), in the sense of: "Except what God the Exalted wills that I possess." This has been objected to, on the grounds that the context of disavowal (of the Prophet's power) rejects that he had any role in bringing about the promise, for that would require explaining that the matter in dispute is something he does not will to possess, peace and blessings be upon him.

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist school) held the connected exception and used this to prove that the servant is independent in his actions, both acts of obedience and acts of disobedience. But you know that this is far from establishing their claim. Yes, some who hold the view of the early generations (salaf), that the servant has an effective power by the permission of God the Exalted, have used it as evidence, not (holding) that he has no power at all, as the Jabriyya (determinists) say, nor that he has a power that is not effective, as is well known of the Ash'ariyya, nor that he has an effective power whether God wills or not, as is the view of the Mu'tazila. (Those who hold the first view) said: The meaning is, "I have no power over any of the harm or benefit, except what God the Exalted wills that I have power over of them; for I have power over it by His will, glory be to Him." Some have said: If possession (milk) is taken in the sense of ability (istita'a), the exception is connected, and if it is kept in its apparent sense, disconnection is necessary. It is not hidden that the original is connection, and one should not depart from it where it is possible without forcing the meaning. In any case, the apparent sense of their statements is that the exception is from the object (of the verb), but on the assumption of disconnection, the meaning is not to exclude the excepted item from the ruling of the item excepted from. Therefore, on that assumption, the ruling was given as "is occurring" rather than "I possess it," for example. So there is no contradiction in the words of one who ruled for disconnection, when he said, in explaining the meaning: that is, "But what God the Exalted wills of that is occurring," pointing by that to harm and benefit. For this is explicit that the excepted item is of the same genus as the item excepted from, which requires connection, because the criterion according to the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) in both matters is exclusion from the ruling or not.

Among what makes one wonder is the claim that the exception is from the subject of ﴿I possess﴾, and that the meaning is: "I do not possess, but God the Exalted is the Possessor of everything; He does what He wills by His will." ﴿For every nation﴾ among the nations who persisted in denying their messengers, ﴿is a term﴾ for their punishment, which descends upon them when it arrives and does not pass to another nation. ﴿When their term comes﴾, that is, the term of each nation, according to what is apparent. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is for increased emphasis, and the annexation is to convey complete definiteness. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the nations implied by "every nation." The reason for expressing "term" annexed to that (the nations) is to convey the intended meaning, which is that each nation reaches its own specific term, and its arrival comes to them specifically from among the nations, through the term being specified by annexation, conveying a general sense of plurality. It is as if it were said: "When their terms come," in the plural, as Ibn Sirin read it: that each one of those nations has its specific term come to it. The term may be interpreted as a specific limit of time, and its arrival in that sense is clear. It may also be interpreted as the duration to which it extends of that time; then its arrival is an expression of its end, for it is then that its arrival is fully realized, that is, "when its time has been completed and ended, their specific term." ﴿Then they cannot delay﴾ from it ﴿an hour﴾, that is, a little of time. ﴿Nor can they advance﴾ upon it. The form (istif'al, "they cannot advance") according to a group is on its original base, and the negation of seeking delay or advance is more emphatic. Others said that it has the meaning of tafa''ul (i.e., "they do not delay and do not advance"). The second clause is either a new sentence, or conjoined to the condition and the conditioned. They prohibited conjoining it to ("they cannot delay"), lest it be objected that advancing after the arrival of the term is not conceivable, so negating it would be pointless. Others permitted it, and the benefit according to them in that is the emphasis on the negation of delay, because when it is placed in the same row, it indicates that it has reached the level of impossibility, so it is impossible in the same way, due to the divine decree, even though it might be possible in itself. It has been said: This is the secret of using the form istif'al, meaning that it has reached such impossibility that it is not sought, since the impossible is not sought. Some answered this objection by saying that ﴿came﴾ means "approached arrival," like your saying: "When winter comes, then prepare for it." It has been objected that restricting the non-delay to nearness and proximity adds no further benefit. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to another answer, which is that "they cannot delay and cannot advance" is a metaphor for its having a fixed limit and a set term which it does not exceed, regardless of advancing or delaying, like the words of the Hamasa poet:

*"Desire has halted me where you are, so I have no one ahead of it, nor one behind it."*

He meant, as al-Marzuqi said: Desire has detained me in a place where you dwell, and I will cling to it and not leave it; and whether I am staying with you or journeying, I do not turn away from you nor incline to another. The reason for placing the statement of the negation of delay before the negation of advance has been mentioned in the verse of al-A'raf, with an extended discussion there. Then, it is not hidden that this verse falls within the scope of the answer, and it was not conjoined to what precedes it, as a notice of its independence in that. The Allamah al-Tibi, may God sanctify his resting place, said: The answer with the words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: I have no power﴾ etc., comes in the wise style, because they did not intend by the question anything but to deem it unlikely that the promise was from God the Exalted, and that he, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, was the one claiming that it was from Him. So they asked him to specify the time, mockingly and sarcastically. So it was said in reply: this mockery is only complete if you claim that you are the one who brings about that promise. If you admit that you are like yourselves in that you do not possess harm or benefit for yourself, how can you claim what is not rightfully yours? Then he began the correct answer, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not turn to their mockery and deeming it unlikely, so he said: ﴿For every nation is a term﴾, etc. Its summary, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is: your punishment has a fixed term with God the Exalted, and a determined limit of time; when that time comes, He will fulfill your promise without doubt, so do not hasten. From here the secret of the omission of the particle fa' (then) from ﴿When their term comes﴾ and its inclusion in ﴿then they cannot delay﴾ becomes known, in contrast to the verse of al-A'raf, where it was used in the first and not the second. That is because when the verse was brought as an answer to their hastening of the promised punishment, as you have just understood, care was taken with the matter of the conditional and its necessity to the utmost care.
