So it was used not as a consequence of anything, as if it were among matters firmly established in themselves, not consequent upon other things. And it strengthened the necessity of the consequent for the antecedent by the addition of the particle fa', by which connection is expressed in such contexts. This is not the case with the verse of al-A'raf, as is not hidden except to the cattle; so keep this in mind, for it is from al-Anfal. This is not contradicted by what was mentioned about the interrogative form at the beginning of the speech, as is clear to those of understanding. Likewise, it is not contradicted by what was said about linking this verse to what precedes it, that it is an explanation of what was left vague in the exception, and a restriction of the generality in the previous decree, which implies that the thing decreed is a matter already accomplished, not dependent on anything other than the coming of the Messenger and the nation's denial. For that, with what is in it, is a denial of the Prophet's involvement in the answer. Perhaps the aim is fulfilled by this alone, since the difference between the contexts of the two verses is achieved by it as well. It may be said: the omission of fa' first is so that the clause occupies the place of an attribute of "term," to magnify its matter and elevate its status, as the context demands. That is: for every nation there is a term described as: when it comes, they cannot delay from it or advance upon it at all. The explicit mention in place of the implicit pronoun is for increased emphasis, as just mentioned, but this is not the best.

Among what makes the dead laugh is what one of the great scholars said, after his thinking had nearly been exhausted: that the secret of the difference between the two verses is an indication from Him, exalted is He, that both are permissible in Arabic. He did not know, may God grant him well-being, that the Noble Qur'an was not sent down to teach Arabic, to explain its rules, or to clarify what is permitted in it and what is not. Rather, it was sent down as a miracle in its eloquence and rhetoric, and in the secrets it contains, for peoples, each of whom is in that matter (like) al-Judhayl al-muhakkak and al-'Udhayq al-murajjab (two proverbial epithets for a man of great expertise and experience).

And one of those who revived the dead in knowledge, whose understanding was purified from the confusion of the people of his age, Safa' al-Din 'Isa al-Bandanji, mentioned that the context of this verse is to strengthen the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and to expand his breast, peace be upon him, against what might constrict him by human nature, from their saying: ﴿When will this promise be, if you are truthful?﴾ And to instruct him, peace and blessings be upon him, to reject their saying that, as the context indicates. So it was appropriate to sever each of the two clauses from the other, so that each of them independently serves to strengthen and to refute, for emphasis and intensification. For this reason the particle fa' was not used at the beginning of the conditional, and it was used in the consequent to increase that, since it indicates the realization of what follows it immediately after what it requires, without delay. The verse of al-A'raf was sent as a threat to the people of Mecca. It is clear that the locus of the benefit in indicating that it is a threat, and that what is more effective in causing fear, is the conditional clause, because it is explicit in the descent of the punishment when the term arrives, and that there is no escape for them from it with Him, not merely (the statement) ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ alone. So the context called for connection and linking, and therefore the particle fa' was used to indicate this and to signal the unity of the two clauses in being a threat. And out of His forbearance, exalted is He, in threatening, the particle fa' was not used in the consequent. End of quotation.

Perhaps what we have put forward is not far from it in one respect, even if it differs from it in another; and each has its direction. And God the Exalted knows best the secrets of His Book.

[Quranic text] "Say," to them, after I had explained to them the state of affairs and the operation of God's practice (sunnah) among nations in general, and had alerted them that their punishment is a decreed and certain matter, which awaits only the arrival of its known term. This is an announcement of how near it is, and a treating of it as if it had already come in reality. ﴿Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you﴾, the punishment you are hastening. The use of "if" (in) here is probably a matter of accommodation (al-mujarah). ﴿By night﴾, meaning at the time of nightly sleep, ﴿or by day﴾, meaning while you are occupied with your affairs. The reason it does not say "by night and by day" is so that the antithesis may appear. The purpose is to convey heedlessness and sleep, and "by night" (al-bayat) covers this, because it is the time when the enemy spends the night and strikes, seizing the opportunity of the other's heedlessness. This meaning is not in the concept of "night" (al-layl) in general, nor is it as well known for night as the daytime is for being occupied with livelihood and affairs, so that relying on the implication (dalalat al-iltizam) would be fitting, as it is for the day. It may be said that the whole day is a place of heedlessness, for it is either a time of occupation with livelihood or a time of midday rest (qaylulah). Night, by contrast, has its heedlessness in the part near its middle, which is the time of "bayat," and so it was singled out for mention. "Bayat" comes both in the sense of spending the night (al-baytutah) and in the sense of attacking by night (al-tabyit), like "salam" in the sense of "taslim." The meaning intended here is built on this. ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾, meaning: what is it of the punishment that they are hastening, when none of it calls for hastening, since all of it is disliked, bitter to the taste, and causes aversion. Here "min" is partitive (li-l-tab'id), and the pronoun refers to the punishment. The indefiniteness of "shay'" (thing) indicates singularity. It is also permissible that the meaning be one of amazement, which is understood from the context, as if it were said: what a terrible calamity they are hastening! In that case "min" is explicative (bayaniyyah) and abstractive (tajridiyyah), based on al-Zamakhshari's counting it as both. It has been said that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He. In that case the meaning on the second reading would be that the benefit of vagueness and specification, and the magnification it contains, disappears.

As for what has been said, that it is more eloquent in the sense of "Do you know what the punishment is? The one who punishes with it is God, glorified is He" (1), this is shared under both readings. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His punishment﴾? "Madha" in the sense of "what thing" is in the accusative position as a fronted object. This is preferable to making it the subject (mubtada'). As for one who did so and estimated a returning pronoun, and one who said that the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ is the linking element (al-rabit) along with interpreting it as the punishment, he inclined to the view that what is hastened of the punishment is comprehensive, so it covers the subject, and thus stands in place of its linking element, because generality in a noun in the apparent (ism zahir) form serves as a link according to the well-known view, so it is more fitting in the pronoun. Abu al-Baqa' claimed that the pronoun refers back to the subject, and that this is the link, and he made this like your saying: "Zayd, I took a dirham from him." This is not correct, as is not hidden. The intended meaning of "the criminals" is the addressees. The turn from the pronoun to this description indicates that because of their crime they should be fearful of the arrival of the punishment, let alone hastening it. It has been said that the point of this is to show their contemptibility and to censure them with this dreadful attribute. The sentence is connected to ﴿Tell me﴾, either as a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) or as being in the place of the accusative as an object. The verb is suspended (mu'allaq) from it because of the interrogative, and it is originally an interrogation about sight, either visual or cognitive. Then it was used in the sense of "inform me," because of the causal and effective relationship in a general sense between seeing and informing. So it is a metaphor for what has been mentioned, and many have gone to this. Abu Hayyan went to the view that this is by way of implicit meaning (tadmin), and that it is not used except for a strange matter. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, meaning: if His punishment comes upon you at one of those two times, you will regret, or you will recognize the error, or then inform me: what is it that the criminals hasten?

Abu Hayyan claimed that the last is definite, because the apodosis is only estimated from what precedes it, either verbally or in estimation. He did not realize that estimating it from a different kind from what was mentioned, when there is evidence for it, is not rare. Even if the validity of the restriction he claimed is granted, what was mentioned is not excluded from it, on the basis that the intent of "Tell me" and "what is it that he hastens from it" etc. is to censure them or to show their ignorance, as some researchers have stated explicitly.

In al-Kashf, as a confirmation of one of the aspects mentioned in al-Kashshaf, it says: "What is it" etc. is the object of the questioning, and the conditional with its omitted apodosis confirms the content of the questioning. For this reason it was placed between them. Since in the interrogation there is ignorance-making and censure, the apodosis was estimated as "you will regret, or you will recognize the error." There is no obstacle to estimating both together, or something that conveys both meanings. For this reason the apodosis is omitted and placed in the middle, as emphasis upon emphasis. End.

It has also been permitted that ﴿What is it that he hastens﴾ is the apodosis of the conditional, like your saying: "If I come to you, what will you feed me?" and the whole thing in its entirety is connected to "Tell me." This was rejected on the grounds that when the apodosis of a conditional is an interrogative, there must be a fa' (then) with it. You say: "If so-and-so visits us, then which man is he?" and it is not omitted except by necessity. It has been expressly stated in al-Mufassal that when the sentence is imperative (insha'iyyah), a fa' must accompany it. The interrogative, even if it is not used in its literal sense, does not leave the category of the imperative. The example is artificial, so one should not rely on it.

[Page 134]

It is answered that al-Radi expressly stated that the occurrence of an interrogative sentence as an apodosis without fa' is established in much eloquent speech. Even if what was mentioned is granted, the saying (qawl) is estimated and its omission is very common and regular without disagreement. It was also raised against this aspect that hastening the punishment occurs before its arrival, so how can it be ordered upon it and be its consequence? It is answered that this is a report about a past state, meaning: "What were you hastening?" This is supported by the explicit "you were" (kuntum) later on, and the Qur'an explains one part of itself by another. You know that this alone does not permit it to be an apodosis, because hastening in the past is not consequent upon the arrival of the punishment. So there must be an estimation such as "you should know," meaning "you should know what," etc.

It has been said that "if it comes upon you" means "if its arrival approaches you," or that what is meant is "if the signs of its punishment come upon you." It has also been said that since the intent is to deny hastening, in the sense of negating it outright, it is valid for it to be an apodosis. It was objected to making the whole conditional sentence suspended from "Tell me" that it cannot be a direct object of it, on the basis that it means "inform me," and this takes "'an" and the sentence does not enter except when it is accompanied by an interrogative. We also say that suspension is permitted, but there is discussion about this in Arabic grammar. It was answered that the one who holds the view of suspension means linguistic suspension, because the meaning is: "Inform me about your conduct if His punishment comes upon you," etc.

The intended meaning of His words, ﴿Then, when it befalls you, will you believe in it?﴾, is an increase in rebuke and reproach. The meaning is: "Is it when the punishment actually occurs and descends upon you that you will believe in it, and your mockery and denial will turn into assent and submission?" The particle ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ (thumma, "then," indicating a delay) is used to show increased remoteness. In this is the implication that this second state is further removed than the first and more fitting for denunciation.

It has also been permitted that this be the response to the condition, with the first interrogative being a parenthetical clause. The meaning would be: "Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you, will you believe in it after its occurrence, at a time when faith will not benefit you?" The underlying sense, as has been said, is: "If His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, and it occurs and is realized, you will believe." Then the particle of delay (ثُمَّ) was used in place of the conjunction "و" (wa, "and") to indicate remoteness. Then the conditional particle was added to indicate that this (second clause) stands on its own in remoteness, and that the first clause serves as a preparation for it. The word ﴿إذا﴾ (idha, "when") was used, emphasized by ﴿ما﴾ (ma), to reinforce the meaning of occurrence and realization, and as an increase in ignorance-reproach, and because they would only believe after it occurred, when it would be of no benefit to them at all. This view is among those permitted by al-Zamakhshari, but it has been criticized as being extremely remote, because ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ is a conjunctive particle, and it has not been heard that an answer is introduced by it, and a clause introduced by an interrogative does not serve as a response without the particle ﴿فَ﴾ (fa, "so"). This objection has been answered by what has already passed.

As for the answer to this objection, that he treated ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ as if it were ﴿فَ﴾, because just as ﴿فَ﴾ originally indicates conjunction and sequence and has connected the conditional response, so too this one does; this is contrary to the consensus of the grammarians, and the analogy of it to ﴿فَ﴾ is not evident. Because of this difficulty, it has been said: al-Zamakhshari's intention is that it indicates the response, and the estimated sense is: "If His punishment comes upon you, you will believe in it after its occurrence," and what is in the noble composition is coordinated with it for emphasis, like His words ﴿Nay, you will soon know﴾ and ﴿Then, nay, you will soon know﴾. This has been criticized as well: its strained character is not hidden, for coordinating an emphasis with ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ while omitting the emphasized element is something that should not be undertaken. And if it were said that the intended meaning is that "you believed" is the response, and ﴿Then, when it befalls?﴾ is a parenthetical clause, then the parenthesis would be with "و" and "ف"; but with ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ no one has adopted this. In sum, much has been said in favor of and against this view, and "the perfumer cannot repair what time has spoiled."

It has been recited as ﴿ثَمَّ﴾ (tham, with a fatha on the thaa), meaning "there" (hunalika). His words ﴿آلآنَ﴾ (a-al-āna, "Now?") are understood with an implied verb of saying, and this is the most apparent and strongest in meaning, i.e., it will be said to them at the time of their belief after the occurrence of the punishment: "Now? You believe in it?" So ﴿الآنَ﴾ (al-āna, "now") is in the accusative position, as an adverb of time for the implied verb ﴿آمَنتُمْ﴾ (āmantum, "you believed"). It has been prohibited that it be an adverb of time for the mentioned verb, because the interrogative has the initial position in the sentence. It has been recited without the interrogative hamza, and in my view the most apparent reading here is that it also relates to an implied verb, because the sentence is built on interrogation. Some have permitted its relation to the mentioned verb, but this is not correct. It is reported from Nafi' that he recited ﴿آلْآنَ﴾ (āl-ān) by deleting the hamza after the lam and placing its vowel on the lam.

His words ﴿وَقَدْ كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ (wa-qad kuntum bihi tasta'jilūn, "while you were hastening for it") occupy the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the implied subject of ﴿آمَنتُمْ﴾. According to what has been said, the sentence proceeds from Him, exalted is He, and is not included under the statement addressed to them to confirm the content of what preceded, namely the denial of delay, and to rebuke them for it. The benefit of the circumstantial clause is the intensification of rebuke and reproach, and the increase of censure and regret. The great scholar al-Tibi said: "Now, you believe in it" would require that after it be said: "And you were denying it," not "you were hastening for it," except that the latter was placed in its position, because what is meant by it is the earlier hastening, which He, exalted is He, related of them in His words ﴿When will this promise be?﴾. That was a mockery from them, denial, and considering it remote. In the change of wording there is a summoning of that shameful statement, so it is more eloquent than "you were denying," and the placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb is for the sake of the consideration of the ﴿fawāṣil﴾ (verse-endings, the rhyming pauses of the surah).

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 10, verse 52:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it will be said﴾ and so on, is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the implied "it will be said" (qīla al-muqaddar) that comes before ﴿Now?﴾, for the emphasis of rebuke. ﴿To those who did wrong﴾, meaning: they placed what they were forbidden from, namely disbelief and denial, in the place of what they were commanded, namely faith and affirmation; or they wronged themselves by exposing themselves to destruction and punishment. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the position of the pronoun serves to censure them by what is in its clause of attribution (ṣilah), and to indicate that it is the cause (ʿilliyyah) of what befell them. ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾, meaning the painful punishment that lasts forever. ﴿Are you being recompensed﴾, meaning: you are not being recompensed today ﴿except for what you used to earn﴾, meaning: except for what you persisted in earning in the worldly life of the kinds of disbelief, of which is included what has passed of hastening (al-istiʿjal). Many commentators in their explanation added all other kinds of sins, on the basis that the disbelievers are responsible for the subsidiary rulings (al-furuʿ), and so they are punished for them. But is the punishment for these sins continuous, following the disbelief, or does it end like the punishment of other disobedient people? It has been said: the apparent view is the second, and by this the texts indicating the lightening of the punishment of the disbelievers are reconciled with what contradicts them. They said: what is lightened is the punishment for sins, while the punishment for disbelief is not lightened.

[Page 136]

﴿They ask you﴾, i.e., they seek information from you, ﴿"Is it true?"﴾, i.e., the punishment that was promised, as this is most fitting to the context, rather than the claim to prophethood which some scholars permitted. It was preferred over that view also on the ground that proving prophethood to those who deny it cannot be achieved by an oath. It has been answered that the purpose of the oath is not to prove prophethood, but to show that this claim is made in earnest and not in jest. Or it may be that the oath is meant for one who can be satisfied by proof of that kind. It may be said that what was mentioned is a shared difficulty of implication, because the promised punishment is not established, in the view of those who claim it is a fabrication, before it occurs, merely by an oath either. So what was mentioned is not suitable as a preponderating factor. The truth is that the oath was not mentioned for the purpose of implication, but as an emphasis on what they denied. The interrogative (al-istifham, the question form) is for denial, and the asking for information (al-istinba') is by way of mockery and ridicule, as is known from their state. Therefore it does not require that it remain on its original meaning. Perhaps it may be said that istinba' in the sense of seeking information is literal, but not about truth and its opposite in the sense that is immediately understood, because they are certain of the second. Rather, what is meant is seriousness and jest, as if they said: "We are certain that what you say is a lie, but we are doubtful whether you are serious or joking, so inform us of the reality of that." A parallel to this is their saying: ﴿Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾ according to what the majority have established. However, that is contrary to the apparent meaning. And ﴿true﴾ is a predicate placed before the subject, which is (huwa), so that it comes immediately after the interrogative particle (al-hamzah), about which the question is asked. It is also permitted that it be a subject, with the pronoun (huwa) as its predicate. It is in the nominative case by virtue of its being a subject, taking the place of the predicate, because it means "established." It is then an adjective that came after the interrogative, so it acts (as a verb) and the nominative noun that follows it can stand in for the predicate, if it is an explicit noun or has the status of one, such as the detached pronoun here. The well-known view is that istanba'a takes two objects: one without an intermediary, and the other with the intermediary of ʿan (about). So the first object according to this is the kaf (the pronoun "you") in yastanbi'unaka. The second object is replaced by this sentence, in the sense of: "They ask you about the answer to this question," since the interrogative itself is not asked about, but rather its answer is asked about. Al-Zamakhshari, seeing that the sentence here cannot be a second object either in meaning, for the reasons you know, or in wording, because ʿan cannot validly be placed before it, made the verb include the meaning of saying, i.e., "They say to you this," and the sentence is in the position of an accusative object of the verb "say."

Al-A'mash read (ālḥaqqu huwa) with the definite article together with the interrogative. This supports the interrogative being for denial, because in it there is an allusion to its falsehood, which requires its denial, since the speech implies restriction by it. It is restriction of the predicate to the subject, according to the well-known view. The meaning is that the truth is what you say, or else its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari took it as restriction of the subject to the predicate, saying: "It is as if it were said: Is it the truth and not the falsehood? Or is it that which you named the truth?" By saying "or," he indicated that the purpose of this aspect does not differ whether the restriction is taken as real, by way of mockery, or as claimed. This was objected to, on the ground that it contradicts what the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani) hold regarding this construction. In al-Kashf it is suggested that the restriction is in the sense of "It is the truth and nothing else," not in the sense of "It is the truth and not the falsehood," according to what they established in their saying: "Zayd is the one who departs," and "the one who departs is Zayd." On this basis, what al-Zamakhshari mentioned does not hold. But this objection is dispelled by what we have verified concerning God's saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾, and that the restriction of each of two terms to the other is considered according to the context. In that case it does not matter whether one is placed first or last. Here the meaning is the restriction of the punishment to truth, not the restriction of truth to the punishment.

He has said there: The verified view is that such expressions as "Zayd is the one who departs" and its reverse are judged to restrict the second term, i.e., departing, to the first, because what is appropriate is the restriction of the general to the specific. Likewise, expressions such as "People are the scholars" and "The scholars are the people," even if there is a partial general and specific relation between them, because the intended meaning is between them. As for expressions such as our saying: "The humble ones are the scholars" and "The scholars are the humble ones," the ruling differs regarding placement first or last, and one of the two restrictions is other than the other. So one should look at what the context requires. If one of them is determined for that, the ruling is given accordingly, whether placed first or last. Otherwise, placement first or last is observed. The restriction may be reciprocal, as in "Zayd is the one who departs," when the known is intended and this is that. Likewise, if the two classes have the same referent, as in your saying: "The laugher is the writer," and so on to the end of what he said. That the meaning here is the restriction of the punishment to truth, and not the reverse, is what is appropriate. The opposition of the scholars of rhetoric is not a novelty from the author of al-Kashshaf and his like, and the truth is not confined to what they hold, as is not hidden. So reflect.

﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾, i.e., say to them, not concerned with their mockery, ignoring what they intend, establishing the matter on the foundation of wisdom: "Yes, that promised punishment is established absolutely." So the pronoun in (innahu, "indeed it") refers to the punishment as well. And (ī, "yes") is a particle of answer and confirmation, meaning "yes." It has been said: it is not used in this way except with an oath specifically, just as hal, in the sense of qad (indeed), is used in questions specifically. For this reason it was heard in their speech connected with the particle of oath wāw, when the thing sworn by is not mentioned, so they say: "iyyū," and they also attach the silent hāʾ (hāʾ al-sakt) to it, so they say: "ayyūh." This word is common today in the speech of the Egyptians and the people of that region. Abu Hayyan claimed that it is permitted to use it with an oath and without it, though the first is more common. He said: What has been mentioned of the reported usage is not evidence, because the language became corrupted through mixing with non-Arabs, so there is no reliance on the reports. Omitting the object of the oath particle wāw and relying on it alone has not been heard from a trustworthy source, and it is contrary to analogy. The answer is emphasized with the most complete forms of emphasis, in accordance with the intensity of their denial and its strength. It is further affirmed and confirmed by His saying, exalted be His majesty: ﴿and you cannot escape﴾ 53, i.e., you cannot escape the punishment, taking it as from fātahu al-amr when the matter has gone away from him. It is also valid to take it as from aʿjazahu, meaning "found him incapable," i.e., you are not those who find the punishment, or who bring it upon you while being incapable of perceiving you and bringing it upon you. Whichever is the case, the sentence is either coordinated with the answer to the oath, or it is a new sentence brought to show their inability to escape, together with what it contains of the confirmation mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 54:

﴿And if every soul that has wronged had all that is on the earth﴾, i.e., by disbelief, or by transgressing against others, or other kinds of wrongdoing, so it is said. It is said that it may be restricted to the first, because it is the complete instance, although the discourse concerns the disbelievers. And "law" (law) is said to mean "inna" (indeed), and it is said to be on its literal meaning, but this was considered far-fetched, and I do not consider it far-fetched. ﴿All that is on the earth﴾, i.e., all that is in the world of its treasures, its wealth, and its benefits, entirely. ﴿would surely ransom itself with it﴾, i.e., it would make it a ransom for itself from the punishment. From iftada (to ransom oneself), in the sense of fada (to ransom), so the object is omitted, i.e., it would ransom its own self with it.

It has been allowed that iftada be intransitive, on the basis that it is the intransitive counterpart (mutawi') of fada, which is transitive. It is said: fadahu, fa-ifta-da (he ransomed him, so he ransomed himself). It was objected that this is not suitable to the context, since what is understood from it is that another ransomed him, because its meaning is "I accepted the ransom," and the one who accepts is other than the one who gives. This was examined: it may be that the one who accepts and the one who gives are the same, since one may ransom himself. Yes, the first is what is understood. ﴿And they will conceal﴾, i.e., the souls indicated by "every soul". The shift to the plural form serves to convey the magnitude of the matter, by the concealment being done together and collectively. What was not observed in what preceded was in order to realize what is intended by assuming that all that is on the earth belongs to each of the souls, and to employ the masculine plural form so that the word "nafs" (soul) is taken as a person, or to give precedence to the masculine denotation over its feminine. Al-israr (concealment) is hiding, i.e., they hid ﴿the regret﴾, i.e., the grief and sorrow over what they had done of wrongdoing. What is meant is the concealment of its traces, such as weeping and biting the hand; otherwise it is among the inner matters that cannot be except secret, and that is due to the intensity of their bewilderment and confusion. ﴿When they see the punishment﴾, i.e., at their witnessing, from the dreadfulness of the situation and the intensity of the terrors what had not occurred to their minds, so their state resembled the state of one brought forward for crucifixion whom the calamity that has overtaken him overwhelms and overcomes, until he cannot utter a word and remains rigid and stunned. It was also said: what is meant by al-israr is sincerity, i.e., they sincerely held the regret; this is either because concealing it is its sincerity, or from their saying: "the secret of a thing" for its pure essence which by nature is hidden, guarded, and treasured. In this there is mockery of them. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Jubba'i said: al-israr here means disclosure. In al-Sihah: "asrartu al-shay'" means I concealed the thing, and also I made it public, and it is among the contradictory terms (addad). Both meanings are explained in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they conceal the regret﴾, and likewise in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"If they had concealed my killing..."

End quote. In al-Qamus also: asarrahu: kataman-hu wa azharahu (he concealed it and he disclosed it), an antonym, and in this there is disagreement among the lexicographers, for al-Azhari among them claimed that using asarra in the sense of azhara is an error, and that the word used in that sense is ashharra with the dotted shin only. Perhaps he himself erred in the charge of error. Accordingly, disclosure too is in terms of its traces, as is not hidden.

Some have allowed that what is meant by al-israr is concealment, except that what is meant by the plural pronoun is the leaders, i.e., their leaders concealed the regret from their followers who had misled them, out of shame before them and fear of their reproach. In this, the pronoun in ﴿asarru﴾ is general, with no indication restricting it; moreover, the terror of the standing is too great for one to reflect along with it on such things. The clause ﴿asarru﴾ is, on the apparent reading, a new (resumptive) sentence. It was said: it is a circumstantial clause with qad implied. And ﴿lamma﴾ in all the other views means "when," in the accusative, governed by ﴿asarru﴾. It has been allowed that it is conditional, with the answer omitted according to the sound opinion, due to what precedes it, i.e., when they saw the punishment, they concealed the regret. And ﴿qudiya﴾, i.e., was judged and decided between them, i.e., between the wrongdoing souls, ﴿with justice﴾, i.e., with equity, ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ at all, for nothing is done to them except what their readiness requires. It was said: the pronoun in ﴿baynahum﴾ refers to the earlier wrongdoers mentioned in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if every soul that has wronged﴾ and to the wronged ones whom they wronged, though they have not been mentioned, yet wrongdoing indicates them by implication. The restriction of wrongdoing to transgression, and the meaning: judgment took place between the wrongdoers and the wronged, and each of them was treated in the manner befitting him. You know that the context does not support this, for if it does not require taking wrongdoing in its greatest instance, which is polytheism, then at least it requires taking it in what falls under it primarily. The apparent view is that the clause ﴿qudiya﴾ is a new sentence, though it was allowed that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿ra'aw﴾, so that it would fall within the scope of ﴿lamma﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 55:

﴿Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: to Him, glorified is He, and not to any other, exalted is He, belongs whatever exists in these great celestial bodies, whether as part of their very reality or as something external to them that is firmly established within them. The word (ma) here is used to give precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what came before, a confirmation and an argument for it, in that whoever owns all existent things and has the disposal of them is capable of what has been mentioned. It has also been said that it is connected to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And if every soul that has wronged had everything on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom﴾. It is as if it is an explanation of their resolve regarding what they would ransom themselves with, and of their lack of ownership of anything, since it conveys that everything in the heavens and the earth is His possession, and no one has any ownership in it besides Him, exalted is He and high is He. But this is not correct, even though some of the eminent scholars mentioned it and restricted themselves to it.

﴿Surely the promise of Allah﴾: that is, all that He has promised, of whatever kind it may be, so that the punishment they hastened for is included in it, along with what was mentioned in the course of explaining their condition, included in the primary sense. The verbal noun (al-masdar) is then in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul). It is also permissible for it to remain in its verbal-noun meaning, that is: His promise, glorified is He, of all that was mentioned. ﴿Is true﴾: that is, established, certain to occur without doubt, or in accordance with reality. The apparent view is that taking the promise in its general sense, such that the mentioned punishment and the retribution for the disobedient are included in it, or the promise of both of them, requires considering the device of giving precedence (taghlib) in the speech. Some have understood the promise as what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, was promised of his victory and of the punishment of whoever does not follow him, and said: considering the device of precedence is a delusion and is not necessary. The making explicit of the Glorious Name is to magnify the matter of the promise and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The opening of the two sentences with the particles of alerting (ala) and affirmation (inna) is to record the certainty of their content, which establishes what preceded of the noble verses, and to call attention to the necessity of keeping it in mind and preserving it.

The Imam mentioned, regarding the reason for the particle of alerting in the first sentence, that the people of this world are occupied with looking at apparent causes, so they attribute things to their apparent metaphorical possessors, saying, for example: the house belongs to Zayd, the boy to 'Amr, the sovereignty to the caliph, and the disposal to the vizier. Thus they were immersed in the sleep of ignorance and heedlessness, supposing these attributions to be valid. Therefore, He, glorified is He, increased them by His saying, mighty is His name: ﴿Surely to Allah belongs﴾ and so on. The attribution of all of that to Him, exalted is His majesty, through ownership, is based on what is established of the necessity of His existence through His essence, glorified is He, and that everything other than Him is possible in its essence, and that what is possible in its essence depends on what is necessary in its essence, either directly or through an intermediary. That requires that the whole belongs to Him, exalted is He. Regarding the use of the particle in the second sentence along this pattern, there is some strain, and the truth is what we indicated in the reason for the opening. The connection of this sentence with what preceded is evident from what we have established. For al-Tabarsi, in explaining this, there is a statement that is not correct.

﴿But most of them﴾: because of the badness of their dispositions, the deficiency of their intellects, and the dominance of heedlessness over them, ﴿do not know﴾ 55, so they say what they say and do what they do.

﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ in this world, with no one having any part in that. This, as is understood from the words of some (scholars), is an argument for the resurrection and the rising again, in the sense that He, exalted is He, gives life and causes death in this world, so He is capable of both in the Hereafter, because one who is capable by His very essence does not lose His capability, and the matter that is inherently receptive to life and death remains receptive to both forever. It is not hidden that the mention of power is an istitrad (digression), having no bearing on the argument for that. The apparent view in my opinion is that it is, like the preceding phrase, a tadhyil (concluding appendix that reinforces what came before). ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ 56 in the Hereafter, by resurrection and gathering.

[Page 139]

...a turning back to them, drawing them toward the truth and bringing them down to accept and follow it, after warning them of the perils of error through what He recited to them of the calamities. It also signals that all of this is directed toward their welfare. This is the connection with what came before. Abu Hayyan said about this: when He (exalted is He) mentioned the proofs of divinity, oneness, and power, He mentioned the indications that prove the validity of prophethood and the path leading to it, which is the one characterized by these attributes. The first view is preferable. The generality of the address does not preclude it, as is the apparent meaning, and al-Tabari chose it, in disagreement with those who restricted it to the Quraysh.

Al-mawʿiẓah (admonition) is like al-waʿẓ and al-ʿiẓah: the reminder of what softens the heart regarding reward and punishment. It was said: it is a rebuke accompanied by intimidation. Al-shifāʾ means the remedy, and it is pluralized as ashfiyah, and the plural of the plural is ashāfī. Al-hudā (guidance) is known from what has passed more than once. Al-raḥmah (mercy) means benevolence, or the intention of it, or an attribute of something other than these two that is fitting for the one in whom it subsists. ﴿Min rabbikum﴾ (from your Lord) is connected to jāʾa (has come). The min is either for the starting point (ibtidāʾiyyah) or is connected to an elided element that occurs as a qualifier of mawʿiẓah, and the min is then partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), and the sentence is according to an elision of a modifier, meaning: an admonition from the admonitions of your Lord.

As for ﴿li-mā﴾ (for what is in), it is either connected to mā ʿindahu (what is in them), with the lām reinforcing, or it is connected to an elided element that occurs as an adjective of it. The same is said regarding what follows, according to what has been said. The intended meaning is: there has come to you a Book comprising these benefits and advantages, revealing the states of deeds, their good and their evil, encouraging the first and deterring from the second, clarifying the true knowledge which removes the diseases of doubts and the corruption of the constitution of belief, and guiding to the path of truth and certainty through directing to reasoning by the signs of the horizons and of the souls. And it is a mercy to the believers, since through it they were saved from the darkness of disbelief and error to the light of faith, and they were freed from the ranks of the fires and ascended to the degrees of the gardens.

Some of the verifiers said: in this there is an indication that the human soul has degrees of perfection, and whoever holds fast to the Qur'an attains them. The first is the refinement of the outward from doing what is not fitting, and to this refers (by the admonition), on the basis that it contains restraint from sins. The second is the refinement of the inward from corrupt beliefs and vile dispositions, and to this refers (by a remedy for what is in the breasts). The third is the adornment of the soul with true beliefs and virtuous morals, and this is not attained except through guidance. The fourth is the manifestation of the lights of divine mercy, and it is specific to the perfect souls prepared for what they have attained of perfection, outward and inward, for that.

The Imam said: the admonition is an indication of the purification of the outward of creation from what is not fitting, and this is the sharīʿah (law). The remedy refers to the purification of the spirits from corrupt beliefs and blameworthy morals, and this is the ṭarīqah (path). The guidance refers to the manifestation of the truth in the hearts of the ṣiddīqīn (the truthful sincere ones), and this is the ḥaqīqah (reality). The mercy refers to the attainment of perfection and radiance, to the point of perfecting others and overflowing upon them, and this is prophethood and the caliphate (khilāfah). These are degrees in which neither advancement nor delay is possible. It is not hidden that this is greatly contrary to the apparent meaning. What the apparent meaning requires is that the mentioned items are attributes of the Qur'an in terms of it being a cause and an instrument for them, and its very self was made [these] for the sake of exaggeration, and there is a general mutual implication between them. The indefiniteness in them is for magnification. And guidance, if it is taken in the sense of indication absolutely, then it is general; or in the sense of indication that reaches its goal, then it is specific. In that case ﴿for the believers﴾ qualifies both matters. What supports restricting guidance to this is His (glorified is He) saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

So the Qur'an is an admonisher through what it contains of intimidation and encouragement, or through what it contains of restraint from sins, whatever they are, accompanied by intimidation only, on the basis of the second explanation of admonition. It is a healer of what is in the breasts from the ailments that lead to destruction, such as ignorance, doubt, polytheism, hypocrisy, and others. It is a guide, by clarifying what is fitting and what is not fitting, to what contains salvation and success with everlasting bliss, or it conveys to that. And it is the cause of mercy for the believers, those who believed in it and carried out the rulings contained in it.

As for when the apparent meaning is set aside, it is said other than what has been said, which you will see, God willing, in the chapter on the allusive (ishārah) interpretation.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti used the verse, as he said, to show that the Qur'an heals bodily diseases just as it heals diseases of the heart. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: I complain of my chest. He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: Recite the Qur'an, for God (exalted is He) says: a healing for what is in the breasts." Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab narrated from Wathilah ibn al-Asqaʿ that "a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) of a pain in his throat, and he said: Upon you is the recitation of the Qur'an."

You know that using the verse for this is hardly sound, and the second report does not indicate it, since there is in it no more than the Prophet's (ﷺ) instruction of the complainer to recite the Qur'an, as guidance to what benefits him and by which his pain would depart. We do not deny that the recitation of the Qur'an has a blessing through which God (exalted is He) may remove diseases and pains, but we deny only the use of the verse for that. The first report, although it is apparent regarding the intended meaning, should nonetheless be interpreted, as when it is said: perhaps he (ﷺ) perceived that in the man's chest there was a spiritual, inward disease, which had become a cause of the physical, sensible disease, so he commanded him to recite the Qur'an so that the first would depart from him, and then the second would depart. It is not improbable that some inward diseases may be a cause of some bodily diseases, for we see that envy and rancor may be a cause of that. And from their sayings to God (exalted is He): "How admirable is envy's justice: it began with its owner and killed him." This is better than taking the statement as an instance of the wise manner of address (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm).

Al-Hasan al-Basri denies that the Qur'an is a healing for diseases. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him that he said: God (exalted is He) made the Qur'an a healing for what is in the breasts, and He did not make it a healing for your diseases. The truth is what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 58:

"Say" (﴿قُلْ﴾) is a shift in address (taltin al-khitab) and a directing of it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he would command the people to seize upon what is in the Mighty Qur'an of bounty and mercy. That is, "Say to them: ﴿With the bounty of Allah and His mercy﴾." The phrase "with the bounty of Allah and His mercy" is connected to a deleted element (mutaʿallaq bi-mahdhuf), and the original sentence is: "Let them rejoice in the bounty of Allah the Exalted and His mercy." Then the prepositional phrase was placed before the verb to convey restriction (ikhtisas) of the action to the prepositional phrase. Then the fa' (fa, "so") was introduced upon it to convey the sense of causation (sababiyyah), so it became "with the bounty of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice." Then His words, glorified is He, were brought: ﴿So in that let them rejoice﴾, for emphasis and affirmation. Then the first verb was deleted because the second indicates it. The first fa' is said to be a conditional (jaza'iyyah) fa', and the second is an extra (za'idah) fa' for emphasis. The original sense is: "If they rejoice in something, then in that let them rejoice, and not in anything else." Then the fa' was added for what has been mentioned. Then the condition was deleted. It has also been said: the first is the extra fa', because the answer of the condition in reality is "let them rejoice," and "in that" is placed first by an inversion of what has been indicated; a fa' was added in it for embellishment (tahsin). For this reason it has been permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for His words, glorified is He: ﴿with the bounty of Allah and His mercy﴾, and in that case there is no need to say that its complement is deleted. A parallel to this in the disagreement over determining the extra element in it is the verse of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

Do not lament if a possession that you had has perished;
but when you have perished, then at that point lament.

Among the rare points of Arabic grammar is what some have indicated: that the verse is an instance of the construction of "occupation" (al-ishtighal), and the demonstrative has been placed in the position of the pronoun of the object, and its singularity is in consideration of what has been mentioned and the like, as is common in it. The reason for its rarity is that the known rule of this construction is the verb being occupied by a pronoun of the object, and none of the grammarians has mentioned the verb being occupied by a demonstrative referring to it. It has also been permitted that the complement of the prepositional phrase be estimated as (so let them take care) (فَلْيَعْتَنُوا), that is: "with the bounty of Allah and His mercy, so let them take care; so in that let them rejoice." The indication of this estimate is that what one rejoices in is among what is cared for and concerned with, or the fronting of the prepositional phrase, as it has been said. Al-Halabi said: "The indication of it from the context is clear, and the condition of an indication is not that it be verbal. So the statement of Abu Hayyan, that this is an omission for which there is no indication, is one that has no basis." It is also permitted that "Has come to you" (جاءَتْكم) be estimated after "Say," indicated by what precedes it, that is: "Say: there has come to you an admonition, a healing, a guidance and a mercy, with the bounty of Allah and His mercy." It is not permitted for it to be connected to the mentioned "has come to you," because "Say" prevents that. In this case, "that" (ذلك) refers to the verbal noun understood from the verb, which is the coming, that is: "So by the coming of the mentioned things, let them rejoice." The repetition of the preposition (ba') in "with His mercy," according to all the other views, is to indicate that each is independent in meriting rejoicing. The meaning of "the bounty and the mercy" is either the genus, which includes what is in the coming of the Qur'an of bounty and mercy by primary inclusion, or what is in its coming of that. This is supported by what is narrated from Mujahid, that the intended meaning of "bounty and mercy" is the Qur'an.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you among its people." This is narrated also from al-Bara' and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a statement of companions (mawquf). A great multitude has also reported that the bounty is the Qur'an and the mercy is Islam, which is in the meaning of the aforementioned hadith. Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the bounty is knowledge and the mercy is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir recorded from him the interpretation of the bounty as the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the mercy as Ali, may Allah honour his face. The well-known description is that the Prophet (ﷺ) is described with mercy, as His words, exalted is He, guide to: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾, without the Commander (Ali), may Allah honour his face, though he was a noble mercy, may Allah be pleased with him and make him pleased. It has also been said: the intended meaning of both is Paradise and deliverance from the Fire. And other things have been said. It is not permitted that "mercy" in the last of the grammatical possibilities mean what was meant by it at first; rather, it is other than the first, as is not hidden.

Ruways narrated from Ya'qub that he read (فَلْتَفْرَحُوا) with the taʾ of address and the lam of command, according to the original form of the addressee which has been dropped, based on the view that the original form of the imperative is the command with lam. So it was deleted together with the taʾ of the present tense, and a hamzat al-wasl was brought in to reach the beginning with a sukun. This is not on the view that it is an original form. This reading has also been reported in a sound hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it has been narrated by a group including Abu Dawud, Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi, by various chains from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, as a statement traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others also recited it. In the glosses of al-Zamakhshari on his Kashshaf: it is as if the Prophet (ﷺ) only preferred the reading with the original form because it is more indicative of the command to rejoice and more explicit in it, signifying that rejoicing in the bounty of Allah and His mercy is strongly recommended, so as to match the affirmation and repetition, and the implication of the meaning of condition for that, and an example of what has been transformed, where what is not eloquent became eloquent, is His words, glorified is He: ﴿And there is not to Him any equal, anyone﴾, from the fronting of the adverbial complement, so that the purpose is the restriction of Oneness. End of quote. This is taken from Ibn Jinni's statement in explaining it. And it is reported from the commentary on al-Lubb in explaining it that since the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to those present and those absent, the lam and the taʾ were combined. It has been said: it seems he meant that since the command was for the whole of the believers, present and absent, the present ones were given precedence in address over the absent ones, and the lam was used to take into account the matter of the absent ones. This is a wonderful point, except that it is a matter open to possibility. What was reported from the author of the Kashshaf is more deserving of acceptance.

It was also read (فافْرَحُوا), and this supports the previous reading, because it is the imperative of the addressee in its original form. It was read (فَلْيَفْرَحُوا) with a kasrah on the lam. (Then:) ﴿is better than what they gather﴾, from wealth, crops, livestock and the rest of the debris of this world, for it is heading toward cessation and about to vanish. The pronoun (هو) refers to the word "that" (ذلك) with regard to its meaning, and that meaning is singular; its wording has been treated in agreement with it, even though it is an expression for the bounty and the mercy.

It is permitted to return the pronoun to both of them directly, by interpreting "that" as "what has been mentioned," as was done with "that," or by placing them as if they were one thing. You may also make it refer to the verbal noun, meaning the coming that has been pointed to. (Ma) may be either a relative or a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle. Ibn 'Amir read (تَجْمَعُونَ) with the second person, addressing those to whom the words "O mankind" (يا أيُّها النّاسُ) were addressed, whether it is general or specific to the Quraysh unbelievers. The pronoun in "so let them rejoice" refers to the believers, that is: "So in that let the believers rejoice; it is better than what you, the addressees, gather." On the reading (فَلْتَفْرَحُوا) and (وافْرَحُوا), the address, as has been said, is to the believers. It is also permitted that it be a shift (iltifat) to them on the reading with the third person as well. It has been objected that the plural is more fitting for others, and even if it is valid to describe them with it in general, it is not proper to commit to a view that entails it, as long as there is an alternative to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 59:

﴿Say: "Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision﴾, meaning: what He has decreed for your benefit from it. Otherwise, provision is not all sent down. The use of *anzala* (sent down) for what is mentioned here is a figurative usage (*majaz*), by naming the effect (*musabbab*) and meaning its cause (*sabab*). It is also permitted for the attribution to be figurative, by attributing the sending down to the provision itself, because its cause, such as rain, is sent down. It has been said that there is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) here that is *makniyyah takhayyuliyyah* (implicit and imaginative), but this is far-fetched. It has also been said that provision is used as a metaphor for its cause, or that a word meaning "cause" is understood, and neither is appropriate.

The word (*ma*) is either a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) in the accusative position, functioning as the first object of *ara'aytum* (have you considered), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning *anzalahu* (He sent it down). The second object is *ma sataraahu inshallahu ta'ala qarIban* (what you will see soon, if God Most High wills). Or the word (*ma*) is an interrogative (*istifhamiyyah*) in the accusative position, functioning as the object of *anzala* (sent down), and it is placed before it because it has the right of initial position (*sadarah*). It suspends the verb preceding it, if we say that suspension (*ta'liq*) applies there. That is: what thing of provision did God Most High send down?

﴿Then you made from it what is unlawful and lawful﴾, meaning: you divided it and split it into unlawful and lawful, and you said: "These are cattle and tilth of restriction (*hijr*), and what is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives," and other such things.

﴿Say: "Has God permitted you [to do this]?"﴾ in making some of it unlawful and some of it lawful.

﴿Or do you invent [lies] against God?﴾ 59

Here (*am*) and the hamzah (interrogative particle) are equivalent (*mut'adilatan*), and the clause is in the position of the second object of *ara'aytum* (have you considered). The word (*qul*) [say] is repeated for emphasis, so this is not prevented. The returning pronoun to the first object is understood. The meaning is: Have you considered the one God Most High sent down to you as provision, and you did with it what you did? Which of the two matters is present in it: permission from God Most High in making it into two parts, or your fabrication? The original form of "Has God permitted you" and so on would have been: "Has God permitted you, or other than Him?" Then it was changed to what is in the clear wording, indicating that the established part is the second one. They attributed that to Him, glory be to Him, so they are fabricators against Him, exalted be His majesty, and not against anyone else. In this there is a great rebuke, as is not hidden. Perhaps this is what is meant by the one who said: the interrogative is for seeking information (*istikhbar*), and he did not intend its literal meaning, so that it would not contradict the certainty of knowledge that permission is absent and fabrication is established. Rather, it was intended for affirmation (*taqrir*), warning, and establishing the proof against them.

It is also permitted that the interrogative is for denying the permission, and (*am*) is then disjunctive (*munqati'ah*) with the meaning of *bal* (rather) for turning away (*idrab*). The intent is to turn away from that, to affirm their fabrication. In this case the clause is governed by *qul* (say), and is not linked to *ara'aytum*. The verb has been satisfied with the first clause, as we indicated. Among the scholars there are those who permitted (*am*) to be connective (*muttasilah*) and also disjunctive, depending on whether the clause is linked to the verb of saying. They required connection if the clause is linked to *ara'aytum*. And making the glorious Name a subject (*mubtada'*) with the clause as its predicate is, according to some, for restriction (*takhsis*), and according to another, for strengthening the ruling. The explicit mention after the place of the pronoun is to announce the complete ugliness of their fabrication. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction absolutely in one view, and for observing the verse endings (*fawasil*) in the first aspect, and for restriction in the second aspect according to another.

The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that the unlawful is not provision. There is no proof for them in it for what we have mentioned, because what is decreed for benefit is the lawful, so what is mentioned here is a part of provision, and it includes both the lawful and the unlawful. The disbelievers only erred in making some of the lawful unlawful. Whoever made the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) a parallel to them in making provision in general divided into two parts has indeed committed a grave slander.

The Qur'anic verse is in ﴿ ﴾ markers, and the commentary follows.

﴿And what do those who fabricate lies against God think?﴾ This is a statement addressed from Him, exalted is He, to explain the terror of what they will encounter. It does not fall under the "saying" that was commanded. Referring to them with the relative pronoun serves to exclude the first possibility of the disjunction, and to brand them with fabrication, while adding "lie" even though fabrication cannot be anything but a lie, in order to show the full ugliness of what they invented and that it is also a lie in their own belief. The (ما) here is interrogative, functioning as a mubtada' (subject), and the word ﴿ظَنُّ﴾ is its khabar (predicate). It is a verbal noun (masdar) that is grammatically annexed to its agent, and its two objects are omitted.

As for His, glorified is He, saying ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, it is a zarf (adverbial complement of time) of the thinking (ظَنّ) itself, not of ﴿they fabricate﴾, because that would be unsound in meaning, nor of an implied verb, because positing an implied element goes against the apparent sense. The meaning is: "What do they think on that Day, that I will do to them?" The intended purpose is threat and warning. That this adverb is attached to the thinking is supported by the reading of Isa ibn Umar, "(وما ظَنَّ)" in the past tense. In this reading (ما) carries the meaning of the thinking and is in the accusative position as a masdar. The use of the past tense expresses the certainty of occurrence, and most descriptions of the Resurrection in the Qur'an are expressed in this way for the reason mentioned. Governing a future time adverb is not prohibited, since the verb is rendered explicitly future by the adverb, and the aforementioned figurative use is permitted, because it can also be treated as past for the sake of its certainty.

It has also been said that the zarf is connected to what their present thinking is about, namely the matters that will occur on the Day of Resurrection, treating that as if it were present and what happens in it of terrors, because the matter is so clearly established and settled in their view, placing it in the position of something known to them. The meaning would then be: "What do they think of what will happen on the Day of Resurrection? Do they suppose that they will not be questioned about their fabrication, or will not be recompensed for it, or will be recompensed with a light punishment?" For this reason, ﴿they do what they do﴾ (يَفْعَلُونَ) is repeated. Then ﴿No! Indeed they are in the severest punishment﴾, because their disobedience is the most severe of disobediences.

As for the preceding verse, it has been said that it is connected to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾ and so on, as if it were said: since they acknowledged that He, glorified is He, is the Provider, say to them: "Have you considered what God has sent down..." and so on. This was reported from Abu Muslim. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O mankind...﴾ and so on, because when He, majestic is His affair, described the Qur'an with what He described, and commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to encourage people to seize what is in it, He followed this with mention of their opposition to what he brought and their prohibition of what He had made lawful. It has also been said that it is connected to the verses that censure them for the corruption of their beliefs, as if He, glorified is He, after censuring them for their foundations, explained the falsehood of their branches. Perhaps the best of these three is the middle one.

﴿Indeed God is full of bounty﴾, that is, great, whose measure cannot be estimated and whose essence cannot be grasped, ﴿toward mankind﴾ all of them, in that He bestowed upon them reason, showed them mercy by sending Messengers and revealing Books, clarified for them what their intellects are not capable of comprehending by themselves, guided them to what concerns them regarding this life and the next, encouraged them and warned them, and explained to them the conditions and the terrors that await the one who deviates from right guidance.

﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾ 60 for that bounty, so they do not benefit from it. Perhaps this clause is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what preceded, affirming its content.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Nor are you engaged in any affair﴾: that is, in a matter of concern. Its root (sha'n) is spelled with a hamza, as in *sa'alahu* (he asked him) when one intends him. Its hamza may be replaced with an alif. Originally it is a verbal noun (masdar), but here the sense is the object (maf'ul), i.e., "a matter" (mash'un). ﴿Nor do you recite from it﴾: the pronoun in *minhu* (from it) refers to the affair. Recitation is the greatest of his affairs, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, which is why it is singled out for mention. Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the Revelation (tanzil). The pronoun is placed before its referent to magnify the matter of Him, the Mighty and Majestic. The *min* (from) in *minhu* is said to be partitive (tab'idiyya) on the first two interpretations, and initial (ibtida'iyya) on the third. The *min* in His words, ﴿of any Qur'an﴾, is extra (za'ida), to emphasise the negation under all the possibilities. This is the view of al-Qutb, while al-Tibi said: the first *min* under the last interpretation is initial and the second is extra; under the first interpretation the first *min* is partitive and the second is explanatory (bayaniyya); under the second interpretation the first *min* is initial and the second is explanatory.

In *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* it is stated that the first pronoun refers to the affair, and the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a recitation which is among the affair; or the pronoun refers to the Revelation, and *min* is initial and partitive; or it refers to Allah, exalted is His affair, and *min* is initial, while the second *min* is extra and initial on the first interpretation, and explanatory or partitive on the second and third. You know that the adverbial phrase may be connected to what comes after it, and the obligation to connect it to a deleted element that qualifies a verbal noun, in the same way under all the possibilities, is unnecessary. Yes, the necessary consequence, according to the well-known view, is that two particles with the same meaning should not be connected to one governed element.

[p. 144]

Abu al-Baqa' held that the first pronoun refers to the affair, and the first *min* is causal (li'l-ajal), as in His words, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ (71:25), and the second *min* is extra, and what follows it is the direct object of *tatlu* (recite). This has a basis. What is among the strangest is what some of them said: it is possible that the pronoun in *minhu* refers to the affair, either by taking *ma tatlu* (what you recite) to mean that recitation is part of your affairs, or by reading the speech as containing a deleted noun, meaning: and you do not recite from it for the sake of the affair, so that some affair occurs to you and you recite the Qur'an because of it. The circumstantial sense (al-haliyya) is something that hardly occurs to anyone with the slightest taste in Arabic. We have not seen the view that a noun is deleted in a sentence where it carries the meaning of causation or the like, and what appears in the words of more than one of the eminent scholars in similar cases is a deletion of meaning, not a deletion of grammatical analysis (i'rab). It is far-fetched to interpret this person's statement in that way, as is not hidden. (This is the end.) Furthermore, the Qur'an is general with respect to what is recited, both as a whole and in part. It is a true meaning in both cases, as has been verified in its proper place. The claim that it is a metaphor for the part, by using the whole and intending the part, is not worth considering. ﴿And you do not do any deed﴾: that is, any deed whatsoever. The first address is specific to the head of the human species and the master of those addressed, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This address is general and includes all servants, the righteous and the wicked, not only the latter two. In each of the two situations, what is fitting has been observed. In the first, in the context of particularity, he used the word "affair" (sha'n), because the deed of a great person is great. In the second, he used the general word "deed" (amal), which applies to both the important and the trivial. It has been said that the first address is also general to the community, as in His words, ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ (65:1). ﴿Without Our being witnesses over you﴾: this is a detached exception (istithna' mufarragh, an exception with no stated object) from the most general state of those addressed with the three verbs. The meaning is: you do not engage in anything of them in any state, except that We are observers, watching over it and guarding it. This is what they said, and from it one understands that the prepositional phrase is connected to what follows it. Perhaps it was placed first for emphasis, to frighten those among the addressees who are meant to be frightened. It seems that for emphasis the pronoun of majesty was used, and that what is meant by watching over them is watching over their deeds. ﴿When you press on with it﴾: that is, you begin it and become engaged in it. The root of *ifada* (pressing on) is rushing forward in abundance or with force. Since the preceding verbs refer to a continuous, habitual state that also relates to past time, the past form was chosen in the exception, and in the adverb the word *idh* was used, which makes the present carry the meaning of the past. This is what has been said, but I have not seen anyone who explains why negation with *ma* was chosen, which by the majority's view makes the present refer to the present in the absence of a contrary indication, in the first two sentences, while negation with *la*, which by most scholars makes the present refer to the future, was used in the third sentence, contrary to the view of Ibn Malik. Perhaps this is one of the effects of the difference of address in terms of particularity and generality, so consider it, for it is very subtle. ﴿Nor is hidden from your Lord﴾: that is, what is far off and what is absent. From this comes the expression "a far-off meadow" (rawd 'azib), and "a remote meadow" (rawd 'az) when it is far from people. The speech contains a deleted noun, meaning: nor is hidden from the knowledge of your Lord, Mighty and Majestic. Or the expression is a metonymy for that. In the mention of the title of Lordship together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, there is an implication of kindness that is not hidden.

Al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *zay* with a kasra (*ya'zib*, as one who is far off). ﴿Of an atom's weight﴾: *min* is extra, to emphasise the negation. *Mithqal* is the name for what balances a thing and matches its weight. Legally it is twenty-four qirat. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this in his tafsir from Abu Ja'far. The correct view is that it did not change between the pre-Islamic period and Islam. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti reported from al-Rafi'i that he said: the people of the first age agreed on the estimate by this weight, namely that the dirham is six daniq, and every ten dirhams are seven mithqals. The mithqal did not change in the pre-Islamic period or in Islam. *Dharra* (atom) is the singular of *dharr*, which is the small red ant. Tha'lab was asked about it and said: a hundred ants weigh one grain, and the *dharra* is one of them. It has also been said that the *dharra* has no weight, and what is meant by it is what is seen in the sunlight entering through a window. ﴿On the earth nor in the heaven﴾: that is, in the two directions of below and above, or in the sphere of existence and possibility, because common people know no other two. Nothing possible is in them or connected to them. The speech also includes them themselves, as is not hidden. The mention of earth before heaven, although heaven is often mentioned before it, and although it occurs in Saba' with this same verse in the parallel position with earth first, is because the discourse concerns the people of the earth, and the aim is to establish proof of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of its details. Heaven is mentioned so that it is not supposed that the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, exalted is He, is restricted to one thing and not another. The sum of the argument is that nothing is hidden from Him, the Exalted, and one whose state is this, how could He not know the condition of the people of the earth and what they are doing with His Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him?

His words, ﴿Nor is there anything smaller than that or greater but it is in a clear register﴾, form an independent sentence. It is not coordinated with what precedes it, nor is *la* a negation of the genus. *Asghar* (smaller) is its subject and is in the accusative because it resembles a noun in construction (mudaf). Likewise *akbar* (greater) is accusative by the assumption of its governing. As for al-Samin's claim that both are built on the fatha, this is weak; it is the view of the Baghdadi grammarians, and he supposed that a later pen had slipped beyond the bounds of acceptance. ﴿In a clear register﴾ is connected to a deleted element functioning as the predicate.

Hamza, Ya'qub, Khalaf and Sahl read with a damma (*la asghara... wa la akbara* in the nominative, as "nor is there anything smaller... nor greater"), as a subject-predicate sentence. Its cancellation is not permitted when it is repeated. As for the statement that a resembling-of-a-noun must be in the accusative, what is meant is the prohibition of building, not the prohibition of the nominative and the cancellation, as some have wrongly supposed. It is also permissible that this is by treating *la* as governing in the manner of *laysa* (is not). It has been said: in the first reading *asghar* is coordinated, in terms of its wording, with *mithqal* or *dharra*, and it was made to be in the genitive instead of the accusative, because it is not declined on account of being a qualifier and its pattern being that of a verb. In the other reading it is coordinated with *mithqal* in terms of its position, because it is the subject, and *min*, as you know, is extra. This raises a difficulty: the meaning becomes "nor is anything smaller than that or greater than it hidden from Him, except that it is in a clear register", and so something is hidden from Him, and this meaning is not correct. The answer is that this is on the assumption that the exception is connected. If the exception is taken as disconnected, the meaning becomes: "but nothing smaller or greater is hidden from Him, except that it is in a clear register", and this confirms His words, ﴿Nothing is hidden from Him﴾, etc. Some answered, on the assumption of connection, that it is in the manner of His words, ﴿They taste not death therein, save the first death﴾ (44:56), and ﴿And that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ (4:23), according to one opinion. So the meaning is: nothing is far from His knowledge except what is in the Preserved Tablet, which is the place of the forms of His known objects, exalted is His affair, based on interpreting the clear register as that; or except what is in His knowledge, based on what has been said, that the Book is knowledge. If that is counted as remoteness, then it is remote from His knowledge, but it is clear that it is not remoteness at all, so nothing is remote from His knowledge at all. It has been reported from some verifiers, in resolving the difficulty, that remoteness is a term for mere distance. Created things are of two kinds. One kind God brought into being without intermediary, like the earth, heaven and the angels, peace be upon them. The other kind He brought into being through the first kind, like the events in the world. The chain of causation and effect may be far from the level of the existence of the Necessary Existent, exalted is He. So the meaning is: not an atom in the earth nor in heaven is far from the level of His existence, except that it is in a clear register, in which He, exalted is He, has recorded those known objects. So it is an detached exception from the most general states. Affirming remoteness in the sense of distance from Him, exalted is He, within the chain of origination, has no objection. This is a subtle view, but it resembles the refinements of the philosophers more, though it differs from what they hold in general.

Al-Kawashi said: the meaning of *ya'zubu* is "become clear and separate", that is: nothing of His creation issues from your Lord except that it is in the Tablet. The summary is that everything is written in it. This was objected to on the grounds that interpreting it as "become clear and separate" is not well known. It has also been said: what is meant by remoteness from the Lord, exalted is He, is distance and departure from His unseen. That is, nothing departs from His unseen except what was in the Tablet, and so it is remote from the unseen and far off, for it no longer remains unseen at that point, because the angels, peace be upon them, and others have knowledge of it. This implies the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, exalted is He, of the unseen and the witnessed.

From here another aspect appears of placing the earth before the heaven. It has also been said that (إلّا, illa) is conjunctive, in the sense of (الواو, wa), as al-Farra' said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿The messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ ﴿except one who has done wrong﴾, and al-Akhfash regarding His words: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those among them who did wrong﴾, and a group regarding His words, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾. Its implied complement follows it, and the speech is complete at His words: ﴿nor anything greater﴾. Then He begins with His words: ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾, meaning, "and it is in a Book."
