Makki transmitted this from Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn Yahya al-Jurjani. Then he said: "This is a good view, were it not that all the Basrans do not recognize (إلّا, illa) as meaning (الواو, wa)." The fair assessment is that it is not appropriate to interpret the speech of the Exalted, the Mighty, in that manner, even if all creation, humans and jinn, agreed that (إلّا, illa) can come in the sense of (الواو, wa).

It has also been said that the exception (الاستثناء, istithna', exception) is from an omitted element indicated by the preceding speech, meaning: "and nothing [is outside] except that it is in a Book." A parallel is His words: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. From the combination of these, the affirmation results that God has knowledge of every object of knowledge, and that everything is written in the Book. Many of the styles of Arabic speech are cited as supporting this, as has been said.

It is also transmitted from the author of the book Tabsirat al-Mutadhakkir that the exception may be connected to what precedes the words of the Exalted: (لا يَعْزُبُ, la ya'zubu, "is not hidden"). The verse would then have an inversion and an arrangement like this: "And you are not engaged in any affair, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an, nor do you do any deed, except that We are witnesses over you when you are immersed in it, and nothing is hidden from your Lord, nor anything smaller or greater, except that it is in a clear Book, and [everything] that is there is in the Preserved Tablet, and We witness it at every moment." Al-Bulqini examined this in his treatise entitled al-Istighna' bi-l-Fath al-Mubin fi al-Istithna' fi ﴿nor anything smaller or greater except that it is in a clear Book﴾. He said that, despite its artificiality, it entails the claim of a construction in the Glorious Speech that has no equivalent in Arabic speech, namely: "except that it is in a clear Book, except that We are witnesses over you," and this is not comparable to the verse of poetry:

*"Amrir rabbahum illa al-fata, illa al-ula, kama la yakhfa"*
[Pass by their lord, except the youth, except the nobility, as is not hidden.]

You know that the least artificial of the views is the view of disconnection (الانقطاع, al-inqita', separation), while the most exalted in rank and the most subtle in meaning is the view of connection (الاتصال, al-ittisal). Placing the speech in the manner of ﴿except what has already passed﴾ and its many counterparts, in prose and verse, is not objectionable. However, the verse is more eloquent under this view. So let it be understood.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 62:

Then, when He (exalted is He) had made His promise and His warning general, applying to all who obey and all who disobey, He (glorified is He) followed this with a description of the states of His sincere awliya' (friends, the close ones of God, wali). So the Mighty One, the Speaker, said: ﴿Surely the friends of God, no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud) it is said that this is an explanation in the form of good tidings and promise, concerning what is the result of the deeds of the believers, and the outcome of what was mentioned before it: that He (glorified is He) is the Guardian over His Prophet (ﷺ) and his community in all that they do and leave undone, and His knowledge (glorified and exalted is He) encompasses them. This came after the mention of the horror of the state of those who fabricate lies against God (exalted is He) on the Day of Resurrection and the terror that will overtake them. It is a general indication by way of threat and warning. The sentence is introduced with the particle of alerting and affirmation (ala) in order to increase the establishment of its content.

Awliya' is the plural of wali (friend), derived from wilaya, which means nearness and closeness. It is said: "He became distant with the distance of a wali," meaning, with closeness. Those meant here are the purified believers, because of their spiritual nearness to Him (glorified is He), as their subsequent explanation makes clear. Wali is also interpreted as muhibb (one who loves), and between the two meanings there is a mutual necessity. The full discussion of this will come shortly, God willing. It also comes with the meaning of nasir (helper), and the words of some scholars point to the validity of considering this meaning here.

What is meant by the two negated, conjoined sentences is the continuing absence of what they signify, as its verification has been explained more than once. It has been said: the meaning is: no fear shall come upon them of an adversity befalling them, nor shall they grieve over the loss of something desired, at all times. That is, nothing that would necessitate these things reaches them at all; not that these things reach them but they do not fear or grieve; nor that fear and grief never reach them at all, but rather they remain in vigour and joy. And how could sensing fear not be so, when fear, out of magnifying the majesty of God (exalted is He) and considering one's own striving and effort in fulfilling the rights of servanthood to be insufficient, is one of the characteristics of the elite and those brought near? Rather, the more a servant draws near to his Lord (glorified is He), the more fear and awe of Him (glorified is He) he has. Many reports and His saying (exalted is He) point to this: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God.﴾ These states overtake them because their aim is nothing but God (exalted is He) and attaining His good pleasure, which brings honour and nearness. That is something about whose attainment there is no doubt and no possibility of its loss, by the necessity of the divine promise. As for all other worldly matters, which hover between being attained and being lost, these are, in their view, more worthless than a wick in the sight of al-Hajjaj. Indeed, the whole world in their eyes is filthier than the foreleg of a dead pig over which a dog has urinated, held in the hand of a leper. So it is far-fetched that these things should fit into the sphere of their purpose, existing or not, such that they would fear the harm they bring or grieve over the loss of their benefit.

It has also been said: what is meant by the absence of fear and grief is their safety from these on the Day of Resurrection, after the establishment of their nearness and happiness. Otherwise, fear and grief befall them before that, whether their cause is worldly or otherworldly. It is not permissible to take it to mean their safety from what has been mentioned in this world, or in what encompasses this world and the Hereafter, because that would be a sense of security from the plotting of God (exalted is He): ﴿None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people.﴾ This is based on the view that the negated fear is attributed to them, but this is not decisive. Some eminent scholars have held that it is attributed to others, meaning: others do not fear for them. It does not follow from this that they do not fear, so that the hadith about the necessity of security would arise. This has been taken as the reason for the variation in the style of the two sentences, and for the departure from "nor do they fear," which would have been more suitable, to what is in the sublime arrangement [of the verse]. It may be said: if what is meant is that nothing befalls them that would necessitate fear and grief, then there remains no room for the hadith about the necessity of security from the plotting of God (exalted is He), as is not hidden from the one who reflects. But the reason for the variation in the style of the two sentences does not become clear through this, nor is it that the variation concerns the condition of fear and grief, by the prevalence of describing the latter as lacking permanence, as it has been said:

"So there is no grief that lasts, nor joy"

as opposed to the first. For this reason it was appropriate to express the first with a noun and the second with a verb indicating occurrence and renewal, as you see.

It has also been said: what is meant is the negation of fear overtaking them, and the negation of grief altogether. What this implies is that they are characterised by fear in some measure, so in this there is an indication that they are, between hope and fear, neither despairing nor secure. For this reason the two sentences were not given in one pattern. Likewise, it did not say "no fear is theirs," for example. But the most correct view in my opinion is what is reported from some eminent scholars: that the meaning of "no fear shall come upon them" is that others do not fear for them, and the first sentence is taken as a metaphor for the goodness of their condition. You are free regarding the second sentence. Fear, according to al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), is the anticipation of something disliked, and its opposite is security. Grief comes from hazan, with a fatha, which is a roughness in the soul caused by distress, and its opposite is joy. On this basis they have explained the meaning as: no fear shall come upon them of an adversity befalling them, nor shall they grieve over the loss of something hoped for.

[Page 148]

**﴿Those who believed﴾**, that is, in everything that came from God, exalted is He. **﴿And used to be God-conscious (yattaqun) 63﴾**, that is, refraining from what must be refrained from, of deeds and abandonments, with constant God-consciousness (ittiqa'an da'iman), as is indicated by combining the two forms, the past and the present (wa-al-mustaqbal). The relative pronoun is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a explanatory resumptive clause (istiʼnaf bayani), as if it were asked: "Who are they? And what is the cause of their success, which the preceding discourse has alluded to?" So it is answered: "They are those who combined faith and God-consciousness, which lead to every good, and who keep away from every evil." You may also restrict the question to "Who are they?", in which case this would be an explanation and clarification of what is meant by the friends (awliya') only. According to the first view, this is together with an indication of what they attained and gained. It has also been said that its position is in the accusative or nominative, as a expression of praise, or that it is a description of the friends (awliya'). This was rejected on the grounds that this involves separating the adjective from the noun it describes by the predicate, and the grammarians have rejected this. Yes, al-Hafid allowed it, and also allowed it to be an appositive (badal). By God-consciousness (taqwa), at the level of gathering, is meant its third rank, which is the God-consciousness commanded in His saying, exalted is He: **﴿Be conscious of God as He deserves to be feared﴾** (Q 3:102). It has been explained as a person's purification from everything that occupies his inner self away from the Truth, and a total devotion to Him, and by this is achieved the witnessing, presence and nearness on which the application of the name (wali) revolves. And thus was the state of those who were included with him, may God bless him and grant him peace, under the address in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: **﴿And you do no deed﴾** (Q 10:61), and so on, except that they have varying degrees in regard to devotion and purification, according to the degrees of the variation in their preparedness. The highest degree is that which the aspirations of the prophets, peace be upon them, reached, so that they combined thereby the leadership of prophethood and guardianship (wilaya). Attachment to the world of bodies did not hinder them from being absorbed in the world of spirits, and involvement with the interests of creation did not prevent them from devotion to the presence of the Truth, glorified be He, mighty and majestic, because of the perfection of their pure souls, supported by holy power. Thus it has been said. Regarding whether the state of everyone who was included with him, may God bless him and grant him peace, under the address, is meant to include all the Companions, may God be pleased with them, the true God-consciousness that is commanded in the verse, through which witnessing, presence and nearness are achieved, is a matter for discussion. The most that has been established, after long dispute, which we mentioned in our answer to the question from the people of Lahore, is that all the Companions are upright (udul): whoever was involved in the strife and whoever was not involved in it. As for the claim that uprightness entails guardianship in the sense mentioned above, if it is established, the aim is achieved; otherwise, it is not.

The verse clearly indicates that the friends are the believers who are God-conscious. The least that suffices for the application of the term wali is drawing near to Him, glorified be He, through the obligatory duties, by carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. The most complete is drawing near to Him, exalted be His glory, through everything that enables nearness. In **al-Mubin al-Mu'in**, the wali is one whom God, exalted is He, takes charge of His affairs Himself, so that he has no action at all, since he has no existence, essence, act or attribute. The construction indicates nearness, so it is as if he is near to Him, mighty and majestic, because of the continuity of his acts of worship and the steadiness of his obedience, and because of his being absorbed in the sea of His knowledge and in beholding the splendor of His greatness, end of quote. In it is the view that wali is an adjective (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and it was allowed that it could be in the sense of an active participle (fa'il), and it was explained as one who takes charge of the worship of God, exalted is He, and His obedience, continuously, without any interruption of disobedience. From al-Qushayri: both descriptions mean that God, exalted is He, takes charge of his affairs, and that taking charge of the worship and obedience of God, exalted is He, is a condition for guardianship, except that the first description predominates in the one who is attracted (majdhub), and the second in the seeker who is striving (salik, murid). It should not be unknown that this statement, and also what came before it, indicates that the intrusion of disobedience is incompatible with guardianship, and this is what the words of many learned men indicate. There is no claim in this of infallibility ('isma), which the community (jama'a) has not affirmed except for the prophets, peace be upon them, rather the most that is in it is the claim of protection (hifz). It has been said: "The friends are protected," and it has been explained as the non-occurrence of sin while it is possible, and the restriction is to exclude infallibility.

Yes, the term 'isma has come with the meaning of protection, explained as mentioned, and on this basis the saying of the author of the **Hizb al-Bahr** came out: "O God, protect me in my movements and my rests," because supplicating for what is among the special attributes of the prophets, peace be upon them, is not permissible, like supplicating for all impossible things, as has been verified in its place. Some have stated without restriction that the intrusion of this is not incompatible, citing what is reported from al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified: he was asked, "Does the knower of God (arif) commit adultery?" He said, "Yes," and [he cited] **﴿And the command of God is a decree decreed﴾** (Q 33:38). This was criticized on the grounds that it is to be understood as possibility in question and answer, and there is no dispute about that; the dispute is only about whether occurrence is incompatible or not incompatible. Some have said: there is no doubt that the description of guardianship does not remain at the time of being engaged in disobedience, since God-consciousness does not exist at that time by consensus, and this description depends on it; and likewise on faith, which at that time is not complete according to the people of truth, and is not realized at all. Rather what is realized is wickedness (fisq) in the intermediate position, or unbelief according to others. Likewise there is no doubt that the occurrence of disobedience does not preclude one's being described as a friend afterward, by one who is afflicted with that returning to God-consciousness and being described by what guardianship depends on. This is like one who becomes described as a believer or as upright, for example, after not having been so described. There remains the discussion about whether occurrence is incompatible with the prior description. If it is said that it is incompatible with it in the sense that, because of it, he was not previously described by what is faith and God-consciousness according to people, then there is also no doubt about the non-incompatibility in this sense, and this is clear. But if it is said that it is incompatible with it in the sense that he was not described by what was mentioned in the sight of God, exalted is He, on the basis that the God-consciousness which is a condition of the friend is perfect God-consciousness, which entails the love of God, exalted is He, and which entails protection, as is indicated in what al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "God, exalted is He, said: Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him. My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have enjoined upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." The hadith.

Some have said regarding the conditional statement: "When I love him, I am the one who guards his senses and limbs, so he does not hear, see, take, or walk except in what pleases Me and what I love, and he turns away from desires and is absorbed in acts of obedience." Close to this is the statement of al-Khattabi: "The meaning is that He facilitates for him the actions he performs with these limbs, meaning that He makes easy for him the path to what He loves, and protects him from agreeing with what He dislikes: from listening to frivolity, looking with his eyes at what is forbidden, striking with his hand what is not lawful, and striving in falsehood with his foot." Likewise is the statement of some: "The meaning is: I make the authority of My love predominate over him, until I strip him of concern with anything other than what brings him close to Me; so he becomes detached from pleasures and avoids desires, wherever he turns and wherever he faces, he meets God, exalted is He, with a sight in it and a hearing from Him, and the love of God, exalted is He, takes hold of the totality of his heart. So he does not hear, see, or do anything except what He loves, and He is for him a helper, supporter and guardian, who protects his limbs and senses." This has a basis, because when disobedience occurs it is known that he was not protected, and by this it is known that he was not beloved, and by that it is known that he was not drawing near to Him, exalted is His glory, nor was he God-conscious as He deserves; and even if people suppose him to be so, he is not among His friends, glorified be He, in reality. Yes, whoever is described with the attributes of friends outwardly must be honored and respected, treated with courtesy, and refrained from harming in any of the kinds of harm for which there is no lawful justification, such as denouncing him out of spite or envy, except in a lawful dispute or contention aimed at extracting a right or clarifying an obscure matter and the like. This is because of what the preceding hadith indicates, which includes the threat against the one who harms, to the utmost extent, and the judgment on the one who is mentioned as a friend is only according to what is apparent, if there is no text from an infallible one indicating its realization in reality. It is not according to what is with God, exalted is He, because there are sins that only the Knower of the unseen can perceive, and among them are the sins of the heart, which are deadly diseases and poisonous venoms; and also because deeds are by their endings, and these are unknown except to the Originator and Restorer, majestic is His majesty.

This is an investigation which bears signs of acceptance. Among people, some have divided guardianship into a lesser (sughra) part, in which sin may occur rarely, but one immediately hastens to repent from it; and the Allamah Ibn Hajar, may God have mercy on him, counted as protected whoever committed a sin in this way and hastened to repent of it. So occurrence, in his view, being rare together with hastening to repent does not contradict protection; what contradicts it is the repeated and frequent occurrence. Likewise, its rarity without hastening to repent. And a greater (kubra) part in which sin never occurs at all, although occurrence is possible, or even if it is impossible, as in the guardianship of the prophets, peace be upon them, and it is claimed that this is among the special features of their guardianship; then protection is more general than infallibility, and this is not improbable. You know that the saying of them, "The prophets are infallible," is clear that infallibility is a consequence of prophethood and is caused by it, and this contradicts that claim, as is not hidden. The division that has been mentioned is good, and it is known from it that most of those who claim guardianship in our time, or for whom it is claimed, have nothing of it except the claim, because of their persistence, God forbid, in major sins that they commit many times a day. May God, exalted is He, keep us and the Muslims safe from that.

And it has come from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in explanation of the friends, what is thought to be contrary to what the verse indicates in that regard. Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Tirmidhi in **Nawadir al-Usul**, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and others have reported on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, who are the friends of God?" He said: **"Those who, when they are seen, God is remembered"**, that is, because of the goodliness of their bearing and their humility.

[Page 149]

And Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi and a group of others narrated from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, God, exalted is He, has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, yet the prophets and the martyrs envy them for their seats and their nearness to God, the Exalted." A Bedouin said: "O Messenger of God, describe them for us." He said: "They are people from the scattered ones among the people and the dispersed of the tribes. Close kinship did not join them. They loved one another for God's sake and embraced one another for God's sake. On the Day of Resurrection, God, exalted is He, will place for them pulpits of light, and they will sit upon them. People will be terrified, while they will not be terrified. They are the friends of God, there is no fear upon them, nor will they grieve."

There is no contradiction in reality. What is indicated here, namely good bearing, humble submission (ikhbat) and loving one another for God's sake, are among the rulings that necessarily accompany faith (iman) and God-consciousness (taqwa), and their particular effects. They are singled out for mention because they are manifest and close to people's understanding. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned each of these according to what the station of guidance and admonition requires, encouraging a questioner or one present with respect to what he singled out for mention of their rulings.

Describing them as those whom the prophets envy for their seats and their nearness refers to their ease, in contrast with what afflicts the prophets (peace be upon them) through preoccupation with their communities. The meaning is that the prophets envy them for the combination of both matters. According to al-Kawashi, this is stated as hyperbole, and the meaning is that if a people with this description were supposed to exist, they would be these. Some verifiers said: this is a depiction of their good condition by way of figurative representation (tamthil). Whichever is the case, there is no proof in it that wilayah (closeness to God and sainthood) is superior to nubuwwah (prophethood), and one who believes that has disbelieved. It may be interpreted to mean that the wilayah of a prophet is superior to his nubuwwah, just as what al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said, which contradicts the more sound view that nubuwwah is superior to risalah (messengership), was interpreted in this manner. Likewise, for something similar to what we have mentioned, the interpretation of Jesus (peace be upon him) of this matter does not contradict what the verse indicates.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Wahb, who said: The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said: "O Jesus, who are the friends of God, exalted is He, those upon whom there is no fear, nor will they grieve?" He (peace be upon him) said: "They are those who looked at the inner reality of this world when people looked at its outward appearance. They looked at the final end of this world when people looked at its immediate pleasure. They put to death of it what they feared it would put to death of them, and they abandoned what they knew would abandon them. Accumulating from it became to them a thing of little worth, mentioning it became to them a loss, their joy in what they obtained from it became sorrow, and what stood between them and its bounty they rejected, and what stood between them and its elevation without right they abased. The world was worn out in their sight, so they do not renew it. It was ruined among them, so they do not rebuild it. It died in their breasts, so they do not revive it. They demolish it, and by it they build their hereafter. They sell it, and by it they acquire what remains for them. They rejected it, so by rejecting it they were the joyful ones. They sold it, so by selling it they were the profitable ones. They looked at its people, fallen down, among whom the exemplary punishments had come to pass, so they revived the remembrance of death and put to death the remembrance of life. They love God, glorified and exalted is He, and they are illuminated by His light and illuminate by it. For them is a wondrous report, and with them is the wondrous report. By them the Book stands, and by it they stand. By them the speech of the writers is spoken, and by it they speak. By them is the knowledge of the Book, and by it they know. They do not see any gain beyond what they have gained, nor any hope beyond what they hope for, nor any fear beyond what they dread."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 64:

﴿For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) introduced in the place of a causal explanation for the negation of their grief and fear, according to one view. According to another view, it is introduced as an explanation of the blessings of both abodes that God, exalted is He, bestowed upon them after He had informed of their deliverance
Page 151
from their evils and their hardships. It is as if, on this view, it was said: "Is there for them, beyond that, any favour and honour?" And it was answered: "For them is good news," etc. The first (the negation of fear and grief) is placed first because clearing away (al-takhliyah, removing what is harmful) precedes adorning (al-tahliyah, bestowing what is good). This also observes the principle of contrast between the good state of the believers and the bad state of the fabricators, and hastens the bringing of joy through the announcement of deliverance from the terrors. The earlier explanation is placed between the clearing away and the adorning to show the complete care for it, along with the indication that the absence of what preceded is due to their faith and their being mindful of God (ittiqa') of the causes that lead to it. Some people explained "the friends (awliya')" as those who take God as their friend through obedience, and whom He takes as His friend through honour, and they made ﴿Those who believed﴾ and what follows an explanation of their taking Him as friend. And this sentence is an explanation of His taking them as friends.

It has been objected that there is no doubt that considering the final condition as part of the concept of friendship is not suitable to the context of encouraging the believers to attain it and to remain steadfast in it, and of giving them good news of its effects and results. Rather, it is detrimental to that, since attainment relates only to what is within one's power, and rejoicing (al-istibshar) occurs only with what is known to have its cause present. The stated condition is neither within their power so that they attain friendship by attaining it, nor known to them at its occurrence so that they recognise that friendship has been attained for them and rejoice in its beautiful effects. Rather, being taken as friend with honour is the very result of friendship. So considering it in the definition of the subject, then the report of the absence of fear and grief, is something not fitting to the dignity of the glorious revelation. End of quotation.

You know that what that party has done is artificial and a deviation from the apparent meaning, so one should not turn toward it, although what the objector mentioned is not free from consideration.

It is permitted that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) be the subject (mubtada') and this sentence its predicate (khabar), and some reports support this. The word ﴿al-bushra (good news)﴾ originally means news that makes joy appear on the surface of the face, and similar to it is al-bishara. It is also applied to the thing announced through it. Some scholars held that both meanings are intended. The two adverbial phrases after it are, on the first view, connected to it. On the second view, they are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. The governing element is the sense of stability contained in the predicate, meaning: for them is good news while it is in this world and while it is in the Hereafter, that is, immediate and deferred. Or the governing element is from the genitive pronoun, meaning: while they are in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.

What is established in most of the narrations is that the good news in the life of this world is the true dream (al-ru'ya al-salihah), which is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood, as is well known. Or it is one part of seventy parts of it, as Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn Majah reported it from the former. Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, al-Bayhaqi, and others reported from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His words, glorified is He: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾. He said: 'It is the true dream that a believer sees, or that is seen for him.'" Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about that, and was answered with what has also been mentioned. He also reported through the chain of Abu Sufyan from Jabir something similar. Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu al-Shaykh, and Abu al-Qasim Ibn Mandah reported through the chain of Abu Ja'far from the aforementioned Jabir, who said: "A man from among the people of the desert came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, inform me about the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of God﴾ ﴿for them is good news﴾,' etc. The Messenger of God (ﷺ), upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿for them is good news in the life of this world﴾, it is the good dream seen by the believer, and he is given good news of it in his worldly life. As for His words, glorified is He: ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, it is the good news to the believer at death, that God has forgiven you and whoever carries you to your grave.'" It has come both as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and as a mawquf (traced to a Companion) from more than one source, that its interpretation is what has been mentioned.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, that the good news in the life of this world is His words, exalted is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And give good news to the believers that for them is a great bounty from God﴾. It was also reported from al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' that it is this and what resembles it from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And give good news to those who believed that for them is a sure standing with their Lord﴾,
Page 152
and His words, glorified is He: ﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him﴾, the verse, and His words, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And give good news to the patient﴾, and so on. Ibn Abi Shaybah and others reported from al-Dahhak that he said concerning this: "They know where they are before they die." What you have heard in the report from Jabir, the last one, has come in the explanation of the good news in the Hereafter.

Ibn Jarir and others reported from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet, that it is Paradise. And from Ata' that the good news in this world is that the angels come to them at death with mercy. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The angels descend upon them, [saying]: "Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in the Paradise you were promised"﴾. As for the good news in the Hereafter, it is that the angels meet them as those who have submitted, given good news of success and honour, and of what they see of the whiteness of their faces, the giving of their records into their right hands, what they read from them, and other good news. It was also said: the intended immediate good news is like victory, conquest, booty, good praise, good remembrance, and people's love, and other such things; as for the deferred good news, it is clear without explanation. You know that one should not turn away from what has been transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in explaining this, if it is authentic. Whoever turned away did so, as far as I think, because he did not come upon it. So it is better to take the good news in both abodes as the announcement of what confirms the negation of fear and grief, whatever it may be. The context guides to this, and for this reason the angels give them this good news from time to time until they enter Paradise. The Noble Book has declared in more than one place this good news from God to us, by His mercy and generosity: ﴿There is no altering of the words of God﴾, meaning there is no changing of His sayings, among which are His promises given as good news to the believing, God-fearing. Thus the good news mentioned here enters into them at the first level, and the impossibility of breaking them is confirmed definitively, out of kindness and generosity. And it was intended, from the non-alteration of His words, glorified is He, on the assumption that the true dream is meant by the good news, the non-contradiction between it and what indicates its establishment and occurrence in what will come by way of the promise, from His words, blessed is His name: ﴿For them is good news﴾, not the non-contradiction between it and its worldly and otherworldly results. I have not perceived its aspect after reflection. It is well known that the true dream does not contradict what it indicates.

It has come from the hadith of al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and others, "from Ubadah, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him concerning the true dream: 'It is a speech by which your Lord speaks to His servant in sleep.'" ﴿That﴾, meaning what has been mentioned, that for them is good news in both abodes, ﴿is the great success﴾ (64), beyond which there is no success. It is permitted that the demonstrative refers to the good news in the sense of the act of giving good news. And it was said: that refers to the bliss through which the good news occurred. Many scholars considered the first sentence and this sentence as a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh), introduced to confirm the thing announced in order to magnify its status. This is based on the permissibility of multiple parenthetical clauses and on the permissibility of its occurring at the end of the speech. For this reason the scholar al-Tibi (al-Tayyibi) said: "If you make the first a parenthetical clause and the second a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the parenthetical clause and for what it is inserted into, and confirming both of them, it would be better, based on the view that what comes at the end of a speech is called a tadhyil, and that it is an i'tiradh, which is merely a terminological convention."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 65:

Whoever takes His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And let not their saying grieve you﴾ as coordinated with the preceding sentence, meaning that the friends of Allah have no fear upon them nor do they grieve, so let not the saying of the enemies of Allah, exalted is He, grieve you, then the parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) for him lies between two connected parts and not at the end of the speech, but it is nothing (lays no weight). What the majority (al-Jumhur) hold is that it is a new sentence (isti'naf) brought to console the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for what he encountered from the enemies in terms of harm arising from their vile and savage utterances, and as a glad tiding to him, peace be upon him, of victory and might following the statement that for him and his followers there is security from every fearful thing and success in every sought-after thing. So it is connected in meaning to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah﴾ etc. It has also been said: it is connected to His, glorified is He, saying: (If they deny you, then say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work") the verse. Al-Tabarsi preferred this, despite its remoteness.

صفحة 153

Naf'i (Nafi') recited ﴿And let not grieve you﴾ with the form of causative (man aḥzana), and in reality it is a prohibition to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, against grief, as if it were said: Do not grieve over their saying, and do not care about everything they utter concerning your matter, of what has no good in it. And it was turned away from to what is in the sublime arrangement only for the sake of emphasis in prohibiting grief, since the prohibition against the effect (ta'thir) is a prohibition against being affected at its root and a negation of it entirely. A parallel to this, as has passed more than once, is their saying: "Let me not see you here" and "Let not the beast of prey devour you" and the like, where the prohibition has been directed to the necessary consequence while the intended meaning is the prohibition of the necessitating cause. It has been said: The specification of the prohibition against grief with mention, along with the general negation preceding it extending to fear as well, is because there was no trace of fear in him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he would be forbidden from it, and perhaps grief would overtake him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at some times, so he was consoled about it. It is not hidden that if we say fear and grief are close in meaning, so that when they are combined they separate, and when they separate they combine, as you have known a moment ago, then the prohibition against grief is also a prohibition against fear. However, the better course is not to take into account what carries the suspicion of attributing fear to his sacred presence, peace be upon him, even though there would be no deficiency in that. For the prohibition of the prophets, peace be upon them, against fear has come just as their prohibition against grief has come; indeed, the attribution of that to them has been established explicitly, and it does not harm the rank of prophethood, since not every fear is a deficiency, that they should be exempted from it, however it may be.

﴿Surely might belongs to Allah entirely﴾ is a new sentence brought to give the reason for the prohibition. It has also been said: it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: Why should it not grieve him? So it was said: Because dominance and subjugation belong to Allah, glorified is He; no one possesses any share of them at all, neither they nor others. So He does not subdue or overcome His friends, rather He subdues them, overcomes them, and protects you from them. Abu Haywa recited (inna) with a fatḥa, as explicit causation, meaning "because." Qutayba ibn Muslim took that as a substitution (badal), then rejected the recitation for it, because it would lead to saying: "So let not grieve you that might belongs to Allah entirely," which is corrupt. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that if it were taken as a substitution it would also have a valid aspect, on the pattern of (and do not be a supporter of the disbelievers) and ﴿and do not call upon another god with Allah﴾, so that it is for stirring up, encouraging and indirect address to someone else; but this is remote.

﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ (65): He hears their sayings concerning you and knows what they conceal against you, so He will requite them for that. What we have mentioned of the verse is the apparent and immediate meaning.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: When they did not benefit from what came to them from Allah, glorified is He, and persisted in their disbelief, that weighed heavily upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so there came to him from Allah, glorified is He, in rebuke to him: ﴿And let not their saying grieve you, that might belongs to Allah entirely; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears what they say and knows it, so if He willed, by His might He would take vengeance on them. It is not hidden that this is very far from the apparent meaning, together with what it contains of attaching knowledge to what has been attached to hearing. Perhaps his narration from the rabbi (al-Habr) is not one to be relied upon.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 66:

﴿Surely, to God belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth.﴾ That is, of the angels and the two weighty ones (the jinn and humankind), as is indicated by the expression "man" (من, man), which is commonly used for rational beings. Giving precedence to the rational beings (al-taghlib) is not appropriate here. The reason for specifying them by mention is to signal that there is no need to state explicitly anything other than them, for they, despite their nobility and high rank, are, if they are servants and possessions of God, glorified be He, then whatever else is among existent things is more deserving of this. The sentence, together with the emphasis it contains on what preceded, namely the exclusivity of might to Him, exalted is His majesty, which necessitates consolation for him, upon him be blessings and peace, and his not being concerned with the statements of the polytheists, serves as a preparation for what follows of His words, glorified be He: ﴿And those who call upon other than God as partners do not follow them﴾, and as evidence for the falsity of their assumptions and their actions based upon them. Restricting it to one of the two matters is deficient, so do not be among the deficient.

"Ma" (ما) is negative, and "shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ) is the object of "yattabi'" (يَتَّبِعُ), and the object of "yad'una" (يَدْعُونَ) is omitted due to its being evident. That is: those who call upon other than God as partners do not follow partners, (partners) in reality, even though they name them partners due to their ignorance. So the intended meaning is the negation of the attribute in reality and in actual fact. What Abu al-Baqa' mentioned regarding the impermissibility of this mode of i'rab (grammatical analysis), because it indicates the negation of their following partners even though they did follow them, arises from heedlessness of what we have mentioned.

It is also permitted that "shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ) mentioned is the object of "yad'una" (يَدْعُونَ), and the object of "yattabi'" (يَتَّبِعُ) is omitted because it is understood from His words, glorified be He: ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾. That is: they do not follow certainty; rather, they follow only their false conjecture, or their conjecture that they are partners, by supposing an object for the conjecture, or by treating it as intransitive. Some have supposed the object of "yattabi'una" (يَتَّبِعُونَ) to be "shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ), inclining toward applying the second (verb) in the case of tanazu' (contention of verbs). This has been criticized: it cannot be of that category, because the object of the first verb is restricted while the second is not, so the object is not unified, and unification is a condition in that matter. That the restriction is incidental after the application, by the indication of its governing verb, does not contradict what is stipulated in that section, as is not hidden.

It is also permitted that "ma" (ما) be interrogative, governed by "yattabi'" (يَتَّبِعُ), and "shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ) be the object of "yad'una" (يَدْعُونَ). That is: what thing do the polytheists follow? That is, what they follow is nothing. And that it be relative, conjoined to "man" (مَن): that is, and for Him, exalted is He, is whatever the polytheists follow, of creation and of angels; so how could it be a partner to Him, glorified be He? The specification of this by mention, although it is included in what preceded, is an expression or an indication of exaggeration in clarifying the falsity of following and the corruption of what they built upon it of conjecture, which is corruption indeed. It is also permitted, on the assumption of the relative reading, that it be a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: false, and the like; or that the predicate be His words, glorified be He: "in following" (أنْ يَتَّبِعُونَ), with the returning pronoun omitted, that is: in His worship, or in their following.

And al-Sulami read "tad'una" (تَدْعُونَ) with the second-person ta' of address, and this is related from Ali, may God honor his face. It is a well-founded reading, contrary to the claim of one who asserts otherwise, for "ma" in it is interrogative for rebuke and reproach, the returning pronoun to "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) is omitted, and "shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it. The intended "alladhina" are the angels, the Messiah and Uzayr, peace be upon them. So it is as if it were said: What thing do those whom you call upon follow, being, in your claim, partners, of the angels and prophets, as an affirmation that they follow God, exalted, and obey Him, and as a reproach to them for not taking them as models in that, like His words, glorified be He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord﴾. The summary of it is that those whom you worship worship God, exalted, and worship none other than Him; so why do you not take them as models and follow them in that? Then the speech turns from address to the third person, so it is said: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and they are only guessing﴾, that is: they only estimate and conjecture that they are partners, an invalid estimation; or they lie in what they attribute to Him, glorified and exalted be He. The "khars" (خَرْص) is either in the sense of estimation and guessing, as is its common primary usage, or in the sense of lying, for its use in that sense has come about because of its prevalence in such contexts.

He is the One who made the night for you that you might rest therein, and the day giving sight (﴿mubsiran﴾). This is an alert to His being singular in complete power and all-encompassing blessing, so that they may be led to recognize His oneness in deserving worship. The definiteness of the two terms (the night and the day) is for restriction (qasr), specifically qasr ta'yin (restriction of specification). This also reaffirms what preceded, namely that all possible existents are under His power and dominion, which makes clear that might belongs exclusively to Him, glory be to Him.

The verb ja'ala (made) may mean innovating and creating, in which case mubsiran is a circumstantial state (hal). If it means making or rendering, then the second object is either ﴿li-taskunu fihi﴾ (that you may rest therein), or it is omitted and indicated by the second object of the second clause, just as the final cause of the second clause is omitted, relying on what is mentioned in the first. The sense is: He is the One who made for you the night dark, that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight, that you may move about in it for your benefits. Thus, from each of the two clauses, something mentioned in the other is omitted, being content with what is stated over what is left out. On this reading the verse contains the rhetorical device of ihtibak (a device in which corresponding elements are dropped from parallel clauses, each clause supplying what is missing from the other). The verse is commonly cited as an example of this, and this is the apparent reading, although it is not strictly necessary. For this reason, a group of scholars held that there is no ihtibak in it. The departure from ﴿li-tubsiru fihi﴾ (that you may see therein), which is what the preceding context would require, to the wording found in this sublime composition, is to distinguish between the prepositional adverbial phrase that is a cause on which the act depends in general.

Attributing sight (ibsar) to the day is a metaphor (majaz), like the usage in the verse of Jarir:

"You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, for travelling by night, yet you slept, while the night of the mounts does not sleep."

and like their saying "its day is fasting," and other usages too numerous to count. Ibn Atiyyah and a group of others took this view. It has also been said that mubsiran is a relative adjective (nisba), like laabin and tamir (having milk and having dates), meaning "possessing sight."

﴿Inna fi dhalika﴾ (Indeed, in that): that is, in the aforementioned making, or in the night and the day. The distance implied in the demonstrative (dhalika) indicates the exalted rank of what is referred to and its high status.

﴿la-ayatin﴾ (are signs): that is, proofs and indications of God's oneness, many in number, or other signs besides what has been mentioned.

﴿li-qawmin yasma'un﴾ (for a people who hear): that is, who hear the proofs in general with the hearing of reflection and consideration. Or it means those who hear these recited verses and their like, which alert to those cosmic signs and command reflection upon them, with that hearing, and so they act in accordance with their requirements. The specific mention of these people, although the signs are set up for the benefit of all, is because they are the ones who benefit from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 68:

﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ This begins the mention of another kind of the polytheists' falsehoods and the demonstration of its invalidity. By "these polytheists" is meant, as has been said, the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, for they said: "The angels are the daughters of God, exalted is He." And the Jews and Christians who said: 'Uzayr and 'Isa, upon them be peace, are His sons, glorified and exalted is He. The verb "ittakhadha" (took) is explicit about adoption, and the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that this is the statement of every polytheist. If it is established that some of them say that begetting and procreation are literal, then what is here is the statement of a part, and one should consider whether the possibility of attributing to the whole what belongs to a part applies here, since its condition is fulfilled, or does not apply for lack of that condition. The word "walad" (son, child) is used in the singular and the plural.

In the Qamus: "al-walad" (with a fatha on the lam, and with a damma, kasra, or fatha on the waw and the lam) is one and plural, and it may be pluralized as "awlad," "walada" and "ildah" (with kasra on both), and "wuld" (with damma), and it includes the male and the female.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: a declaration of His transcendence and holiness, exalted above what they attribute to Him, according to the basic meaning of "subhan." It may also be used figuratively to express wonder, and it is valid to intend that here, the meaning being wonder at their foolish statement. Some combined between the declaration of transcendence and the expression of wonder, and perhaps this is based on the view that wonder is a kinaya (implicit meaning), and that it is valid to intend the literal meaning within the kinaya, which is one of the two opinions on the question. It was said, however, that it is not necessary that the meaning of wonder be derived from the use of the word in it; rather it is among the secondary meanings (al-ma'ani al-thawani).

His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾, meaning, free of need of everything, in every respect. It is a reason for His exalted transcendence above that, and an indication that taking a son results from need, which is either fear of poverty or, for example, the preservation of the species.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning, of rational and non-rational beings. It is an affirmation of the meaning of "Self-Sufficient," because the owner of all existents is the Self-Sufficient, and all else is needy. It was also said that it is a second reason for transcendence above adoption, because it contradicts ownership.

His saying, majestic is His dignity: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, meaning, no proof for this, that is, for what has been mentioned of the false statement. It is a clarification of its invalidity by establishing that the clear proof presented is free from any opposition or contradiction. The particle "in" is negative, and "min" is extra, for the emphasis of negation; its governed noun is the subject, and the preceding adverbial phrase is its predicate, or it is in the nominative as the agent, since it relies on the negation. "Bihadha" (for this) is connected either to "sultan" (authority), because it means proof as you have heard, or to something omitted that occurs as its attribute. It was said it occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of the hidden pronoun in the adverbial phrase which refers back to it. Or it is connected to the meaning of settledness contained in ﴿ʿindakum﴾ (with you), and on this view it is necessary that "sultan" be the agent of the adverbial phrase, lest there be a separation between the implicit operator and its complement by a foreign element. The turn to address (second person) is for greater emphasis in imposing obligation and confounding, and for reinforcing what is in His saying, exalted is He:
Page 156
﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ 68, of rebuke and reproach for their ignorance and fabrication. In the verse there is evidence that every statement for which there is no proof is ignorance, that beliefs must have a decisive basis, and that imitation (taqlid) is far from guidance. It is not suitable as a ground for rejecting analogy (qiyas) and acting on solitary reports (khabar al-ahad), because that concerns the branches (furu'), whereas this verse is specific to the fundamentals (usul), on account of the proofs that have established its specification, even though its apparent wording is general.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 69:

﴿Say﴾ is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning of the address toward the master of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so as to make clear the evil of their outcome and the grimness of their end. In this there is a warning to them against persisting in what they are in, and to others against falling into the like of it. ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah﴾ in every matter. The fabrication (iftira') includes, in the first instance, attributing a son and a partner to Him, exalted is He, and this is more appropriate than restricting the statement to what the discussion is about. In that case, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is meant to cover those addressed and others, i.e., whoever has this attribute, whoever they may be. ﴿Will not succeed﴾ (la yuflihun) means they will not be saved from any harm, nor will they attain any desired thing at all. Included in this is their not being saved from the Fire and not attaining Paradise. Restricting it to this (i.e., the Fire and Paradise) is in the context of intensifying the rebuke against fabricating lies about Him, glorified is He, rather than generalizing it as the context allows.

﴿Mata'un fi al-dunya﴾ [a comfort of this worldly life] is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "It is" or "That is a comfort." The tanwin (nunation) is for belittling and diminishing. The adverbial phrase "fi al-dunya" is attached to a deleted verb-phrase that functions as a qualifier (na't) of the noun. The sentence is a resumptive statement (kalam mustani'af), brought as an answer to an assumed question about what appears to be the case for them outwardly, namely their attaining their desires and achieving worldly portions in general, or within the context of their fabrication, and as an explanation that this is far from being of the kind of success (falah). It is as if it were said: "How could they not prosper while they are in prosperity and luxury?" So it is said: "That is a petty, little comfort in the worldly life, and it is not success in attaining what is sought." Then, the absence of deliverance from what is disliked is also indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then to Us is their return﴾, meaning: their return to Our judgment by death, so they will meet everlasting misery. ﴿Then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: because of their persistent disbelief, or because of their disbelief in the worldly life. So where are they from success?

What we have mentioned, that "mata'un" is the predicate of a deleted subject, is the view taken by more than one of the grammarians (mu'arribin). However, Abu al-Baqa' and others among them estimated the subject to be "their life," or "their turning about," or "their fabrication." The last estimate has been objected to on the grounds that "mata'" is only applied to what is inclined toward by the soul, desired in itself, enjoyed and benefited from; the reason it is not regarded is its rapid disappearance, whereas fabrication against Him, glorified is He, is in itself among the worst of ugly things in the soul, let alone being inclined toward by it. It has been answered that the application of "mata'" to that is based on the consideration that it is inclined toward by their evil souls, and that there is benefit for them in it according to what they consider to be a benefit, even if it is among the worst of ugly things and not truly beneficial in reality. It is not hidden that the first view, despite this, is more preferable. It has also been said that the mentioned term is a subject with a deleted predicate, meaning: "For them is a comfort," etc., and this is not far-fetched. The verse is either conveyed from Him, glorified is He, to establish that they will not prosper, not part of the speech commanded to be delivered, which is what the apparent sense of His words, glorified is He, ﴿Then to Us is their return﴾ and His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then We will make them taste﴾ indicates; or it is part of it, on the basis that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to convey it and relate it from Him, exalted is His majesty, and the Noble Book contains parallels to this.

﴿And recite to them﴾, that is, to the polytheists among the people of Makkah and others, to confirm what has preceded concerning the failure of the fabricators, the fact that what they enjoy is on the verge of passing away, and that they are on the brink of everlasting misery and severe punishment. ﴿The account of Noah﴾, that is, his report, which has significance and importance, concerning his people, who are similar to your people in disbelief and obstinacy.

[Page 157]

So that they may reflect upon what it contains of admonition, and perhaps they will desist from what they are upon, or the severity of their stubbornness will be broken. Perhaps also some of those who hear this from you, among those who denied the validity of your prophethood, will acknowledge its validity and believe in you, by way of its having become established for them that what is recited agrees with what it contains, without any contradiction to it at all. Then he will recall that you did not hear that from anyone, nor did you acquire it from a book, so there is no way for you to know it except through revelation, which is the basis of prophethood.

In this there is a confirmation of what has preceded, namely that all belongs to Allah, Glorified is He, that might is exclusively His, Exalted is He, that there is no fear for His friends and no grief for them, an encouragement of the Prophet (ﷺ), and an urging upon him not to care about them and their words and deeds, which is evident. Restricting this to some of it is deficient. The discussion concerning Noah, peace be upon him, has already been mentioned.

﴿When he said to his people﴾: the lam (اللّامُ) is for communication (lil-tabligh) or for causation (lil-ta'lil), and (إذْ, "when") is either a badal (substitute) for (نَبَأ, "account") as badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), or it is an operand governed by it (معمولة له), not by (اتْلُ, "recite"), because that would corrupt the meaning. Abu al-Baqa' permitted its being attached to an implied element that functions as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of (نَبَأ). In any case, what is meant is only part of his account, peace be upon him, not everything that took place between him and his people. They were, as al-Ajhuri said, from the descendants of Qabil.

﴿O my people, if my standing﴾ has been burdensome to you, that is, has been great and difficult for you, ﴿my standing﴾, that is, my self, though it is originally a noun of place, and it is intended to mean the self by way of indirect metonymy (kināya īmā'iyya), as one says: "the exalted assembly." It may also be a mīmī verbal noun meaning residence, as one says: "I stood in the place" and "I resided (aqamtu)," meaning: my residence among you for a lengthy period. That it was, as Allah the Exalted mentioned, a thousand years less fifty years, requires that the statement be in the last part of his life and the end of his affair, which would need transmission. Or the intended meaning is his standing in calling them, and close to this is his standing to remind and admonish them, because the preacher used to stand among those he admonished, since that is more prominent and more conducive to listening, as is related about Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to preach to the disciples while standing and they were seated. Our Prophet (ﷺ) often stood on the pulpit and admonished the congregation while they were seated. Thus "standing" is made a metonym or metaphor for that, or it is an expression for the establishment and consolidation of that.

﴿And my reminding﴾ you ﴿with the signs of Allah﴾, which indicate His oneness and nullify what you are upon of polytheism, ﴿then upon Allah I have relied﴾, not upon other than Him. The clause is the response of the conditional, and it is an expression for his not caring and not turning his attention to their hostility. It is also permissible that it stands in the place of the response. It was said that the response is omitted, and this (the following clause) is coordinated with it, meaning: so do what you wish. It was also said that what is meant is continuance in restricting reliance to Him, Exalted is He, and it is permissible that what is meant is the producing of a specific rank among the ranks of reliance, since otherwise he, peace be upon him, is always relying upon Him, Glorified is He, and not upon other than Him.

His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾ is, according to the majority, coordinated with the stated response, and the fa' (فاء) is for the sequencing of the command to resolve upon reliance, not for the sequencing of resolving itself upon it. It was also said that it is the response itself, and what preceded is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), and this would be introduced by the fa'. So know this, for the knowledge of a person benefits him.

Perhaps this is less problematic than what preceded, given what you have heard, along with what it involves of the coordination of an imperative upon a declarative, and there is discussion on this.

(أجْمِعُوا, "resolve") is with a cut hamza, and it is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, from (أجْمَعْتُ عَلى الأمْرِ, "I resolved upon the matter") when one has determined upon it, except that the preposition was dropped, so the verb reached its object directly. It was said that (أجْمَعَ) is transitive by itself, and he cited for it the verse of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

They resolved their affair at night, but when they arose in the morning, a clamor was theirs.

Al-Sudusi stated that omitting (عَلى, "upon") as in (أجْمَعْتُ الأمْرَ, "I resolved the matter") is more eloquent than including it as in (أجْمَعْتُ عَلى الأمْرِ). Abu al-Haytham said: the meaning of (أجْمَعَ أمْرَهُ, "he gathered his affair") is that he made it gathered after it had been scattered, and (تَفَرَّقْتُهُ, "to scatter it") is that one says at one time "I will do this," and at another time "I will do that." When he determines, he has gathered what was scattered of his determination. Then it came to mean determination, to the extent that it reached (عَلى, "upon"), though its original transitivity is directly. According to some there is no difference between (أجْمَعَ) and (جَمَعَ, "gathered"), while others distinguished between them, saying the former is used for abstract meanings and the latter for concrete objects. So one says "I resolved my affair" and "I gathered the army." Perhaps it is more frequent but not constant. The meaning of "affair" here is something like scheming and plotting.

﴿And your partners﴾, that is, those whom you claimed to be partners of Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He. It is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (مَفْعُولٌ مَعَهُ) from the subject (of the verb), because the partners are the ones resolving, not the ones resolved upon. This is supported by the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and 'Isa al-Thaqafi in the nominative, for then it is apparently coordinated with the attached pronoun in the nominative, and the presence of the intervening element serves in place of emphasis with the detached pronoun.

It was also said that it is a subject with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your partners will gather," and similar. It was also said that the accusative is by coordination upon (أمْرَكُمْ, "your affair"), with an omitted modifying element, meaning "and the affair of your partners," based on the view that (أجْمَعَ) relates to abstract meanings, and the speech is in the manner of mockery, on the basis that the partners meant are idols. It was also said that it is on its apparent sense, and what is meant by them is those who follow their religion. It was also permitted that there is no omission, and the speech is an attribution to the metaphorical object, in the manner of what has been said about ﴿and ask the town﴾. It was also said that this is by way of the object of a hidden verb, as has been said about his saying: "I fed her chaff and cold water," meaning: "and call upon your partners," as Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, read.

Nafi' read (فاجْمَعُوا) with a joined hamza and a fatha on the mim, from (جَمَعَ, "to gather"). The coordination of "partners" upon "affair" in this reading is clear, based on the idea that one says "I gathered my partners" just as one says "I gathered my affair." Some claimed that the meaning is "let your affair be gathered," but as you see, this is not the case. The meaning is that he commanded them to determine and resolve upon his killing, and to strive to destroy him by whatever means would enable them to scheme and the like, trusting in Allah, the Exalted, and due to their lack of concern. The intended meaning is not the literal command.

﴿Then let not your affair﴾ be ﴿a concealed matter upon you﴾, that is, covered, from (غَمَّهُ, "he covered it") when he covered it. From this is the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr: "There is no concealment (ghumma) in the obligations of Allah, the Exalted," meaning it is not hidden or concealed, but rather it is manifested and announced. The prepositional phrase is attached to (غُمَّةَ, "concealment"). The intended meaning is a prohibition against them engaging in what would make it concealed, for a command is not prohibited, and this entails a command to manifestation. So the meaning is: make that manifest and openly declare it to me, for concealment is only resorted to in order to block the door of seeking deliverance by flight or the like. Since that is impossible in my case, there is no point in concealment. The word (ثُمَّ, "then") here is for delay in rank. Using the explicit noun "affair" in place of the pronoun is for the increase of emphasis. It was said: it is more apparent, because what is meant by it is what befalls them from him, peace be upon him, of severe distress that is disagreeable to them, not the first matter. What is meant by "concealment" is distress, like "anguish" and "grief." The prepositional phrase is attached to an implied element that functions as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of it. (ثُمَّ, "then") here is for delay in time, and the meaning is: then let your state not be a grief upon you, and be released by my destruction from the burden of my standing and my reminding with the signs of Allah. This has been objected to on the grounds that it is not supported by His saying, Exalted is His glory: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite﴾, that is, deliver to me that matter which you intend and do not delay me, on the basis that (القَضاءُ, "decision") is from (قَضى دَيْنَهُ, "he settled his debt") when he paid it, and its object is omitted as we have indicated. In this there is an implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya), and "decision" is an imaginative element (takhyīl). Some have explained "decision" as judgment, meaning: judge by what you deliver to me, and in this there is an implicit metaphor (tadmīn) and also an implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya), because placing what occurs after destruction between the command to resolve upon its beginnings and the command to carry out its decision is like separating wood from its bark. The first interpretation is free of this, and it is evident. It was said: what is meant by "concealment" is the first meaning, by "affair" what has preceded, and by the prohibition the command to consult, meaning: resolve your affair, then consult about it, and after it, because neither of the two orders indicated by them is manifest. Then, whether the reading of the majority or the reading of Nafi' in (اجْمَعُوا) is considered, it was read (أفْضُوا إلَيَّ, "come forth to me") with a fa', meaning: reach me with your evil, or: bring yourselves out to me, from (أفْضى, "he went out into the open space") when he went out into the open area, like (أبْرَزَ, "he came out") when he went out into the open ground (al-birāz), which is a wide place.

﴿Then if you turn away﴾, meaning: you remain in your aversion to my admonition, or you newly adopt a specific aversion to it after you have come to know my affair and witnessed from me what confirms the truth of my words. [Page 159] ﴿then I have not asked you﴾ in return for my reminder and admonition, ﴿for any wage﴾ that you would pay me, so that it would be paid back to you, up to the point of your turning away, either because you accuse me of greed, or because paying what is asked of you is burdensome, or so that your turning away, which leads to deprivation, would harm me. The first reading serves to show the invalidity of turning away by explaining the absence of what would validate it, and the second serves to show that he, peace be upon him, was indifferent to whether they existed or did not exist. On either reading, the first ﴿fa﴾ (then) marks the consequence of this condition upon the response before it, and the second ﴿fa﴾ marks the condition as a cause for informing about the content of the response after it, as one of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin) mentioned. That is: if you turn away, then know that there is no validator for it at first, so that it is affected by it, in the manner said regarding the Almighty's words: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none who can remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent﴾.

Some scholars held that the answer to the condition is omitted, and what was mentioned, which is its cause, has taken its place. That is: there is no incentive for you to turn away and no reason for it; or: then there is no harm to me from that. The words of some indicate that, with the consideration of the omission and the substitution mentioned, the consideration of the condition as a cause for informing comes in, and this is what taste (dhawq) inclines towards. The ﴿min﴾ (from) is extra, for emphasis, meaning: ﴿so I have not asked you any wage﴾. The Almighty's words ﴿My wage is only from Allah﴾ are an emphasis of what precedes it on the first meaning, and a justification for his, peace be upon him, being independent of them on the second meaning. That is: my reward for the exhortation and reminder is only from Him, the Exalted; He rewards me for it, whether you believe or turn away. The words of the Glorified: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among those who submit﴾ (72) are a tadhyil (concluding appendix) to what precedes, according to what has been said, confirming its content. The meaning is: I have been commanded to be included among the Muslims who take no payment for teaching the religion and do not seek worldly gain through it. In this there is the interpretation of Islam as synonymous with faith, with consideration of the restriction. Some scholars turned away from this because of what it contains of a kind of strain, and so they interpreted Islam as submission and compliance, without restriction, meaning: I have been commanded to be among those who yield to His judgment, not opposing His command and not hoping for other than Him. In this, on this meaning too, there is of the emphasis of what came before and the confirmation of its content what is not hidden. The emphasis does not become clear on the assumption that the meaning is "among those who submit to every affliction that befalls them in obedience to Allah, the Exalted"; its manifestness is on the two previous assumptions.

In sum: he, peace be upon him, did not fall short in guiding them with this speech, and he reached the utmost extent in it.

Some scholars mentioned the reason for the composition in this style according to some of the possible aspects, and said: He, peace be upon him, said at the beginning: ﴿In Allah I have put my trust﴾, thereby showing his reliance on his Lord, the Glorified; meaning: I have trusted in Him, so do not suppose that your threat to kill and harm me prevents me from calling to Allah, the Exalted. Then he presented to them what indicates the truth of his claim, saying: ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾, as if he were saying: gather together all that you are able to do of the things that bring about the attainment of your aim. Then he did not limit himself to that, but commanded them to add to themselves their partners whom they used to claim would strengthen their state by their standing and by drawing near to them. Then he did not limit himself to these two, but added a third to them, which is his saying: ﴿Then let not your affair be obscured to you﴾, so he wanted them to strive in their affair to the utmost effort and exert themselves to the utmost exertion, until their life would be pleasant. Then he did not limit himself to that, until he added a fourth to it, saying: ﴿Then carry it out upon me﴾, commanding them to deliver all of that to him. Then he added to that a fifth: ﴿and do not give me respite﴾, forbidding them from delaying. In this there is an indication that he, peace be upon him, had reached the utmost extent in trusting in Allah, the Glorified, and that he was certain that their plot would not harm him nor reach him, and that their scheme would not take effect against him, which is clearer than the sun and more evident than yesterday.

Then, peace be upon him, wanted to make the proof binding upon them and to clear his own position, so he negated that he asked them for any part of a wage, and confirmed this by saying that his wage is with Allah, the Glorified, not with anyone else, pointing to the abundance of [Page 160] His generosity, the Exalted in majesty, and that He rewards him for his act, whether he asked for a wage or did not ask. For this reason he did not say: "My asking for a wage is only from Allah, the Exalted." Then he did not suffice with that, until he added that he was commanded to what includes not asking them and not looking to what they possess, and to be characterized by it in its most perfect form, because ﴿among the Muslims﴾ is more eloquent than "Muslim," as has been established in its proper place. In this there is a cutting off of whatever might come between them and answering his call and taking heed of his admonition. However, the people had reached the utmost extent of obstinacy and rebellion.

﴿So they denied him﴾, i.e., they persisted after he, peace be upon him, had left them no means of escape in the bow of argument (*qaws al-ilzam*), and in the cup of clarification no pretext for their turning away except rebellion, drunk down. This is their continued denial, which the preceding and following context indicates. It is a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon the clause "﴿He said to his people﴾." The *fa'* in "﴿So We saved him﴾" is *fasihah* (an explanatory *fa'*, one that signals an omitted condition) according to one opinion, meaning: "So the word of punishment was due against them, and We saved him." Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) denied this and claimed that the mention of what it points to in the wording of some exegetes (*mufassirun*) is a preparation for the consequent clause (*tawtiʾah lil-tafriʿ*), not an indication that the *fa'* is *fasihah*. I see no harm in the first view, but the estimate "so We dealt with each as wisdom requires" and the like is, in my view, preferable.
