The object of the saving is omitted, i.e., from the drowning, as the context indicates. It was also said: from the hands of the disbelievers, so We delivered him from that. ﴿And those with him﴾ refers to the believers in him. According to the well-known report they were forty men and forty women, and it was said fewer than that. ﴿In the ship﴾, i.e., the ark, here in the singular (*mufrad*). The prepositional phrase, as al-Ajhuri and others said, is connected to "We saved him," i.e., the saving took place in the ship. It may also be connected to the "settling" (*al-istiqrar*) to which the adverbial phrase before it is attached as a relative clause: "and those who settled with him in the ship."

﴿And We made them successors﴾ of those who had perished by drowning in the flood. *Khala'if* is the plural of *khalifah*. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, and they are the rest of his people. Referring to them by the relative pronoun signals that the content of the relative clause is the cause of the drowning. The mention of the drowning is delayed after the mention of the saving and the succession, in order to show complete concern with the matter of the first mentioned, to hasten joy for the hearers, and to signal that mercy, which is among the requirements of lordship, precedes wrath, which is among the consequences of the crimes of the guilty.

﴿Then see how was the end of those warned﴾, i.e., those made to fear God and His punishment. By them are meant the deniers. Referring to them in this way indicates their persistence in denial, since the warning had no effect on them and did not benefit them at all. It is God's customary practice not to destroy a people by annihilation except after warning, for whoever is warned has been given an excuse. Looking (*al-nazar*), as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is by the eye and by insight, and the latter is more common among the elite. The speech is brought to magnify what befell them, to warn whoever denies the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to console him, may God bless him and grant him peace. The meaning is: consider what God has reported, for it is not possible that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, or those he warned, look at it directly.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 74:

﴿Then We sent﴾, i.e., We sent after him, that is, after Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿messengers﴾, i.e., noble ones possessing a great deal of excuse (ʿudhr). The indefinite form ﴿messengers﴾ is for magnification and multiplication. ﴿To their peoples﴾. It has been said: i.e., to their nations, in the sense that every messenger of God was sent to a particular people, such as Hud to ʿAd, Salih to Thamud, and others, whether those whose stories are told or those whose stories are not told. It does not mean that every messenger was sent to the peoples of all of them, or to whatever people they were. In this there is an indication that the universality of the message to mankind was not established for any of those messengers, peace be upon them. The apparent sense of their statements is a consensus (ijmaʿ) that this universality is specific to our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and was not established for anyone sent after Noah. There is a difference of opinion concerning Noah, peace be upon him, as to whether he was sent to the people of the earth in its entirety or to a region of it. Upon this depends the discussion of whether the Flood covered all the people of the earth or was only for some of them, namely the people of his call who denied him, as the apparent meaning of many verses and hadiths indicates. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The preferred view among the scholars who verify (muhaqqiqun) is the second, and many of the people of the earth, such as the people of China and others, deny the universality of the Flood. The first view does not contradict the claim that the universality of the message, in the well-known sense of universality lying between general and specific, is specific to our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, because it applies to those after him until the Day of Resurrection.

Some have claimed that the Flood was general while the mission was specific. There is no barrier to God, exalted is He, destroying those who have no offense together with those who do have one, and there is no objection against Him, glorified is He, regarding what He has done, for He disposes of His own pure dominion and is not questioned about what He does. In His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾ there is a kind of indication of this. Yes, universality of the message has been established for Noah, peace be upon him, in its outcome, since after the Deluge nothing remained on the face of the earth except those who were with him, and they were all the people of the earth at that time. Thus the difference between his message, peace be upon him, and the message of our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, is clear, for the message of our Prophet, peace be upon him, is universal both at the beginning and at the end, while his, peace be upon him, is universal at the end but not at the beginning. This is not free from examination. The better view is that the universality of our Prophet's message, peace be upon him, be considered in terms of its applying to those after him until the Day of Resurrection, for the absence of this being established for any of the messengers, peace be upon them, before or after Noah is not disputed. All of this applies when jinn are not taken into account in the universality, and likewise the angels if they are taken into account, as His saying, glorified is He, indicates: ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾. So the matter of specificity is clearer and clearer.

﴿Then they came to them﴾, i.e., each messenger came to his specific people ﴿with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident miracles indicating the truth of what they said. The preposition (bi) is either connected to the verb ʿinda-ma (before), on the basis that it is for transitivity, or to a omitted element which functions as a circumstantial (ḥal) from the nominative pronoun, i.e., ﴿being furnished with clear proofs﴾. However, this does not mean that each messenger came only with one proof, but rather with one proof or with many proofs specific to him, determined according to what wisdom requires. Shaykh al-Islam, in negating both the intention of coming with a single proof and the intention of coming with many proofs, held this view, and then said: The consideration of the distribution of units over units applies only to the two pronouns in (they came to them), as has been indicated. Perhaps our approach is better than his. It is understood from the words of some of the scholars who verify that the implication of sending each messenger to his own people derives from the attribution of "people" to the pronoun in ﴿messengers﴾, and this is not from the juxtaposition of plural with plural which requires the distribution of units over units. There is no doubt that the implication of each messenger coming to his specific people follows from this. After all this, if the juxtaposition of plural with plural in (they came to them) with clear proofs is considered, and it is said that units are distributed over units, it does not follow that each messenger had a proof which he brought, just as (the people sold their animals) does not require that each one of the people had one single animal which he sold, for its meaning is that each of the people sold what he had of animals, and this covers a single animal and others. This is unlike (the people rode their animals), for in that case the intention of each one of the animals is definitely required, since it is impossible for a person to ride two animals, for example. The scholar Abu al-Qasim al-Samarqandi, in his glosses on al-Mutawwal, explicitly stated that the juxtaposition of plural with plural does not require the distribution of units over units, in the sense that each member of one of the two plurals has one member of the other plural. This is evident in what we have said. What is relied upon in classifying the verse under the first example is an external matter, for it is known that one messenger among the messengers, peace be upon them, came to his people with more than one proof.

﴿So they were not to believe﴾: an explanation of the continuation of their non-belief in past time, i.e., it was not correct nor fitting at any time that they should believe, because of the severity of their obstinacy and the great extent of their stubbornness. The plural pronoun here refers to the people to whom the messenger was sent, and likewise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because they had denied it before﴾. The preposition (bi) in it is connected to (yuʾminu, "believe"), and (ma) is a relative pronoun whose referent is all the laws that each messenger brought, both their roots and their branches. What is meant by their non-belief in them is their persistence in that after the repeated appeals and the warnings, and by their denial before it is their denial from the time the messengers, peace be upon them, came until the time of persistence and obstinacy. This is on the basis that what is narrated is the last of their states, as the narration of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, indicates. Denial was not made the primary object as non-belief was made so, to indicate that it is clear in itself and needs no explanation, and what is in need of explanation is their non-belief after the repeated clear proofs and the manifest miracles which would have compelled them to accept, had they been people of intellect. If what is narrated is all the states of those peoples, then what is meant by the negation of their belief stated earlier is their continuous unbelief from the time the messengers, peace be upon them, came until the time of their persistence, and by their non-belief understood from the clause of the relative is their unbelief before the coming of the messengers, peace be upon them. Then what is meant by the relative is the roots of the laws on which all the messengers agreed and to which they called their nations, such as monotheism (tawhid) and its necessary consequences, which cannot be changed or altered. The meaning of their denial of that before the coming of their messengers is that they were not a people of ignorance such that they had never heard of it at all; rather, each people was hearing it from the remnants of those before them, and so they denied it. Then their state after the coming of the messengers was like their state before that, as if no one had been sent to them. It has been said: What is meant is that they did not benefit from the mission, and their state after the mission was like their state before it in being a people of ignorance. The first is better. The specification of denial and non-belief with respect to what has been mentioned of the roots is because the state of the rest becomes evident by the implication of the text, for when they did not believe in what all nations agreed upon, then they would be even less likely to believe in what only some of them held alone. The reason this denial is not made a primary object is that what the matter of punishment depends upon when both forms of denial are combined is the denial occurring after the mission and the call, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾. Something that occurred earlier was only mentioned to explain their deep-rootedness in unbelief and denial. Some have separated the pronouns, saying: the pronoun in ﴿they were﴾ and (yuʾminu) refers to the people of the messengers, and the pronoun in ﴿they denied﴾ refers to the people of Noah, peace be upon him. That is: the people of the messengers were not to believe in what the people of Noah denied, i.e., in its like. What is meant by it is what the messengers, peace be upon them, were sent to convey.

It has been permitted on this view that the relative refers to Noah himself, i.e., the people of the messengers were not to believe in Noah, peace be upon him, for if they had believed in him they would have believed in their prophets, peace be upon them. What is in this is not hidden. Some people have made the (bi) causal and (ma) a verbal-noun (masdariyya), and the meaning is: they denied their messengers, so their punishment from God, exalted is He, was that they would not believe, because of their denial before. This was supported by the verse that follows. In this there is opposition to the majority, who make the verbal-noun (ma) a noun, as is the view of al-Akhfash and Ibn al-Sarraj, so that the pronoun may return to it. In returning it to the truth, on the claim that it is established in minds, there is what is not hidden of far-fetchedness. It has been said: (ma) is a qualifying (mawsufa) and the (bi) is also causal, or for accompaniment, i.e., they denied with something, which is obstinacy and rebellion. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that firm sealing ﴿We seal﴾. The demonstrative here is according to the principle established in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ and its parallels among what has passed. To take the demonstrative as referring to the drowning, as al-Khazin did, is nothing. Sealing (tabʿ) is applied both to the influence of a thing by the impression of a stamp, and to the mark resulting from the impression, and the seal (khatm) is similar to it in that, according to what al-Raghib also stated. He mentioned that it is making a thing take on some form, like the stamping of coins and dirhams, and that it is more general than sealing and more specific than impression. Most of them interpret it as sealing, meaning by it prevention, i.e., we seal ﴿upon the hearts of the transgressors﴾ (74). That is, those who exceed the known limits in unbelief and obstinacy, and we prevent them thereby from accepting the truth and following the path of right guidance. Sealing has also come in the sense of tarnish or defilement, as in the tarnish of a sword due to its rust and dirt. Some have interpreted what is in the verse according to that. The Muʿtazilites, wherever it is attributed to Him, exalted is He, interpreted it as abandonment (khidhlan), in conformity with their doctrine. From this, al-Zamakhshari said: It works in the manner of a metaphor for their obstinacy and persistence in stubbornness, because whoever is obstinate and persists in stubbornness, God, exalted is He, abandons him and withholds from him success and grace, so he continues in that until the rust and the seal accumulate upon his heart. What he means, as it has been said, is that (naṭbaʿu) means (nakhdhulu), "We abandon," by way of explicit subordinate metaphor. However, since the sealing, which is abandonment, follows their obstinacy and stubbornness and is necessarily connected with them, it is treated as a metaphor for them. It has been read as (yaṭbaʿu) with the (ya) prefix, with the pronoun referring to God, glorified and exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 75:

﴿Then We sent﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿Then We sent after them messengers to their peoples﴾; it is the coordination of one narrative (qiṣṣa) upon another narrative. ﴿After them﴾ means: after those messengers, peace be upon them, Musa and Harun. He chose to state explicitly their sending, peace be upon them both, along with a particular detailing, to signal the gravity of the matter of this narrative and the magnitude of its impact. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ means: the nobles of his people, who gather around an opinion, who fill the eye with splendour and the souls with majesty and radiance. Singling them out by mention is due to their foundational role in establishing the public interests and important affairs, and to the fact that everyone refers to them in calamities and grave difficulties. It has also been said that what is meant by them here is the people in general, by the usage of the specific for the general. ﴿With Our signs﴾ means: with Our proofs and Our miracles, which are the signs detailed in al-A'raf. The ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasa), meaning: while being endowed with them. ﴿But they behaved arrogantly﴾ means: they acted with pride, were self-impressed, and exalted themselves against following. The fa' is an explanatory fa' (faṣīḥa), meaning: so they came to them and conveyed the message, but they behaved arrogantly. By this arrogance is alluded to what occurred from them at the outset, from the saying of the accursed one to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Did we not bring you up among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life?﴾ and other things. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ (75) is a parenthetical clause of concluding (tadhyīl) character. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with qad implied. On both readings it indicates their habitual commission of crime, which is the committing of a great sin, meaning: they were a people whose condition and habit was that.

It may be derived from what has been mentioned that the cause of their arrogance is being explained, and taking it as a plain coordination does not suit or accord with Qur'anic eloquence, for this degree is known from their prior attributes.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 76:**

﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us﴾. The *fa'* here is also *fasihah* (the *fa'* that signals an implied clause), expressing what has been stated explicitly in other places, as if it were said: Musa said, "Indeed I have come to you with a clear sign from your Lord," up to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾ ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾. Then when the truth came to them, ﴿they said﴾, out of the extremity of their obstinacy and arrogance together with the utmost of their incapacity: ﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾ (76). That is, its being magic is evident, or it is clear in its kind and surpassing its peers. *Mubin* is from *abana*, meaning "appeared and became clear," not from *abana* meaning "made manifest and clarified," although the latter is one of its two meanings.

The reference of *al-haqq* ("the truth") that came to them is, as many have said, the signs, and it has been put in place of the pronoun to indicate that its truth is manifest to everyone. Attributing coming to it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) which also indicates the extreme of its manifestness and the intensity of its radiance, such that it is not hidden from anyone with the least discernment. From here it was said regarding the meaning: "When the truth came to them from Us and they recognized it, they said," etc. The objection to this, that there is no indication in the speech of this recognition and that it is known only from another place, such as His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾, is answered by saying that it stems from scarcity of knowledge, given the clarity of the indication of what you know. Likewise, what they said is based on what is said about its indicating acknowledgment and the extreme of their incapacity.

It was also read *lasahirun* (لَساحِرٌ). By it they meant Musa, peace be upon him, because he is the one on whose hand appeared what overwhelmed them.

[p. 164]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 10, verse 77:

﴿Said Moses﴾ is a *istinaf bayani* (an explanatory resumptive clause), as if it were said: "What did Moses, peace be upon him, say to them?" So it was said: he said to them, in the form of a rebuking, denying question: ﴿Do you say of the truth﴾ which is the furthest thing from magic, which is sheer falsehood, ﴿when it has come to you﴾, that is, at the time of its coming to you and your witnessing it. This is what is required by what was indicated just before, or [it means] from the very beginning, without reflection and contemplation, as has been said. Whichever it is, it contradicts the statement that falls under the question. The object of the saying is omitted, relying on the indication of what precedes and follows it, and as a notice that it is something that should not be uttered even in the manner of reporting. That is: do you say to it what you say, that it is manifest magic? He means that it is something that no speaker could say or utter. It is also permitted that the object of the saying is the words of Him, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ on the basis that their purpose in the question is to have him, peace be upon him, affirm it, not a genuine question, since they had already decided that it was magic, so how would they ask about it? The reported speech in one of the two places is the meaning of their statement, and its sense; otherwise the story is one and what proceeded from them in it, according to the apparent sense, is one of the two sayings. Its weakness is not hidden. It is also possible that the saying means defamation and slander, from the expression: "So-and-so fears *al-qala* (gossip)," and "there is *tuqawul* (back-biting) among the people," when some say to others what displeases him. A parallel to this is the use of *dhikr* in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿We heard a youth mention them, called Abraham﴾. In that case the object and the *lam* are dispensed with to indicate what is being disparaged, as in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Come, for you﴾, meaning: do you blame him and slander him? In this way, and likewise in the first way, His statement, Glorified is He: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a denial newly begun on the part of Moses, peace be upon him, that it is magic, and a repudiation of their saying, and a rebuke to them for it, following rebuke and ignorance following ignorance. As for the first way, this is clear. As for the last way, the reason for choosing the denial that it is magic over the denial that it is defective, by saying: "Is there in it any defect?" (as the apparent sense of the previous denial requires), is the explicit rejection of what they found fault with in particular, after alerting to the first denial, that there is in it no trace of any defect. The fronting of the predicate is to signal that it is the target of the denial. And the sense of nearness in the demonstrative is to increase the specification of what is pointed to, and to bring to mind the qualities in it that show it to be a striking sign from the signs of God, Exalted is He, which declare the impossibility of its being magic: this, whose matter is clear and evident, and whose state is observed and known, such that no one who has a seeing eye can doubt it.

His statement, Glorified is He: ﴿And the magicians do not prosper﴾ (77) is an emphasis of the previous denial and of the rebuke and ignorance contained in it. The claim that it is magic necessarily entails the claim that the one who brought it is a magician. The clause is in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun of the addressees, and the linking element is the *waw* without a pronoun, as in the verse: "Winter has come, and I possess no provision," and your saying: "Zayd has come, and the sun has not risen." That is: do you say of the truth that it is magic while the state is that its practitioner does not prosper, that is, does not attain his aim and does not escape harm? Whereas I have prospered and won through the proof, and escaped destruction. The clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is parenthetical between the circumstantial clause and what follows it, to emphasise the previous denial by explaining the impossibility of its being magic in respect of its own essence, before explaining its impossibility in respect of its proceeding from him, peace be upon him. Whoever makes it the object of the saying keeps the circumstantial sense as it is, and there is no parenthetical clause in his view. The meaning on that basis would be: "Do you compel me to acknowledge that it is magic, when what I am upon of success is evidence that between it and magic is a greater distance than between east and west?"

It has been said: this clause may be like the preceding one within the scope of their saying, and it is also circumstantial, but in another mode, and the question is directed to it. The meaning would be: "Have you come to us with magic, seeking to prosper by it, while the state is that the magician does not prosper?" Or: "They marvel at his prosperity while he is a magician." But it is not hidden that the context (*sibaq*) and the wider context (*siyaq*) reject this possibility, so the glorious text should not be read in that way.

Page 165

In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim* it is said that the permission that the whole [passage] is the object of the saying is something the glorious text does not support at all. First, because what they said is simply the judgement that it is magic, with nothing in it indicating the meaning that is forced upon it in any way, so that his answer, peace be upon him, would be turned away from the explicit content of what they addressed him with to something not understood from it, which the revelation must be declared free of such things. As for the denial's being a parenthetical interruption that turns the previous denial into a stronger denial, I do not see that it is fitting to turn in this place to accepting that permission in the words of God, the Mighty.

Second, because the mention of the magicians' failure to prosper in absolute terms is the task of one who holds to the manifest truth, not of the unbelievers who cling to the skirts of some of them in opposing him, peace be upon him. Had that been their saying, it would have been appropriate to restrict the non-prosperity to those whom they assumed to be magicians, on the basis that most of those who come with it are magicians. The excuse that clinging to the skirts of some magicians does not contradict the mention of their failure to prosper in absolute terms, since it is possible that their belief is non-prosperity absolutely, and their clinging afterwards to what they clung to is of the kind of "receiving falsehood with falsehood," I do not see except as the clinging of a drowning man to grass.

As for the third point, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said: "Have you come to us..."﴾ and so on, is placed here to show that he, peace be upon him, silenced them. They were cut off from producing any statement related to his words, let alone a sound reply, and they were compelled to cling to the hem of *taqlid* (blind imitation), which is the habit of every defeated and incapable person and the custom of every obstinate contender. This is on the basis that it is a resumption (*isti'naf*) answering what he, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, had said before it, in the manner of ﴿Moses said﴾, as has been indicated. It is as if it were said: "What did they say to Moses, peace be upon him, when he said to them what he said?" And so it was answered: "They said, unable to argue: Have you come to us ﴿to turn us away﴾, that is, to divert us," and between *laft* (turning away) and *fatl* (twisting) there is a semantic and etymological relationship. Many scholars have stated that the two are cognate roots, and neither is a metathesis of the other, as al-Azhari said. ﴿from what we found our fathers upon﴾, that is, from the worship of other than God Most High. There is no doubt that this can only be realized if what is mentioned is a continuation of his, peace be upon him, speech in the way that has been explained. For if it were reported as coming from them, his, peace be upon him, reply would be devoid of the rebuke that compelled them to abandon the ways of argument. And there is no doubt that there is no connection between their words, ﴿Have you come to us...﴾ and so on, and his, peace be upon him, denunciation of what was reported from them, that would make it a valid answer to it. This is evident, except to one who has been veiled from grasping self-evident truths. In sum, the truth is that there is no justification for that supposition in any way, and defending it is superfluous, as is not hidden. ﴿and that greatness may be yours both﴾, that is, sovereignty, as was narrated from Mujahid. This is then the use of the cause (*malzum*) to mean the effect (*lazim*). Al-Zajjaj said that sovereignty was called *kibriya'* (greatness) only because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It was also said: that is, greatness and haughtiness over people by making them followers. Hammad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Bakr, and Zayd narrated from Ya'qub, reading (*yakuna*, "may be") with the yaa' of the third person, because the feminine gender here is not real and there is an intervening separator.

﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land of Egypt. It was also said that the generic sense is intended. The prepositional phrase is connected either to *takuna* (may be), or to *al-kibriya'* (greatness), or to the sense of settledness within *lakuma* (for you both), since it falls as a predicate, or to an implied element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of *al-kibriya'*, or of the pronoun in *lakuma*, since it bears the meaning. ﴿We shall not believe you both﴾, that is, we shall not give credence to what you have brought at all. In this there is emphasis on what is understood from the earlier denial. The pronoun of the addressees refers to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both. The reason they did not single out Moses, peace be upon him, for address here, as they did earlier, is that he was the one who spoke to them directly with rebuke and denial, in order to magnify the matter that is, in meaning, one of the two causes of their turning away, and for the sake of intensifying the vexation of Moses, peace be upon him, and making him despair of faith in what he had brought. In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim* it is stated that the use of the dual pronoun in these two places, after the singular in the earlier contexts, is due to the fact that greatness includes both of them, peace be upon them, and that affirming one of them entails affirming the other. As for turning away and coming to him, since they are among the distinctive features of the bearer of the Law, they were attributed to Moses, peace be upon him, alone. End of quotation. So reflect.

[Page 166]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 79:

﴿And Pharaoh said﴾. The verb is attributed to him alone, because command is among his own functions, not those of the chiefs (al-mala', the council of notables). This is unlike the earlier actions, such as arrogance and the like, which are attributed to him and to his chiefs. However, the apparent meaning is that he was not among those who spoke ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾, because he—may the curse of God be upon him—did not used to openly display the worship of anyone as his chiefs and the rest of his people did. That is, he said to his chiefs, instructing them in the initial steps of enforcing the matter by action after despairing of enforcing it by word. ﴿Bring me every learned sorcerer﴾ (79), skilled and proficient in the various arts of magic. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (sahhar), (sahhar being the intensive form).

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 80:**

﴿Then when the sorcerers came﴾ is conjoined to an implied element that the context calls for, which has been omitted to indicate how swiftly they carried out the command. This is the usual function of the *fa' al-fasihah* (the "eloquent fa'," which signals an omitted step). A parallel to this is explicitly stated in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So We said, "Strike the rock with your staff," and it burst forth﴾. The meaning is: they brought it, and then, when they came, ﴿Moses said to them, "Throw what you are going to throw" 80﴾. That is, "Throw what you have resolved and settled your opinion upon throwing, whatever kinds of sorcery it may be." The basic meaning of *al-ilqa'* (throwing) is casting a thing where you encounter it, i.e., see it. Then in common usage it became a term for any casting. This statement from him, peace be upon him, came after they had said to him what is related of them in the other surahs, such as their saying: ﴿Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw﴾, and similar things. It was not at the beginning of their coming.

Here *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), the sentence after it is its clause (*silah*), and the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*) is omitted. The meaning is: "what you are throwing it (i.e., *ma* + *ulqunahu*)." The contemptuous effect of this vagueness, and its suggestion of indifference, is not hidden. The intent is to command them to put forward what they had determined to do, so that its falsehood might become manifest. The intent is not a command to practise sorcery or an approval of it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 81:**

﴿So when they had cast﴾, that is, what they had cast of staves and ropes, ﴿and they had struck fear into the people and produced a great magic﴾. ﴿Moses said﴾ to them, ﴿paying no heed to them or to what they had done: "What you have brought is magic"﴾. Here (*ma*) is a relative pronoun serving as the subject, and (*al-sihr*, "magic") is the predicate. The (*al*) in it is for the genus (*jins*) and for definiteness (*ta'rif*), in order to convey restriction (*qasr*) in the sense of exclusivity. That is: what you have brought is magic and nothing else, not what Pharaoh and his chiefs called magic, namely signs of God the Exalted. This is the genus usage. It is also transmitted from al-Farra' that the (*al*) is for prior reference (*'ahd*), because magic was mentioned earlier in God's words: ﴿Indeed, this is surely magic﴾. This was rejected on the grounds that the condition for it to be a prior reference is that the earlier and later mentions be identical in essence, as in ﴿We have sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ and ﴿Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾. There is no such identity here, since the earlier magic was what Moses (peace be upon him) brought, and this is what the sorcerers brought. Some scholars have denied the requirement of essential identity, claiming that identity in kind is sufficient. They said of God's words ﴿And peace be upon me﴾ that the (*al*) is for prior reference, although the peace upon Jesus (peace be upon him) is not essentially the same as the peace upon John (peace be upon him). The apparent view is that this identity is required, and that identity in kind is not sufficient. Otherwise it would be valid to say, in "I saw a man and I honoured the man," if the first was Zayd and the second 'Amr for example, that the (*al*) is for prior reference because the identity in kind is evident. No one has said this, and I do not think anyone would entertain it. What is in the verse is not of this kind. Rather, the difference between the earlier and the later is clearer, since the first is metaphorical magic and the second is real. The (*al-salam*) in "what they said" is a single referent, and the multiplicity of those upon whom it falls does not make it multiple in common usage. Philosophical hair-splitting is not to be heeded in such matters.

Some researchers have mentioned that claiming the definite article is for prior reference while also claiming that restriction is derived from it are mutually contradictory, because restriction arises only when the article is for genus. Yes, if the indefinite noun mentioned first was not intended as a specific referent and was then made definite, the genus-definiteness does not contradict prior-reference definiteness, since the indefinite noun is equivalent to genus-definiteness. In that case prior-reference definiteness does not contradict restriction. Although their speech appears to contradict this, let it be examined. [End of quotation]

I say: al-Farra's claim here of prior reference is not something to be heeded. Perhaps he meant genus, though he expressed it as prior reference, following what al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in *Hamʿ al-Hawamiʿ* citing Ibn ʿUsfur, who said: "It is not far from my view that the two letters *alif* and *lam* which mark genus definiteness be called prior-reference ones, because genera are known to rational people from the moment they understand them, and prior reference presupposes prior knowledge." Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf ibn Maʿzuz claimed that *al* is only ever for prior reference and interpreted it in a way similar to what was mentioned, except that the apparent reasoning does not support that. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read *siḥrun* with an indefinite article, and Ubayy (ibn Kaʿb) read *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun*. The reasoning under these readings also conveys restriction, but indirectly, since it stands in contrast to their words ﴿Indeed, this is manifest magic﴾. In all these readings it is also permitted that (*ma*) be interrogative, with *al-siḥr* as the predicate of an omitted subject. Abu ʿAmr and Abu Jaʿfar read *ālsiḥr* with a cut and extended *alif* as an interrogative, so *mā* is an interrogative in the nominative as subject, ﴿you have brought﴾ is its predicate, and *al-siḥr* is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "a great thing you have brought, is it magic, or is magic it?" It may also be that *al-siḥr* is in apposition to (*ma*), as you say "What do you have, a dinar or a dirham?" Also, (*ma*) may be put in the accusative by an omitted verb supposed to follow it, meaning "whatever you have brought," with ﴿you have brought﴾ explaining it. For *al-siḥr* the first two possibilities hold.

It is also permitted that (*ma*) be a relative pronoun as subject, with the nominal clause, that is, "it is magic" or "magic is it," as its predicate. In this case it involves giving a predicate that is a non-declarative utterance (*insha'i*). On this reading it cannot be put in the accusative by an omitted verb which the stated word would explain, because what does not govern cannot explain a governing verb.

﴿Indeed God will nullify it﴾, that is, He will utterly annihilate it by manifesting through the hands of (Moses) a miracle, so that no trace of it remains at all; or, its falsehood and corruption will become evident to the people. The *sin* (of *sayubtiluhu*) is for emphasis. ﴿Indeed God does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾ (81). That is, the kind of them in general, so that the sorcerers are included in it primarily. It is also permitted that the corrupters mean those being addressed, in which case it is the placing of an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, to brand them with corruption and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) explaining and reinforcing what precedes. The meaning of not setting right that is not establishing it, or not strengthening it with divine support, not that corrupt things cannot be made sound, since that is evidently not something that can happen. That is, He, glorified is He, does not establish the work of the corrupters, nor let it endure, but removes it and annihilates it; or He does not strengthen it or support it, but shows its falsehood and makes it known.

The verse has been cited as evidence that magic is corruption and deception without reality. You know that making an absolute claim that magic has no reality is a matter for debate. The truth is that some of it has real effect, and some of it is false imagination, called conjuring (*sha'badha*) and trickery (*sha'wadha*).

(Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah Yunus, verse 82)

﴿And Allah establishes the truth by His words﴾. That is, He confirms it and strengthens it. This is coordinated (ʿatf) with His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿He will nullify it﴾. The mention of the Exalted Name in both places serves to instil awe and to cultivate reverence.

﴿By His words﴾: that is, by His commands (awamir) and decrees (qadaya). It is reported from al-Hasan (ʿan al-Hasan) that it means: by His promise of victory to whoever brings it, and He, glorified is He, does not break that promise. It is reported from al-Jubba'i (ʿan al-Jubba'i) that it means: by what He sends down, clarifying the meanings of the verses which His Prophet (ﷺ) brought.

It has been read as (bikalimatihi) in the singular, and it has been explained as "the command," the singular of "awamir" (commands), just as "kalimat" has been explained as "awamir." The intended sense is the genus, so the two readings agree. It has also been said: it is possible that by it is meant the word "Be" (kun), and that by it is meant the command, the singular of "umur" (affairs), with "kalimat" meaning the affairs and matters.

﴿Even if the criminals dislike it﴾ (82). By them is meant everyone characterised by criminality, including the sorcerers and others.

[Page 168]

﴿So none believed in Moses﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied clause (muqaddar), which is detailed in another place, meaning: ﴿Then Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they had fabricated﴾, and so on. It was not mentioned because it is relied upon, for the sake of brevity (ījāz), and to indicate that His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah will nullify it﴾, are something that cannot admit of falsehood at all. Perhaps its conjunction to that with "fa" (then) is in view of the newly occurring affirmation (ījāb), which is one of the two concepts (mafhūm) of restriction (ḥaṣr). For they say: the meaning of "None stood up except Zayd" is "Zayd stood up, and no one else stood up." Some did not take this into account and said: its conjunction with "fa" to that, despite being a continuous negation (ʿadam mustamirr), is of the same type as in His words, ﴿so they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, and as in your saying, "I admonished him but he did not heed, and I shouted at him but he did not desist." The secret in this is that the bringing of a thing after the arrival of what necessitates abstaining from it, even if it is a continuation upon it, is nonetheless, by way of its description (ʿunwān), a new act and a fresh deed. That is, none believed in him, peace be upon him, at the beginning of his mission, except a offspring (dhurriyyah) from his people, that is, the children of some of the Children of Israel, since he, peace be upon him, called the fathers, but they did not respond to him out of fear of Pharaoh, and a group of their youths responded to him. Thus by "dhurriyyah" is meant the youths, not the children.

"Min" (from) is for partitive (tabʿīḍ). It is also permitted that it be for beginning (ibtidāʾ), and the partitive is derived from the tanwīn and the pronoun referring to Moses, peace be upon him, as is one of the two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Ibn Jarīr narrated from him that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh, and a group held this view. Thus the believers were from other than the Children of Israel, and among them were his wife Āsiyah, his hairdresser, the believer of Pharaoh's family, the treasurer, and his wife. There is some obscurity in applying the term "dhurriyyah" to these. Some preferred to return the pronoun to Moses, peace be upon him, on the ground that he is the one being spoken of, and that on the other view the suitable form would be the pronoun after it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah preferred returning the pronoun to Pharaoh, on the ground that it is well known in the narratives that the Children of Israel were under the oppression of Pharaoh, and they had been given good news that their deliverance would be at the hands of a boy who would be a prophet, with such and such a description. When Moses, peace be upon him, appeared, they followed him, and it is not known that any of them opposed him. Therefore the second view is apparent. What was mentioned, that the one being spoken of is Moses, peace be upon him, is not free of something, for one may counter that by saying the discourse concerns the people of Pharaoh, because they are the ones who said he is a sorcerer, and because the admonition and warning of the people of Mecca, to which the verses are directed, indicates that the intent here is to explain their circumstances. You know that there is room for discussion in this. And the known matter, after granting that it is known, does not harm the first view, because the meaning then is: none manifested his faith and declared it except a offspring from the Children of Israel, and not others, for they concealed it and did not reveal it. ﴿Out of fear﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "dhurriyyah," and "ʿalā" is in the sense of "maʿa" (with), as it has been said regarding His words, ﴿and gave wealth despite love for it﴾. The tanwīn is for magnification, that is, existing with a great fear. ﴿From Pharaoh and their chieftains﴾: the pronoun refers to Pharaoh, and the plural form, according to more than one scholar, is as is customary in the pronouns of the great. It was rebutted that what occurs in the speech of the Arabs is the plural in the pronoun of the speaker, as in "we," and the pronoun of the addressee, as in His words, ﴿My Lord, return me﴾, and the verse: "Ah, have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad." It is not transmitted in the pronoun of the absent third person, as was transmitted from al-Raḍī. It is answered that al-Thaʿālibī and al-Fārisī transmitted it for the absent person as well, and the affirmative is given precedence over the negative. Also, it does not suit the magnification of Pharaoh; if it is according to his claim and his people's claim, it is only fitting in a speech which is said to be reported from them, and it is not so. It may be answered that the intent of magnification is to place him in the position of the plural. And that it does not suit, being a matter of prohibition, why should it not be possible that it suits because of what it contains of indicating the greatness of the fear, which entails increased praise of the believers? It has been said that this occurs according to their custom in their discourses, in the mere use of the plural for the pronoun of the great, even if magnification is not intended at all. So consider it. It is also permitted that the plural is because the intent of "Pharaoh" is his household, as one says "Rabīʿah" and "Muḍar." It has been objected that this is known only for a tribe and its father, since the name of the father is applied to them, whereas Pharaoh is not of this kind. Moreover, it has been said that applying "father" in the manner of a tribe to it is not permitted unless it is heard and it is established that it is made a proper name for it. Do you not see that they do not say: "So-and-so is from Hāshim, or from ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib," but rather "from the Banū Hāshim and the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib"? So how can the household of Pharaoh be intended by "Pharaoh," when it has not been established that it is made a proper name for them? The claim of establishment here is the very point in question. Therefore the view that the plural is because what is intended is his household, like Rabīʿah, is nothing, unless what is meant is that Pharaoh and his like among kings, when mentioned, bring to mind the status of his followers with him, so the pronoun returns to what is in the mind. Its illustration by what was mentioned is because it resembles it in general terms. Then, it is not hidden that if the household of Pharaoh is intended by "Pharaoh," it should be that Pharaoh and his household are intended by "the household of Pharaoh," by way of predominance (taghlīb). It has also been said that the speech is by omission of a modifier (muḍāf), that is, "the household of Pharaoh," so the pronoun returns to that omitted term. In this there is the point that omission depends on a clue, and there is no clue here, and the plural pronoun may refer to something other than that omitted term, as you will know shortly, Allah willing. Thus it is not suitable to be a clue. As for the claim that an omitted term is not referred back to by a pronoun, as Abū al-Baqāʾ said, it is not so, for if it is meant that it is never referred back to, this is incorrect; and if it is meant that when it is omitted because of a clue, this is disputed, for in that case it is in the status of what is mentioned, and the return of the pronoun to it in this manner has been frequent in the speech of the Arabs. Close to this view is the claim that there is an omitted conjoined term to which the pronoun returns, that is, "out of fear of Pharaoh and his people and their chieftains." This is also refuted by what has been said: that this omission is weak and not regular.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to the offspring, or to the people; that is, out of fear of Pharaoh and of the nobles of the Children of Israel, since they used to prevent them out of fear of Pharaoh against them, or out of fear for themselves; or out of fear of the nobles and chiefs of the Copts, since they used to prevent them in support of Pharaoh. Perhaps what comes to mind is that it returns to the offspring, and the plural is in view of meaning, and the meaning is interpreted as: they believed out of fear of Pharaoh and of the nobles of their own people. ﴿Lest he should afflict them﴾, that is, test them and punish them. The root of "fitan," as al-Rāghib said, is putting gold into fire to show its quality from its inferiority; and it is used for putting a person into fire, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿the Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾. What results in punishment is called "fitnah," and it is used for testing, and in the sense of trial and hardship, which is what is meant here. "An" (that) and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun which occurs as a substitute for Pharaoh, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), that is, out of fear of Pharaoh's affliction of them. It is also permitted that it be the object of "khawf" (fear), since it is an indefinite verbal noun which is frequently made to govern. It has also been said that it is the object for the sake of which (mafʿūl lahu), and the original is "li-an yaftinahum," so the preposition is omitted, and this is among the things in which omission is regular. This does not harm in such a case the non-unity of the agent of the verbal noun and of that for which it is done. Moreover, the view of some imams is that unity of agent is not a condition for permitting the accusative, and al-Raḍī inclined to this and supported it with what we mentioned in our glosses on the commentary of al-Qaṭr by the author. The attribution of the verb to Pharaoh specifically is because he is the locus of the matter of torment. In the speech there is istikhdām in one opinion, since by "Pharaoh" first his household is intended, and second he alone is intended. You know what is in it.

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾, that is, he was dominant and overpowering in the land of Egypt, and the use of "ʿuluw" (haughtiness) for dominance and overpowering is a well-known metaphor. ﴿And indeed, he was among the extravagant﴾ (83): that is, those who exceed the limit in wrongdoing and corruption through killing and shedding blood, or in arrogance and insolence, to the point that he claimed lordship and enslaved the descendants of the prophets, peace be upon them. The two clauses are a concluding parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī) confirming the content of what preceded, and in them there is emphasis that is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 84:**

﴿And Moses said﴾, when he saw the fear of the believers: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in God﴾, meaning, if you have affirmed Him and His signs, ﴿then upon Him rely﴾, meaning, depend on Him and not on anyone other than Him, for He, glorified is He, is sufficient for you against every evil and harm.

[Page 170]

﴿if you are submitting﴾, meaning, surrendering to the decree of God, exalted is He, and sincerely devoted to Him. This is not the suspension of a ruling on two conditions. Rather, it is the suspension of two things on two conditions. He suspended the obligation of reliance (tawakkul), which is understood from the command, and placed before it the element connected with faith (iman), since faith is what necessitates it. He suspended the very act of reliance and its existence on submission (islam) and sincerity (ikhlas), because it is not realized alongside corruption (takhlit). A parallel to this is: "If Zayd calls you, then answer him, if you are able to," for the obligation to answer is suspended on the calling, and the calling itself is suspended on ability. The summary of this is: if you have believed in God, then reliance upon Him, glorified is He, is obligatory for you, so do it and be characterized by it, if you are submitting to Him, exalted is He.

This type, according to what is in al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'an commentary of al-Zamakhshari), indicates an emphasis in the ordering of the consequent upon the condition, as in: "If you enter the house, then you are divorced, if you are my wife." Some scholars have regarded it as belonging to the category of suspension on two conditions, which entails that the second condition precedes the first in existence. So if one says: "If I speak to Zayd, then you are divorced, if you enter the house," she is not divorced unless she enters the house before the speaking, because the second condition is a condition for the first, so its precedence over it is necessary. He established this by stating that there are three things here: faith, reliance, and submission. By faith is meant affirmation (tasdiq), by reliance is meant ascribing affairs to Him, mighty and majestic is He, and by submission is meant surrendering oneself to Him, glorified is He, and cutting off the means. So He suspended reliance on affirmation after suspending it on submission, because the consequent is suspended on the first condition and is an explanation of the second consequent. It is as if it were said: "If you are affirming God, exalted is He, and His signs, then single Him out by ascribing all affairs to Him. This is not attained except after you are sincere to God, blessed and exalted is He, surrendering yourselves to Him, glorified is He, having no share of Satan in you. Otherwise, abandon the matter of reliance."

It is known from this that not every one of the believers is permitted to engage in reliance; rather, it is for individuals among them, and that the station of reliance is below the station of submission. Most scholars hold the former view, and perhaps it is more subtle in its consideration.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 85:

﴿Then they said﴾, answering him (peace be upon him) without hesitation or swallowing of saliva in that: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, not in anyone else, Glorified is He. From this restriction (qasr) and from the use of the past tense "tawakkalna" (we have put our trust) rather than "natawakkalu" (we put our trust), it is inferred that they were sincere believers. It has been said: for this reason their supplication was answered: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ [85], meaning a place of trial and punishment for them, by Your giving them power over us so that they torment us, or tempt us away from our religion, or are themselves tempted through us and say: "If these people were upon the truth, they would not have been afflicted."

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 10, verse 86:

﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ This is a supplication for deliverance from the evil of their company and from the evil of their conduct after deliverance from their oppression. For this reason he described them as disbelievers after having described them as wrongdoers, and this is the placing of an explicit noun in the position of a pronoun. It is also permissible that what is meant by "the people who are wrongdoers" are the chiefs (al-mala') whom they feared, and by "the disbelieving people" is everything that includes them and others. In placing reliance (tawakkul) before supplication (du'a), even though it explains the compliance with Musa's (Moses, peace be upon him) command to them, there is a hint that the one who supplicates should base his supplication on reliance upon Allah, the Exalted, for it is more hopeful of being answered. Let no one imagine that tawakkul contradicts du'a, because du'a is one of the means to the desired end. Tawakkul is the abandonment of means, because what is meant by it is setting aside regard for ordinary means, restricting it to the One who causes them, Mighty and Majestic, and believing that the matter is tied to His will, Glorified is He. Whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. The scholars have stated that a person who engages in means while holding this belief is also considered a mutawakkil (one who relies upon Allah). Similar to tawakkul in not contradicting du'a, as the verse indicates, is istislam (submission). Yes, in the statement of some of them that submission is one of the attributes of Ibrahim (Abraham, peace be upon him), and among its effects was leaving off du'a when he was thrown into the fire, and his peace be upon him being content with the knowledge alluded to in his saying: "It is enough for me in my asking that He knows my state," this does indicate a contradiction. Whoever knows the stations and reflects deeply, the matter of reconciling these will be easy for him.

[Page 171]

﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother: "Settle⁽¹⁾ ..."﴾ *(an)* is *mufassira* (explanatory, introducing a clarification) because revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the meaning of speech. It may also be *masdariyya* (the particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun), meaning the verb is taken as a verbal noun. *Tabawwu'* means taking a *mubā'a*, that is, a dwelling place (*manzil*), just as *tawaṭṭun* means taking a homeland (*waṭan*). The majority read the hamza (*tahqīq al-hamza*, pronouncing it fully). Some read *tabawwayā* and made it a *yā'*, which is a substitution of the hamza for ease of pronunciation. The verb, according to what has been said, is transitive to one object: one says *tabawwa'a Zaydun kadhā* ("Zayd settled such-and-such"). But if the *lām* is introduced on the agent, as in *tabawwa'a li-Zaydin kadhā* ("Zayd settled for such-and-such"), it becomes transitive to two objects, since the agent has become an object by means of the *lām*. The verse is interpreted in this way, so *li-qawmikumā* is one of the two objects. It has also been said that the verb is transitive to one object, and *li-qawmikumā* is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of *al-buyūt* (the houses). In both cases the *lām* is not superfluous. Abū ʿAlī said: the verb is transitive by itself to two objects, and the *lām* is superfluous, as in ﴿radifa lakum﴾ ("it followed you"). *Fa'ala* and *tafa''ala* may have the same meaning, as in *allaqtuhā* and *ta'allaqtuhā* ("I hung it"). The implied sense is: "Settle your people in houses in which they will live or to which they will return for worship."

*Miṣr* is not declined (*ghayr munṣarif*) because it is a feminine proper noun. If you were to decline it because of its lightness, as you decline *Hind*, that would be permissible. The prepositional phrase is connected to *tabawwa'ā*. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial qualifier of *buyūtan* (houses), or of *qawmikumā* (your people), or of the agent pronoun in *tabawwa'ā*, though this last option is weak.

﴿And make⁽²⁾ ...﴾ You two and your people, so there is a prevalence of the addressed (*taghlīb al-mukhāṭab*) over others. ﴿your houses﴾ those, so the annexation is to a known referent (*li-l-ʿahd*). ﴿as a qiblah﴾ means a place of prayer (*muṣallā*). It has also been said: mosques oriented toward the *qibla*, meaning the Kaʿba, for Moses (peace be upon him) used to pray facing it. In both explanations, *qibla* is metaphorical for what it is explained as, by way of a relation of necessity (*ʿalāqat al-luzūm*) or of whole and part (*al-kulliyya wa-l-juz'iyya*). The disagreement about the intended meaning here reflects the disagreement over whether those constructed houses were for dwelling or for prayer. If the former, then *qibla* is a metaphor for the place of prayer; if the latter, then it is a metaphor for mosques.

The view that *qibla* refers to mosques oriented toward the Kaʿba has been objected to: the explicitly stated thing in the authentic hadith is that the Jews faced the Rock (*al-Ṣakhra*) and the Christians faced the rising of the sun. It is not well known that Moses (peace be upon him) faced the Kaʿba in his prayer, so saying so is strange. Even stranger is what al-ʿAlāʾī said: that the prophets (peace be upon them) all had the Kaʿba as their *qibla*. It has been said: making the houses places of prayer is contradicted by the hadith: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration (*masjid*) and a means of purification (*ṭahūr*)." It is also contradicted by the report that earlier nations used to pray only in their churches. This is answered by saying that the restriction applies when they are not compelled; when they are compelled, prayer in their homes becomes permitted for them, just as the prayer of fear was permitted for us. Pharaoh, may God curse him, destroyed their places of worship and forbade them from praying, so He revealed to them: "Pray in your houses," as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr. It may also be said that there is no contradiction at all, on the basis that what is intended is designating the houses for prayer and the invalidity of prayer elsewhere. Their ruling at that time would then be the ruling of the churches today. What is particular to this community is the validity of prayer in any place on earth and the absence of any specific place being designated for it. So there is no need for what is said: that considering the whole earth a mosque is a particularity, in view of what the law of Moses (peace be upon him) was established upon, namely the requirement to pray in churches and the impermissibility of praying in any place the worshipper chose on earth.

As for the Jews' facing of the Rock mentioned earlier: it is well known that this was in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). As for before and after the revelation of the Torah (*al-Tawrāt*), they used to face the ark (*al-tābūt*), which was placed in the tent (*qubba*) of Moses (peace be upon him). It has also been said that facing in Bayt al-Maqdis was also toward the ark, and they would place it upon the Rock, so facing it was facing the Rock. As for their facing in Egypt, it may have been toward the Kaʿba, as narrated from al-Ḥasan. What is in the hadith is to be understood as referring to the last of their states. It is also possible that it was toward the Rock, as it is today. Other possibilities exist too, and God Most High knows the reality of the matter best.

It has been said that the meaning of *qiblatan* is "facing one another" (*mutaqābila*). Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with both of them, meaning: "Make your houses face one another, some of them facing others."

﴿And establish the prayer⁽³⁾﴾ in them. It has been said: they were commanded to do this at the beginning of their affair, so that the disbelievers would not gain the upper hand over them, harm them, and tempt them away from their religion. This is based on the view that *al-buyūt* means dwellings. If, however, it is intended to mean mosques, then this does not hold, as is not hidden. The likely reason for this direction is that they were commanded to pray so that they might seek help through its blessing for their purpose, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Prayer in mosques is more excellent, so it is more likely to bring benefit.

﴿And give good news to the believers 87﴾ of the attainment of their purpose. It has been said: of victory in this world in response to their supplication, and of Paradise in the Hereafter. The pronoun was dual at first because settling a people and taking places of worship are matters handled by the leaders of a people through consultation. Then it was plural a second time, because making houses into mosques and praying in them is something every person does. Moreover, including Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them both) together with the people in the two matters mentioned is an encouragement for them to comply. Then it was singular a third time, because giving good news to the community is the function of the bearer of the law, and it is among the greatest things, more joyful and more impressive to the soul. The phrase "the believers" was placed in the position of "the people" in order to praise them for their faith, and to indicate that faith is the basis for receiving good news.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 88:**

﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment"﴾ i.e., that with which they adorn themselves, of clothing, mounts and the like; it is also used as a verbal noun. ﴿And wealth﴾ i.e., many kinds of wealth, as the plural and the indefinite (tanwin) indicate. Mentioning this after "adornment" is the mention of the general after the specific, for comprehensiveness, though it may also be restricted to what lies beyond adornment by the contrast in context. Some scholars interpreted "adornment" as beauty, bodily soundness, tallness of stature and the like. ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way﴾ i.e., so that they may go astray from it. This is a causal clause (ta'lil) for the preceding giving. The speech is Moses, peace be upon him, informing that God, exalted is He, only furnished them with adornment and wealth as a gradual leading on (istidraj), so that they would increase in sin and error, as He, glorified is He, informed of their likes in His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾. Al-Farra' went to the view that the lam is causal, and the apparent meaning is that it is literal; so that error would be the will of God, exalted is He. What the Mu'tazilites said does not follow, namely that if it is willed, they must be obedient to it, based on the premise that will is a command or entails one, since this premise has been shown to be invalid in speech. Some scholars, to avoid this, estimated a negation to avoid error, as was estimated in ﴿We bear witness that you should not say﴾: "We bear witness that you do not say." There is no need for this. It was also said that the causality is figurative, since when they went astray because of it, its giving was treated as if it were for the sake of error, so there is a metaphor of consequence (isti'ara tab'iyya) in the lam. Al-Akhfash said: the lam is for consequence (lam al-'aqiba), so that this would be a report from him, peace be upon him, based on his experience with them and his insight into them, or on knowledge through revelation, as it is said, that the outcome of that giving is error.

The difference between figurative causality and this, if we say that it too is a figurative sense, is that in causality the cause is mentioned, but its giving was not because it is a cause; whereas in the lam of consequence no cause is mentioned at all. It is like the metaphorical use of one of two opposites for the other. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is for supplication (du'a'), and there is no fault in Moses, peace be upon him, in supplicating against them for error, either because he, peace be upon him, knew through experience or the like that it would certainly occur, so he prayed for it; and its essence is that it is a supplication for what can only be that, so it is an explicit statement of what God's decree has brought about, like the saying "May God curse Satan." Or because it is not truly a supplication, and the concern is not whether the thing asked is immediately effected or not, but rather the description of them as obstinate and the clearing of his excuse, peace be upon him, in the call. Thus on this view it is an allusive metonymy (kinaya ima'iyya). As for what was said: "This is a testimony to their bad state by way of metonymy within metonymy, because error accompanies misguidance, which is withholding grace; so error is used as a metonymy for misguidance, and misguidance accompanies their being as if sealed; so this is a disclosure and clarification of their state by way of metonymy." Though there is something in it, it is not needed, because sealing is explicitly mentioned afterwards; rather the concern here is the essence and kernel of all these matters.

The words of al-Zamakhshari suggest a preference for its being supplication. In al-Intisaf it is said that this is a Mu'tazilite doctrine more subtle than the crawling of an ant, such that discovering it almost amounts to unveiling. The apparent meaning is that it is causal. The author of al-Fara'id said: were it not for causality, His saying ﴿You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment﴾ would not be coherent and would not fit together. It was also objected that it contradicts the purpose of the mission, which is calling to faith and guidance. It is not hidden that the answer to this is known from what we have set forth just now. As for how the speech fits together, it is as several have said: Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned His saying ﴿You have given﴾ and so on as a preface for reaching the supplication against them, i.e., "You bestowed this blessing upon them so that they would worship You and give thanks to You, but that only increased them in rebellion and disbelief. When the situation is thus, let them go astray from Your way." Had he supplicated at the outset, it would not have been fitting, since perhaps he would not have been excused; so he first presented the complaint against them and the lament over their evil conduct, so that he could ascend from it to the supplication, while observing the cohesion of the speech in the sequence of the supplications arranged in one order, and avoiding the need to excuse the repetition of the address, as the causal view needed to be excused by saying that it is for emphasis and to indicate that the purpose is to display their error and ingratitude as a prelude to the supplication against them afterwards. Al-Tibi claimed that there is no room for the view of an objection (i'tiraD), because it is only fitting in its place when the soul delights in hearing it; and for this reason the saying of al-Nabigha was criticized: "Perhaps Ziyad, you have no father, is heedless."

In his speech there is an inclination to the view that the lam is for supplication, and this, in the view of the impartial, goes against the apparent meaning, and what they mentioned for it does not render it more apparent.

It is read ﴿li-yudillu﴾ with the yā' vowelled with a ḍamma and with a fatḥa. ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾ i.e., destroy it, as Mujahid said. So ṭamas means destruction, and its verb is of the pattern of ḍaraba and dakhala. The reading ﴿iṭmus﴾ with a ḍamma on the mīm supports this, and it is both transitive and intransitive. It also comes in the sense of erasing a trace and changing, and most exegetes explained it this way, saying: the meaning is, "Our Lord, alter it from the aspect of its benefit to an aspect from which they gain nothing."

You know that altering it from the aspect of its benefit is also a destruction of it, so this does not contradict what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak, that after this supplication their dirhams, dinars, copper and iron became engraved stones. It is also related from Muhammad al-Qurazi that he said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked me about this verse, and I informed him that God, exalted is He, obliterated the wealth of Pharaoh and the people of Pharaoh until it became stones. Umar said, "Wait where you are until I come to you," and he called for a sealed bag, opened it, and in it was an egg split open, and it was stone; and likewise the dirhams, dinars and similar things. In another report from him, it is said that their sugar became stones, and that a man, while he was with his wife, they both became two stones, and while a woman was standing baking bread, she became like that. This is something that hardly can be authentic at all, and there is nothing in the verse that points to it in any way. In my view, reports of their wealth changing into stones are not free of weakness, so they should not be relied upon. Perhaps the better view is that by its obliteration is meant its destruction by them in the most complete manner, and by "wealth" is meant what includes adornment of garments, mounts and other things. ﴿And harden their hearts﴾ i.e., make them hard, and seal over them so that they are not opened to faith, as is the character of their state. ﴿So that they will not believe﴾ is the answer to the supplication, namely "harden," not "obliterate"; so it is in the accusative. It is possible that it is a supplication in the form of a prohibition, like "My God, do not punish me," in which case it is in the jussive. It is also permitted that it be coordinated with ﴿li-yudillu﴾, with what lies between them being an intervening supplication; then it is in the accusative or the jussive according to the disagreement you know about regarding the lam.

﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾ (88) i.e., that they witness it and are certain of it, to the point that this will not benefit them at that time. What is meant is the category of painful punishment. Several have related from Ibn Abbas that it is to be explained as drowning.

Some scholars used this verse to argue that invoking disbelief upon a person is not considered disbelief if it is not in the manner of demanding or approving of disbelief, but rather in the manner of wishing that God may take the sharpest vengeance upon that person. Shaykh al-Islam Khawahir-zadah went to this view. So their saying, "Contentment with another's disbelief," is not on its absolute footing in his view, but is restricted to the case where it is in the manner of approval. But the author of al-Dhakhira said: We have come across a report from Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, that contentment with another's disbelief is disbelief without distinction, while what is transmitted from the Imam of Guidance Abu Mansur al-Maturidi is the distinction. So there is disagreement on the matter. It was said: what is relied upon is that contentment with disbelief as disbelief is disbelief, while contentment with it not from this aspect but from the aspect of its being a cause of painful punishment, or its being one of the effects of God's decree and destiny, for example, is not disbelief. By this the contradiction between their saying, "Contentment with disbelief is disbelief," and their saying, "Contentment with the decree is obligatory," is resolved, on the basis that the decree here is taken to mean the thing decreed. On this view, what was said does not hold: that a servant's contentment with his own disbelief is disbelief without doubt on its absolute footing, but rather the same distinction previously mentioned for contentment with another's disbelief applies to it too. From this verification it is known what is in their saying that whoever is approached by a disbeliever who wants to become Muslim and he says to him, "Wait until I perform ablution," or delays him, becomes a disbeliever because he is content with his disbelief for a period of time in view. This is supported by what is in the sound hadith about the conquest of Mecca: that Ibn Abi Sarh was brought by Uthman, may God be pleased with him, to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he said, "O Messenger of God, accept his allegiance." The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, withheld his hand from accepting his allegiance and looked at him three times, each time he refused to pledge allegiance to him; then he pledged allegiance to him after the third time. Then the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, turned to his companions and said, "Was there not among you a rightly-guided man who would stand up to this one when he saw that I withheld my hand from his allegiance, and kill him?" They said, "How would we know, O Messenger of God, what is in your mind? Why did you not signal to us with your eye?" He, peace be upon him, said, "It is not fitting for a prophet to have a betrayal of the eyes." This was related by Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and it is well known in the biographies. It is evident from it that withholding in general is not disbelief as they said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 89 (part 1 of 3):

He said, ﴿Your supplication has indeed been answered﴾. This is addressed to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both. Its apparent meaning is that Harun, peace be upon him, made a supplication like the one Musa, peace be upon him, made, in actuality. However, the text only reports the supplication of Musa, peace be upon him, because he was the Messenger in his own right, so there was no need to report Harun's supplication separately. Harun was associated with the good news to show his honour, peace be upon him. It is also possible that he did not actually supplicate, but the supplication was attributed to him as well, on the basis that Musa's supplication has the same ruling as his, since he was Musa's follower and minister. What is established by the reports is that he, peace be upon him, used to say "Amin" to his brother's supplication, and "Amin" is a supplication, for its meaning is "answer" (istajib). It is not one of the Names of God, as they narrate from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him. It has been said that because it is a supplication, the Hanafis (the Hanafi school) recommend saying it silently. But this is open to question, because the apparent basis for recommending silent or audible recitation is not that it is a supplication. The Shafi'is (the Shafi'i school) recommend saying it aloud, while what is well known from them is that they also hold that it is a supplication. The apparent meaning of the words of some verifiers is that the attachment of the word "Lord" to the pronoun of the speaker in the plural form in the three places indicates that he, peace be upon him, used to say "Amin" to the supplication of Musa, peace be upon him. The weakness of this indication is not hidden. It is also recited as (your supplications) in the plural, and its basis is clear.

﴿So go straight﴾: proceed in accordance with My command, and remain steadfast in what you are upon of calling to the truth and establishing the proof. And do not hasten, for what you have requested will certainly occur at its appointed time.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "They claim that Pharaoh remained for forty years after this supplication." Ibn Jarir also reported a similar account from Ibn Jurayj. al-Tirmidhi reported from Mujahid that the supplication was answered after forty years, but he did not mention the claim.

﴿And do not follow the path of those who do not know﴾ 89: this refers to the customs of God, the Exalted, in making matters depend on wisdoms and interests; or the path of the ignorant in not trusting the promise of God, glorified is He.
