The prohibition does not imply that the forbidden act is actually occurring, for it is common for a person to be forbidden from something that is impossible for him to do. Perhaps the purpose here is merely to emphasize the matter of the promise and to convey that in delaying its fulfilment there are divine wisdoms. [p. 175]

It is reported from Ibn 'Amir that he recited (wa la tattabi'ani) with a light nun, kasra-vowelled, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn al-Hajib explained this by saying that (la) is a negative particle and the nun is the sign of the nominative case. The clause is either in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the nominative pronoun in (istaqima), as if it were said: "Go straight, not following." A present-tense negated verbal clause with (la) that functions as a circumstantial phrase may or may not be linked with the conjunction "wa", contrary to those who claimed that it must not be linked with "wa" unless a subject is implied. Or it is coordinated with the imperative clause that precedes it, which, although declarative in form, is imperative in meaning, since what is intended by it is a prohibition, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You believe in God and His Messenger﴾ and (you do not worship except God). A prohibition expressed in the form of a statement is more emphatic than a prohibition expressed in its own form. It is also possible to take the clause as a new sentence informing that they do not follow the path of the ignorant. Some people have taken (la) in the recitation of the majority to be a negative particle too, but this is weak, because according to the correct view, a negation does not emphasize. It has also been said that (la) is a prohibitive particle and the nun is the light emphatic nun, kasra-vowelled because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. This is a weak analysis, for al-Kisa'i and Sibawayh do not permit it, because they prohibit the light nun from occurring after the alif, whether it is the alif of the dual or the alif separating the feminine plural nun from the emphatic nun, as in: "Will you two (f.) strike, O women?" Also, when the light nun is followed by a quiescent letter, it must be dropped according to the majority, and it may not be vowelled. But Yunus and al-Farra' permitted this, and there are two reports from them: that it remains quiescent, because the alif, being light, is equivalent to a fatha, and its kasra follows the original rule for the meeting of two quiescent letters. On this basis, that analysis is complete.

It has been said that this nun is the heavy emphatic nun, but it was lightened. This is as you see, weak. It is also reported from him (ibn 'Amir): (wa la tatba'anni) with the second ta' lightened and quiescent, and with a doubled nun, from the triliteral (tabi'a). Also: ﴿wa la tattaba'anni﴾, which is like the first, except that the nun is quiescent according to one of the two reports from those mentioned before, on the basis of the quiescence of the light nun after the alif according to the original rule, and of disregarding the meeting of two quiescent letters when the first of them is an alif, as in (mahyaya).

Then know that it is well known to explain the kasra of the nun in the recitation of the majority as being due to the meeting of two quiescent letters. Its apparent meaning is that by this the meeting of two quiescent letters is removed, but this is not so, for the two quiescent letters are the alif and the first nun, and neither of them is vowelled; the vowelled letter is only the second nun. For this reason, some verifying grammarians said: the original reason for vowelling is to make assimilation (idgham) possible, and its being with a kasra is in imitation of the nun of the dual. The meeting of the two quiescent letters, namely the alif and the first nun, is not harmful, according to what they stated about its permissibility when the first is a letter of prolongation and the second is assimilated into a similar letter, as in (dabbatin), because the tongue is raised for both of them together at that point. This has been verified in its proper place, so let it be consulted. This is what I have to say, and Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

* * *

From the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ He, glorified is He, indicated that they listen, but their situation is that of the deaf in not benefiting, and this is because of their lack of readiness in actuality, or in ruling, in that it exists but its light is veiled by the firm establishment of dark states. The same applies to what follows. Then He, exalted is His majesty, removed what might be imagined, that their being in that state is an injustice from Him, glorified is He, toward them, by His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong people at all﴾ by depriving them of their senses and intellects, for example. ﴿But people wrong themselves﴾, in that He sought their readiness, which was not made by Him to be that. ﴿And on the Day He gathers them, it will seem as if they had not remained except an hour of the day﴾ because of their bewilderment, through the thickening of the darkness of sins upon their hearts. ﴿They will recognize one another﴾ by the rule of the earlier companionship and the call of desire that is necessary for the original kinship. This recognition may remain if they are united in direction and agree in purpose, and it may not remain if the desires differ and the opinions diverge; then the states derived from the attachments of the upbringing vary, and mutual denial and the accidents of habit occur. ﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have certainly lost, and they were not guided﴾ [p. 176] to that by which they might benefit. ﴿And for every nation there is a messenger﴾ from among their own kind, so that they may be able to draw benefit from him. ﴿So when their messenger comes, judgment will be made between them﴾ by saving those who were guided by him and rewarding them, and by destroying those who turned away from him and punishing them, because the causes of that become manifest with his presence. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, so that they are treated contrary to what they deserve. ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ This is a denial of the Resurrection, due to their being veiled by the density they are in. ﴿Say, "I do not possess for myself any benefit or harm except what God wills."﴾ This is a negation of his independence in influencing, and a statement that he does not possess except what God, exalted is He, permits; and this is a kind of the Oneness of Actions (tawhid al-af'al). In it there is guidance for them that he does not possess the ability to hasten what he has promised them. ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾, that is, a purification of your souls by the promise, the threat, and the warning against sins that cause punishment, and the encouragement to obedience that brings reward by the grace of God, exalted is He. ﴿And a healing for what is in the breasts﴾, that is, a remedy for the hearts from their diseases, which are more severe than the diseases of the bodies, such as doubt, hypocrisy, envy, rancour, and the like, through teaching the realities and wisdoms that produce certainty, purification, and readiness for the manifestations of the true attributes. ﴿And guidance﴾ for your spirits toward the essential witnessing. ﴿And mercy﴾ by the bestowal of the perfections suitable for each of the three stations, after the readiness has been attained: in the station of the self by admonition, the station of the heart by purification, and the station of the spirit by guidance, for the believers, first by assent, then by certainty, and third by direct vision.

Some of them mentioned that the admonition is for the seekers, the healing for the lovers, the guidance for the knowers, and the mercy for those who find intimacy. All of them are believers, but the degrees of faith vary, and the address in the verse is to them. In it is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. It is said that He, glorified is He, began with admonition for the one sick with His love, because it is a purgative to purge his desires. When he is cleansed of that, He gives him to drink the draught of His subtle kindnesses, and this becomes a healing for him from what afflicts him. When he is healed, He nourishes him with His guidance toward Himself. When he is perfected through companionship with Him, He purifies him with the waters of His mercy from the filth of the disease and the scum of the trial.

﴿Say, "By the grace of God"﴾: by His granting success in acceptance at the stations. ﴿And by His mercy﴾: by the moral, practical, and unveiling gifts within them. ﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾, not in the transient worldly matters, few in quantity and base in value. ﴿It is better than what they accumulate﴾ of base and insignificant things.

Some of them interpreted the grace (fadl) as the unveiling of the dawn of pre-eternity to the eyes of the spirits of the seekers, and the increase of its clarity in a moment, until the suns of the attributes and the moons of the Essence rise, and they fly in the lights of that with the wings of attractions to wherever God, the Exalted, wills. And the mercy is the successive arrival of the states of the unseen to the hearts, in the manner of singularity (tafrid), without interruption. For this reason, the lion-thicket of Sufism, Abu Bakr al-Shibli, may his secret be sanctified, said: "My time is everlasting and my sea has no shore." It is also said: His grace is union, and His mercy is protection against separation. It is said: His grace is casting the fires of love into the hearts of the seekers, and His mercy is His drawing the spirits of the longing ones. It is said: His grace, glorified is He, upon the knowers is the unveiling of the Essence, upon the lovers the unveiling of the attributes, and upon the seekers the unveiling of the lights of the signs. His mercy, exalted is His majesty, upon the knowers is care, upon the lovers sufficiency, and upon the seekers protection. Al-Junayd said: "The grace of God, exalted is He, is at the beginning, and His mercy is at the end," and this is consistent with what we have said. Al-Kattani said: "The grace of God, exalted is He, is the apparent blessings, and His mercy is the hidden blessings." Other things have also been said.

﴿Say, "Have you considered what God has sent down to you"﴾: that is, tell me what God, glorified is He, has sent down of spiritual provision, such as the true knowledge and the religious ethics. ﴿And you have made of it lawful and unlawful﴾: as in the first category, in that you denied it to its people and accused them of heresy; and as in the second category, in that you accepted it. ﴿Say, "Has God permitted you [to do so], or do you invent [falsehood] against God?"﴾ in judging things lawful and unlawful. Then He, glorified is He, threatened the inventors by His saying, mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent falsehood against God?﴾ and so on. So in the verse there is an allusion to the bad state of those who deny those who are adorned with the divine knowledge. Perhaps the origin of this is their assumption that knowledge is confined [p. 177] to what they possess, and they do not know that beyond their sciences there are countless sciences which God, exalted is He, bestows upon whom He wills. In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge"﴾ there is an allusion to this. How fitting it is that they should be told: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little.﴾

It is strange that when they hear something from the people of God, exalted is He, that differs from what their own scholars hold, they reject it and say: "Deviation and misguidance." They rely in that merely on that difference, supposing that the truth is confined to what one of those scholars has brought, even though the disagreement has never ceased to exist among them, in a continuous manner.

Moreover, it may be said to them: What assures you that this speaker, whom you heard saying what you heard and whom you denounced, is not also a mujtahid, like your own mujtahids? If they say: The mujtahid has known conditions, and these are not present in him, we reply: Are these conditions that have been laid down for the mujtahid in the religion of Allah Most High transmitted explicitly from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or did you devise them yourselves, or did the mujtahid devise them? If they were transmitted from the Messenger, peace be upon him, then bring them forward, recite them, and establish their transmission, if you are truthful. But that is far-fetched. If you were the ones who laid them down, and you are more ignorant than the son of a day (i.e., a newborn), then they are rejected against you, with no affection or honour for them. Furthermore, to accept them is to take the word of one who is not a mujtahid, which you yourselves do not permit. If the one who laid them down was the mujtahid, then establishing that he is a mujtahid depends on accepting those conditions, and accepting those conditions depends on establishing that he is a mujtahid. Is this anything but circular reasoning, which is impossible, if you understood it? Also, why should it not be possible that those conditions are conditions for the mujtahid of transmission (al-mujtahid al-naqli), while there is another mujtahid whose condition is the purification of the soul, its cleansing, its adornment with the divine character, its readiness and its preparedness to receive knowledge from Allah Most High? What prevents Allah Most High from creating knowledge in one whose soul is purified, who has prepared himself through poverty and turning to Allah Most High, whose resolve in seeking is sincere, and who does not rely on his own power and strength, just as He creates it in one who has fulfilled the conditions of ijtihad according to you, so that he exerts himself and directs his thought and reflection? To claim that He, glory be to Him, creates knowledge in this one and not in that one is a restriction upon Allah Most High and a departure from fairness, as is not hidden. Therefore, it is not fitting for the author, who knows that grace is in the hand of Allah, who gives it to whomever He wills of His servants, to refuse to accept what is brought by one in whom the traces of purification and readiness have appeared and upon whom the lights of adorning oneself with the divine character have shone, even if no mujtahid has brought it, so long as it does not contradict what is known to have come from the religion by necessity. Allah Most High refuses that anything similar to what has been mentioned should come from one who is not so.

However, our master, the Divine Imam and renewer of the second millennium, may Allah sanctify his secret, mentioned in some of his Persian letters that it is not permissible to follow the people of kashf (unveiling) in their unveilings, because kashf is not a proof binding upon others. It may be said: This amounts only to a prohibition of following the people of kashf, whereas the point of dispute is denouncing them and accusing them, may Allah protect us, of heresy (zandaqa), and there is not the slightest trace of that in the statement. As is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, Allah is full of grace to mankind﴾ through the two kinds of knowledge and their bestowal after preparing the readiness to receive them. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾ for that, nor do they recognize its worth, so they are withheld from increase. ﴿And you are not engaged in any affair, nor do you recite any part of the Qur'an, nor do you do any deed, but We are witnesses over you when you are busy with it﴾. This is an announcement from Him, exalted is He, of His great awareness of the thoughts and what passes through the hearts; nothing—no thought and no inner secret—is hidden from Him, exalted is His majesty.

﴿Does He not know, who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾. Then He, exalted and high, informed of the extent of His encompassing power over every atom, from the Throne to what is beneath the earth, by His saying, blessed is His name: ﴿And not an atom's weight escapes your Lord, either on earth or in heaven﴾. That is, His knowledge, glory be to Him, encompasses what is in the lower and upper worlds, so every atom of His atoms falls within the scope of His knowledge. How could it not, when all of them subsist by Him, exalted is His majesty, who looks upon each one at every moment with the gaze of preservation and care? Were it not so, the atoms would perish and all existing things would vanish. ﴿Indeed, the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them﴾, since no remnant remains in them by which they would fear deprivation, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾, because the loss of any of the perfections and delights is impossible for them. ﴿Those who believed﴾ with true belief, ﴿and were mindful of Allah﴾, of their remnants and the appearance of their fluctuations (talawwunat). ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, through the existence of steadfastness and the characters that announce the Garden of the souls; ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, through the appearance upon them of the lights of attributes and realities, which announce the Garden of the hearts. The apparent meaning is that the relative clause is an explanation of "the friends of Allah", so the wali is the believer who is mindful of Allah to a perfect degree. For the term there are various expressions, some of which have been mentioned earlier.

In al-Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya by Ibn Arabi): the wali is the one whom Allah Most High has taken as His ally with His support in the station of striving against the four enemies: desire, the self, Satan and the world. In it there is also a division of the friends of Allah into several categories, among them the qutbs (poles), the awtad (pegs), the abdal (substitutes), the nuqaba' (chiefs) and the nukhaba' (choice ones). This has been related both as marfu' and mawquf from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Anas, Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Ubada ibn al-Samit, Ibn Abbas, Abdullah ibn Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Awf ibn Malik, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Wathila ibn al-Asqa', Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Darda', and Umm Salama; and from the mursal reports of al-Hasan, Ata' and Bakr ibn Khunays; and from the reports from the Successors and those after them, which are innumerable. Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti mentioned this in a separate treatise of his, and he strengthened its pillars, while some (of those whom we have mentioned earlier) denied it. The truth is with those who affirm it, and I, praise be to Allah Most High, am among them, although I have not previously strengthened its pillars. Also (mentioned are) the a'imma (imams), the hawariyyun (disciples), the rajabiyyun, the khatm, the malamiyya, the fuqara' (the poor), saqit al-rafraf (the fallen one of the rafraf), the son of the fallen one of the Throne, the umana' (trustees), the muhdathun (the newly inspired), and other categories. The Greatest Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, counted the messengers and prophets, peace be upon them, among them; and the statement of the verse applies to them, peace be upon them, in the fullest manner.

It is attributed to him, may Allah Most High be pleased with him, that he held the view that the wali is superior to the prophet and the messenger, and many of the deniers engaged in this, to the point that they declared him a disbeliever—may Allah forbid it for him—because of this. Yet he stated in more than one place in his al-Futuhat, and likewise in the rest of his works, what contradicts this view as the deniers understood it. In his book al-Qurba he mentioned that whoever hears an ambiguous expression from a realised gnostic, such as saying "Wilaya is the greatest prophethood," or "The gnostic wali's rank is above the rank of the messenger," should seek to establish the intended meaning and should not hasten to attack it. Then, in explaining what he had mentioned, he said the following text: "I know that a person has no standing merely as a human being; there is no excellence or nobility in the species by an essential judgement. Rather, distinction occurs through ranks. The prophets, may Allah's blessings be upon them, did not excel creation except through these ranks. The Prophet (ﷺ) possessed the rank of wilaya, of gnosis, and of messengerhood. The rank of wilaya and gnosis is everlasting, while the rank of messengerhood is terminated, for it ends with the delivery (of the message), and excellence belongs to what is lasting and enduring. The gnostic wali abides in the presence of Allah, glory be to Him, while the messenger goes forth, and the state of abiding is higher than the state of going forth. Thus he, may Allah's blessings be upon him, is higher and more noble in respect of being a wali and a gnostic than in respect of being a messenger. He, may Allah's blessings be upon him, is the same person, but his ranks differ; it is not that the wali among us is higher than the messenger—we seek refuge in Allah Most High from abandonment. Upon this principle, the people of unveiling and existence speak that word, for we consider only stations and speak only of them, not of persons, since speaking of persons may at times be backbiting. Speaking of stations and states is among the attributes of men. For each of us there is a known portion of drink and an apportioned provision." End of quotation. This is explicit that he, may Allah sanctify his secret, neither said, nor did any of his group say, that the wali is superior to the prophet, as is attributed to him.

Al-Sha'rani transmitted from him that he said: "There was opened to me a portion the size of the eye of a needle of the station of prophethood, as a manifestation (tajalli), not as entry, and I nearly burned." Therefore, all that appears to suggest that view should be interpreted, such as his reports in his book al-Tajalliyyat and elsewhere of his meeting with some of the prophets, peace be upon them, and his conveying to them of knowledge that they did not possess. Likewise the saying of Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, may Allah sanctify his secret, which has been mentioned previously: "O company of prophets, you were given titles, and we were given what you were not given," and so on. For the belief that a wali of the awliya' is superior to a prophet of the prophets is great disbelief and far-off error. Even if it were permissible to prefer a wali over a prophet, the greatest of the truthful (al-Siddiq al-Akbar), may Allah Most High be pleased with him, would be preferred over any of the prophets, because he is the highest of the awliya' in rank, as the People of the Sunna maintain. The Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, also stated this in his book al-Qurba, although he was not preferred in that way; rather, he was preferred over all others, as he expressed: "The sun has not risen nor set upon anyone after the prophets who is more excellent than Abu Bakr al-Siddiq." So if al-Siddiq is not preferred, though he is the one in whose breast there settled what settled and who attained perfection beyond counting, how could anyone else be preferred?

Many of the Shi'a, however, preferred Ali, may Allah honour his face, and likewise his descendants, the pure Imams, may Allah be pleased with them all, over many of the prophets and messengers, including the Ulu al-'Azm (the prophets of steadfast resolve) and others. They have no basis for this except false reports and mistaken opinions.

In sum, whenever we see a person who is a believer and God-fearing, we judge him to be a friend of God (wali) based on the outward state, and it is obligatory for us to treat him with what befits him of honor and reverence, without exaggerating about him by preferring him over a messenger, a prophet, or the like. This is what the common people today do in their treatment of someone they believe to be a friend of God, which is most like the treatment of the polytheists toward someone they believe to be a god. We ask God Most High for pardon and well-being. Nor is it required that a marvel (karamah, a miraculous favor of God granted to a saint) occur at his hand, as a miracle (mu'jizah) must occur at the hand of a messenger. Steadfastness (istiqamah) suffices him as a marvel, as is shown by what is famously reported of Abu Yazid, may his secret be sanctified. Indeed, the perfect friend of God pays no attention to marvels and does not desire that they occur at his hand, unless they contain a benefit for the Muslims, specifically or generally. In al-Jawahir wa'l-Durar of al-Sha'rani, it is said: "I heard our shaykh say: If the friend of God slips and does not return to the right course in time, he is punished with a veil, which is that he consents to the manifestation of breaking customary patterns, called marvels in the language of the common people, so he shows them and says: 'If I were being held accountable for this slip, the power of disposal would have been withdrawn from me.' He overlooks that this is a gradual trap (istidraj). Rather, even if he is free from slips, it is obligatory for him to fear deception and gradual trap." Some of them said: "The marvel is the menstruation of men, and whoever is deceived by marvels dies in his sleep. The most harmful of marvels to the friend of God is what causes fame, for fame is a calamity." It has been reported from the elite that it diminishes the rank of perfection, and they supported this with the well-known report: "Whoever people know is singled out for trial." Yes, it is mentioned in Asrar al-Qur'an that friendship is not complete except by four stations. The first is the station of love (mahabbah), the second is the station of longing (shawq), the third is the station of passionate love (ishq), and the fourth is the station of gnosis (ma'rifah). Love does not occur except by unveiling of beauty, longing does not occur except by inhaling the breeze of union, passionate love does not occur except by the nearness of lights, and gnosis does not occur except by companionship. Companionship is realized by the unveiling of divinity together with the manifestation of the lights of the attributes. The attainment of this has signs and marks mentioned in that book, so whoever wants them should consult it. Discussion of this station is extensive, and the books of this people are full of it, and what we have mentioned suffices for our purpose. The best thing to rely on in recognizing the friend of God is following the radiant Sacred Law (shari'ah) and treading the white path. Whoever departs from it by the breadth of a finger is far removed from friendship by many stages, so he should not be called a friend of God, even if he brings a thousand thousand extraordinary acts. The lawful friend of God today is rarer than the red sulphur, and there is no power nor might except in God.

As for the tents, they are like their tents, but I see the women of the tribe are not its women.

﴿There is no changing the words of God﴾, that is, for what has preceded for them in eternity of good care. Or: there is no changing of His realities, Glory be to Him, that descend upon them, and His names that are unveiled to them, and the rulings of His manifestations, exalted and high, that come down upon them first. Or: there is no changing of their natural disposition (fitrah) upon which He created them. And every created thing is called a word (kalimah), because it is the effect of the Word. ﴿And let not their saying grieve you﴾, that is, do not be affected by it. ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to God﴾; no one other than Him possesses any of it. So God Most High will suffice you against them and will subdue them. ﴿He is the All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what should be done to them.

Page 180

﴿Unquestionably, to God belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, that is, everyone in them is under His dominion, Glory be to Him, His disposal, and His subjugation; they have no power over anything without His permission. So it is like an emphasis on what the previous verse conveyed. Or: among those in them are the angels and the two weighty ones (jinn and humans), who are the noblest of possible beings, all servants of Him, Glory be to Him, none of whom is fit for lordship. So what cannot be rationally conceived is more deserving of not being fit for it. Thus it is like evidence for His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And those who call upon other than God do not follow partners﴾, they follow only what they imagine and fancy to be a partner, while there is no partnership for Him in reality. ﴿It is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾. This is an allusion to the rest of lovers and longing ones in the night when it extends its ropes and spreads its cloak, and their inclination toward conversing with their Beloved, their attraction to beholding what they seek, their delight in the divine arrivals that come upon them, and their absorption in the various kinds of Lordly manifestations. From here one of them said: "Were it not for the night, I would not have loved to remain in this world." This is the state of the lovers of the Presence, and they are the true lovers. May God Most High benefit us through them. And one of the metaphorical poets recited:

I spend my day in talk and in hopes, and the night gathers me with worry, a gatherer.
My day is the day of people, until the night appears to me, and beds stir me toward you.

﴿And the day as something to see﴾, that is, He clothed it in the garment of the lights of power, so that you may fulfill your necessary needs therein. It is said: the allusion by that is to the night of the body and the day of the spirit, so that you may see by it the realities of things and what you are guided by. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, the words of God Most High, so they uphold its inner meanings and its limits, and they become aware through it of His attributes and names, Glory be to Him.

﴿And they said: God has taken a son﴾, that is, a derivative that shares His nature. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, that is, I declare Him exalted, Most High, above that. ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾, whose existence is by His essence, and by Him exists everything; and that contradicts neediness. He emphasized His self-sufficiency, exalted is His majesty, by His saying, Most High: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, etc. And His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah﴾, etc. is a command to him, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, to recite to them the news of Noah, peace be upon him, concerning the soundness of his trust in God Most High, and his looking at his people and their partners with the eye of self-sufficiency, and his indifference to them and their schemes, so that they may take lesson from his condition, peace and blessings be upon him. For the prophets, peace be upon them, are in the creed of monotheism, standing by God Most High, and not turning toward creation, whether... Or it is a command to him, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, to recite the news of Noah with his people, so that his people may be admonished and refrain from what they are upon that leads to their destruction. ﴿And Moses said: O my people, if you have believed in God﴾, that is, with true faith, ﴿then upon Him rely, if you are Muslims﴾, that is, submissive. That is: if your faith is sound with certainty, then upon Him rely, on the condition that you have no action of your own, and you do not see for yourselves or for others any power or influence, but rather you are submissive like the dead before his washer. For the condition of the validity of trust is the annihilation of the remnants of actions and powers. ﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered, so remain steadfast﴾, that is, upon what you are in terms of supplication, in gratitude for that answer. It was also said: remain steadfast upon your knowledge of the station of asking, which is the station of contentment, so that it may be answered for you after you supplicate. For whoever does not know the station of asking may bring him to something outside its station, so he violates etiquette and is not answered. It was also said: this is a rebuke to them both, peace be upon them, that is: your supplication has been answered because of your weakness in bearing the onset of My trial, so remain steadfast after that in bearing My affliction and patience in it, for that is fitting to your station. It has been said: knowledge requires contentment with the decree and tranquility in affliction. It was also said: that is, remain steadfast in your supplication. Steadfastness in supplication is, as Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri said, that the supplicant does not become angry at the delay of the answer, and does not ask a request of specificity. We ask God Most High to grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with.

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea.﴾ *Jāwaza al-makān* means he crossed the place, meaning he traversed it and went beyond it. The verb is transitive to its first object, which was originally the agent with the preposition *bi-* (*bi-*), and to the second object directly. The meaning is: We made them cross the sea, by making it dry and by preserving them until they reached the shore. Al-Ḥasan read *(jawwaznā)* with gemination. The form *fa''ala* here has the meaning of *fā'il*, so it derives from *al-tajwīz* (causing to pass), which is synonymous with *al-mujāwaza* in the sense mentioned above. It does not mean *nafadha* (to pass through), because that does not require transitivity with *bi-*. It is transitive to the second object with *fī*, as in the line of poetry:

*"And there must be a guide who permits its path, as he permitted the going-in at the door, so let him be careful."*

Accordingly, the correct form linguistically would have been: *"wa-jawwaznā Banī Isrā'īla al-baḥra,"* meaning, *"We made the Children of Israel pass through the sea,"* that is, *"We led them through it and made them enter it."* In the verse there is an indication of their separation from the sea, and of the divine care accompanying them during the crossing, as is well known in the distinction between *adhhabahu* (he took it away) and *dhahaba bihi* (he went away with it).

﴿So Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them.﴾ Al-Rāghib said: It is said *tabi'ahu* and *atba'ahu* when one follows his trace, either physically or by imitation and obedience. The apparent meaning is that the two verbs have the same sense.

Some of the verifiers said: It is said *tabi'tuhu ḥattā atba'tuhu* when he was ahead of you and you caught up with him. So the meaning here is that he overtook them and reached them. ﴿Pharaoh and his soldiers,﴾ until the two groups came into view of each other and the two hosts were almost meeting. ﴿In transgression and enmity,﴾ that is, in injustice and aggression. These are two verbal nouns in the accusative, functioning as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) in the sense of the active participle, meaning *bāghīna* (transgressing) and *ʿādīna* (aggressing). Or they are an accusative of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*), meaning for the sake of transgression and aggression.

Al-Ḥasan read *(ʿudūwan)* with a damma on the *ʿayn* and the *dāl*, and with gemination of the *wāw*. The reason is that when God, glorified and exalted, informed Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, that their prayer had been answered, He commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night. As one of many has mentioned, they numbered six hundred thousand. He brought them out while Pharaoh and his chiefs were heedless. When he perceived this, he went out himself with his soldiers in pursuit of them, hastening. The people turned around and behold, the great calamity was behind them. They said: "O Moses, here is Pharaoh and his soldiers behind us, and here is the sea before us. So how can we be saved?" Then God, exalted, revealed to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff." He struck it, and it split into twelve parts, each part like a great mountain, and each tribe had a path. They walked along them. Pharaoh and those with him reached the shore, having come out of the sea, and their passage remained as it was, with all of them in it. When the last of them had entered and the first of them were about to come out, the sea covered them with what covered them. ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him,﴾ that is, reached him. The intended sense of his being overtaken is that he fell into it and was entangled in its first effects. It has been said that the meaning of *adraka-hu* is that he was close to reaching it, like the saying *jā'a al-shitā'u fa-ta'ahhab* (winter has come, so prepare yourself). This is because the reality of being overtaken prevents the statement that God recounted with His words, exalted is His majesty: ﴿He said: I believe﴾ and so on. Some people kept *idrāk* (overtaking) in its apparent meaning and understood the saying as the inner speech (*kalām nafsī*). They claimed that the verse is evidence for the existence of inner speech. This was criticized on the grounds that the presence of the possibility of another meaning invalidates the soundness of the argument. Whatever the case, the intended meaning is not an announcement of a previous faith, as has been said, but rather the creation of a faith at that moment. ﴿That there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe.﴾ That is, *bi-annahu* (in that). The preposition was assumed to be elided because faith, and likewise disbelief, is transitive with *bi-*. The position of its complement after its elision, whether in the genitive or the accusative, is a well-known point of disagreement. To make it transitive directly, without any assumed preposition, is contrary to the well-known usage of the verb.

Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read *(innahu)* with a kasra, based on the implied verb of saying (*iḍmār al-qawl*), meaning "and he said: indeed he..." Or it is a new resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) explaining his faith. Or it is a substitution (*ibdāl*) from the sentence *āmantu*. A nominal sentence may be substituted for a verbal one, and the resumption is in the sense of substitution with regard to what is reported, not with regard to the reporting, because the first sentence is in his speech, and the first sentence in his speech is resumptive, and what is substituted from a resumptive sentence is resumptive. The pronoun refers to the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*). God, exalted, expressed it with the relative pronoun and made its relative clause the faith of the Children of Israel in Him, exalted, and did not say, as the sorcerers said:

*﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron.﴾* This is to indicate his return from obstinacy and his following of those who were leading them, hoping for acceptance and for being included with them in the line of salvation. ﴿And I am among the Muslims.﴾ That is, those who submitted themselves to God, exalted; that is, they made them pure and sound for Him, glorified is He. By "them" is intended either the Children of Israel specifically, or the category, and they were at that time included in it by primary inclusion. The apparent meaning is that the sentence, in both cases, is conjoined to the sentence "āmanat" (believed), and the choice of the nominal form is for claiming continuity and persistence.

It has also been said: On the first view it is conjoined, and on the second it may also be circumstantial (*ḥāl*) from the speaker's pronoun, meaning: "I believed sincerely for God, exalted, being included in the line of those firmly established in that." He repeated the single meaning in three expressions and went to great lengths, eager for acceptance, which entails salvation. Would that some of this had been at the time when faith would benefit him, and that was before despair, for the faith of despair is not accepted, as the eminent scholars have held.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 91:

﴿Now?﴾ The interrogative (istifham) here is for denunciation and reproach. The adverbial phrase (zarf) depends on a deleted element that is understood as postponed, meaning: "Now you believe, when you have despaired of life and become certain of death?" It is understood as postponed so that the denunciation and reproach are directed at delaying faith to a point where its acceptance is impossible. The speech is understood with the implied verb "said" (al-qawl), meaning: "So it was said to him." This is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿he said﴾, and this whole passage up to ﴿a sign﴾ is a narration of what God, glorified be He, did in anger toward the forsaken one, and of the response to what he displayed with a dreadful rejection, and a rebuke for his disobedience and corruption, and so on. Omitting the mentioned verb and presenting the narrated report in the form of a performative speech (insha') indicates the great degree of wrath and the intensity of anger, which is evident.

As for who said this to him, it is said: it is God, exalted is He. It is said: it is Gabriel, peace be upon him. It is said: it is Michael, peace be upon him. Abu al-Shaykh narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to me: 'I have never hated any of God's creatures as I hated Iblis on the day he was commanded to prostrate and refused to prostrate. And I have never hated anything more intensely than Pharaoh. When the day of drowning came, I feared that he would hold fast to the word of sincerity and be saved, so I took a handful of mud and struck it into his mouth. Then I found God, exalted is He, to be more angry with him than I was, so He commanded Michael, who came to him and said: Now?'" And what this report contains of Gabriel's action has come in other reports. Among these is what al-Tayalisi, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Hakim narrated, and which they both declared sound, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: Gabriel said to me: 'If you had seen me, as I took from the sea's bed and pushed it into Pharaoh's mouth, fearing that the mercy would reach him.'" This reason (ta'lil) has been found problematic.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that this is among the additions of those who slander God and His angels, peace be upon them. In this there are two errors. The first is that faith is valid in the heart, like the faith of a mute person, so the state of the sea does not prevent it. The second is that whoever dislikes the faith of an unbeliever and loves his remaining in disbelief is himself an unbeliever, because contentment with disbelief is disbelief. Ibn al-Munir approved of this, saying: "He denounced a denounceable thing and became angry for God and His angels, peace be upon them, as is their due." The majority holds the opposite view, because the hadith is sound according to the trustworthy imams, such as al-Tirmidhi, who is preferred over the later narrators of hadith after Muslim and others. They have labored to explain its meaning so that no difficulty remains in it.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that the intended meaning of "mercy" is worldly mercy, that is, deliverance, which is what the forsaken one sought. It is not necessary for its attainment that faith be valid, as in the case of the people of Jonah, peace be upon him, so that from disliking it there would follow what cannot be imagined regarding Gabriel, peace be upon him, namely contentment with disbelief. There is no impossibility in this mercy being bestowed merely upon uttering the word of faith, even if that was in a state of distress and despair. Thus his, peace be upon him, pushing of the mud is interpreted as closing the door to a remote possibility, due to complete rage and intense anger, and the quotation ends.

[Page 183]

It is not hidden that interpreting "mercy" as worldly mercy is far-fetched, and what al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, almost rejects it: "The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to me: 'If you had seen me, O Muhammad, when I was pressing down on Pharaoh with one of my hands and pushing the mud into his mouth, fearing that the mercy of God, exalted is He, would reach him, so that he would be forgiven.'" For in it forgiveness is arranged upon the attainment of mercy, and this is clear that the intended meaning is not worldly mercy, because forgiveness is not consequent upon it. What is consequent upon it is only deliverance.

Some scholarly verifiers said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, did what he did out of anger at him for what had proceeded from him, and out of fear that if he repeated that, it might perhaps be accepted from him by way of breaking the customary course, because of the vastness of the sea of mercy that encompasses everything. As for contentment with disbelief, the truth is that it is not disbelief absolutely; rather, it is disbelief when one approves of it, and disbelief is only one's contentment with one's own disbelief, as in al-Ta'wilat by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi (known as 'Alam al-Huda), and the quotation ends. What relates to this issue has already been mentioned just above, so recall it, for "what is in the covenant is from antiquity." Yes, it is said: contentment with one's own disbelief occurs only when he is already a disbeliever, so there is no sense in counting it as disbelief, since disbelief has already been established before it. This has what it has and what it lacks, and it is another discussion that does not harm what we are dealing with.

Al-Tibi, after answering with what he answered, added to it his statement: "Furthermore, there is no room for reason in such a sound report except acceptance and attributing deficiency to the self. It may be said: when a report contradicts clear reason, or includes attributing to a person what cannot be conceived in terms of the Law, and it is not possible to interpret it in a way that agrees with the judgment of reason and removes the attribution of deficiency, then it is not sound. Accusing the narrator of something that weakens the credibility of his report is easier than accusing clear reason and attributing deficiency to it, rather than attributing deficiency to one whom God, exalted is He, and His Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, have testified to be preserved from error and perfect. So reflect. And God is the Granter of success."

As for His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿and you had disobeyed before﴾, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the verb governing the adverbial phrase. It was brought to intensify the reproach and rebuke for delaying faith until this moment, by clarifying that the delay was not for any excuse that might be counted, but was in the manner of rejection, defiance, and corruption. For His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and you were among the corrupters﴾ (91) is coordinated ('atf) with ﴿you had disobeyed﴾ and falls within the scope of the circumstantial clause. The meaning is: "And you were among the corrupters who went to excess in misguidance and in leading others astray from faith." This is an expression for his corruption, which returns to himself and spreads to others through injustice, transgression, and barring the Children of Israel from the path. The first refers to his disobedience that was specific to him.

[p. 183]

His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿So today We shall save you in your body﴾ is mockery of him, a disappointing of him, and a complete cutting off of his hopes. The meaning is: today We shall bring you out of what your people fell into, from the depths of the sea, and We shall make you float, clothed in your body, stripped of the soul. He expressed that by "saving" (tanjiyah) metaphorically (majaz). He made the prepositional phrase "in your body" a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the addressed pronoun, which also hints that his purpose in faith was salvation. It has also been said that the meaning of the circumstantial clause is "stripped of clothing," or "with all his limbs complete."

Some of the distinguished scholars took the speech to be an instance of tajrid (abstraction, a rhetorical device in which a speaker addresses himself as if he were another person). It is permissible that the bāʾ (in bi-badanika, "in your body") is extra (zāʾidah), and "your body" is a substitute (badal al-baʿḍ) for the addressed pronoun, as if it were said: "We shall save your body." It has also been held that the bāʾ indicates instrumentality, so that the construction follows the pattern of your saying "I took him with your hand" and "I looked at him with your eye," as an announcement that this remote object had been attained. This is a view, but it is not a commendable one, as is not hidden.

It has also been said that "tanjiyah" means throwing onto a najwah, which is an elevated place. It was said: it was named so because it saves one from the flood. Yunus ibn Habib the grammarian followed this view. Ibn al-Anbari and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him that he said: the meaning is "We shall place you on an elevation of the land so that the Children of Israel see you and know that you have died."

The interpretation of "body" (badan) as "armour" (dir') has also come down, and this was narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ubayy. He had an armour of gold by which he was recognised. In another report it was of pearl.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Jahdam Musa ibn Salim that Pharaoh had a garment he wore called "the badan," which gleamed.

Ya'qub recited (nunjīka) from the form of if'al, which has the same meaning as the form tafʿīl (intensive/causative), in its two earlier senses. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted from Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' al-Yamani and Yazid al-Barbari that they both recited (nunaḥḥīka) with the unpointed ḥāʾ, and it is attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-Sammal. That means: We shall place you in a side (nāḥiyah) and cast you onto the shore.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, recited (bi-abdānika) in the plural form, by making each limb equivalent to the body, so he applied the whole to the part by way of metaphor. On this basis is the plural of "limbs" (ijrām) in the verse:

"How many a place, had I not been, you would have fallen as one falls
from the top of a cliff, sliding down by his own limbs."

Or it means "your armours," on the basis that the one abandoned was wearing one armour over another.

Ibn al-Anbari transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited (bi-nidā'ika), that is, "with your call" (bi-du'ā'ika).

﴿So that you may be a sign to those after you﴾: that is, so that you may be a sign to those who come after you among the nations, when they hear the account of your condition, from one who witnessed your state and what befell you, as a lesson and a deterrent against tyranny, or as a proof showing them that man, however far he reaches in greatness of rank, height of pride and strength of authority, is a slave, subdued, far from the places of divinity and lordship.

It has been said that by "those after him" is meant those who remained after him of the Children of Israel, that is, that it might be a sign for them of the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him, since in their souls there was such awe of the two of them that it led them to imagine that he would not perish. So they denied Musa's report of his destruction until they saw him on their path along the shore, red and short, like a bull. This was narrated from Mujahid.

It was recited (li-man khalafaka) as a past verb, meaning "came to occupy your place." It is attributed to Ibn al-Sumayqa' and Abu al-Simal that both recited (li-man khalaqaka) with a fatha on the lām and the qāf, meaning "that it be a sign for your Creator, like the other signs." For His, glory be to Him, singling you out for casting onto the shore is evidence that He intended by it, may His majesty be exalted, to expose your forgery, remove doubts about your affair, and be a clear proof of His perfect knowledge, power, wisdom and will. This is a meaning with no harm in it, and the verse may be interpreted by it also on the well-known recitation.

It is mentioned in al-Nashr that among what is not reliably transmitted is the recitation of Ibn al-Sumayqa' and Abu al-Sammal (nunaḥḥīka) with the ḥāʾ and (li-man khalaqaka) with the qāf. Regarding the explanation of his rescue by what has been mentioned, as some of the verifiers have said, there is an indication that it was not for his honour or for another benefit returning to him, but for the complete contempt for him, exposing him before the eyes of witnesses and increasing the horror of his state. It is like one who is killed and then his body is dragged through the markets and thrown as carrion in the square, or who is carried around on his head in the regions and cities.

The first lām is connected to the verb, and the second is connected to a deleted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to (āyatan), meaning: existing for those after you. The response to this abandoned one came in the manner of what was said in His saying: ﴿I believe that He﴾ etc., in its inclusion of exaggeration, as is not hidden to one who reflects on the verse.

He confirmed the sense of what was reported by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs﴾ 92: that is, they do not reflect upon them nor take lessons from them. This is a concluding parenthetical remark (i'tiraḍ tadhyīl) placed at the point of relating this and similar verses.

Consensus (ijma') has been established on the disbelief of the abandoned one and the non-acceptance of his faith. What also bears witness to this is what Ibn 'Adi and al-Tabarani narrated, that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Allah created Yahya ibn Zakariyya in his mother's womb a believer, and He created Pharaoh in his mother's womb a disbeliever." So he is among the people of the Fire, abiding therein forever, without doubt.

On this the Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, spoke at the beginning of his book al-Futuhat, in the sixty-second chapter of it, where he mentioned that those whom Allah forsook among the servants He divided into two groups. One group is not harmed by the sins they committed, and to them is the indication in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾. These are not touched by the Fire, by what Allah has turned to them in repentance, and by the seeking of forgiveness of the Exalted Assembly and their supplication for them.

He divided the other group into two parts. One part Allah brings out of the Fire by intercession, and they are a group of believers and people of monotheism who died without their sins having been expiated. The other part He leaves in the Fire, and they are specifically the criminals, to whom it will be said on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾, and to them is said "people of the Fire," because they are the ones who inhabit it. They are of four groups, all of them in the Fire, not coming out of it.

The first group: those who are arrogant toward Allah, Exalted, like Pharaoh and those like him, who claimed lordship for himself and denied it of Allah, Exalted, saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾, and said: ﴿I am your most high lord﴾, meaning by it "other than me in the heavens." Likewise Nimrod and others.

The second: the polytheists, who affirmed Allah, Exalted, but made other gods along with Him, and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾.

The third: the "mu'attilah" (deniers), who negated God entirely, so they did not affirm any god for the world at all.

The fourth: the hypocrites, who displayed faith out of the compulsion by which judgment was passed upon them, while in their souls they held to one of these three groups. These four categories are the people of the Fire who do not come out of it, from among jinn and humans," and the quotation ends.

This is explicit in what we have said. However, in another place of the same book he went against it, saying in the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, in substance: When Allah, Exalted, knew that He had sealed every heart that manifests greatness and pride, and that Pharaoh in his soul was the most abased of the abased, He commanded Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, to treat him with mercy and gentleness, in accordance with the inner state of his soul and to draw out his outward greatness and pride. So He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Speak to him gently; perhaps he will remember or fear﴾. The "perhaps" and "maybe" from Allah, Exalted, are obligatory. So be mindful, by the gentleness and humility which confronted him, of what he was in his inner self, so that the outer and the inner would be equal. That leaven continued to work within him, with the divine expectation whose fulfilment is obligatory, and its judgment grew stronger until the time when his despair of following them was cut off. When the drowning came between him and his hopes, he resorted to what had been hidden in his inner self of humiliation and need, so that the divine hope would be realised before the believers. So he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾. Thus one doubt was removed by another doubt, just as the sorcerers said when they believed: ﴿We believed in the Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾, that is, the one to whom the two of them call. So they brought this to repel suspicion and remove doubt. His saying: "and I am of the Muslims" is an address from him to the Real, Exalted, since he knew that He, glory be to Him, hears him and sees him. So the Real addressed him in the language of the unseen, and he heard it: "Now? You have displayed what you were already knowing, and you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters to your followers." He did not say to him "and you were among the corrupters," so it is a word of good news to him, which He made known to us so that we might hope for His mercy despite our excess and our crimes.

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿So today We shall save you in your body so that you may be a sign to those after you﴾, meaning: so that salvation may be a sign for whoever comes after you, that is, a mark: if he says what you said, salvation will be for him as it was for you. What the verse indicates is not that the punishment of the Hereafter is lifted and his faith was not accepted; rather what it indicates is that the punishment of this world is not lifted from one upon whom it descends, if he believes at the time of its descent, except the people of Yunus, peace be upon him.

So His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So today We shall save you in your body﴾ means that punishment attaches only to your outward part, and We have shown the creation his salvation from punishment. The beginning of the drowning was a punishment, so death in it became a pure, innocent martyrdom, into which no disobedience had entered, and so he was taken at the best of deeds, which is uttering faith. All of this is so that no one despairs of the mercy of Allah, Exalted, and "deeds are by their endings." Faith in Allah, Exalted, kept circulating within his inner self, and the divine, essential seal in creation stood between pride and human subtleties, so pride never entered it at all.

As for His, Exalted, saying: ﴿Then their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾, it is a verified statement, perfectly clear, for the one who benefits is Allah, Exalted, and so it was not benefit except

[p. 184]

He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The way of Allah which has passed before among His servants﴾. By this is meant the faith at the sight of an unusual calamity. Exalted is He, has also said: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾. So the most that this faith can be is unwilling, and the Truth, glorified is He, has attributed it to Himself, and unwillingness has its locus in the heart, and so is faith. Allah, exalted is He, does not hold the servant to burdensome deeds on account of the hardship he finds in them, but rather multiplies his reward for them. As for this situation, hardship is far from it. Rather, he came willingly in his faith. He did not live after that but was taken [in death], and was not delayed, lest he return to what he had been upon of claiming [divinity]. Had the passengers of the sea, concerning whom He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Gone astray is whoever you invoke except Him﴾, been taken [in death] upon their deliverance, they would have died as monotheists, and deliverance had been granted to them.

Then His statement, exalted is He, in completing this story: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs﴾, in the sense that: your deliverance has appeared as a sign (ayah), i.e., a sign of the attainment of deliverance. So most of the people were heedless of this sign, and they decided against the believer with wretchedness.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So He will lead them to the Fire﴾, there is nothing in it indicating that he entered it with them. Rather, He, exalted and high is He, said: ﴿Cause the people of Pharaoh to enter the severest punishment﴾, and He did not say: "Cause Pharaoh and his people to enter." And the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, is too vast for Him not to accept the faith of one in distress. And what distress is greater than the distress of Pharaoh in the state of drowning? And Allah, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him and removes the evil?﴾ So He joined, for the distressed one who calls upon Him, the response and the removal of evil from him. And this one [Pharaoh] believed in Allah, exalted is He, sincerely, and did not call upon Him for remaining alive in this world, out of fear of the accidents [of life] and that there be placed between him and this sincerity which came to him in this state. So he preferred the side of meeting Allah, exalted is He, over remaining, by uttering the faith. And He made that drowning a punishment (nakal) of the Hereafter and the First [life]. So his punishment was no more than the distress of the salty water, and his seizure was in the best of attributes. And this is what the apparent wording gives, and it is the meaning of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾, meaning: in His taking him as a punishment (nakal) of the Hereafter and the First.

And He, glorified is He, mentioned the Hereafter before the First so that it would be known that that punishment, i.e., the punishment of drowning, is the punishment (nakal) of the Hereafter. And this is the great favor. End of quotation. It is explicit regarding his faith, indeed regarding his being among the martyrs, on the basis that death by drowning is a martyrdom for the believers, as the leading scholars of religion have agreed, with a difference of opinion concerning the death by drowning of one who was negligent in learning to swim, whether it is counted as martyrdom or not. For some of the Shafi'is held that the negligent one mentioned, if he dies by drowning, dies disobedient and not a martyr, and that the martyr is only one who dies thus while knowing how to swim, or who was not negligent in learning it but did not learn. It seems that the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, did not hold this distinction, or he knew that Pharaoh was among those who knew how to swim, or among those who were not negligent in learning it. Or he held that faith expiated for him every sin before it, and among that is the sin of negligence, for example, which is less than his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ and ﴿I know for you no god other than me﴾ by a thousand thousand degrees. But I do not know whether the drowned one is a martyr in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, as he is in our law, or whether this matter is among the distinctive features of this law, which Allah, exalted is He, has bestowed upon its people with what He has bestowed, as an honor for its Prophet, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace.

And he [Ibn 'Arabi], may his secret be sanctified, went in his book Fusus al-Hikam to something similar to what he went to later in his book al-Futuhat. Many have objected to him on this account. Yet in my view it is not greater than his saying, may his secret be sanctified, concerning the faith of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, and many of their likes, and their deliverance on the Day of Resurrection. He stated this explicitly in the Fusus. And it is strange that his objectors were not as numerous in this matter as they were in saying that Pharaoh believed. Some people have defended him, and among them, most famously, al-Jalal al-Dawani, and he has a treatise on this, in which he brought what is counted as nothing by the junior students. But in the History of Aleppo by the learned al-Halabi, as my master al-Shihab said, it is said that it is not by al-Jalal, but is by a man named Muhammad ibn Hilal al-Nahwi. And al-Qazwini refuted it,
[p. 187]
and reproached him, saying: "His example is that of a man of obscure fame who, when he came to Mecca, urinated in Zamzam in order to become known among the people." And there is a proverb: "Oppose, and you will be known." What confirms that it is not by al-Jalal is that he was a Shafi'i in school of law, as his marginal notes on al-Anwar testify to this. And in the fatawa of Ibn Hajar: some of our jurists declared unbelievers those who held the faith of Pharaoh, despite what that treatise contains of defective expression, evident weakness, and its lack of resemblance to the rest of his compositions. Had I not feared prolixity I would have recounted them to you. In sum, the apparent meanings of the verses are explicit in the unbelief of Pharaoh and the non-acceptance of his faith. And among that is His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And Ad and Thamud, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings, and Satan made their deeds appealing to them, and he averted them from the way, though they were discerning﴾ ﴿And Qarun and Pharaoh and Haman, and Moses had come to them with clear proofs, but they were arrogant in the land, and they were not those who outstrip﴾ ﴿So each We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those seized by the blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah was not to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾. For it is clearly indicative of Pharaoh's continuance in disbelief and in the sins that brought about what befell him, as is shown by the use of kana (was) and the present tense verb. And with faith there is no continuance. Moreover, that He placed him in the row of those mentioned with him is also clearly evident for the claim.

Some have added to this His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then the enemy of Mine and his enemy will take him﴾, on the basis that ʿaduww is an adjective of the form ṣifah mushabbahah, which indicates permanence, and so it indicates the permanence of his enmity toward Allah, exalted is He, and his enmity toward His Messenger, peace be upon him. And the permanence of one of the two enmities suffices for his evil state, contrary to whoever has made a mistake. They have also explicitly stated that the faith of the moment of calamity and of despair is not accepted. And there is no doubt that the faith of the forsaken one was of that kind, and his denial was obstinacy. The consensus of the mujtahid imams on non-acceptance has been related. Their basis for this is the Book and the Sunnah. What is transmitted from Imam Malik regarding acceptance has not been established according to those who are informed of the views and differences of the mujtahids. Yes, the Imam, Qadi ʿAbd al-Samad, from our masters the Hanafis, explicitly stated in his tafsir that the position of the Sufis is that faith benefits even at the witnessing of punishment. And this imam preceded the Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, by about a hundred years. Then the reporting of consensus becomes problematic, unless it is said: the authenticity of that from the Sufis, who are among the mujtahids relied upon, is not granted, because it contradicts the apparent indication of non-benefit. So that does not undermine the consensus. And in al-Zawajir: even granting it, that does not harm us regarding the claim of the consensus of the Community on the unbelief of Pharaoh, because we judge him an unbeliever not merely because of his faith at the moment of calamity, but also because of what was joined to it: that he did not believe in Allah, exalted is He, with a sound faith, but it was pure imitation. The evidence is His statement: ﴿except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed﴾. So it is as if he acknowledged that he did not know Allah, exalted is He, but only heard from the Children of Israel that the world has a god, so he believed in that god whose existence he heard the Children of Israel affirm. And this is pure imitation, which is not accepted, especially from one like Pharaoh, who was a dahri denying the existence of the Creator. For he needs a decisive proof that removes the corrupt belief he held, which reached the utmost of ugliness and vileness. Also, the conversion of a dahri and the like, of one who had adhered to something, requires that he acknowledge the falsehood of that thing in which he disbelieved. So if he had said, "I believe in the One besides whom there is no god," he would not be a Muslim. And Pharaoh did not acknowledge the falsehood of what he had disbelieved in, namely the denial of the Creator and the claim to divinity for his own wicked self. And his saying: ﴿except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed﴾ — it is not known what he intended by it. Therefore the imams have explicitly stated that "I believe in the One besides whom there is no god" does not yield faith, because of the possibility [of other meanings]; likewise what he said. And even granting it, the consensus is established that belief in Allah, exalted is He, without belief in the Messenger is not valid. So even if we grant that Pharaoh believed in Allah, exalted is He, with a sound faith, he did not believe in Moses, peace be upon him, nor did he address him at all. Thus his faith was not beneficial. Do you not see that if a disbeliever said a thousand times, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah," or "except the One in whom the Muslims believe," he would not be a believer until he says, "and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."
[p. 188]

The Sahara (magicians) exposed their faith to faith in Moses (peace be upon him) by saying: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron." So it is not said that Pharaoh's faith was of the same kind as theirs. Their faith, when they believed, was based on the miracle of Moses (peace be upon him), and faith in God Most High together with faith in the miracle of the Messenger is faith in the Messenger. Thus they believed in Moses (peace be upon him). Pharaoh, by contrast, did not expose his faith to faith in him (peace be upon him) at all. Rather, in mentioning the Children of Israel without him, [the Qur'an indicates] that he is the Messenger who knows God and what befits Him, and who guides to His path, which is a hint that he remained in disbelief in him. What the Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn al-'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, said in explaining the verse ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾ and so on lies outside the taste of Arabic speech, and is a forced effort with no meaning. What guides you to part of this is that he, may his secret be sanctified, understood the words of God Most High ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before﴾ and so on as a rebuke and good news. Yet it is not hidden that if his faith and submission were valid, the more fitting [phrasing] for the station of grace toward which the Shaykh's gaze aspired would be to say to him: "Now we accept you and honour you," since the validity of his faith entails the pleasure of the Truth with him, and one with whom the pleasure [of God] has come is not addressed with such an address, as will not be hidden from one who has knowledge of the styles and conversational usages of the Arabs. Also, how can one be addressed who had his disobedience and corruption erased by faith, with words that are clearly pure reproach, unmixed rebuke and sheer censure? That is nothing but to establish the greatest laws of wrath against him and to remind him of his ugly deeds that he had committed, and to inform him that they were what prevented him, when he uttered faith, from [reaching a point] where it would benefit him. Likewise his interpretation of ﴿so their faith did not benefit them﴾ as meaning that the one who benefits is God Most High. Yet the convention of the Book and the Sunna is to attribute things to their causes, affirmatively and negatively. So when it is said, "Faith does not benefit," its legal meaning is nothing but a judgement that it is invalid and not to be counted. And what meaning justifies restricting God Most High's benefit to this [moment], which is the time of the descent of punishment, while looking at what is actually the case, namely that God Most High is the true Benefactor at every time? Had He benefited them, He would not have uprooted them with punishment. And the words of God Most High ﴿And there the falsifiers will lose﴾ are clear evidence that what is meant by ﴿it did not benefit them﴾ is that they remained, with that faith, in disbelief, and other matters not hidden from one who reflects on his words, may his secret be sanctified. Therefore, what should be relied upon is what he first held. It has been said: when a scholar's words conflict, what is taken is what agrees with the clear evidences, and what opposes them is set aside. There is no doubt that what he first held is what agrees with that. Moreover, even if the only thing from him, may his secret be sanctified, were the saying that his faith is accepted, we would not be obliged to follow him in that, nor to act upon it, since it opposes what the Book and the Sunna indicate and what the leading Companions, the Successors, and the mujtahids after them testified to. The eminence of the one who says it does not make it binding. Mālik and others said: "Everyone's words are taken and rejected, except for the occupant of this grave," meaning the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him). And from 'Ali, may God honour his face: "Do not look at who said it; look at what was said." It seems that the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, said that by way of nazar (rational reflection), and nazar may err or be correct. Whoever knows that the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) had ijtihad (independent reasoning) and that revelation came contrary to it, will not regard what has been said about the Shaykh as too great, even if he is who he is. Moreover, even if he said that by way of kashf (mystical unveiling), but presented the argument for the sake of instruction and guidance, indicating that his understanding does not oppose what the Book indicates, we would still not be obliged to follow him by taqlid (imitation). Indeed, it has already been reported from the Divine Imam, may his secret be sanctified, that it is not permissible to imitate kashf, and more than one scholar has stated that it is not a proof for others, like ilham (inspiration), and no legal ruling is established by it. You know that if each of the two statements came by way of kashf, kashf would have to be divided into correct and incorrect, like nazar, since affirmation and negation cannot both be true or both be false. This is evident. Some have said that it is divided, though its reasoning is obscure. Among the people is one who interpreted the Shaykh's words affirming the acceptance of faith as meaning that by Pharaoh is meant the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara), and by Moses and Aaron, the two commanded to speak gently, Moses is the spirit (al-ruh) and Aaron is the heart (al-qalb). He began to establish the discourse along these lines. It is not hidden that committing to this, with its evident strain, is something the Shaykh's words reject, and it is likely contrary to the aim of his gaze. For this reason his eminent companions did not adopt it, but left his words upon their outward meaning, which is the apparent one. And declaring unbelief upon some who deny him in this is misguidance, and what a misguidance and a great injustice that deserves punishment. For he, may his secret be sanctified, has a basis for this, as do others who oppose him, even if they differ in strength and weakness. Moreover, grasping the reality of this question is not something we have been obligated to, so ignorance of it does not harm one's religion. And God Most High is the guide to the right way.

[Page 189]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 93:**

﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a goodly abode﴾ is a resumed statement, brought to explain in general terms the abundant blessings bestowed upon them after the blessing of deliverance, and their failure to give thanks for them. *Bawwa* here means *anzala* (to settle, to lodge), like *aba'a*. Its noun form is *al-bi'ah* with a kasra, as in the *al-Qamus* (Al-Firuzabadi's dictionary). It is said: *bawwa'hu manzilan* ("he settled him in a dwelling"), *bawwa'hu fi manzil* ("he settled him in a dwelling"), and likewise *bawwa'tu lahu makanan* ("I prepared a place for him") when you made it ready. It is transitive, taking one or two objects. The meaning is: We settled them after We had delivered them and destroyed their enemies.

﴿*Mubawwa' sidq*﴾ means a suitable, praiseworthy dwelling. It is a noun of place in the accusative, functioning as an adverb of place (*zarf makan*). It may also be read as a verbal noun (*masdar*) with an omitted modifier, meaning "the place of a settlement." It may also be taken as a second object. The root meaning of *sidq* is the opposite of *kadhib* (falsehood). However, it is the custom of the Arabs that when they praise something they attribute it to *sidq*, so they say, for example, *rajul sidq* ("a man of truth") when he is perfect in his qualities and suited to the purpose intended for him. It is as if they observed that everything that is thought well of is truthful. The intended meaning of this *mubawwa'* is, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from al-Dahhak, Syria and Egypt. The Children of Israel who were in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and who are the intended group here, possessed that land, according to what a number of the scholars have held.
