Abu al-Shaykh and others narrated from Qatadah that the intended meaning is Syria and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Some scholars preferred this view on the basis that those people did not return to Egypt after that. You should know that, of the two opinions, the "Children of Israel" should be understood as including their descendants, on the basis that they did not enter Syria during the lifetime of Moses, peace be upon him, but it was their sons who entered it. You have already been given what relates to this point, so recall it.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of *mubawwa'* is the outskirts of the city toward the direction of Syria, and that by the "Children of Israel" are meant the Children of Israel who lived in the time of our Prophet, upon whom be the best of blessings and the most complete of peace.

﴿And We provided them with good things﴾, that is, delights. It has been said that it may be interpreted as "a year's provision" (*al-hawl*).

﴿So they did not differ﴾ regarding the matters of their religion, but rather they were followers of the command of their Messenger, peace be upon him,

﴿until knowledge came to them﴾, that is, only after they had come to know it through reading the Torah and understanding its rulings. It has also been said that the meaning is: they did not differ concerning the affair of Muhammad, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, except after they had come to know the truth of his prophethood through his described attributes mentioned in their Book and through the manifest evidence of his miracles. This is clearly the meaning on the last opinion regarding who is meant by the Children of Israel who were settled. As for the first opinion, there is a difficulty in it, because those settled people who were in the age of Moses, peace be upon him, did not differ concerning the affair of our Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, by necessity, so that this difference could be attributed to them in reality. This is not like the statement of the Exalted: (*and when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh*), etc., nor like His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿*Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah?*﴾, so that a figurative usage (*majaz*) could be considered. Al-Tabarsi claimed that the meaning is that they were all upon disbelief and did not differ about it until Moses, peace be upon him, was sent to them and the Torah was revealed, in which was the judgment of Allah the Exalted; then some of them believed and some of them persisted in their disbelief. But this is nothing at all, as is not hidden.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that in which they used to differ﴾ (93), so He will distinguish between the truth and the falsehood by reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 94:

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾: that is, in doubt about what flows (from the Qur'an). The address is said to be to him, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and the meaning is: if you are in doubt about that by way of supposition and assumption, because doubt cannot be conceived of him, upon him be peace, since the veil has been lifted for him. For this reason the verse uses "in" (in), which is generally used for what is not certain, so that it may be used even for what is impossible by reason or by habit,

[Page 190]

as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth﴾. The truth of a conditional sentence (al-shartiyyah, the conditional clause) does not depend on the occurrence of its condition, as is evident. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "what") refers to the narratives (al-qasas), that is: if you are in doubt about the narratives sent down to you, among which is the story of Pharaoh and his people and the reports of the Children of Israel. ﴿Then ask those who read the Scripture before you﴾, for that is established among them and confirmed in their books, in accordance with what We have sent down to you. The narratives were singled out for mention because the rulings sent down to him, upon him be peace, abrogate (naskh, the annulment of an earlier ruling by a later one) their rulings and oppose them, so it cannot be conceived that they would be asked about them. By "the Scripture" is meant the genus (jins) of scripture, so it includes the Torah and the Gospel, and this is what is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. This is supported by the fact that it was recited as (al-Kutub, "the Scriptures") in the plural. The relative pronoun has also been explained as referring to those among the People of the Book who did not believe, because their informing (the Prophet) of what agrees with what was sent down, which follows from the question, is more beneficial for the purpose. Some of them explained it as referring to the believers among them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and Tamim al-Dari, and this is attributed to Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Mujahid.

It has been objected that Ibn Salam and others embraced Islam in Medina, while this surah is Meccan. What appears to be intended is the argument for the truth of what was sent down and the citing of what is in the earlier books, as mentioned, and that the Qur'an confirms them. The sum of this is that the benefit is removing doubt if it should arise for someone other than him, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, through proof; or describing the People of the Book as firmly rooted in knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood, may God's peace and blessings be upon him; or rebuking them for abandoning faith; or stirring the Messenger, upon him be peace, and increasing his steadfastness. The purpose is not to affirm the possibility that doubt could occur to him, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, at all. For this reason, when this verse came to him, upon him be peace, he said, as Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada: "I do not doubt, and I will not ask."

Al-Zajjaj claimed that "in" (in) is a negation, and that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿then ask﴾, is the response of the conditional, with the response being implied, that is: "You were not in doubt about what We sent down to you; but if you wish to increase in certainty, then ask." This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and what has been mentioned is sufficient without it. Similar to this is what has been said: that doubt here means constriction and hardship, by what he (the Prophet) witnesses of his people's obstinacy and harm, that is: if you become constricted by what you encounter of your people's harm and obstinacy, then ask the People of the Book how the prophets, upon them be peace, endured the harm and obstinacy of their peoples, and be patient likewise. Rather, this is far more remote than that. It has also been said that the address is to him, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, but what is meant is his community, or anyone who hears: that is, if you, O listener, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you through the tongue of our Prophet, then ask. According to this, (fa-anzalna ilayk, "so We sent down to you") is similar to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾. In making the recitation (al-qira'ah, the reading) the complement of the relative clause, there is an indication that the answer does not depend on more than it. The verse also alerts that whoever is troubled by a doubt in religion should consult those among the people of knowledge who can remove it, indeed should hasten to do so, as indicated by the consequential fa' (the "fa" of the apodosis, al-fa' al-jaza'iyyah, which marks what follows as a consequence), on the basis that it denotes sequence. ﴿Indeed, the truth has come to you﴾, the clear truth from which there is no turning away and about whose truth there is no doubt, ﴿from your Lord﴾, who manages what is good for your affairs. ﴿So never be among the waverers﴾: that is, by wavering from what you are upon of firmness and certainty. Remain upon that as you were before. Al-imtira' is doubt and hesitation, and it is lighter than denial, which is why it is mentioned first.

Then He, glory be to Him, followed with His words: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., any of them, ﴿for you would then be﴾ by that ﴿among the losers﴾ (95), in themselves and in their deeds. The expression "the losers" is more evident in warning than the expression "the disbelievers." The purpose of the prohibition in both places is incitement and stirring up (al-tahyij wa'l-ilhab), like what has passed. What is meant by this is to inform that doubting and denying have reached such ugliness and a degree of being forbidden that one should be prohibited from them even if he is someone who cannot possibly be characterized by them, so how about someone for whom such characterization is possible? And in this there is a cutting off of the hopes of the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 96:

Page 191
﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified﴾ etc. The explanation of the source is the persistence of the disbelievers in what they are upon of disbelief and error, to the point that they do not benefit from faith. That is: indeed, those upon whom ﴿the word of your Lord﴾ has been established, i.e. His judgment and decree, which is interpreted by the Ash'arites as His eternal will, related to things as they are, regarding what has not ceased to be that they will die in disbelief or be made to abide forever in the Fire, ﴿they will not believe, 96﴾, since it is not possible that His decree be annulled or His will be contravened, exalted is His majesty and glorified is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 10, verse 97:**

﴿Even if every sign came to them﴾, one whose meaning is clear and acceptable to minds, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾: drowning and the like. Then it will be said to them, "You let the milk go to waste in summer" (a proverb). Al-Zamakhshari explained the word (kalimah) as referring to God's decree that He wrote on the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), and which He informed the angels about, that they would die as disbelievers. He made that writing the writing of knowledge (kitab ma'lum), not the writing of decree and will (kitab muqaddar wa murad). There is no evidence in the explanation of the word for this, except that making the writing a writing of knowledge rather than a writing of decree and will is founded on the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilism, a rationalist school of theology).

What the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) hold is that all the actions of the servants, in their entirety, are known to Him, may He be exalted, and willed by Him. Nothing occurs except what He wills, and what He knows and wills, may His majesty be glorified, are in agreement. Opposition between them is not permitted. His knowledge, may He be glorified, relates only to what the thing is in itself. He wills only what He knows, and He decrees only what He wills. There is no compulsion (jabr) there and no delegation (tafwid), but a matter between two matters.

Al-Mawla al-Kurani explained this in his commentary on the four premises mentioned in Tawdih al-Usul (a work of usul), namely that the servant is compelled by his own choice (majbur bi-ikhtiyarihi). He elaborated on this in a way that cannot be surpassed, and by affirming the predisposition (isti'dad), and that it is not created (ghayr majul), the conclusive proof becomes clear. He expanded the discussion in ilm al-kalam (speculative theology). Some of what is useful for this matter has already been mentioned. If you want what settles the heart and opens the inner conscience, then turn to the treatises of that Mawla on this subject, for their paths are clear in attaining certainty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 98:

﴿Why was there not⁠﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) that establishes their destruction. Here "lawla" (why not) is a tahdid (exhortation, from the particle ḥaḍḍ, "urging") that carries the sense of reproach, like "halla" (why not). A parallel is found in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"You count the slaughter of she-camels the best of your glory,
O sons of Dawtari, when there was not the al-Kamā al-muqanna'."

This is supported by the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with both of them, which has "fahallā" (so why not). The reproach is, as transmitted from al-Saffaqsi, for abandoning the faith mentioned afterwards. "Kāna" (was) is, as some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have chosen, a defective (nāqiṣa) verb. Allah's statement ﴿a town⁠﴾ is its subject, and the clause ﴿believed⁠﴾ is its predicate. His statement ﴿so its faith benefited it⁠﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the predicate, meaning: "Why was there not a town among the towns that We destroyed with total annihilation (ihlāk al-istiṣāl) that believed before witnessing the punishment, and did not delay its faith until the time of seeing it, as Pharaoh delayed his faith, so that its faith benefited it, in that Allah accepted it from them and lifted the punishment from them because of it?"

Al-Samin and others went to the view that the verb is complete (tāmma), so "a town" is its agent (fā'il), the clause ﴿believed⁠﴾ is a qualifier (ṣifa), and ﴿benefited it⁠﴾ is coordinated with it. This was objected to on the grounds that the exhortation and reproach would then be about existence, which is not the intended meaning. It was answered that there is no barrier to the exhortation being about the qualifier, and in that case there is no difficulty in what has been said. In any case, "the town" means its people by a common figurative usage (majāz shā'i'), and the indication (qarīna) here is too clear to be hidden.

Allah's statement, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿except the people of Yunus⁠﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), as said by al-Zajjaj, Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i and most grammarians. That is: "but the people of Yunus, ﴿when they believed⁠﴾ at the moment they saw the signs of the punishment, and they did not delay until it descended, ﴿We lifted from them the punishment of disgrace⁠﴾, that is the humiliation and degradation, ﴿in the life of this world⁠﴾ after it had overshadowed them and was about to descend upon them. ﴿And We let them enjoy⁠﴾ the enjoyments of this world after the lifting of the punishment from them, ﴿for a time⁠﴾, that is a period of time determined for them in Allah's knowledge.

It is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is until the Day of Resurrection, so they are alive today, except that Allah has concealed them from people, in the manner that is said about al-Khidr, peace be upon him. I have seen in some books something agreeing with this, except that it mentions that they will appear in the days of the Mahdi and will be among his helpers, and then they will die. All of this has no soundness.

Others said: the exception is continuous (muttasil), and by "town" is meant its people who were on the brink of destruction.

It was also said: the disobedient. The negation that is implied by the exhortation is taken into account, and the exhortation also implies a command, which is why they treated it as having the same ruling. However, it is not valid to take this into account on the assumption of continuity, because it would entail that faith would be among the excluded things, which is not sought, and it is not sought; rather it is corrupt. It was also said: there is no barrier to this on that assumption, because the people of the towns are being urged to beneficial faith, and the people of Yunus are not being urged to it, because they had believed. Taste (al-dhawq) refuses anything except taking the negation alone when continuity is taken into account. And His statement, glorified is He, ﴿when they believed⁠﴾ would be a resumption (isti'nāf) explaining the benefit of their faith.

It is also read "illā qawmu" (with the nominative) in the sense of an apposition (badal) from "qarya" (town), meaning its people. Those who held the view of continuity and taking the negation into account were strengthened by this, because an apposition can only occur in a non-affirmative context. Some grammarians have explained this reading as follows: "illā" is in the sense of "ghayr" (other than), and it is a qualifier whose grammatical case (i'rab) appears in what follows it, as in the verse of one poet:

"Every brother from whom his brother parts ... by the life of your father, except the two Farqads (stars)."

The apparent sense of their statement is that the exception is absolutely from "qarya." It is reported from al-Zamakhshari that on the first view it is from "qarya," not from the pronoun in "believed," and he gave as reason that the disjunctive exception means "but," and so it lies between two different statements, so one does not rely on what is not self-standing; and because the qualifier, meaning faith, has no place in the excluded element (mustathnā minhu), so the exception is from the original sentence. As for the second view, it is an exception from the pronoun in terms of meaning, made into a word from it, or from "qarya," since there is no difference in your saying: "The people were departing, except Zayd," between making it from the noun or from the pronoun in the predicate, because the ruling is only completed by the predicate. The difference only arises in a sentence like: "I struck the people, the worlds, except Zayd." He then said: a parallel to this in both views is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿We have been sent to a people who are criminals⁠﴾ ﴿except the family of Lut⁠﴾, and the reason for this is clear.

In al-Kashf, the point of similarity is that the meaning of destruction differs according to the two views, just as the meaning of sending differs there according to the two views. It seems he meant by destruction the one taken as a restriction in His statement "why was there not a town among the towns that We destroyed," so reflect on this.

As for "Yunus," there are dialectal readings with the three vowels on the nun, both hamzated and unhamzated, and the one that is transmitted with full reliability (mutawātir) is the damma (u) without hamza.

The story of these people, according to what has been related from more than one source, is that Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to the people of Nineveh, in the land of Mosul, and they were people of disbelief and polytheism. He invited them to faith in Allah alone and to abandoning the idols they worshipped, but they refused him and denied him. So he informed them that the punishment would strike them in the morning within three (days). When the third night came, it departed from them in the middle of the night. When they woke up, the punishment enveloped them, and it was above their heads, with nothing between them and it except the distance of two-thirds of a mile. It is also reported that the sky became covered with a black, terrifying cloud, emitting intense smoke. It descended until it enveloped their city, and their rooftops turned black. When they became certain of destruction, they sought their prophet but did not find him. So they went out into the desert with themselves, their women, their children and their animals. They wore sackcloth and displayed faith and repentance, and they separated the mothers from their children, among the people and the animals. So some longed for others, and the voices rose, and they all cried out and humbled themselves before Him, exalted is He, and sincerely intended (their devotion). So their Lord had mercy on them, answered their supplication, and lifted from them the punishment that had descended upon them. That was on the Day of 'Ashura, and it was a Friday.

Ibn Mas'ud said: their repentance reached the point that they restored injustices among themselves, to the extent that a man would come to a stone on which he had laid the foundation of his building, pull it up and return it to its owner. It is reported in a narration from Qatada that they cried out to Allah for forty mornings until He lifted what had descended upon them. Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn Ghaylan, who said: When the punishment overtook the people of Yunus, they walked to an elder from among the remnants of their scholars and said: "What do you see?" He said: "Say: O Living, when there is no living; O Living, Giver of life to the dead; O Living, there is no god but You." They said it, and He lifted the punishment from them. Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: They said: "O Allah, our sins have grown great and magnificent, and You are greater and more magnificent. So deal with us as You are worthy of, and do not deal with us as we are worthy of."

Yunus, peace be upon him, when he had departed from them, sat on the road asking for news, as has come in a raised (marfu') report. A man passed by him and said to him: "What did the people of Yunus do?" So he told him what they had done. He said: "I will not return to a people who have called me a liar," and he set off angry, as Allah related in another place, which will come, Allah willing.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the people witnessed the punishment, because of the word ﴿We lifted⁠﴾. This is what most reports imply, and many exegetes went to it. The benefit of faith for them after witnessing it is among their particularities, for the faith of disbelievers after witnessing what they were promised is faith of force (īmān ba's), which is not beneficial, since the obligation is then lifted, and Allah's custom is to destroy them without respite, as He destroyed Pharaoh. The view that he remained alive until what Allah willed and settled in the land of Mosul is among the fabrications of the Jews.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 10, verse 99:

﴿If your Lord had willed, everyone on earth would have believed﴾: This establishes that the faith of all accountable beings, in existence and non-existence, turns on the pivot of His, glorified is He, absolute will. This follows the explanation that the disbelief of the disbelievers is subordinate to His word. The object of the will (*mash'ah*, divine will) is omitted here, as is customary in its parallels. That is, if He, glorified is He, willed the faith of everyone on earth from among the two categories (humans and jinn), all of them would have believed, such that not one of them would have deviated. ﴿All together﴾, that is, gathered in faith, not differing regarding it. But He did not will that, because He, glorified is He, wills only what He knows, and He knows only what has a reality in itself. Concerning what has no reality at all, He does not know it, and what He does not know He does not will. To this rationale al-Kurani, may God have mercy on him, went, and he extended the discussion in clarifying and defending it in more than one treatise. But the majority hold that He, glorified is He, does not will it, because it contradicts the wisdom upon which the foundation of creation and legislation is built.

The verse is also a proof against the Mu'tazilah (a theological school), who claim that God, exalted is He, willed the faith of all creation, yet only some of them believed. According to them, will (*mashi'ah*) is of two kinds: a permissive will (*tafwidiyyah*), from which the thing may be absent, and a compelling will (*qasriyyah*), from which it cannot be absent. They interpreted what is in the verse according to this latter kind. So the meaning, in their view, is: if your Lord had willed a will of compulsion and coercion for the faith of the two categories, they would have believed. But He, glorified is He, did not will it in that way; rather, He commanded them to believe, created for them a choice for it and for its opposite, and delegated the matter to them: whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. This is their practice regarding every verse that came to them that clearly nullifies what they hold to. In reply: there is no indication that restricts it, and furthermore His, glorified is He, saying ﴿Will you then compel the people?﴾ contradicts this, as it is said. For the interrogative particle (*hamzah*) indicates denial, and because it has the right of initial position, it is placed before the conjunction, contrary to what the majority hold, and the *fa'* (then) is for sequencing. The intended meaning is that the denial follows from what came before. There is no benefit (in restricting it to compulsion), indeed there is no basis for taking the will of compulsion and coercion alone in the sequencing of the denial.

It has also been said that the interrogative particle is in its proper place, and the conjunction is upon an implied element that the speech encompasses, as if it were said: Does your Lord not will that? So will you compel them ﴿until they become believers﴾? The denial is directed at the ordering of the mentioned compulsion upon His, exalted is He, not willing it. The phrase "the denial is the denial" means that we must take the will in its unrestricted sense. By "the people" is meant those upon whom sealing has been set, or it is all of them for emphasis. It is permitted that *anta* (you) be the subject of an implied verb, which the following clause explains, and that it be the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is the clause after it. They count it as a semantic subject (*fa'il ma'nawi*), and its being placed first serves to strengthen the ruling of denial, as al-Sharif, sanctify his secret, went in his commentary on *Sharh al-Miftah* (commentary on *Miftah al-'Ulum*), and he mentioned in it that the intended meaning is the denial of the action's issuing from the addressee, not the denial that he is the doer while the act itself is established. It has also been said that the placing first is for restriction. In it is an announcement that compulsion is a possible matter, but the real question is who is compelled, and what it is: none but Him, glorified is He, alone, with no partner in it, because He, may His majesty be exalted, is the One able to act upon their hearts in a way that forces them into faith, and that is not within human capacity.

[p. 194]

﴿And it is not for any soul﴾ is an explanation of the dependence of the faith of those souls whose faith God, exalted is He, knows, on His will, exalted is He, in existence and non-existence, after the general dependence has been stated in this way. It has also been said that it is a confirmation of what the preceding discourse indicates, namely that opposition to the will is impossible. That is: it is not valid or proper for any soul among the souls whose faith God, exalted is He, knows, ﴿to believe except by the permission of God﴾, that is, by His will and His decree, glorified is He. The basic meaning of permission (idhn) for something is informing of its permissibility, granting leave for it, and lifting the prohibition against it. They considered what was mentioned to be among its necessary implications, like the facilitation that some of them mentioned in its interpretation. The soul was specified by the mentioned attribute and was not made to belong to the category of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of God﴾ (3:145). It has been said that this is because the exception is a "reduced exception" (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general circumstances. That is: it is not for any soul to believe in any of its circumstances except in a circumstance in which it is associated with His permission, glorified is He. Therefore, faith must be among the things to which its state leads, just as death is a state for every soul from which there is no escape. Thus, specification by what has been mentioned is necessary, for the souls whose non-faith God, exalted is He, knows, have no state in which they believe, such that they could make an exception of that state from others. End of quotation.

It may be said that this exception, with regard to the soul which God, exalted is He, knows will not believe, is informative of its non-belief in the most complete manner, in the same way as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ (4:23). So it is as if it were said: it is not for a soul which God, exalted is He, knows will not believe, to believe in any of the circumstances, such as soundness of intellect, health of body, and others, except in a circumstance in which it is associated with God's permission and His will that it believe. And this (permission) follows His knowledge of that, and His knowledge of it is impossible, because He has known its opposite, so the knowledge would turn into ignorance, and thus His will for that would be impossible, and so its faith would be impossible, since what depends on the impossible is impossible.

In the Hawashi al-Shihabiyya it is stated that if (ma kana) means "what was found," it requires restricting the soul to those whom He knows will believe; but if it means "what is valid/proper," it does not require that. For this reason, whoever mentioned it mentioned it, and whoever left it out left it out. There is obscurity in this, so reflect.

﴿And He places the rijs﴾, that is, disbelief, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So it increased them in rijs to their rijs﴾ (9:125), by the indication of what precedes it. Its origin is a corrupt and loathsome thing, and it was expressed by this term because it is a sign of corruption and loathsomeness. It has also been said that what is meant by it is punishment, and it was expressed by this term because the two share the quality of being abhorrent and repulsive. And the meaning of disbelief from it is by consideration that it was first transferred from "loathsome" to "punishment" because of their sharing in what was mentioned, and then it was applied to disbelief because it is its cause; so it is a metaphor at the second level. The Imam preferred the first interpretation, out of reluctance toward what is involved in applying "loathsome" to God's punishment, in terms of repulsiveness. He favored the second interpretation because the word ʿalā (upon) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿upon those who do not reason﴾ (10:100), that is, who do not use their intellects to consider the proofs and signs, or do not understand His indications and rulings, implies that it is due to the seal (tab') upon their hearts. The first interpretation is rejected by this. It was objected that the meaning is that He decrees it upon them, so there is no rejection; and it interprets ﴿those who do not reason﴾ in a way that makes it an establishing statement (ta'sis), as you have heard in its interpretation. From this you know that the verb is treated as occupying the position of the preposition (lam), and its first object is an implied object. It may be distinguished between the two interpretations by saying that according to the first, they have not been deprived of the capacity for reflection, but they were not granted success in it; and according to the second, the opposite. The forthcoming command is clearly in the first sense. The sentence is conjoined to an implied element, as if it were said: "So He permits some of them to believe, and places..." etc., or: "So He permits them to believe, and places..." etc.

It was read as (al-rijz) with a zay. Hammad and Yahya, from Abu Bakr, read (wa-najʿalu) with a nun.

[Page 195]

﴿Say: Look﴾. This is an address to the master of those addressed (ﷺ), commanding him to direct the disbelievers among whom he lived to reflect on the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth and what is in them of wondrous signs, both the horizonal (āfāqiyyah) signs and those within the self (anfusiyyah). The purpose is to make clear to him (ﷺ) that they are among those who do not use their reason. It seems to be connected with what came before it, and its connection to His words, glorified is He: ﴿Will you then compel the people...﴾ and so on, is according to the meaning: do not compel people to faith, but command them with what customarily leads to it, namely looking, which is not free of consideration.

It was also said: when He, exalted is He, had shown in what preceded that faith comes by His creation, that no one believes except by His permission, and that those upon whom the Word has been justified will not believe, He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to command looking, lest he become disinclined to it after that information. I consider the first view more preferable.

The letter lām in قُلِ may be read with a damma or a kasra, and both are canonical (sab'iyyah) recitations. His words, glorified is He: ﴿what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are in a position of accusative (naṣb) by the omission of the preposition, because the verb before it is suspended (mu'allaq) by the interrogative, since (مَا) is interrogative (istifhāmiyyah) and is the subject (mubtada'), and (ذا) has the meaning of (الذي, "that which"), with the adverbial phrase as its relative clause (ṣilah), and it is the predicate of the subject. It is also permissible that (ماذا) as a whole be an interrogative noun in the nominative as subject, with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, meaning: what wondrous thing in the heavens and the earth, from the marvels of His, exalted is He, craftsmanship, which indicate His oneness and the perfection of His power, exalted is His majesty.

It is also permitted that (ماذا) as a whole be a relative pronoun meaning (الذي), in a position of accusative by the verb before it. Al-Samin considered this weak, because in that case the looking must be either mental, as is apparent, and then it is transitive with (في), or visual, and then it is transitive with (إلى).

﴿And signs and warnings will not avail a people who do not believe﴾ (101). That is: they will not suffice them and will not benefit them. It is read in the masculine (بالتذكير), and "the signs" means what was pointed to by His words, glorified is He: ﴿what is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Thus there is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. "The warnings" (النذر) is the plural of nadhīr in the sense of mundhir (warner), that is, the warning messengers, or in the sense of inḏhār (warning), that is, the warnings, and it is plural because the types are intended. It is also permitted that "al-nudhur" itself be a verbal noun meaning warning. By "these people" is meant the people upon whose hearts a seal has been set, that is, they will not believe in the knowledge and judgment of Allah, exalted is He. The (مَا) is negating, and the clause is parenthetical (i'tiraḍiyyah). It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (قُلْ), and in the view that makes it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (انْظُرُوا) there is something to consider. It is necessarily parenthetical if (ما) is made interrogative in the sense of denial (istifhām inkāriyyah), and then it is in a position of accusative as an infinitive (maṣdariyyah) for the verb after it, or as its direct object. The object on this reading, and likewise on the possibility of negation, is omitted unless it takes the place of an intransitive verb, meaning: they will not avail anything.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 102:**

﴿Then do they await﴾, that is, these who were commanded to reflect, from among the polytheists of Makkah and their leaders, ﴿anything but like the days of those who passed away﴾, that is, like the events that befell them and the descent of God Most High's punishment upon them, since they deserve nothing other than that. The use of "days" for events occurs, as in their saying "the days of the Arabs" (ayyam al-'Arab), and it is a well-known figurative usage (majaz) of expressing a time by what took place in it, as one says "the Maghrib (prayer)" for the prayer that occurs in it. The intended sense of the relative clause is the polytheists of the earlier nations. ﴿Before them﴾ is related to "passed away" and was brought for emphasis and to indicate that they too will pass away as those before them passed away. ﴿Say﴾ as a threat to them, ﴿"Then wait﴾ for that, ﴿indeed I am with you among those waiting﴾ for it."

Page 196

So the object of the waiting is one in essence, and this is the apparent meaning. It is also permitted that it be different in essence but the same in kind, that is: "Wait for my destruction; indeed I am with you among those awaiting your destruction."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 103:

﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ (nunajji rusulana) is read with the shaddah (tashdid) by the majority, while al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it without shaddah (takhfif). It is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element indicated by His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿like the days of those who passed away before them﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) brought in to hasten to the threat and to emphasize the severity of the warning. It is as if it were said: We destroy the nations, then We save the messenger sent to them ﴿and those who believe﴾ in them. He used the present tense (mudari') to narrate a past state, to magnify its horror by bringing its images to mind, and he delayed the narration of the salvation after the narration of the destruction, contrary to what occurs in other places, so that His saying, may He be exalted, may be connected to it: ﴿Thus it is a duty upon Us; We shall save the believers﴾ (103), i.e. We save them with a salvation like that salvation which was for those before them. It is said that the demonstrative refers to the salvation, and the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is linked to an implied element that functions as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun (masdar). It is also permitted that the kaf be in the accusative position, in the sense of "like", serving in place of the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). According to some, it may be in the position of an adverbial accusative (hal) from the salvation contained in ﴿nunajji﴾, with the sense "We do the saving in a state of being like that saving". It may also be in the place of the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e. "the matter is thus". And ﴿haqqan﴾ is in the accusative governed by its implied verb, i.e. "that is due, as a due matter". The clause is a parenthesis between the governing element and the governed, on the assumption that ﴿kadhalika﴾ is an object of the verb mentioned after it. Its purpose is to emphasize the salvation and to state that it is certain to occur, and this is what is meant by "truth" (al-haqq). It is also possible that it means "obligatory" (al-wajib). The sense of salvation being obligatory is that it is like a matter obligatory upon Him, may He be exalted; otherwise there is no obligation upon Him in reality, may He be glorified. Several grammarians have stated that the clause is parenthetical, and it is inferred from this that there is no harm in a parenthetical clause when some of its complements remain. It is also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the kaf which is in the sense of "like", or for the omitted element it replaces.

It is said: ﴿kadhalika﴾ is in the accusative governed by the first ﴿nunajji﴾, and ﴿haqqan﴾ is in the accusative governed by the second, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. By ﴿al-mu'minin﴾ is meant either the category that includes the messengers, upon them be peace, and their followers, or the followers alone; and the omission of mention of the messengers is a notification that there is no need to mention them. In either case, there is an indication that the basis of salvation is faith. This clause was brought as a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, affirming its meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 104:

﴿Say﴾ to all who doubt your religion and disbelieve in you: ﴿O mankind﴾. The address is made with the generic noun, introduced by the particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbih), in order to generalize the conveying of the message and to show the utmost concern for what has reached them. ﴿If you are in doubt about my religion﴾, which I worship God Most High by and call you to, and you have not known what it is nor its attribute, so that you said, "He has apostatized."

﴿Then I do not worship those whom you worship besides God﴾ at any time whatsoever. ﴿But I worship God, who causes you to die﴾, and then does to you what He does of the various kinds of punishment. The clause has been made, in view of its meaning, a response (jawab) by way of interpreting it as a statement (ta'wil al-akhbar); otherwise there is no apparent consequence for the condition. So the meaning is: if you are in doubt about that, then I inform you that worship is restricted to Him, the Exalted, and the abandonment of the worship of anything other than Him, such as idols and others, which you worship out of ignorance. It is common for a statement, in its sense as a clause, to be made the apodosis, as in: "If you honor me today, I honored you yesterday." On this same pattern is His, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾. For the existence of the blessing is not the cause of its coming from God, Exalted is He; rather the matter is the reverse. It is only the cause of the statement that it comes from Him, Exalted is He, as Ibn al-Hajib established.

Page 197

It may also be that the meaning is: if you are in doubt about the soundness of my religion and its rectitude, then I inform you that its essence is worship directed to Him alone, this being its nature, unlike what you worship, which is far removed from that nature. So present this to your intellects, ponder it with your thoughts, and look with an eye of fairness, so that you may know its soundness and truth. Some have mentioned that in this reading there is no need to make the cause the informing and notifying; rather the apodosis is regarded as the command to present what has been mentioned to their intellects and to reflect upon it. The more apparent view is to regard the informing as the apodosis, as in the first meaning. The expression of what they are upon as "doubt," although they are certain of its invalidity, is to signal that the most that can afflict a rational person in this matter is doubt about its soundness, whereas certainty of its invalidity is something for which there is no path. It has been said: we do not grant that they were certain; rather they were in doubt and agitation upon seeing the miracles. And "bi-anna" (that) was brought for indication, but this is not fitting, since there exists what removes it.

It is permissible that the meaning be: if you are in doubt about my religion and about what I am upon, whether I will remain steadfast upon it or abandon it and conform to you, then do not entertain impossible notions, do not doubt my matter, cut off your hopes from me, and know that I do not worship those whom you worship besides God, nor do I choose error over guidance, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: O disbelievers! I do not worship what you worship﴾. It is not hidden that what came before is more suitable to the context. The priority of abandoning the worship of other than God, Exalted is He, over worshipping Him, glory be to Him, is due to the precedence of clearing away (takhliyah) over adorning (tahliyah), as in the statement of Tawhid, and to signal opposition from the very beginning. The singling out of death (tawaffi) from among the rest of the attributes of action, mentioned in relation to them, is for the purpose of instilling fear, for there is nothing more severe for them than death. It has also been said: the intended meaning is, "I worship God who created you, then causes you to die, then will return you," and in this there is an allusion to the Resurrection which they deny, and it is among the principal foundations of the religion. Then both extremes were omitted and the middle was retained so that it would indicate them, for these two have frequently been mentioned together with it in the Qur'an. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾ (104). That is: God, Exalted is He, has made it obligatory upon me. Thus the obligation of faith in God, Exalted is He, is legal (shar'i), like the rest of the obligations. Mawla Sadr al-Shari'a mentioned that "legal" (shar'i) has two meanings: that which depends on the Shari'a, such as the obligation of prayer and fasting; and that which the Shari'a has stated but which does not depend on the Shari'a, such as the obligation of faith in God, glory be to Him, and the obligation of affirming the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, for it does not depend on the Shari'a. Thus it is not legal in the first sense. That is because the establishment of the Shari'a depends on faith in the existence of the Creator, may He be exalted, and His knowledge, power and speech, and on affirming the prophethood of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, by the indication of his miracles. So if any of these rulings depended on the Shari'a, circularity (dawr) would follow. Someone may object that the Shari'a's dependence on the obligation of faith and the like is not established, whether by "Shari'a" is meant the address of God, Exalted is He, or the Shari'a of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. The dependence of affirming the validity of the Shari'a of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, on faith in God, Exalted is He, and His attributes, and on affirming the prophethood of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the indication of his miracles, does not require that it depend on the obligation of faith and affirmation, nor on knowledge of their obligation. At most it depends on faith and affirmation themselves, which does not entail that it depends on their obligation; and it is not inconsistent with the dependence of the obligation of faith and the like on the Shari'a, as is the doctrine held by them, that there is no obligation except through revelation (sam'). As for Zamakhshari's statement here, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded by reason and revelation, it is not free from a Mu'tazilite tinge, as is his habit in many places. And whoever among our exegetes said that he was obligated to that by reason and revelation meant by "reason" that which follows what is heard through the Shari'a, so there is no contradiction. The speech is on the basis of the omission of the preposition, that is: I was commanded that I should be; and the omission of the preposition before "an" and "anna" is regular. Even if one sets that aside, the omission after "amara" is a heard usage from the Arabs, as in the poet's saying:

Page 198

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded, for I have left you possessing wealth and property."

Some have included this clause within the apodosis, but this is not necessarily so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 105:

﴿And that I should set your face toward the religion﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf), as more than one scholar has said, to ﴿that I should be﴾, and there is an objection that the (an) in the coordinated-to clause is without dispute a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, because of its governing the accusative, whereas the one on the side of the coordinated clause cannot be like that, since an imperative (amr) falls after it. Likewise, it cannot be an explanatory (mufassirah) particle, for its coordination to the verbal one, and because the hidden preposition (bāʾ) would then have to enter upon it, and the explanatory one does not admit that. This is answered by choosing that it is verbal, and the imperative falling after it does no harm in this regard, for it has been transmitted from Sibawayh that it is permissible to connect it to it. There is also no difference, in the relative clause of the literal (ḥarfī) relative pronoun, between a demand (ṭalab) and a declarative statement (khabar), because it is only forbidden in the nominal (ismī) relative pronoun, since that was set for the purpose of attaching by means of it a description of definite nouns with sentences, and demand-sentences cannot be a description. What is intended by saying that after it is mentioned what indicates the verbal noun (maṣdar) by which it is interpreted, and this occurs with every verb. As for the objection that its interpretation removes the meaning of the command intended from it, it is answered that it is interpreted, as we pointed out earlier in regard to the command to establish, for just as the verbal noun is taken from the root, it may also be taken from the form, though there is no need for this here, due to the indication of the Exalted's words: ﴿I have been commanded﴾ upon it. In al-Fara'id it is said that it is permissible to estimate: "and it was revealed to me that I should establish." Al-Tibi criticised this, saying that this is grammatically valid, but that in that coordination there is a semantic benefit, namely that "and that I should establish" etc. is like an explanation of "that I should be" etc., in the style of "Zayd pleased me, and his generosity," being included with him in the ruling of the one commanded. So if that were estimated, the purpose of the explanation would be lost, and the sentence would be independent, coordinated to its like. In this there is room for reflection, since it is possible that this sentence explains the coordinated sentence upon which it stands. Abu Hayyan estimated that, and claimed that "an" then may be verbal and may be explanatory, because the hidden verb carries the meaning of saying without its letters, and that on this basis the difficulty of the coordination disappears, and the address in "your face" stands in its place. It is refuted by saying that an explanatory sentence may not be omitted, and as for the validity of the verbal particle occurring as subject or object, that is not necessary, and there is no difficulty in the coordination he intended, and the matter of address is easy, since it is for consideration of the reported speech and the command mentioned with it.

Establishing the face for the religion is a metonymy (kināyah) for directing the self wholly to His worship and turning away from whatever is other than Him, for whoever wishes to look at something with careful attention sets his face opposite it such that he does not turn right or left, since if he turned, the facing would be void. The apparent meaning is that the face here is on its literal sense. It is permissible that by it is meant the essence, and the intention is: direct your essence and entirety to the religion, and strive in performing the obligations and refraining from vices, so the lam is linked to "establish." It has been said: the face is in its literal sense, and establishing it is directing it to the qiblah, i.e., face the qiblah and do not turn to the right or the left, so the lam is for causation. This is not the case, and similar to it is the saying that this is a metonymy for turning the intellect wholly to seeking the religion.

﴿ḥanīfan﴾, i.e., inclining away from the false religions. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), either from "the face" or from "the religion." On the first, it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, since establishing the face includes turning to the truth and turning away from falsehood. On the second, it has been said that it is a separate (muntaqilah) circumstantial clause, but there is scrutiny in this. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "establish."

﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ (105) is coordinated to "establish," falling under the command, and it is an emphasis of it, i.e., do not be among them in belief or in action.

**Page 199**

*"And do not invoke, besides Allah, that which neither benefits you by itself, if you invoke it to avert some harm or bring about some desired thing, nor harms you if you abandon it by depriving you of something desired, whether by way of removal, lifting, or inflicting something disliked"* — whether invoked independently or in association (with Allah). The sentence is said to be coordinated with the prohibitive sentence preceding it. Some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) preferred to coordinate it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: O mankind⦆, so it does not fall under the command, because what follows it, up to the end of the two verses, is coherent, and it is not possible to separate some of it from the rest. There is no basis for placing the whole under the command. You know that if the verb of revelation (al-iyha') is assumed in ﴿and that I should establish⦆, as Abu Hayyan and the author of al-Fara'id did, there is no obstacle to coordination, as is apparent, with the prohibitive sentence which is coordinated with the first sentence, and to placing all the coherent parts under the revelation. That assumption is sometimes preferred because it avoids committing a departure from the apparent meaning by coordinating with a distant element. It has also been said: there is no need to assume the revelation and the coordination as stated, and the earlier command carries the sense of revelation, as if it were said: "And it was revealed to me that I should be..." etc. Inclusion under this is then not objectionable. However, this is as you see, and I do not think you would accept it.

﴿So if you do, then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers. 106⦆ That is, counted among them. The verb is a metonymy (kinaya) for invoking, as if it were said: "If you invoke what neither benefits nor harms." It is said that this was expressed indirectly to exalt his status (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) and to draw attention to the loftiness of his station, (preventing him) from being associated with the worship of other than Allah, even within a conditional sentence.

The discussion on the purpose of a prohibition of this kind has already passed just now. The answer to the condition, according to what is in the prohibition, is the clause ﴿then you⦆ and its predicate, namely ﴿among the wrongdoers⦆. The word ﴿idhan⦆ (then/in that case) was placed between the subject and the predicate, although its proper position is after the predicate, for the sake of the verse-ending (fasila).

In al-Kashshaf, ﴿idhan⦆ is a response to the condition and an answer to an assumed question, as if a questioner asked about the consequence of worshipping idols, so he was made "among the wrongdoers," because there is no greater wrong than associating partners (with Allah). ﴿Indeed, associating partners is a great wrong⦆. This is the phrasing of the grammarians, and it was explained, as al-Shihab said, to mean that it indicates that what follows it is caused by a condition, whether realized or assumed, and is an answer to a statement, whether realized or assumed.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in Jam' al-Jawami', after clarifying that the temporal ﴿idha⦆ may have part of the sentence it is attached to omitted, or all of it, so that tanwin is substituted for it, and it is vowelled with a kasra for the sake of two consecutive unvowelled letters, not for i'rab (grammatical case), contrary to al-Akhfash, and it may be vowelled with a fatha: his teacher al-Kafiyaji added ﴿idhan⦆ to these. Then he said in his commentary on Hamʿ al-Hawami': "I indicated in my words, 'and our teacher added to these in that respect "idhan"', to a strange question which few have addressed. It is that I heard our teacher, may Allah have mercy on him, say concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you obey a human like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers⦆ that this ﴿idhan⦆ is not the familiar word, but rather it is the conditional ﴿idha⦆ whose clause to which it is attached has been omitted, and tanwin has been substituted for it, as in ﴿yawma'idhin⦆ (on that day). I used to find this very admirable, and I thought that the Shaykh had no predecessor in that, until I saw that some later scholars inclined to what the Shaykh inclined to. I have elaborated on this in the margin of al-Mughni." End of quotation.

You know that the verse he cited is like the verse we are dealing with. What he mentioned is something the heart inclines to, and I see no harm in it. Perhaps it is preferable to what the author of al-Kashshaf and his followers said, so the verse should be understood in its light. This had often occurred to me, but I hardly dared to affirm it until I saw it attributed to another person whose merit no one denies, so I affirm it, praising Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 107:

﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾ is a confirmation of what was mentioned in the clause concerning the denial of benefit from the false objects of worship, and a depiction of His exclusive possession of it, glorified is He; that is, "and if He afflicts you with some evil," ﴿then there is no remover of it﴾ from you, whoever he may be and whatever he may be, ﴿except Him﴾ alone. Thus the non-removal of harm by the idols is established by way of demonstrative proof. This is also an explanation of the absence of benefit in removing what is disliked, which necessarily entails the absence of benefit in bringing what is loved, by an apparent implication, for removing what is disliked is the lowest degree of benefit; so when it is negated, benefit is negated altogether. ﴿And if He intends you with good﴾ is a verification of the negation of harm mentioned in the clause; that is, if He intends to afflict you with good, ﴿then there is no repeller of His bounty﴾, of which what He intends for you of good is part. So this is an indication of the answer to the conditional, not the answer itself.
Page 200
It also signifies that the overflowing of good from Him, may He be exalted, is by way of grace and generosity, without any obligation upon Him, glorified is He; that is, no one is able to turn it back, whoever he may be, so the idols are included in this primarily. This is an explanation of the absence of their harm by the repelling of what is loved before it occurs, which necessarily entails the absence of their harm by removing it, or by inflicting what is disliked, by a clear implication. Perhaps the mention of intending with regard to good and touching with regard to harm, though the two are interrelated, is because what He, glorified is He, intends comes to pass, and what comes to pass only happens by His intention, may He be exalted; this signifies that good is intended by God, may He be exalted, in itself, while harm occurs only as recompense for deeds and is not intended in itself. It is also possible that the meaning of both verbs is intended in each of good and harm, since the context requires emphasizing each of encouragement and warning; but he intended brevity in speech, so he mentioned touching in one and intending in the other, so that what is mentioned in each side indicates what was left out on the other side. Thus the verse contains a type of rhetorical device called ihtibak, which has been mentioned in other verses. He, glorified is He, did not make an exception in the case of good, to show complete care for it; and this is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He afflicts with it whom He wills of His servants﴾, where He, may His majesty be great, explicitly stated affliction with the bounty encompassing what He willed of good. It has been said: the reason He, may He be exalted, did not make an exception in that is that He has assumed that the attachment of good to Him occurs by His will, may He be exalted, and the validity of an exception would require willing its opposite at that time, which is impossible; whereas this differs from touching harm, for the will to remove it does not entail the impossibility of the attachment of two opposite wills at one time. In departing from "and if He wills you good" to what is in the sublime arrangement, there is an allusion, as has been said, that the intended one is man, and all other goods are created for his sake. What we have pointed to, that the pronoun in (with it) refers to the bounty, is the apparent and fitting reading; its return to what was mentioned has been permitted, but that is not the case. Taking the bounty in general, first and last, as you have learned, is what some verifiers adopted, refuting those who made it a reference to that very good, on the grounds that mentioning it first is an apparent use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to show the benefit mentioned; but His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿of His servants whom He wills﴾ rejects that, because it proclaims generality. In my view it is permissible that the speech be of the type "I have a dirham and its half." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ (107) is a concluding statement to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He afflicts with it﴾, etc., confirming its meaning; and all of it is a concluding statement to the last conditional clause, confirming its meaning.

Al-Imam mentioned in these verses that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ cannot be a prohibition from worshipping idols, because that is stated in His saying, glorified is He, at the beginning of the verse: ﴿I do not worship those you worship besides Allah﴾; so this statement must be taken to contain an additional benefit, namely that whoever has known his Master, if he turns after that to other than Him, that would be shirk, which the people of the hearts call hidden shirk. And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not call upon, besides Allah, what neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ is made an allusion to a station which is the last of the degrees of the knowers, because whatever is other than the Real is possible in its essence, existing by His bringing into being; and what is possible in its essence is nonexistent considered in its own essence, and existent by the bringing into being of the Real. Then there is no benefactor except the Real, and no harmer except Him, and "everything perishes except His Face"; and if this is so, there is no return except to Him, may His majesty be great, in both abodes.

The meaning of ﴿So if you do﴾ etc. is: if you occupy yourself with seeking benefit or avoiding harm from other than Allah, may He be exalted, then you are ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who place a thing in other than its proper place, since everything other than Allah, may He be exalted, is removed from disposing of affairs; so attributing disposition to it is placing a thing in other than its place, and that is injustice. Seeking benefit from things which Allah, may He be exalted, created for benefit, such as food, drink and the like, does not contradict returning entirely to Allah, may He be exalted, on condition that the eye of the intellect, when turning to any of those things, witnesses the power, existence, and beneficence of Allah, may He be exalted, in bringing those existent things into being and depositing those benefits in them, while firmly believing that in themselves and in their essences they are nonexistent and perishing, having no existence, no permanence, and no influence except by the bringing into being of Allah, may He be exalted, His sustaining of them, and the outpouring upon them of what properties are in them, by His munificence and beneficence.

His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah touches you﴾ etc. is a confirmation that all possible things are dependent upon Him, glorified is He, and exalted, and that there is no reliance except upon Him, may His majesty be great; and this is a fine statement. However, his claim that His saying, may He be exalted: "And do not be among the polytheists" cannot be a prohibition from worshipping idols, etc., is not free from problems.

Our Sufi masters have also mentioned something similar to this in the verses. In the Secrets of the Qur'an it is said that He, glorified is He, warned His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, against turning to other than Him in his devotion to Him, by His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾, that is, among those who seek other than Me and prefer over the beauty of My witnessing what is unbecoming of created things. They have also mentioned that establishing the upright religion is by correcting knowledge, which cannot be except by abandoning looking at anything other than the Real, may His majesty be exalted. Then He, may He be exalted, increased the emphasis on turning to Him and turning away from other than Him by His saying, may His majesty be great: ﴿And do not call upon﴾ etc., where He indicated that whoever seeks benefit or harm from other than Him, the Exalted, is a wrongdoer, that is, one who places lordship in other than its place. From here Shaqiq al-Balkhi said: The wrongdoer is one who seeks benefit from one who does not possess benefit for himself, and seeks to repel harm from one who cannot defend himself; and whoever is unable to sustain himself, how can he sustain another? He confirmed this by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if He touches you﴾ etc.

From this, Ibn 'Ata' said: He, may He be exalted, cut off from His servants fear and hope except from Him and toward Him, by informing them that He is the Harmer and the Benefiter. The harm may also be an allusion to the veil, and the good an allusion to the unveiling of beauty; that is, "if Allah touches you with the harm of the veil, then there is no remover of your harm except Him, by the appearance of the lights of His union; and if He intends you with the unveiling of His beauty, then there is no repeller of the bounty of His union from any cause or reason, for the one specially chosen in eternity for union is not veiled by any of the things, because in the preceding grace he is preserved from the flow of compulsion." (This), and perhaps it suffices, from the aspect of allusion in the verses, instead of further discussion, as is the custom in the Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 108:

﴿Say﴾: O Messenger, addressing those disbelievers after you have conveyed to them what was revealed to you, or addressing the responsible people in general, as al-Tabarsi said: ﴿O mankind, the truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾. This refers to the Great Qur'an, whose indication is clear, which includes the excellent rulings, among them the fundamentals of the religion mentioned just before, and you have come to know what it contains of clear proofs and guidance, so no excuse remains for you. It has been said that the intended "truth" is the Prophet (ﷺ). But there is in this much exaggeration, which is not hidden. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid that the truth is what is indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾ and so on. But this, as you see, is not [convincing]. ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ by faith and following, ﴿then he is only guided for [the benefit of] himself﴾, meaning the benefit of his guidance returns to himself. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ by disbelief and turning away, ﴿then he only goes astray to his own detriment﴾, meaning the burden of his misguidance falls upon himself. It has also been said that the purpose is to declare the Message free from any trace of a motive returning to him (peace be upon him), such as seeking benefit or repelling harm. This is hinted at by the attribution of the coming to the truth without any indication that this happens through his mediation (ﷺ). ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, meaning a keeper to whom your affairs are entrusted; ﴿I am only a bringer of good news and a warner﴾. In the verse there is an indication that he (peace be upon him) does not compel them to faith nor force them to it; his duty is only to convey. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is abrogated (naskh, the lifting of a earlier ruling by a later one) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 10, verse 109:

﴿Wattabi'** ﴾ in all your affairs,
Page 202
what is revealed to you of belief and action and conveyance (al-tabligh), following the manner of renewal and continuity. The expression "the reaching of the truth, which is explained by the Qur'an, to them by coming" and "to him (ﷺ) by revelation" is an indication of the contrast between the two ranks. And if by "the truth" is meant what has been said, then the matter is very clear.

﴿Wasbir﴾ over what befalls you of the hardships of conveyance and the harm from those who have gone astray, ﴿until Allah judges﴾ by granting victory over them, or by commanding fighting against them, ﴿and He is the best of judges﴾ (109), since error is impossible in His judgment, He being aware of the inner secrets just as He is aware of the outward appearances. Others among judges, may His majesty be exalted, only know the outward appearances, so error occurs in their judgment. And there is no concealing what these verses contain of excellent admonition, consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), a promise to the believers, and a warning to the disbelievers. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon the master of the messengers, whose remembrance cheers the hearts of those who affirm God's oneness, and upon his family and all his companions.
